stem:
A 7-year-old boy weighing 22 kg is brought into John Hunter Hospital trauma bay after being hit by a car at low speed. Primary survey: airway patent, breathing equal but rapid, circulation tachycardic with weak peripheral pulses, conscious GCS 14. T 36.5, HR 156, RR 38, BP 86/52, capillary refill 4 seconds. He has bruising over the right lower abdomen, no obvious external bleeding, no long-bone deformity.

The trauma team leader requests the first fluid resuscitation order, and the registrar must distinguish between the paediatric trauma bolus volume and the paediatric medical sepsis bolus volume.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 156, RR 38, BP 86/52, CRT 4 sec, GCS 14, weight 22 kg.
data_table.Examination: Bruising RLQ, abdomen guarding, no peritonism yet, no external bleeding, no long-bone deformity.
data_table.Investigations: FAST scan pending; blood group + crossmatch sent; bedside lactate 4.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which volume and fluid type should be administered as the first bolus, recognising that the paediatric trauma cut-off differs from the paediatric sepsis cut-off?

options.text: 20 mL/kg crystalloid (440 mL) over 5-10 min - standard paediatric sepsis bolus
10 mL/kg crystalloid (220 mL) over 5-10 min then transition to packed red cells 10 mL/kg if persistent shock; activate paediatric massive transfusion protocol
40 mL/kg crystalloid (880 mL) over 30 min - aggressive volume resuscitation as per ATLS adult protocol
20 mL/kg of 4% albumin colloid - colloid resuscitation for trauma
Withhold all fluids until CT abdomen confirms intra-abdominal injury and surgical control achieved

subtopic_detail: Paediatric trauma vs sepsis fluid bolus discrimination

stem:
A 9-month-old girl is referred to paediatric cardiology at the John Hunter Children's Hospital for a murmur picked up at the 8-month vaccination visit. Birth was at term, weight 2.8 kg (10th centile), no antenatal concerns. She has fed well but feeds slowly. Her mother volunteers that she has the most outgoing personality of any baby in the family. Examination: weight on 5th centile (down from 10th at birth), interactive smile, prominent forehead and short upturned nose, full cheeks, wide mouth, small chin, mild infraorbital fullness.

Cardiac auscultation: harsh ejection systolic murmur loudest at the right upper sternal edge with a thrill, transmitted to the carotids, no diastolic murmur. Femoral pulses present and equal. Mild generalised hypotonia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 36, BP arm 108/68 (right) and 96/62 (left), no postductal differential, SpO2 99%.
data_table.Examination: Dysmorphic facies (prominent forehead, upturned nose, full cheeks, wide mouth), small chin, mild hypotonia, harsh ESM with thrill at right upper sternal edge, normal femoral pulses.
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram pending. Random ionised calcium 1.42 mmol/L (high, ref 1.15-1.32). Random glucose 4.2 mmol/L. UEC otherwise normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely unifying diagnosis, and which targeted genetic test should be requested?

options.text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21); request karyotype and atrioventricular septal defect echocardiography
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion); request FISH for 22q11.2 and cardiac imaging for conotruncal defects
Williams syndrome (7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene); request FISH for ELN deletion and cardiology assessment for supravalvular AS and peripheral pulmonary stenosis
Noonan syndrome (PTPN11 mutation); request gene panel and ECG for pulmonary valve stenosis
Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation); request gene panel and echocardiogram for aortic root dilatation

subtopic_detail: Williams syndrome constellation recognition + ELN deletion confirmation

stem: A 4-year-old child is brought to a regional emergency department in Tamworth (Hunter New England LHD) after ingesting an unknown quantity of an over-the-counter medication that acts as a competitive, lipophilic antagonist at central and peripheral muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. There is no nicotinic activity. The agent crosses the blood-brain barrier readily. Onset was approximately 60 minutes ago. The grandparent who called the ambulance is unsure what was taken; the empty blister pack has been brought in but the label is unreadable.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, mumbling speech, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 148, BP 102/64, dry axillae, flushed dry skin, dilated minimally reactive pupils, bowel sounds absent, bladder palpable.
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.36, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L, paracetamol level <10 micromol/L, salicylate not detected, ECG sinus tachycardia QRS 88 ms QTc 440 ms.

lead_in: Based purely on the receptor mechanism described, which clinical feature is the single best discriminator from a sympathomimetic toxidrome?

options.text: Dry flushed skin with absent bowel sounds and urinary retention
Tachycardia with hypertension and mydriasis
Hyperthermia with agitated delirium
Pinpoint pupils with bradycardia and bronchorrhoea
Hypotension with miosis and hyporeflexia

subtopic_detail: Anticholinergic vs sympathomimetic toxidrome discrimination by mechanism

stem: A 12-month-old infant weighing 9.4 kg is brought to John Hunter Hospital paediatric ED 90 minutes after the parent inadvertently gave the child five doses of paracetamol 250 mg/5 mL suspension instead of paracetamol 120 mg/5 mL suspension, at the prescribed paediatric volume of 6 mL per dose, over the past 16 hours (one dose every 4 hours; the 5th dose was 90 minutes ago). The child is alert, well, afebrile, drinking, and has no abdominal pain or vomiting. No other agent was co-ingested. Pre-existing health is unremarkable. The parent has brought the bottle and the dosing syringe.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 28, BP 92/58, T 36.9 deg C, SpO2 99% room air.
data_table.Examination: Alert, hydrated, abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Pending - clinician calculating total ingested dose to determine NAC eligibility.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management based on the calculated cumulative dose?

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting; cumulative dose below the staggered-ingestion treatment threshold
Commence IV N-acetylcysteine using the 21-hour Prescott regimen and check paracetamol concentration and ALT now
Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram at 4 hours post the most recent dose to decide NAC
Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally to limit further absorption
Repeat paracetamol level at 24 hours post the most recent dose and decide on NAC then

stem:
A 16-year-old boy presents to a Tamworth paediatric ED with 24 hours of mild central chest discomfort, no syncope, no palpitations, no exertional symptoms. Exam normal, no pericardial rub, no murmur. ECG sinus rhythm, no ST changes, no PR depression. Troponin I 87 ng/L (upper limit of normal 14). He received his second dose of an mRNA COVID-19 booster 48 hours ago.

He has no past cardiac history, no family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death, no recent viral illness, no drug use, no stimulant medications. Echocardiogram requested.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 78, BP 118/72, SpO2 99% room air.
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds normal, no rub, no murmur, no peripheral oedema, chest non-tender.
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus normal axis, no ischaemia or pericarditis. Troponin I 87 ng/L (ULN 14). CRP 12. FBC normal. Echocardiogram pending.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge with safety-netting; troponin rise is fully explained by recent vaccination and requires no investigation
Admit for telemetry, complete echocardiography, repeat troponin at 6 hours, paediatric cardiology review, and recognise post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis as the most likely cause
Commence empirical aspirin 300 mg orally and admit as suspected acute coronary syndrome
Order CT coronary angiogram before any other intervention
Reassure and arrange outpatient stress test in 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: Post-mRNA-vaccine myocarditis vs alternative myocardial injury

stem:
A 4-year-old previously well girl is brought to Maitland Hospital paediatric ED with 5 days of bloody diarrhoea, 24 hours of pallor, and 12 hours of reduced urine output. Her family returned 9 days ago from a 3-week farm-stay holiday on the NSW mid-north coast where the children regularly fed unpasteurised milk to orphan calves. Initial GP-ordered stool PCR is pending.

Today she appears pale, irritable, with abdominal tenderness but no peritonism. She has had no antibiotic exposure for this illness. There is no rash, no jaundice, no recent vaccinations, no medication exposure. Family history is unremarkable for renal or haematological disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4, HR 138, BP 105/72 (above the 95th centile for age), RR 26, SpO2 98%, weight 16 kg, urine output 0.4 mL/kg/h over 12 h.
data_table.Examination: Pallor, mild scleral icterus, generalised abdominal tenderness, no peritonism, no organomegaly, no rash, no peripheral oedema (yet).
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, WCC 14, blood film: schistocytes ++ and helmet cells. Reticulocytes elevated. Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline unknown, eGFR markedly reduced for age). LDH 1840 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, INR/aPTT normal, Coombs negative. Bilirubin 38 micromol/L (mostly unconjugated). Stool PCR pending.

lead_in: Which is the single most likely diagnosis, and which clinical action is contraindicated?

options.text: Immune thrombocytopaenic purpura; commence prednisolone 2 mg/kg orally
STEC-associated haemolytic uraemic syndrome (D+HUS); supportive management and avoid empirical antibiotics
Acute leukaemia with disseminated intravascular coagulation; commence empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics
Acute glomerulonephritis post-infectious; commence furosemide and start ACE inhibitor
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia; commence prednisolone 2 mg/kg and IVIG

stem:
A 3-year-old boy weighing 14 kg is triaged at John Hunter Hospital paediatric ED at 0220 with 18 hours of fever, lethargy and decreased oral intake. Parents describe a non-blanching rash that developed in the last hour on both legs. He has not been immunised. Initial assessment: T 39.4, HR 178, RR 44, capillary refill 4 seconds peripherally and 3 seconds centrally, mottled extremities, BP 88/52, SpO2 96% room air.

He is drowsy but rousable, no neck stiffness on initial exam but obtunded enough to limit reliable testing. Blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L. The triage nurse is initiating the NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 deg C, HR 178, RR 44, BP 88/52, SpO2 96% RA, CRT 4 sec peripheral, weight 14 kg.
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable, mottled extremities, non-blanching petechial rash both legs, dry mucous membranes, no obvious focus.
data_table.Investigations: Initial venous gas pending; bedside lactate 4.8 mmol/L; FBC, UEC, CRP, blood cultures, meningococcal PCR all sent.

lead_in: Within the NSW Health Paediatric Sepsis Pathway, what is the most appropriate fluid resuscitation and antibiotic decision for the first hour?

options.text: 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 minutes and reassess; defer antibiotics until lumbar puncture and CT brain are completed
10-20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 5-10 minutes, reassess after each bolus to a usual maximum of 40-60 mL/kg, plus ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) IV within 60 minutes
40 mL/kg of 4% albumin as a single rapid push to address capillary leak, plus intravenous vancomycin and meropenem within 60 minutes
Defer fluid resuscitation and commence a peripheral adrenaline infusion at 0.5 mcg/kg/min immediately as primary therapy before any crystalloid bolus
20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 60 minutes plus benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg intravenously, with immediate lumbar puncture during the bolus

subtopic_detail: NSW Health paediatric sepsis pathway cut-offs
Bronchiolitis admission criteria and feeding support
stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 6-week-old term infant in winter with 3 days of coryza and increasing work of breathing. Mum reports feeds have dropped from 100 to 40 mL every 3 hours over the last 24 hours, and the baby is becoming sweaty during feeds. There is no apnoea history. Older sibling has a viral URTI.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 91% RA (rises to 95% on 0.5 L/min nasal prong), BP 78/46
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession; tracheal tug; bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and wheeze; capillary refill 2 s; mucous membranes slightly dry
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate RSV positive; no bloods or chest x-ray; weight 4.6 kg (50th centile)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose; review at 1 hour
Admit; commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen to maintain SpO2 90% (RCH target); nasogastric feeds at two thirds maintenance
Discharge home with safety-net advice; review by general practitioner in 24 hours and red-flag information for parents
Admit for high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min from arrival; nil by mouth and intravenous maintenance fluids
Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg and gentamicin 7 mg/kg; chest x-ray and full septic workup including lumbar puncture

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice phototherapy threshold and DAT
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term breastfed boy on the postnatal ward. The midwife noted increasing yellowing of the face and chest. The infant is feeding 8 times in 24 hours, settled, with normal stool and urine. Birth weight 3.6 kg, now 3.42 kg. Maternal blood group O Rhesus positive. Antenatal antibody screen was negative. The infant's serum bilirubin has just returned.

data_table.Examination: Mild jaundice to upper chest; no hepatosplenomegaly; tone normal; reflexes intact; well perfused
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 290 micromol/L total, conjugated 8; DAT positive; FBC Hb 198 g/L, reticulocytes 6%; blood group A Rh+

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and recheck serum bilirubin in 24 hours; advise increased feed frequency in the interim
Withhold breastfeeding and substitute formula for 24 hours; recheck serum bilirubin at the end of the formula trial
Commence intensive phototherapy and recheck serum bilirubin at 4 to 6 hours; ensure hydration with continued breastfeeding
Arrange immediate double-volume exchange transfusion; transfer to neonatal intensive care for line insertion
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg over 2 hours; defer phototherapy pending response to immunoglobulin

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 5-week-old term infant brought in by his parents with a documented temperature of 38.4 at home and irritability over 6 hours. He is alert in the cot, feeding well, with no respiratory or skin findings. His parents recall a recent viral illness in an older sibling. He has no risk factors for invasive group B Streptococcus and was discharged well at day 3.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.5, HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 98% RA, BP 78/44; capillary glucose 4.6
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused; anterior fontanelle soft; clear chest; soft abdomen; no rash; no focal source
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 14.2 (neutrophils 9.2), Hb 132, plt 320; CRP 32; urine collected by SPA pending; blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally as required and general practitioner review in 24 hours; safety-net advice
Admit; observe without antibiotics or lumbar puncture pending 24-hour blood and urine culture results
Admit; commence intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg; defer lumbar puncture pending repeat clinical assessment in 6 hours
Admit; perform lumbar puncture, commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg, gentamicin 5 mg/kg and cefotaxime 50 mg/kg
Perform urine dipstick on bag urine only; commence oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily and discharge home with review

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing an 8-year-old girl with a 2-week history of polyuria and weight loss. Today she developed vomiting and is now drowsy but rousable, breathing deeply. She has no fever or sick contacts. The team weighs her at 26 kg. The first venous gas and ketones are back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 142, RR 32 deep, BP 96/62, SpO2 99% RA, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Kussmaul respiration; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 s; reduced skin turgor; clear chest; soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.10, bicarbonate 8, BSL 28, beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8, Na 138 (corrected 142), K 4.2, urea 8.4, Cr 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin strategy in the first hour?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes as bolus; start IV insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour immediately with the bolus
0.45% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 1 hour; commence subcutaneous insulin glargine 0.3 unit/kg immediately for maintenance cover
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct acidosis; defer insulin until pH above 7.20
0.9% sodium chloride 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes as resuscitation bolus regardless of perfusion; reassess after 30 minutes only
0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes for perfusion; start IV insulin 0.05 to 0.1 unit/kg/hour after 1 hour of fluid

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar managing a 9-year-old girl with known asthma now in resus. She received three 12-puff burst-doses of salbutamol with spacer plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg 60 minutes ago. She remains in marked respiratory distress, with subcostal recession and accessory muscle use, only managing single-word sentences. She has had no recent viral illness; her last hospitalisation was 8 months ago. There is no fever.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 152, RR 38, SpO2 89% on 6 L/min mask, BP 108/68
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal recession; accessory muscle use; minimal air entry; widespread expiratory wheeze; alert
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.34, pCO2 38, lactate 2.4; capillary glucose 6.8; no CXR yet
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 12 puff x3 in 1 hour; oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg; ipratropium 250 mcg x3

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) over 20 minutes; continue back-to-back nebulised salbutamol
Intravenous aminophylline loading dose 10 mg/kg over 1 hour; start maintenance aminophylline infusion immediately afterwards
Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) of 1 in 1000; repeat at 15-minute intervals as required
Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine 1.5 mg/kg and rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg; transfer to paediatric intensive care
High-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min in 100% oxygen alone; cease bronchodilators and reassess in 30 minutes

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease with coronary involvement
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-month-old boy with 7 days of fever to 39.5. He has mild conjunctival injection, one cracked lip, and a faint trunk rash. He has no cervical adenopathy and no peripheral changes. He is irritable but feeding. Blood tests and an urgent transthoracic echocardiogram are now available. The Kawasaki classic criteria are not all met.

data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral non-suppurative conjunctivitis; cracked lower lip; faint truncal exanthem; no adenopathy; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2 (neutrophils 14), Hb 96, platelets 580, CRP 165, ESR 78, albumin 28, ALT 92, Na 132; urine WCC raised; echo shows LAD Z score 3.1 with mild dilatation
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg PRN; ibuprofen ceased 2 days ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and ceftriaxone for occult bacterial infection; defer further immune therapy pending blood cultures
Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus oral aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg per day in 4 divided doses
Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily alone; outpatient cardiology follow up in 2 weeks for repeat echocardiogram
Intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg single dose; cardiology review in 24 hours with repeat coronary artery measurement
Oral aspirin 5 mg/kg daily alone as antiplatelet cover; repeat echocardiogram in 6 weeks to monitor coronary calibre

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 7-year-old boy with asthma at his routine 3-monthly clinic visit. He currently uses inhaled budesonide 100 micrograms twice daily with spacer and salbutamol as required. Over the past 3 months he has needed his salbutamol 3 to 4 times a week, woken at night with cough twice, and missed 2 days of school for an exacerbation managed by oral prednisolone. His inhaler technique is excellent on demonstration. There is no environmental trigger he can identify and no smoke exposure at home.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear today; no wheeze; growth on 50th centile; no eczema flare
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry FEV1 78% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.78, bronchodilator response +14%
data_table.Medications: Budesonide 100 mcg BD with spacer; salbutamol 100 mcg PRN; nil oral

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase inhaled budesonide to 200 micrograms twice daily; reinforce trigger avoidance and review in 6 weeks
Add montelukast 5 mg orally each evening; continue current inhaled budesonide and salbutamol
Switch budesonide to inhaled fluticasone/salmeterol combination 50/25 micrograms twice daily for combined therapy
Cease budesonide and start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days; review at completion of course
Continue current regimen and provide written action plan; review only if further exacerbation requires hospital

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 22-month-old boy whose mother is worried that he looks pale and tires easily on outings. He drinks 800 mL of cow's milk daily from a bottle since 9 months of age and eats little solid food, refusing meat and vegetables. He was born at term, breastfed for 4 months. He is otherwise well, with no jaundice, splenomegaly or recent infection. His growth has tracked the 25th centile. Bloods returned this morning.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no jaundice; soft abdomen, no organomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78, MCV 62, MCH 19, ferritin 7 microg/L, transferrin saturation 7%, CRP 2, reticulocytes 1.2%

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL/day and start oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg elemental iron/kg daily; recheck in 1 month
Refer to paediatric haematology for bone marrow examination; defer iron therapy pending specialist review
Arrange same-day intravenous iron polymaltose infusion under sedation; admit for observation overnight
Transfuse packed red cells 10 mL/kg over 4 hours; admit for paediatric review and post-transfusion bloods
Send haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassaemia trait; defer iron therapy until results return

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old infant in ED with 1 week of progressive paroxysmal cough, vomiting after coughing fits, and an apnoeic episode at home today. There is no fever. His 4-year-old sister has had a 3-week persistent cough recently labelled as a viral URTI. The infant has had no vaccinations yet; the family declined antenatal pertussis vaccination. Nasopharyngeal swab PCR for Bordetella pertussis is positive.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 168, RR 56, SpO2 92% RA (recovers between paroxysms), BP 78/46
data_table.Examination: Paroxysmal cough with inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomit observed; chest otherwise clear
data_table.Investigations: Pertussis PCR positive; WCC 28 (lymphocyte predominant 18); CXR mild perihilar streaking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of the infant and household contacts?

options.text: Treat the infant with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and reserve chemoprophylaxis for symptomatic household contacts only
Treat the infant with oral amoxicillin and offer prophylaxis only to household contacts under 6 months of age
Manage the infant supportively without antibiotics; arrange vaccination of household contacts but no chemoprophylaxis
Treat the infant with oral azithromycin and arrange azithromycin chemoprophylaxis for all close household contacts regardless of vaccination status
Admit the infant for observation only; commence household antibiotics only if the older sibling tests positive on swab

stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy with 12 hours of episodic inconsolable crying, drawing his legs up, and now passing a small amount of dark stool with mucus per rectum. He has had two episodes of bile-stained vomit. Between attacks he appears lethargic but is now pale and clammy. He is well perfused but the abdomen feels fullness in the right upper quadrant. There has been no recent viral illness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 99% RA, BP 92/58, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between paroxysms; soft abdomen with palpable RUQ sausage-shaped mass; PR exam shows blood-stained mucus
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal ultrasound shows target sign at the hepatic flexure; FBC and UEC unremarkable; lactate 1.4

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange same-admission air enema reduction by interventional radiology with paediatric surgical team in attendance
Commence empirical IV ceftriaxone and metronidazole; observe for 6 hours before deciding on intervention
Proceed directly to laparotomy and manual reduction with potential resection; no enema attempt
Discharge with safety-netting and arrange outpatient ultrasound in 24 hours if symptoms persist or worsen
Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage and trial of bowel rest for 12 hours; reimage if no improvement

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old girl admitted 3 days ago with her first febrile urinary tract infection. The catheter specimen grew Escherichia coli sensitive to her current IV antibiotic. She defervesced within 36 hours and is now feeding well, with normal observations. The bladder ultrasound performed during admission showed mild left renal pelvis dilatation but no hydroureter. The team is preparing her discharge plan and follow up.

data_table.Examination: Well, alert, feeding normally; abdomen soft, no masses
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine: E. coli sensitive; bladder ultrasound: mild left pelvis dilatation, normal right; FBC and CRP normalised; UEC normal
data_table.Medications: IV gentamicin and amoxicillin during admission; switching to oral cefalexin for discharge

lead_in: What is the most appropriate further imaging plan?

options.text: Magnetic resonance urogram at 3 months to characterise the pelvis and rule out pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction in this child
Routine micturating cystourethrogram within 2 weeks for every infant after a first febrile UTI regardless of imaging findings shown
DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring; no MCUG unless DMSA is abnormal or recurrent UTI develops
No further imaging is required after this ultrasound; outpatient paediatric follow-up and parental advice for prompt presentation with any future fever
Continuous prophylactic trimethoprim 2 mg/kg nocte for 12 months and no further imaging unless she becomes symptomatic again later

stem: You are the GP working in a regional clinic when parents rush in carrying their 18-month-old boy who suddenly began choking on a peanut 2 minutes ago. The toddler is conscious, distressed, and making weak ineffective coughing sounds with audible stridor. He is making poor air entry on auscultation and his lips are starting to look dusky. He cannot vocalise. The nearest hospital with paediatric emergency capability is 25 minutes away by ambulance.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 168, RR 50, SpO2 86% on room air, BP not yet checked
data_table.Examination: Conscious, distressed, making feeble coughs with stridor; reduced air entry bilaterally; dusky lips
data_table.Investigations: Clinical assessment; no time for imaging

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Perform 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) immediately and call for senior assistance
Encourage the child to keep coughing and call an ambulance; provide oxygen by mask while waiting for transport
Perform a blind finger sweep of the oropharynx to locate the foreign body before attempting back blows
Give 5 back blows between the scapulae with the child head-down, followed by 5 chest thrusts if obstruction persists
Lay the child supine and commence chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute until ambulance arrives

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy whose parents are concerned about ongoing daytime soiling for 8 months. He passes small hard pellets every 3 to 4 days and has multiple episodes of liquid stool leakage into his underwear daily. He was toilet-trained at 3 years. He withholds and crosses his legs. His diet is poor in fibre. There is no blood, abdominal pain, weight loss or red-flag history. Abdominal examination is consistent with faecal loading.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa and suprapubic region; perianal skin normal; no anal fissure; gait and lower limb neurology normal
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; no imaging indicated; growth on 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step in management?

options.text: Commence twice daily oral docusate 12.5 mg without disimpaction and review fibre intake over the next 6 weeks
Disimpaction with high-dose oral macrogol (PEG 3350) over 3 to 7 days, followed by daily maintenance dosing and behavioural toilet program
Refer for anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease before any laxative intervention
Recommend daily phosphate enemas for 14 days as primary therapy and review symptoms at the end of the course
Refer to paediatric psychology for behavioural management of encopresis without medication for the first 3 months

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 26-month-old boy at his routine health check. His parents report he has only 5 single words and does not combine them. He does not point to show interest, prefers to line up cars repetitively, and resists eye contact. He had no significant birth or perinatal history and his hearing screen at birth was normal. He has no regression of skills. His motor development is normal and he walks well. There is no family history of intellectual disability.

data_table.Examination: No dysmorphic features; growth 50th centile; gait and tone normal; no neurocutaneous stigmata; HEADSS not yet applicable
data_table.Investigations: Hearing screen at birth normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to speech pathology only and review in 6 months; defer paediatric review unless speech therapy alone fails to improve language
Reassure parents that boys develop language later and review at age 3 years if expressive language has not advanced over the next 9 months
Commence a 6-week trial of a Mediterranean-style diet and omega-3 supplementation and review behaviour and language at the end of trial
Order karyotype and Fragile X testing as the first investigation step before any specialist therapy referral or further developmental assessment
Refer for audiology assessment and to a developmental paediatrician for multidisciplinary autism assessment; arrange early intervention referral

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing an 18-month-old boy whose mother is worried about three episodes of him going limp and turning blue around his lips for around 20 seconds after he was scolded or denied something he wanted. Each episode ended with rapid recovery, no post-event drowsiness, no incontinence and no jerking movements observed. He is meeting all developmental milestones and is otherwise well. There is no family history of sudden death, syncope or seizures.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful; no dysmorphic features; cardiovascular and neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: FBC Hb 118, MCV 78, ferritin 24 microg/L; ECG sinus rhythm with QTc 410 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure parents about the benign self-limiting nature of cyanotic breath-holding spells and provide simple first-aid safety advice
Commence sodium valproate 10 mg/kg/day in two divided doses with serum drug-level monitoring every three months in clinic
Arrange outpatient sleep-deprived EEG and 24-hour ambulatory video-EEG monitoring to exclude an underlying focal epilepsy syndrome
Refer to paediatric cardiology for 24-hour Holter monitoring and exercise stress echocardiogram to exclude long QT syndrome
Commence oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg/day elemental iron for empirical supplementation despite ferritin within the normal reference range

subtopic_detail: Immediate antibiotic threshold in bilateral acute OM under 2 years
stem: A 15-month-old boy presents to your GP clinic with 24 hours of fever, irritability and right ear-tugging. He has no significant past medical history, is fully immunised, and is non-Aboriginal. He has no allergies. On examination he has a temperature of 38.7, both tympanic membranes bulging with reduced light reflex, and red middle ear effusion bilaterally. There is no mastoid tenderness and no facial weakness. He is alert and drinking.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulging red tympanic membranes; no mastoid tenderness; no neck stiffness; well perfused; drinking 60 percent of usual

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents, advise paracetamol or ibuprofen for analgesia, and review in 48 hours if symptoms persist
Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin ear drops twice daily for 5 days as first-line treatment for acute otitis media
Prescribe amoxicillin 30 mg/kg every 8 hours orally for 5 days plus regular paracetamol or ibuprofen analgesia
Prescribe cefuroxime 15 mg/kg twice daily orally for 7 days as the first-line agent in childhood otitis media
Refer to ENT for urgent tympanostomy tube placement given the bilateral nature of his presentation today

subtopic_detail: Supportive management thresholds in infant bronchiolitis
stem: A 10-month-old boy presents to your ED in late autumn with 3 days of coryza, rhinorrhoea, mild fever and 24 hours of wheezing and cough. His older sister had a cold last week. He has no prior wheeze, no atopy in the family, and is breastfed plus solid food. He is fully immunised. He has had no prior salbutamol use. He has 30 percent reduced feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 140, RR 50, SpO2 95 percent RA
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, widespread wheeze and bilateral fine crackles, mild dehydration with capillary refill 2 seconds; alert
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer with reassessment of respiratory effort and oxygen saturation at 20 minutes
Supportive care with feeds and oxygen monitoring; admit if SpO2 below 90% (RCH target) or feeds below 50 percent of normal
Commence high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min as first-line therapy without trialling standard low-flow oxygen
Administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days to reduce airway inflammation and shorten time to discharge
Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 strength with continuous monitoring for 4 hours before reassessment

subtopic_detail: Normal stooling variation in a thriving fully breastfed infant
stem: A 7-week-old exclusively breastfed boy has not opened his bowels for six days. His mother reports that he strains and goes red in the face, then passes a large soft stool without blood.

data_table.Growth: Passed meconium at 12 hours of age; weight tracking on the 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Alert and settled; soft abdomen with no mass; normal anus and normal spine

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the mother that this stooling pattern is normal
Commence oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes at a maintenance dose
Refer to paediatric surgery for a suction rectal biopsy
Advise a trial of an extensively hydrolysed infant formula
Give a glycerol suppository now and repeat it in two days

subtopic_detail: Toddler iron deficiency anaemia with cow's milk excess
stem: A 22-month-old girl is brought to your GP clinic for review of pallor. Her mother reports she drinks 750 mL of cow's milk per day from a bottle, eats variably, and refuses red meat. She is otherwise well, walks normally, and has met all developmental milestones. She is fully immunised. She has 5 episodes per day of upset and is described as fussy by her mother.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no koilonychia, no hepatosplenomegaly, weight on 50th centile, height on 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 64 fL, ferritin 7 mcg/L, transferrin saturation 6 percent, CRP under 5; coeliac serology negative; blood film microcytic hypochromic; reticulocyte count 1.8 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that the anaemia is mild and continue current diet with a routine review in 4 months
Order serum lead level and refer urgently to paediatric haematology for further workup before treatment
Commence vitamin B12 1000 micrograms intramuscularly weekly for 4 weeks then 3-monthly maintenance
Prescribe oral ferrous fumarate 100 mg daily without dietary advice or milk reduction during this visit
Prescribe oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg daily, limit cow's milk to 500 mL/day, advise iron-rich foods, recheck in 8 weeks

subtopic_detail: Empiric IV antibiotic regimen in febrile infant under 3 months
stem: A 2-month-old infant is brought to your ED with 24 hours of fever (38.6 by parents), poor feeding, irritability, and a single episode of vomiting. He has no upper respiratory or other localising symptoms. He is fully immunised for age. On examination he is alert but irritable, with a temperature of 38.7, capillary refill 2 seconds, no rash, no meningism, and clear chest. His urine is collected by clean catch.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 165, RR 50, SpO2 99 percent RA, weight 5.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; no rash; anterior fontanelle soft; chest clear; no abdominal tenderness; perfusion adequate
data_table.Investigations: Bedside urine dipstick positive for leukocytes and nitrites; FBC, CRP, blood cultures, blood gas pending; LP being arranged

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin empiric coverage following blood and urine cultures and lumbar puncture
Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg/dose four times daily for 7 days as outpatient management with GP follow-up
Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy at 50 mg/kg once daily without need for second agent
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole orally as suitable empiric treatment for outpatient management of UTI
Withhold antibiotics until urine culture is back at 48 hours and reassess clinically before commencing therapy

subtopic_detail: IVIG and aspirin for classic Kawasaki disease
stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to your ED on day 6 of high spiking fevers up to 40, accompanied by a polymorphous rash on day 2, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis on day 3, a strawberry tongue with red cracked lips on day 4, and unilateral right cervical lymphadenopathy 2.5 cm. His feet became swollen yesterday with red palms. He is irritable and lethargic. He has been seen twice by his GP for viral illness.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.8, HR 145, RR 32, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis; cracked red lips and strawberry tongue; polymorphous rash trunk and limbs; right cervical lymphadenopathy 2.5 cm; oedema and erythema of palms and soles; no signs of meningism
data_table.Investigations: FBC WCC 18, neutrophils 13, platelets 580; CRP 198; ESR 78; Na 132; albumin 28; ALT 78; urinary sediment with 15 WCC; echocardiogram pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence amoxicillin and observe for clinical response over 48 hours before further investigations are arranged
Treat as scarlet fever with oral phenoxymethylpenicillin and observe response over the next 72 hours
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with high-dose aspirin and arrange urgent echocardiogram
Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg as monotherapy without immunoglobulin or aspirin
Reassure parents of viral exanthem, advise paracetamol, and arrange GP review of progress in 48 hours

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to your GP clinic with a 1-week history of a palpable purpuric rash on his buttocks and lower legs, abdominal pain, and 24 hours of left knee swelling. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. He is otherwise well, has a good appetite, and no haematuria reported by parents. Examination shows palpable non-blanching purpura on extensor surfaces of legs, mild ankle and knee swelling without joint effusion, and a soft non-tender abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura extensor lower limbs and buttocks; bilateral mild ankle swelling, painful left knee; soft non-tender abdomen with normal bowel sounds; no testicular involvement
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick clear (no blood, no protein); FBC normal platelets 380; coagulation normal; UEC normal; ASOT positive 380 U; throat swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate monitoring plan?

options.text: Single review in 4 weeks with FBC and creatinine to confirm resolution of symptoms before discharge
Weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 4 weeks, then fortnightly for 8 weeks, then 3-monthly to 12 months
Daily urinalysis at home with creatinine and proteinuria measurement performed monthly for 1 year
Renal biopsy at 6 weeks regardless of urinalysis findings as routine screening in this presentation
Single urinalysis and blood pressure check at 6 months in line with general practice protocols

subtopic_detail: Bilious vomiting in shocked neonate - malrotation with midgut volvulus
stem: A 5-day-old term infant born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth (birth weight 3300 g) is brought to your tertiary neonatal ED with 6 hours of bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and decreased feeding. The baby was breastfeeding well at home. He was discharged on day 1 of life. On arrival he is pale, peripherally cool, with capillary refill 4 seconds, and a distended tender abdomen.

data_table.Vital signs: T 35.8, BP 56/35, HR 175, RR 65, SpO2 96 percent on room air, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Pale, peripherally shut down, tense distended abdomen with reduced bowel sounds; no obvious external mass; testes descended; no perianal abnormality
data_table.Investigations: BSL 2.4 mmol/L; ABG pH 7.20, bicarbonate 12, lactate 5.8; Hb 110, WCC 8.2, platelets 90; UEC: Na 132, K 5.8, urea 8.2, creatinine 56; CRP 18; clotted blood for cross-match sent; abdominal radiograph shows non-specific gas pattern with no obvious pneumatosis or free air; nasogastric aspirate is bile-stained

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate management priority?

options.text: Commence empiric intravenous gentamicin, ampicillin and metronidazole and observe the abdomen at frequent intervals while monitoring vital signs
Commence broad-spectrum antibiotics and arrange contrast upper gastrointestinal series within 2 hours to confirm diagnosis
Insert nasogastric tube, commence intravenous fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and admit for clinical observation overnight
Administer 20 mL/kg fluid bolus, commence broad-spectrum antibiotics, and arrange CT abdomen with contrast to clarify the cause
Resuscitate with fluid and blood products, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, and arrange immediate paediatric surgical consultation for laparotomy

subtopic_detail: Empiric oral antibiotic for first febrile UTI in well toddler
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18-month-old girl in the short-stay unit with 24 hours of fever and reduced feeding. She is alert with no rash and tolerating sips. A clean-catch urine collected after meatal cleaning shows leucocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, and microscopy with 200 white cells per microlitre. Local antibiogram shows E. coli trimethoprim resistance of 28 percent and cefalexin resistance of 6 percent.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99 percent, BP 96/58
data_table.Examination: Alert, hydrated, soft non-tender abdomen, no flank tenderness, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine LE positive, nitrites positive, WCC 200/microL, urine culture pending; venous blood gas pH 7.38, lactate 1.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric oral antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 7 days starting now in the short-stay unit
Withhold antibiotics until urine culture sensitivities are reported tomorrow morning before commencing any oral therapy
Oral trimethoprim 4 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 7 days starting now as the empiric first-line oral antibiotic
Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days starting now as the first-line empirical oral antibiotic
Intravenous gentamicin 7 mg/kg daily admit for 48 hours then switch to oral therapy guided by culture sensitivities

subtopic_detail: Postexposure prophylaxis for household contacts of confirmed pertussis
stem: You are the GP registrar seeing a family after their 7-year-old son was diagnosed with PCR-confirmed pertussis 2 days ago. The household includes the index case, his 32-year-old mother who is 34 weeks pregnant, his 38-year-old father, an 8-week-old sister who is fully vaccinated for age, and a 4-year-old brother whose immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: All household members afebrile and asymptomatic at presentation today
data_table.Examination: Index case isolating at home with paroxysmal cough; other family members no respiratory symptoms
data_table.Investigations: Index case pertussis PCR positive 2 days ago; other family members no testing performed

lead_in: Which household members should receive antibiotic postexposure prophylaxis today?

options.text: Only the 8-week-old sister receives azithromycin while other contacts are observed at home
No prophylaxis is given because all household contacts are currently asymptomatic on review
Mother, 8-week-old sister, 4-year-old brother, and father all receive azithromycin
Only the mother and 8-week-old sister receive azithromycin while other contacts are observed
All household contacts receive trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole as the preferred first-line agent

subtopic_detail: Pharmacotherapy choice for moderate croup in ED
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy with a 12-hour history of barking cough, hoarseness, and intermittent stridor at rest. He is alert and accepts oral medications. There is no drooling, history of foreign body, or recent vaccinations missed. Local supply of dexamethasone oral solution is currently available.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 138, RR 36, SpO2 97 percent on air
data_table.Examination: Barking cough, stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, alert, normal air entry bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Westley croup score 4 (moderate); no investigations indicated for typical croup
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol given by parents 4 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as initial inhaled corticosteroid because oral intake is uncertain
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now and reassess in 30 minutes
Salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and observation pending resolution of stridor
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 alone now without corticosteroid
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose tried first because dexamethasone is unavailable

subtopic_detail: IM adrenaline weight-band dosing and route in school-age child with anaphylaxis
stem: You are the ED registrar called to resuscitation as an 8-year-old boy arrives by ambulance after eating a peanut snack at school 20 minutes ago. He developed lip swelling, generalised urticaria, then dyspnoea and one episode of vomiting. Paramedics administered 300 micrograms intramuscular adrenaline 10 minutes ago via his school auto-injector. He weighs 32 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 154, RR 38, SpO2 91 percent on 6 L/min oxygen, BP 78/42
data_table.Examination: Widespread urticaria, perioral swelling, audible wheeze bilaterally, prolonged capillary refill, anxious
data_table.Investigations: Bedside venous gas pH 7.30, lactate 3.2
data_table.Medications: Adrenaline 300 micrograms IM 10 minutes ago (auto-injector); now 20 minutes since exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next adrenaline order while you secure IV access and prepare a fluid bolus?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 as the next adrenaline dose for upper airway oedema
Subcutaneous adrenaline 300 micrograms in the deltoid as a second dose for ongoing wheeze and hypotension
Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms in the anterolateral thigh as the appropriate paediatric weight-band dose
Intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg push as a single bolus over 30 seconds while preparing fluid
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 micrograms in the anterolateral thigh now and repeat at 5 minute intervals as needed

subtopic_detail: Empiric antibiotic and LP timing in late onset suspected neonatal sepsis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 12-day-old term boy brought in by his mother with poor feeding and reduced activity for 8 hours. He is now lethargic and grunting. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, breastfed, and discharged at 36 hours. He has not received any maternal antibiotics in labour. The local cefotaxime supply is unavailable due to a national shortage and ceftriaxone is being used as the substitute despite the patient being a term neonate without jaundice.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 192, RR 68, SpO2 94 percent, BP 62/38, prolonged capillary refill
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, grunting, mottled, anterior fontanelle full, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.22 base excess -10, glucose 2.6, lactate 4.2, WCC 22, CRP 78, blood culture taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next set of antimicrobial actions?

options.text: Commence IV cefazolin and gentamicin then add aciclovir if seizures or focal CNS signs develop later
Commence IV vancomycin and meropenem to cover resistant gram negatives and methicillin resistant staph
Commence IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin alone given a term neonate with cefotaxime unavailable on site
Start IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and ceftriaxone immediately then proceed to lumbar puncture when stabilised
Perform lumbar puncture first then commence IV benzylpenicillin and gentamicin only after CSF is obtained

subtopic_detail: Initial workup of weight faltering in 9-month-old without organic red flags
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 9-month-old boy whose weight has dropped from the 25th to the 3rd centile across the last three reviews. He was born at term, weighed 3.2 kg, and is exclusively breastfed with one daily solids tasting. His mother describes long unsettled feeds and reports she eats no extra protein. He smiles, transfers objects, and sits unsupported. There is no diarrhoea, vomiting, recurrent infection, or family history of coeliac disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 124, RR 30, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Growth: Weight 6.4 kg (3rd centile, dropping), length 70 cm (25th), head circ 44 cm (25th)
data_table.Examination: Alert, no dysmorphism, no organomegaly, normal cardiac exam, soft non-distended abdomen, no rashes
data_table.Feeding: Breast feeds 6-8 times daily; offered pureed vegetable and rice cereal once daily; no formula

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for paediatric admission and inpatient nasogastric supplemental feeding trial
Arrange a structured feeding history with three-day diet diary and observe a feed
Order coeliac serology, full blood count, and renal function as the next investigation
Advise immediate cessation of breastfeeding and introduction of full-strength formula
Reassure the mother that weight tracking on the 3rd centile is normal variation

subtopic_detail: HPV vaccine routine schedule for 12-year-old at school-based program
stem: You are the school-based immunisation doctor reviewing a 12-year-old girl in Year 7 attending the routine school program. She is fit, well, has had no severe vaccine reactions, and is not immunocompromised. Her mother has consented in writing and asks whether she will need a second dose later this year or next.

data_table.Examination: Well, no acute illness, BMI on the 60th centile
data_table.Immunisations: Up to date with childhood schedule; never received HPV
data_table.Other: No pregnancy, no immunosuppression, no current febrile illness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate HPV immunisation plan?

options.text: Administer Gardasil 9 today and book a second dose at six months
Administer Gardasil 9 today as a single dose with no further doses required
Defer vaccination until she turns 14 years to align with menarche cohort outcomes
Administer Gardasil 9 today and book three total doses across six months
Decline routine vaccination and instead recommend cervical screening once eligible

subtopic_detail: Differentiating paraphimosis from physiological phimosis in 4-year-old boy
stem: You are the ED registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy whose father retracted his foreskin during a bath two hours ago to clean underneath. The foreskin has not returned over the glans and the child is now crying with marked penile discomfort. There has been no trauma, fever, or urinary symptoms, and he passes urine without difficulty. The father describes the foreskin as previously non-retractable until tonight.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 124, RR 24, BP 96/60, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Foreskin retracted behind a swollen, painful glans with a constricting band; glans pink, warm, non-dusky; no urinary retention
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis clear; no imaging performed
data_table.Past history: Otherwise well, immunisations up to date, no surgical history

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Reassure the family that the foreskin is non-retractable and arrange GP review
Apply topical lidocaine gel and attempt manual reduction with sustained glans compression
Refer to urology for elective circumcision booking and discharge with paracetamol
Apply topical corticosteroid cream twice daily for six weeks and review in clinic
Insert urinary catheter to relieve urinary retention and admit for intravenous antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Suspected foreign body inhalation in toddler with focal wheeze and stable airway
stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing an 18-month-old girl who began coughing during a family dinner two hours ago. Her grandmother saw her chewing peanuts before the choking episode. She is now alert, tolerating sips, with mild intermittent cough but no stridor or cyanosis. On auscultation she has decreased air entry and end-expiratory wheeze localised to the right side.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 96 percent on air, BP 98/60
data_table.Examination: Sitting comfortably, no tripod posture, mild intercostal recession, focal right wheeze and reduced air entry
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray inspiration: subtle right hyperinflation; expiration film: persistent right hyperinflation with mediastinal shift to the left
data_table.Past history: Well child, full immunisation, no asthma

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial salbutamol via spacer and review in two hours before any procedural plan
Refer urgently to ENT or paediatric surgery for rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia
Perform five back blows and five chest thrusts and admit for observation overnight
Order high-resolution chest CT to confirm radiolucent foreign body before any referral
Discharge home with chest physiotherapy advice and GP review in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Suspected button battery oesophageal ingestion in 2-year-old with delayed presentation
stem: You are the rural ED consultant reviewing a 2-year-old boy whose mother found him near a hearing-aid box six hours ago. He vomited once, refused dinner, and is now drooling with retrosternal discomfort. The nearest endoscopy service is at a tertiary hospital 90 minutes away by road retrieval. He has no stridor, intact saturation, and looks well perfused. The mother offered him milk to drink an hour ago; he kept it down.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 134, RR 30, SpO2 99 percent on air, BP 98/56
data_table.Examination: Drooling, refusing oral intake, mildly distressed; chest clear; no haemoptysis; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Chest and abdominal X-ray: 20 mm circular radiopaque object with double-rim halo lodged at the level of the thoracic inlet; no free air; no pneumomediastinum

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention before retrieval?

options.text: Administer 10 mL aliquots of oral honey every 10 minutes while awaiting retrieval transport
Withhold all oral intake and arrange immediate endoscopic removal at the local hospital
Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac to attempt expulsion before transfer to the tertiary centre
Give oral activated charcoal 1 g/kg via cup to bind the battery contents before retrieval departure
Insert a wide-bore nasogastric tube and attempt mechanical dislodgement of the battery toward the stomach

subtopic_detail: First-line investigation for global developmental delay with no syndromic features
stem: You are the paediatrician reviewing a 3-year-old boy referred for delay in all developmental domains. He is non-verbal, walks unsteadily, and has poor social engagement. There is no parental consanguinity, no regression, no seizures, and no dysmorphism. Hearing and vision testing are normal. Newborn screening was unremarkable and no metabolic decompensation history exists. Family is keen to identify a cause to guide reproductive counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 100, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Growth: Weight 75th centile, height 70th centile, OFC 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Non-dysmorphic, normal cardiac and abdominal examination, normal genitalia, normal skin findings
data_table.Investigations: TSH, ferritin, creatine kinase, urine metabolic screen all normal; MRI brain not yet done

lead_in: What is the single best next investigation?

options.text: Karyotype with G-banding to screen for whole chromosome aneuploidy as a first step
Chromosomal microarray as the first-tier genetic investigation for unexplained global delay
MRI brain with contrast as the highest yield single investigation in this clinical setting
Whole exome sequencing as the first genetic test to bypass microarray triage entirely
EEG to exclude epileptic encephalopathy as the underlying cause of the delay

subtopic_detail: Sentinel facial features in fetal alcohol spectrum disorder assessment
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic reviewing a 4-year-old boy referred by his kindergarten teacher for behavioural concerns and slow language. His birth mother has been open about ongoing alcohol use through the pregnancy. He is in long-term foster care. His foster mother reports impulsivity, poor emotion regulation, and difficulty following two-step instructions. Growth is below the 3rd centile for weight and length. There is no history of perinatal infection, head trauma, or seizures, and metabolic screening done at school entry was normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight 13.1 kg (<3rd centile), height 95 cm (<3rd centile), head circumference 47.5 cm (<3rd centile)
data_table.Facial findings: Short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper vermilion border
data_table.Development: Receptive language 2 years 6 months, expressive language 2 years, gross motor age-appropriate
data_table.Hearing and vision: Audiology and ophthalmology screening normal in the last 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming the suspected diagnosis?

options.text: Send a chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing as the next investigation
Refer for multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental assessment with standardised facial measurement
Commence a 6-week trial of methylphenidate for presumed attentional and impulse difficulties
Arrange brain MRI to exclude a structural cause of the developmental delay
Reassure the family and re-review developmental progress in 6 months in clinic

subtopic_detail: Diagnostic pathway for suspected Hirschsprung disease in delayed meconium passage
stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to assess a term male newborn on day 3 who has not passed meconium since birth and now has bilious vomiting after each feed. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth at 39 weeks. His abdomen is progressively distended, and a digital rectal examination produces a forceful expulsion of meconium and gas. He has not had any prior abdominal surgery. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis, and the newborn screening blood spot is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 158, RR 52, SpO2 98 percent on room air
data_table.Examination: Distended soft non-tender abdomen, visible bowel loops, no inguinal hernia, anus normally sited and patent
data_table.Hydration: Capillary refill 2 seconds, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.36, lactate 2.1 mmol/L; supine abdominal radiograph shows dilated bowel loops with paucity of rectal gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.text: Proceed directly to laparotomy and intraoperative levelling biopsies under anaesthesia
Request a water-soluble contrast enema to characterise the transition zone in colonic anatomy
Arrange a suction rectal biopsy for histological assessment of ganglion cells
Trial high-dose oral lactulose and review the response over the next 48 hours
Send sweat chloride testing to exclude meconium ileus from cystic fibrosis

subtopic_detail: Application of revised Jones criteria for acute rheumatic fever in high-risk populations
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a regional Northern Territory hospital reviewing an 8-year-old Aboriginal girl with a 5-day history of migratory polyarthralgia and intermittent fevers. She had a sore throat 4 weeks ago that resolved without medical review. Her parents report she is no longer able to walk on the right knee. On examination she has a soft mid-systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and tender swelling of the right knee and left wrist.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 132, RR 24, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Investigations: ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP 92 mg/L, ASOT 800 IU/mL, ECG PR interval 180 ms (age-corrected upper limit), throat swab pending
data_table.Echocardiography: Pending; transthoracic study available later today
data_table.Skin findings: No subcutaneous nodules or erythema marginatum identified

lead_in: Which diagnostic conclusion is best supported by the available findings under the 2015 revised Jones criteria?

options.text: Definite acute rheumatic fever can be diagnosed on the current clinical and laboratory findings
Probable acute rheumatic fever is the most that can be assigned without echocardiography confirmation
Possible acute rheumatic fever is the appropriate label until subcutaneous nodules develop on review
Reactive arthritis is the more likely diagnosis given the migratory pattern of joint symptoms
Septic arthritis must be excluded by joint aspiration before any rheumatic fever diagnosis

subtopic_detail: Stepwise escalation of atopic eczema flare beyond moisturiser and mild topical steroid
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 3-year-old girl with a severe atopic eczema flare across the trunk and limbs. Her mother has applied liberal sorbolene and 1 percent hydrocortisone cream twice daily for 7 days with worsening lichenification and excoriation. There is no honey-coloured crusting, fever, or vesicular lesions. The family demonstrates good technique with moisturiser. Her sleep has been disturbed for 4 nights.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Skin examination: Diffuse erythema with lichenification at antecubital and popliteal fossae, excoriations, no pustules or oozing crust
data_table.Atopic background: Egg-allergy infancy, sibling with asthma, dust mite specific IgE strongly positive
data_table.Previous treatments: Sorbolene 3 times daily, 1 percent hydrocortisone twice daily for 7 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Continue 1 percent hydrocortisone twice daily and review the response again in 7 days
Refer to a paediatric dermatologist for ciclosporin or methotrexate consideration
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 5 days to settle the flare quickly
Step up to methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1 percent once daily with wet-wrap bandages overnight
Switch to topical pimecrolimus twice daily as steroid-sparing maintenance therapy

subtopic_detail: Renal monitoring and referral thresholds in Henoch-Schonlein purpura nephritis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy 4 weeks after a presentation with palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower limbs, abdominal pain, and bilateral ankle arthritis. He met clinical criteria for Henoch-Schonlein purpura and his skin and joint symptoms resolved within 10 days. His mother reports cola-coloured urine over the last 2 days. He is otherwise well, eating and drinking normally, with no oedema. The local emergency department sent a urine sample at the time of presentation that was negative for blood and protein.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 96, RR 20, BP 122/78 mmHg (>95th centile for height)
data_table.Blood results: Creatinine 78 micromol/L (baseline 35), urea 9.1 mmol/L, albumin 28 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange a repeat urine dipstick and blood pressure check in 4 weeks
Start oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks and review in clinic in 2 weeks
Start oral aspirin and discharge with a 2-week clinic review for joint symptoms
Order renal ultrasound and discharge with general practitioner urinalysis monitoring weekly
Refer immediately to paediatric nephrology for inpatient assessment and renal biopsy planning

subtopic_detail: Non-IgE mediated cow milk protein allergy management ladder in infancy
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 5-month-old infant with a 6-week history of loose blood-streaked stools, eczema flare, and unsettled feeding. He is exclusively breastfed and his weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile. There has been no acute reaction to any food, no hives, no swelling, and no vomiting. The mother has tried eliminating dairy from her own diet for 1 week with partial improvement. Skin prick testing to cow milk is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 122, RR 30, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Growth: Weight 6.5 kg (25th centile, dropping), length 65 cm (25th centile), head circ 42 cm (25th centile)
data_table.Stool examination: Mucus and visible blood streaks, no diarrhoea
data_table.Examination: Mild eczema in antecubital fossae, soft non-tender abdomen, no perianal fissure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue maternal dairy exclusion strictly for at least 2 to 4 weeks with dietitian support
Switch immediately to extensively hydrolysed formula and cease breastfeeding now
Switch immediately to amino acid based formula given the bleeding per rectum
Refer for paediatric gastroscopy and colonoscopy to exclude infantile inflammatory bowel disease
Trial soy formula for 2 weeks and review symptoms in clinic at the end of the trial

subtopic_detail: Recognition and treatment of incomplete (atypical) Kawasaki disease in infants
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy on day 6 of unexplained high fevers despite appropriate empiric ceftriaxone. He has a fine truncal rash, conjunctival injection without exudate, and red dry lips but no extremity changes, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and no oral cavity changes. Blood and urine cultures are sterile at 48 hours. Respiratory viral PCR is negative. Inflammatory markers are markedly elevated.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2, HR 168, RR 38, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 12.1 x10^9/L, platelets 540 x10^9/L, ALT 85 U/L, albumin 27 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue empiric ceftriaxone for a further 48 hours and review for clinical change
Discharge with safety-net advice and arrange community paediatrician review in 1 week
Obtain echocardiography and treat with IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin given supplemental criteria are met
Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 5 days as first-line monotherapy
Order a chest computed tomography to investigate alternative infectious aetiologies

subtopic_detail: Indications and timing of adenotonsillectomy in paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea
stem: You are the GP referred a 5-year-old girl by her preschool teacher for daytime inattention and morning headaches. Her parents describe loud nightly snoring with witnessed apnoeic pauses and restless sleep. She has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile for weight. There is no rhinitis, no recurrent tonsillitis, and no atopic history. She has tonsils that touch the uvula and a Mallampati class III oropharynx.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 96, RR 22, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 96 percent room air awake
data_table.Growth: Weight 16 kg (10th centile, falling), height 110 cm (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Mouth breathing, mild adenoidal facies, no inspiratory stridor, no rhinitis
data_table.Polysomnography (recent): Obstructive apnoea-hypopnoea index 8.4 per hour, nadir SpO2 87 percent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ENT for adenotonsillectomy as the first-line treatment of moderate paediatric OSA
Trial intranasal mometasone for 6 weeks before any referral for surgical intervention
Commence trial of continuous positive airway pressure overnight while awaiting outpatient review
Order MRI airway to characterise the anatomy before any surgical referral is generated
Reassure parents and arrange a sleep position trial with lateral positioning at night

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called by the neonatal nurse about a term baby born at 39+5 weeks gestation, now 60 hours of age. The baby is appropriate weight for age (3.4 kg), exclusively breastfed, and has been admitted to the special care nursery for visible jaundice extending to the legs. The infant is feeding well, alert, with no neurological abnormality.

Mother is blood group O Rh positive; baby is group A Rh positive with positive direct Coombs test. Bloods show total serum bilirubin 410 micromol/L, unconjugated 390, conjugated 20, Hb 142 g/L, reticulocytes 5%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 44, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.9, weight 3.4 kg
data_table.Examination: Jaundice to legs (Kramer zone 4); alert; tone normal; no opisthotonus or high-pitched cry
data_table.Investigations: TSB 410 micromol/L (unconjugated 390, conjugated 20); Hb 142, retic 5%; DAT positive; baby A Rh+, mother O Rh+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Discharge home with general practitioner heel-prick total serum bilirubin re-check arranged within 24 hours of leaving the special care nursery
Stop breastfeeding completely and switch to exclusive infant formula feeding for the next 48 hours while keeping the infant in special care nursery
Commence intensive multiple-bank phototherapy, ensure adequate hydration, and recheck the serum bilirubin in 4-6 hours without scavenger therapy
Start intensive multi-bank phototherapy, give IVIG 0.5-1 g/kg over 2 hours, ensure hydration, prepare for exchange transfusion via tertiary unit
Administer oral phenobarbital 5 mg/kg as hepatic enzyme induction therapy to enhance bilirubin clearance over the next 24-48 hour treatment period

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department reviewing an 11-month-old boy brought in by his parents with three episodes of inconsolable crying with leg-drawing each lasting around 8 minutes over the past four hours. Between episodes he is pale but responsive. He vomited bile-stained fluid once. His last bowel motion 90 minutes ago had a small amount of dark-red jelly-like material.

Examination reveals a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, no peritonism, and capillary refill of 2 seconds. Abdominal ultrasound confirms ileocolic intussusception. There is no free air on AXR.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, BP 88/52, RR 36, SpO2 99%, Temp 37.4, weight 9.2 kg, CRT 2 s
data_table.Examination: Lethargic between episodes; soft abdomen with palpable sausage mass RUQ; no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: target sign at ileocaecal junction with no free fluid; FBC, UEC, glucose normal; lactate 1.4; AXR no free air or obstruction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management step now?

options.text: Discharge home with detailed parental safety-netting advice and primary care review arranged within 12 hours of leaving the emergency department
Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and observe for the next 24 hours before deciding on further imaging or operative interventions
Resuscitate with isotonic IV fluid bolus 10-20 mL/kg, then transfer for air enema reduction by interventional radiology with paediatric surgery standby
Proceed directly to operative laparotomy and surgical reduction without first attempting any non-operative pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction
Trial a barium contrast enema with a delayed abdominal radiograph at 8 hours to confirm reduction before considering surgical intervention pathways

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in the ED reviewing a 7-week-old infant brought in by her mother with a 9-day history of progressively worsening cough. The infant has paroxysms of cough up to 12 per day, three episodes of apnoea overnight noted by the parents, and occasional cyanosis with coughing. She feeds intermittently. She has had her 6-week immunisations. Her older brother (4 years) had a coryzal illness with cough two weeks ago that has now resolved. On examination the chest is clear between paroxysms. NPA is sent for pertussis PCR. SpO2 between paroxysms is 96%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 50 between paroxysms, SpO2 96% between paroxysms, Temp 37.1, weight 4.6 kg
data_table.Examination: Vigorous baby between episodes; paroxysmal cough with cyanosis and three apnoeas overnight; chest clear; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 28 with lymphocytosis 22; CXR clear; pertussis NPA PCR pending

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate antimicrobial?

options.text: Amoxicillin 25 mg/kg orally three times daily for a 7-day course as the principal antimicrobial therapy in this case
Azithromycin 10 mg/kg orally once daily for a 5-day course as first-line antimicrobial in this young infant presentation
Erythromycin 10 mg/kg orally four times daily for a 14-day course as the first-line macrolide for young infant pertussis
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 8/40 mg/kg orally twice daily for 14 days as first-choice antimicrobial in this young infant pertussis case
Ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg orally twice daily for a 7-day course as first-line antimicrobial therapy in this young infant pertussis presentation

stem:
A 5-week-old male infant is referred to your paediatric surgical unit with a two-week history of progressively worsening non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds. He is hungry between feeds. Examination reveals a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis. He has dry mucous membranes, capillary refill of 3 seconds, and depressed fontanelle. Weight has dropped from 4.0 kg to 3.6 kg over two weeks.

VBG shows pH 7.55, HCO3 38, base excess +14, Cl 86, Na 134, K 2.9. Ultrasound confirms pyloric stenosis with muscle thickness 4.5 mm and channel length 18 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 38, SpO2 99%, weight 3.6 kg (was 4.0 kg), CRT 3 s
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, depressed fontanelle, palpable olive RUQ, visible peristalsis; lethargic but rousable
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.55, HCO3 38, BE +14, Cl 86, Na 134, K 2.9, glucose 4.2; ultrasound: muscle thickness 4.5 mm, channel 18 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Proceed directly to definitive pyloromyotomy operatively within the first hour of arrival to the paediatric surgical receiving unit
Commence 5% dextrose at a maintenance rate of 5 mL/kg/h with no sodium chloride or potassium electrolyte additives prescribed initially
Bolus 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg, then 0.45% saline with 5% dextrose plus KCl 20-40 mmol/L at 1.5 x maintenance, book surgery when Cl >100 HCO3 <30
Give 40 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline followed by intravenous sodium bicarbonate to correct the metabolic alkalosis prior to operative planning
Place a nasogastric tube on free drainage and continue trial of small frequent oral feeds while awaiting elective surgical fixation in 24 hours

stem: A 6-year-old girl with ALL on maintenance chemotherapy presents to your tertiary paediatric ED via ambulance with a 2-hour history of fever 39.0 degrees and lethargy. She had vincristine 5 days ago. She has a tunnelled central venous catheter in situ. Capillary refill is 3 seconds, BP 88/52, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 98%. The line site is clean. She has no penicillin allergy. Her last neutrophil count three days ago was 0.4 x 10^9/L. Blood cultures are about to be drawn from line and peripherally.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 88/52, RR 28, SpO2 98%, Temp 39.0, weight 22 kg, CRT 3 s
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries, alert but tired; CVC site clean; no focal source on full examination
data_table.Investigations: Bloods drawn peripherally and from line; FBC pending; previous ANC 0.4 x 10^9/L three days ago
data_table.Medications: 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate, recent vincristine; allopurinol; cotrimoxazole prophylaxis on Mondays and Tuesdays

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial regimen to commence within the first hour?

options.text: Piperacillin-tazobactam 100 mg/kg IV after cultures, adding vancomycin only for haemodynamic instability, mucositis or proven line infection
