Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 25 mg/kg three times daily with outpatient discharge and clinic review at 24 hours in haematology day unit
Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg intravenously once daily as empiric monotherapy throughout the first 48 hours of suspected febrile neutropenia in this child
Meropenem 20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours plus amikacin 15 mg/kg IV once daily as routine first-line empiric combination for all febrile neutropenia
Withhold all antibiotics until the central venous catheter is removed and the blood culture microbiology results have returned to clinical team

subtopic_detail: Perthes vs slipped upper femoral epiphysis
stem:
A 12-year-old boy is brought to your general practice by his mother with a 3-week history of intermittent right hip pain and a limp. He is in the 95th centile for weight at 78 kg and 50th for height. He has noticed his right foot turns outward when he walks, and he keeps the leg externally rotated when sitting. There is no fever, no recent illness, and no trauma.

Examination shows restricted internal rotation of the right hip with obligate external rotation when the hip is flexed (positive Drehmann sign). Bilateral AP and frog-leg lateral radiographs of both hips show mild posteromedial slippage of the right capital femoral epiphysis along the Klein line.

data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait with externally rotated right limb; restricted internal rotation right hip; obligate external rotation on hip flexion (positive Drehmann); no warmth or effusion
data_table.Investigations: AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis: right capital femoral epiphysis posteromedially displaced relative to Klein line; left hip: equivocal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommend gradual weight loss and arrange clinic review with repeat plain radiographs of both hips in three months from today's primary care visit
Commence ibuprofen analgesia and physiotherapy with planned outpatient orthopaedic review in six weeks once the symptoms have begun to improve
Make him non-weight-bearing immediately, admit to paediatric orthopaedics, refer for urgent in-situ percutaneous single-screw fixation per RCH protocol
Order MRI of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis radiographically before referring on for orthopaedic surgical opinion and operative planning later
Manage as Perthes disease with abduction bracing and physiotherapy with quarterly clinical and radiographic review by primary care general practitioner

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the special care nursery to a previously well-appearing term male neonate born at 39 weeks who is now 60 hours of age. Over the past 12 hours he has become progressively lethargic, then irritable with hyperventilation, refusing feeds, with a brief tonic-clonic seizure 30 minutes ago. He has had no fever. There is no perinatal sepsis history.

There was no antenatal newborn screening result yet because the heel prick was taken at 48 hours. Bloods show NH3 540 micromol/L, respiratory alkalosis (pH 7.51, PaCO2 26, HCO3 22), glucose 4.1, lactate 2.0, anion gap 12, normal LFTs, normal coagulation, normal infection markers. There is no ketonuria.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 70 (hyperventilation), Temp 36.7, SpO2 99%, weight 3.4 kg
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, hyperventilating, post-ictal; soft anterior fontanelle; tone normal
data_table.Investigations: NH3 540 micromol/L; ABG pH 7.51, PaCO2 26, HCO3 22, BE -1; glucose 4.1; lactate 2.0; anion gap 12; no ketosis; LFTs normal; coagulation normal; CRP <5; CSF acellular

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate emergency management?

options.text: Increase enteral protein intake aggressively to drive metabolic ammonia clearance via the residual ureagenesis catabolic pathway in this neonate
Withhold all treatment until a definitive enzymatic urea cycle diagnosis is confirmed by tertiary metabolic biochemistry and molecular genetic testing
Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and gut decontamination with oral lactulose to reduce enteric ammoniagenesis and clear circulating ammonia
Stop protein, give 10% dextrose with intralipid, sodium benzoate plus phenylbutyrate plus arginine scavengers, prepare haemodialysis if NH3 stays >400-500
Administer intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg as the principal pharmacological intervention to reverse acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy in this neonatal presentation

stem:
A 2-year-old previously well boy presents to your emergency department with one day of barking cough, hoarse voice and now severe inspiratory stridor at rest with marked sternal and intercostal recession. He is alert but anxious. The triage nurse reports oxygen saturations 93% on room air. He had a low-grade fever the day before. His vaccinations are up to date.

He has no drooling, has been drinking small volumes, and there is no neck swelling. The nurse asks what treatment to give immediately at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, BP not done, RR 42, SpO2 93% on RA, Temp 37.4
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest; marked recession; anxious; mild reduction in air entry both fields
data_table.Investigations: Westley score 8 (severe); clinical diagnosis; no bloods or imaging required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate initial management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with concurrent single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kilogram while preparing escalation pathway with anaesthetics
Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram once and clinical observation for two hours without nebulised adrenaline because of stimulation and possible distress on application
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg per kilogram now for presumed epiglottitis and call ENT for direct laryngoscopy in the operating theatre without delay regardless of vaccination status
Heliox 70 of 30 with concurrent nebulised salbutamol as first-line therapy for severe upper airway obstruction in this preschool child without prior wheeze history
Reassure parents and discharge home with humidified air at home as evidence-based first-line therapy for moderate to severe croup with safety-net advice about deterioration

subtopic_detail: Febrile UTI in infants under 3 months
stem: A 6-week-old infant girl is brought to your emergency department by her parents because of a tactile fever today, feeding refusal and increased sleepiness. She has not had any cough, coryza or rash. She was born at term, has been growing normally on the 50th centile, and was vaccinated at 6 weeks two days ago. On examination she has a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius rectally, is mildly irritable when handled and has no obvious focus of infection on careful examination including ears, throat and chest.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, BP 86/54, RR 48, SpO2 98% on RA, Temp 38.4 rectal
data_table.Examination: Mildly irritable; AF flat; no rash; no respiratory distress; no focus on examination
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4; CRP 38; venous pH 7.36, lactate 2.4; urine pending; chest X-ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Send a bag urine sample for culture and discharge home with safety-net advice and paediatric follow-up at the local general practice clinic in 24 hours
Admit, take blood cultures, lumbar puncture and a clean catch or suprapubic aspirate urine, then commence intravenous benzylpenicillin plus cefotaxime empirically as a septic workup approach
Reassure family that her recent vaccination explains the fever and observe for 4 hours without bloods, urine, lumbar puncture or empirical antibiotic therapy at the present time
Perform a urinalysis only and treat as a presumed urinary tract infection with oral cefalexin for ten days while awaiting culture confirmation from the bag sample collected today
Order a chest X-ray and respiratory viral PCR only to identify the likely viral cause of the fever before deciding on the need for any antibiotic therapy in this infant

stem: A 3-year-old boy presents to your emergency department on day 6 of an illness characterised by persistent fever above 38.5 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, strawberry tongue with cracked red lips, a polymorphous truncal rash, oedema of the hands and feet and a unilateral 2.5 cm cervical lymph node. He is irritable and his bloods show CRP 124 mg per litre, WCC 18.4, platelets 540, ALT 78 and a normocytic anaemia. Urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. Echocardiography has been requested and will occur within hours.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral conjunctival injection; strawberry tongue; cracked lips; polymorphous rash; oedema of hands and feet; 2.5 cm right cervical node
data_table.Investigations: CRP 124; WCC 18.4 with neutrophilia; platelets 540; ALT 78; Hb 96 (microcytic); urine sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Wait until day 10 of illness to confirm coronary artery aneurysm on echocardiography before commencing intravenous immunoglobulin therapy and aspirin antiplatelet therapy together
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for presumed streptococcal toxic shock syndrome while awaiting blood cultures and discontinue if cultures are negative at 48 hours
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kilogram over 10 to 12 hours plus aspirin 30 to 50 mg per kilogram per day in four divided doses initially in hospital
Treat with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg per kilogram daily for three days as first-line monotherapy without intravenous immunoglobulin in routine Kawasaki disease management
Discharge with oral ibuprofen and paediatric outpatient review in three days if the fever persists beyond day 8 of illness with no other planned investigations or interventions today

stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to your paediatric clinic for follow-up of IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) diagnosed three weeks ago by characteristic palpable purpura over the buttocks and lower limbs with mild abdominal pain. He has had no melaena, intussusception or arthritis. The previous review four days ago was unremarkable. Today his mother reports brown-coloured urine in the morning, ankle swelling and a blood pressure recorded at the local pharmacy as 132/86 mmHg. His urinalysis in your rooms shows haematuria 3+, proteinuria 3+ and red cell casts.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 134/88 (>95th centile), RR 18, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Faded purpura on lower limbs; mild bilateral ankle oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 3+, protein 3+; RBC casts; Cr 78 (was 38); albumin 28; urine PCR 380 mg/mmol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase fluid intake and recheck urinalysis and renal function in two weeks with attendance at general practice if proteinuria worsens or new symptoms develop with no other intervention today
Reassure family that haematuria after IgA vasculitis is universal and reviewing the urinalysis in three months is sufficient management without escalation of investigations today
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg per kilogram per day at the next routine general practice visit without specialist nephrology input or escalation of investigations today
Refer urgently to a paediatric nephrologist for renal biopsy assessment and consideration of immunosuppressive therapy alongside renin-angiotensin system blockade for proteinuria
Commence intravenous cyclophosphamide 750 mg per square metre as outpatient therapy in your general practice rooms today for the severe IgA vasculitis nephritic flare currently

stem: A 5-month-old boy is referred to your paediatric inpatient team after a third hospital admission with severe pneumonia, this time with Pneumocystis jirovecii on bronchoalveolar lavage. He had oral candidiasis at 8 weeks, persistent watery diarrhoea since 3 months with documented failure to thrive crossing two major weight centiles downward, and chronic perianal excoriation. His maternal uncle died of overwhelming infection at 7 months. Vaccinations include BCG at birth, with no localised reaction at the BCG site. Lymphocyte counts on previous admissions have been persistently low.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, BP 84/52, RR 56, SpO2 91% on 2 L NP, Temp 38.7
data_table.Examination: Cachectic; oral candidiasis; bibasal crackles; perianal excoriation
data_table.Investigations: Lymphocytes 0.4 (low for age); IgG 1.8 g/L (low); BAL Pneumocystis positive; CXR diffuse interstitial

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral itraconazole prophylaxis alone and arrange routine paediatric outpatient follow-up in six weeks without immunology referral or hospital admission for further investigation
Continue co-trimoxazole, plan rotavirus catch-up vaccination this admission alongside MMR booster at 6 months and discharge once afebrile and feeding without further investigation
Transfuse 10 mL per kilogram of non-irradiated packed red cells for an anticipated drop in haemoglobin during this acute respiratory illness without further immunology consultation today
Reassure the family that recurrent infections are normal at this age and continue routine immunisation schedule including BCG booster at 6 months of age in next month
Avoid live vaccines, place in protective isolation, withhold any non-irradiated blood products and refer urgently to a paediatric immunology centre for SCID confirmation and definitive treatment

stem:
A 9-year-old boy with a diagnosis of asthma attends a routine review at the general practice where you work as a registrar. He has been on budesonide-formoterol 100/6 micrograms two inhalations twice daily as maintenance for the past 12 months. He reports no daytime symptoms over the past three months, no night waking, and full participation in school sport without pre-exercise reliever.

His mother is keen to reduce his medication burden. He has had no oral corticosteroid courses in the past 18 months and no hospital presentations. His inhaler technique with a spacer is excellent and adherence has been confirmed by pharmacy refill data.

data_table.Examination: Weight 30 kg, chest clear, no nasal polyps, no eczema flare
data_table.Investigations: Office spirometry FEV1 105% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.88, bronchodilator response negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his asthma plan?

options.text: Switch to fluticasone propionate 250 micrograms twice daily and review symptoms in 3 months
Continue current dose unchanged for a further 6 months before reassessing step-down options
Cease budesonide-formoterol and prescribe salbutamol 100 micrograms as a reliever only when needed
Switch to montelukast 5 mg orally once daily as maintenance monotherapy and stop inhaled therapy
Reduce maintenance to budesonide-formoterol 100/6 micrograms one inhalation twice daily and review in 3 months

stem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the paediatric emergency department where you are the registrar with two weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 3 kg weight loss. Today she has been vomiting and is drowsy but rousable. Capillary blood glucose reads HIGH on the ward meter. Capillary ketones are 4.8 mmol/L. She weighs 26 kg. Her father describes her as alert but exhausted. She has no significant past history and takes no medications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 32 deep and sighing, Temp 36.5 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes dry, capillary refill 3 seconds, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6)
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, glucose 32 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid management in the first hour?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg intravenously over 30 minutes to correct the acidosis before any further fluid
Sodium chloride 0.9% as a 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes, then commence insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour
Hartmann's solution at maintenance rate alone, without an initial bolus, while awaiting electrolyte results
Sodium chloride 0.45% with 5% dextrose and 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at 1.5 times maintenance from the outset
Sodium chloride 0.9% as a 10 mL/kg bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, then reassess perfusion before further fluids

stem: A 7-month-old boy is brought to the paediatric ward where you are the registrar with eight days of fever to 39.5 degrees C, persistent irritability, and refusal of feeds. He has a maculopapular rash on his trunk and conjunctival injection without exudate. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy and his oral mucosa is unremarkable. His mother reports a brief peeling at the fingertips noted yesterday. He has been treated with two courses of oral amoxicillin without improvement. There is no respiratory distress and no organomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, BP 92/56 mmHg, RR 36, Temp 39.2 degrees C, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: BCG scar site erythematous, mild perineal desquamation, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CRP 162 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, platelets 612 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 88 U/L, sterile pyuria on urinalysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent echocardiography and commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg plus high-dose aspirin
Continue supportive care with paracetamol and reassess after a further 48 hours of observation
Switch to intravenous ceftriaxone for occult bacterial infection and add doxycycline for atypical pathogens
Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse therapy alone for inflammatory vasculitis
Perform a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid culture and commence empirical aciclovir intravenously

subtopic_detail: Severe early jaundice with positive DAT
stem: You are the paediatric registrar covering the postnatal ward. A term male infant born at 39+4 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery is now 28 hours old and clinically jaundiced to the lower abdomen. His mother is blood group O Rh-positive, with anti-c antibodies detected at 28 weeks at a titre of 1:32. Cord blood at delivery showed haemoglobin 138 g/L and direct antiglobulin test positive. The infant is feeding eagerly. Birth weight was 3450 g and weight today is 3320 g. The transcutaneous bilirubin reading is 290 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 bpm, RR 42, Temp 36.9 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, vigorous suck, no hepatosplenomegaly, scleral icterus to mid-trunk
data_table.Investigations: Serum total bilirubin 318 micromol/L, conjugated 8 micromol/L, Hb 132 g/L, reticulocytes 8%, blood group A Rh-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with community midwife follow-up and a repeat bilirubin sample in 24 hours
Commence intensive multi-light phototherapy and prepare for possible exchange transfusion at this level
Commence single-bank conventional phototherapy and recheck the bilirubin at 24 hours
Administer oral phenobarbital 5 mg/kg daily as a hepatic enzyme inducer and avoid phototherapy
Withhold treatment and arrange repeat transcutaneous bilirubin in 6 hours before deciding on therapy

stem: A 6-week-old girl is brought to the emergency department where you are the registrar after a single episode at home where she became limp and pale for around 20 seconds during a feed before returning to her normal state. She has fed and behaved normally since. She was born at 38 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery. There is no fever, no respiratory symptoms, no preceding illness, and no family history of sudden infant death. Examination on arrival is normal. Her parents are very anxious but the child appears completely well on your assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142 bpm, RR 38, Temp 36.8 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, normal tone, anterior fontanelle soft, chest clear, no rash, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood glucose 4.6 mmol/L, paired pre-and-post-ductal saturations both 99%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and commence empirical intravenous antibiotics
Discharge home with shared follow-up by the general practitioner within 24 hours and infant CPR education
Admit for at least 4 hours of monitored observation with paired saturation checks before discharge planning
Arrange outpatient electroencephalography and discharge home pending the test result in 2 weeks
Arrange immediate outpatient 24-hour Holter monitoring and discharge home with cardiology phone advice only

stem: An 8-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with 3 days of coryza and an increasing wheeze. He has taken 60% of his usual feeds over the past 12 hours but is still having normal wet nappies. There is no fever and no history of choking. He was born at 38 weeks gestation and has had three previous episodes of viral wheeze. His father has asthma. On arrival he is alert and pink, with mild subcostal recession and a wet productive cough between feeds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 48, SpO2 91% room air, Temp 36.9
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession; bilateral fine inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheeze; CRT 2s; alert
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab pending; chest X-ray not performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Admit for supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 90% (RCH target) with small-volume oral or nasogastric feeds
Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess clinical response over the next 30 minutes
Commence inhaled fluticasone via spacer and review with the general practitioner in 48 hours
Administer nebulised hypertonic 3% saline three times daily plus a short course of oral prednisolone
Discharge home with oral amoxicillin to cover likely lower respiratory bacterial co-infection

stem: A 2-year-old boy presents to a regional emergency department in the early hours with a barking cough and inspiratory stridor that wakes him from sleep. The cough started 24 hours earlier with rhinorrhoea and a low-grade fever. He has otherwise been well, is fully vaccinated, and has had no choking or drooling. While in the cubicle he is settled on his mother's lap, taking sips of juice with no audible stridor at rest, and his voice sounds hoarse but normal in volume. He has had one previous episode 6 months ago which resolved without treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Barking cough on examination; no stridor at rest; mild intermittent suprasternal tug only when crying; air entry normal bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate management at this point?

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 and prepare for paediatric retrieval team transfer
Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg and observe for until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) before discharge
Reassure the parents and discharge home with humidified air advice and paracetamol as needed
Take a lateral neck radiograph to exclude epiglottitis before initiating any pharmacological treatment
Commence oral amoxicillin and review with the general practitioner the following morning for re-examination

stem: A 4-year-old boy is admitted with 6 days of fever to 39.5, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a polymorphous truncal rash, cracked red lips, a strawberry tongue, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy of 1.8 cm. He received intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg over 12 hours and oral aspirin 5 mg per kg per day starting 36 hours ago. Despite this, his temperature has remained above 38 and his C-reactive protein has not improved on repeat testing. An echocardiogram performed before treatment showed mild dilation of the proximal left main coronary artery. He has no known immunodeficiency.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 26, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 38.7 (post-IVIG)
data_table.Examination: Persistent conjunctival injection; cracked lips; rash fading; cervical node 1.5 cm
data_table.Investigations: CRP 145 (was 180), Hb 92, platelets 480, albumin 28, ALT 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue current aspirin dose and reassess clinically in 48 hours before considering further therapy
Switch aspirin from anti-inflammatory to antiplatelet dosing and continue observation for another 24 hours
Commence intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically targeting toxic shock syndrome and septicaemia
Administer a second dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g per kg and add intravenous methylprednisolone
Switch aspirin to clopidogrel and commence oral prednisolone alone as a steroid-sparing maintenance regimen

stem: A 9-year-old girl with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes presents with 48 hours of polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, and rapid breathing. She is alert with sunken eyes and a dry tongue. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 8 mmol/L, glucose 28 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L. She weighs 30 kg. She has had no recent fluid intake. Her initial 10 mL per kg normal saline bolus has been completed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 134, BP 96/58, RR 36 (Kussmaul), SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Alert; capillary refill 3 seconds; dry mucous membranes; mild abdominal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 28, pH 7.10, HCO3 8, ketones 5.6, K+ 4.2, Na+ 138; BSL on point-of-care confirms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid and insulin plan for the next phase?

options.text: Continue saline boluses at 20 mL per kg per hour until the heart rate normalises, then start insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour
Commence intravenous insulin infusion 0.1 units per kg per hour immediately before any further fluid replacement
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol per kg over 1 hour given the severity of the acidaemia on venous gas
Switch to 5% dextrose with potassium chloride 40 mmol per litre immediately and titrate to capillary blood glucose
Replace a 5 to 7% deficit over 48 hours with 0.9% saline plus potassium and start insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units per kg per hour at 1 hour

stem:
A 5-year-old girl presents with her father to the general practitioner with 8 weeks of large, painful, hard bowel motions occurring once every 5 to 7 days. She has been soiling her underwear with small amounts of soft stool most days. She is otherwise well, fully toilet-trained for urine, and started prep this year. Her diet is varied but limited in fluids.

She has had no abdominal distension since infancy, normal growth, and no delayed passage of meconium. Abdominal examination reveals a palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa with no other findings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with palpable left iliac fossa faecal mass; no perianal abnormality; growth on 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric gastroenterologist for rectal manometry to exclude Hirschsprung disease before any therapy
Recommend dietary fibre, increased fluids, and a daily fruit-juice trial without any laxatives initially
Prescribe a single phosphate enema to disimpact and then review need for ongoing oral laxative therapy
Commence oral macrogol disimpaction regimen with escalating daily doses over 3 to 7 days, then move to a maintenance dose
Start senna 7.5 mg nightly for 6 weeks without disimpaction phase and review at the end of the course

stem:
A 16-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother after the mother found a written plan to take 30 paracetamol tablets the next day, alongside the cached tablets in her bedroom. The young woman is currently calm, articulate, and minimises the plan, saying it was a moment of frustration after an argument. She has been treated for moderate depression by her general practitioner for 4 months with limited response to sertraline 100 mg daily.

She lives with her mother who is supportive; her father has limited contact. She has had two emergency presentations in the past 6 months for superficial cutting; nothing has been ingested today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 110/68, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Composed; mood flat; no thought disorder; HEADSSS reveals social withdrawal and disordered sleep
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; paracetamol level not relevant (no ingestion); urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition plan?

options.text: Discharge home with safety planning, mother as primary supervisor, and outpatient psychology follow-up within 7 days
Refer to school-based counselling and increase sertraline to 150 mg daily without acute admission
Admit only if she expresses ongoing intent within the next 2 hours during repeat interview by the registrar
Discharge under a verbal contract of safety with the mother removing tablets at home and a phone call from CYMHS in 72 hours
Admit to a paediatric ward for safety, urgent child and youth mental health service review, and means restriction at home

stem:
A 22-month-old boy is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by his parents with 36 hours of watery diarrhoea (8 episodes) and 6 episodes of non-bilious vomiting, last vomit 90 minutes ago. He is alert but irritable and refuses solid food, though he accepted 50 mL of water at triage without further vomiting. There has been no blood in the stool, no fever above 38.5, and no travel.

Two children at his childcare centre have similar symptoms. He has had normal wet nappies but fewer in the past 12 hours. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and skin turgor is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 37.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and irritable, dry mouth, no sunken eyes, normal turgor, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; clinical assessment suggests 3 to 5% dehydration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration strategy?

options.text: Trial oral rehydration solution at 50 mL per kg over 4 hours given in small frequent sips with reassessment
Insert a peripheral cannula and infuse 0.9% saline at 100 mL per kg over 6 hours empirically for dehydration
Commence a single intravenous bolus of 20 mL per kg 0.9% saline and recheck electrolytes in 2 hours
Administer ondansetron orodispersible 4 mg and reassess feeding tolerance, then admit overnight irrespective of response
Withhold fluids and food for 6 hours to rest the gut, then trial dilute apple juice as the first rehydration agent

stem:
A 7-year-old boy attends a follow-up appointment with his general practitioner after 6 months on inhaled fluticasone 50 mcg twice daily via spacer. Despite reliable adherence (verified by pharmacy refill records), he has needed his salbutamol reliever on 4 days a week and has been waking with cough twice a week. He has had two short courses of oral prednisolone in the past 3 months but no admissions.

There is no smoking in the household, his inhaler technique was reviewed last visit, and his weight and height are on the 50th centile. He has known house dust mite and grass pollen allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation; spacer technique reviewed and adequate; no eczema today
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; spirometry FEV1 82% predicted at last visit

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his preventer therapy?

options.text: Continue current fluticasone dose and add montelukast 5 mg nightly as a leukotriene receptor antagonist
Increase fluticasone to 100 mcg twice daily and reassess control and inhaler technique in 4 to 6 weeks
Switch fluticasone to budesonide-formoterol as maintenance and reliever therapy (MART) in this age group
Stop fluticasone and trial a short course of oral prednisolone followed by environmental allergen avoidance only
Refer for omalizumab subcutaneous monthly therapy given his allergic phenotype and current symptom burden

stem: A previously well 6-year-old girl was diagnosed with Henoch Schonlein purpura (IgA vasculitis) 10 days ago after a palpable purpuric rash on the lower limbs, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, and bilateral ankle swelling. At initial review her urinalysis was negative, blood pressure was normotensive, and she had no haematuria or proteinuria. She has been managed at home with paracetamol and her family reports the rash is fading. She has returned today for follow-up and her urinalysis today shows blood 3+ and protein 2+. Her blood pressure is 118/78.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 118/78 (>95th centile for age and height), RR 20, SpO2 99%, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Fading purpura on lower limbs; soft non-tender abdomen; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 3+ protein 2+; urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPCR) pending; creatinine 38; albumin 36

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure the family the rash is resolving and review with urinalysis again in 4 weeks at the next scheduled visit
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg without specialist consultation and continue urinalysis weekly at home
Refer urgently to paediatric nephrology for assessment including UPCR, eGFR estimation and consideration of biopsy
Recommend an angiotensin receptor blocker via the general practitioner without specialist nephrology input now
Admit for intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg per kg daily for three days irrespective of biopsy result

stem:
A 14-year-old boy presents to a regional emergency department on day 4 of a sore throat originally treated with phenoxymethylpenicillin by his general practitioner 48 hours ago after a positive throat swab for group A Streptococcus. Over the past 12 hours his throat pain has become severe and predominantly right-sided; he has trouble swallowing his own saliva and his voice has become muffled.

He has no stridor, no drooling whilst sitting upright, and no neck stiffness. On examination, he has trismus opening only 2 cm, deviation of the uvula to the left, and a fluctuant bulge on the right superior tonsillar pole.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 38.6
data_table.Examination: Trismus 2 cm, uvula deviated to the left, fluctuant right superior tonsillar pole; no stridor
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ultrasound shows hypoechoic fluid collection 2.5 cm at right tonsillar pole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Switch from phenoxymethylpenicillin to oral clindamycin and continue review with the general practitioner tomorrow
Arrange contrast-enhanced CT neck to confirm abscess before any drainage despite confirmatory ultrasound findings
Arrange urgent tonsillectomy under general anaesthesia within 24 hours as definitive management in adolescents
Refer urgently for needle aspiration or incision and drainage with intravenous benzylpenicillin and metronidazole
Commence high-dose dexamethasone alone without drainage to reduce swelling and reassess at 24 hours

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the general practitioner with worsening eczema flares for 3 months affecting her flexures, face and trunk. Her parents are applying QV cream once daily but have stopped using hydrocortisone 1% after reading online about steroid concerns. She is itchy enough to wake at night and has new excoriations across the antecubital fossae. There is no oozing, no honey-coloured crusting, and no systemic upset. She is fully vaccinated and is otherwise growing well. There is a strong atopic family history including asthma and allergic rhinitis.

data_table.Vital signs: Apyrexial; growth 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema and lichenification in flexures; excoriations; no impetiginisation; no eyelid swelling
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate skin care plan?

options.text: Continue QV cream only and avoid all topical steroids; trial a hypoallergenic diet for 6 weeks instead
Switch hydrocortisone for a topical calcineurin inhibitor as first-line therapy for paediatric flexural eczema
Wet-wrap a high-potency topical steroid (mometasone furoate) twice daily across all affected areas for 4 weeks
Commence oral antihistamine cetirizine nightly and topical antibiotic mupirocin to all eczematous skin
Educate family on regular emollients with methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% to affected areas once daily for 1 to 2 weeks

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to a general practice clinic with pallor noted by her grandmother and reduced energy at playgroup over 6 weeks. She drinks 800 mL of cow's milk daily, eats limited solids (mainly white bread and pasta), and has no overt blood loss. She was born at term, exclusively breastfed for the first 4 months, and has been gaining weight on the 25th centile track.

She has had no recurrent infections, no jaundice, and there is no family history of haemoglobinopathy. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and palmar creases but no jaundice or hepatosplenomegaly.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no jaundice; soft non-tender abdomen; no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 64 fL, MCH 22 pg, ferritin 5 mcg/L, CRP 4, reticulocytes low; faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Empirical oral antibiotics for occult bacterial infection and recheck full blood count in 4 weeks before iron replacement
Recommend intramuscular iron polymaltose injection given likely poor oral adherence in toddlers under 2 years
Refer urgently to paediatric haematology for bone marrow biopsy and haemoglobinopathy electrophoresis screen
Start oral elemental iron 3 mg per kg daily, reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL daily, and recheck haemoglobin at 6 weeks
Transfuse packed red cells now as a one-off given the symptomatic anaemia, then commence ongoing oral supplementation

stem:
A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with 4 weeks of gradually worsening left groin and knee pain after no specific injury. His parents note that he has started walking with the left foot turned outwards. He has gained 12 kg in the past year; his body mass index is now on the 97th centile. There is no fever, no rash, no morning stiffness, and no other joint involvement.

His mother has type 2 diabetes. On examination, his left leg is held in slight external rotation; passive hip flexion causes obligate external rotation; he can weight-bear with a limp but not stand on the left leg alone without pain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 118/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Left leg externally rotated; obligate external rotation on hip flexion; antalgic limp; no joint effusion of knee
data_table.Investigations: AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis radiographs available; CRP 6, WCC 8.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and outpatient physiotherapy review in 1 week for an irritable hip diagnosis
Recommend a low-impact exercise program with weight loss advice and rheumatology review in 4 weeks
Order a bone scan to characterise the lesion before any orthopaedic referral or weight-bearing restrictions
Aspirate the hip under ultrasound guidance to exclude septic arthritis before further definitive imaging or referral
Make the patient strictly non-weight-bearing, refer for urgent orthopaedic review with AP and frog-leg lateral radiographs

stem:
A term-born baby boy is 72 hours old and reviewed on the postnatal ward by the paediatric registrar after the midwife noticed visible jaundice extending to the trunk. He is breastfed every 2 to 3 hours, has had appropriate wet nappies and has lost 6% of birth weight. He was born at 39+2 weeks, the pregnancy was uncomplicated and the mother is O Rh positive.

The baby is alert, feeds vigorously, and has no organomegaly or pallor. There is no family history of haemolytic anaemia. His transcutaneous bilirubinometer reading is 285 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.9
data_table.Examination: Alert, jaundice to mid-trunk, no hepatosplenomegaly, vigorous feeding
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 295 micromol/L (transcutaneous 285); DAT negative; blood group O+; FBC normal; reticulocytes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy with a fibre-optic blanket or bank of lights and recheck serum bilirubin in 6 to 12 hours
Recommend supplementary formula feeding to accelerate clearance and recheck bilirubin in 24 hours after observation
Discharge home with sunlight exposure advice and review with the general practitioner in 48 to 72 hours after discharge
Arrange exchange transfusion within 24 hours regardless of the rate of bilirubin rise and clinical response observed
Withhold any treatment and repeat serum bilirubin in 24 hours assuming physiological jaundice in a healthy infant

stem:
A previously well 5-month-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department by her parents with 24 hours of fever to 39 and one episode of vomiting. She is feeding 70% of normal and has decreased wet nappies overnight. She has no rash, no cough, no diarrhoea, no obvious focus on examination, and her ears, throat and chest are clear.

She has not received antibiotics recently. A clean catch urine collected by the midwife shows leucocyte esterase 3+ and nitrites 2+ on dipstick; microscopy shows pyuria. Blood cultures and urine culture have been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 42, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 39.1
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; no rash; soft abdomen; clear chest; ears normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick LE 3+ nitrites 2+; microscopy pyuria and gram-negative rods; WCC 19; CRP 75; blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg per kg twice daily for 5 days with general practitioner review in 48 hours after discharge
Admit for intravenous gentamicin and intravenous benzylpenicillin or ampicillin pending sensitivities and clinical response
Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy for 7 days irrespective of culture results once initial blood culture is drawn
Oral trimethoprim for 7 days with renal ultrasound at 6 weeks if symptoms persist beyond 5 days of therapy
Oral nitrofurantoin for 5 days, encouraging increased fluid intake and follow-up urine culture in 1 week

stem: A 3-month-old boy with bronchiolitis admitted 18 hours ago to a metropolitan paediatric ward has deteriorated. He has been on high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L per kg per minute with FiO2 0.4 for 6 hours. Despite this his work of breathing has increased with marked subcostal and intercostal recession; he is now only intermittently rousable. His latest capillary blood gas shows pH 7.20, pCO2 9.1 kPa, HCO3 22 mmol/L, lactate 2.4 mmol/L. He is being suctioned hourly and has stopped feeding orally. The treating registrar phones the local paediatric intensive care service.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188, RR 72, SpO2 92% on HFNC FiO2 0.4, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession; only intermittently rousable; sluggish capillary refill 3s
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.20 pCO2 9.1 kPa HCO3 22 lactate 2.4; chest X-ray shows hyperinflation with peri-hilar streaking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase HFNC flow to 3 L per kg per minute and continue current FiO2 with reassessment in 60 minutes before any other escalation
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back for 30 minutes before any further respiratory support escalation step
Prepare for intubation and arrange paediatric intensive care retrieval team transfer to a tertiary paediatric ICU
Commence non-invasive bilevel ventilation locally and continue oral feeds while awaiting tertiary paediatric ICU advice
Administer intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg per kg and start broad-spectrum antibiotics empirically for bacterial superinfection

subtopic_detail: Mandatory reporting of suspected child abuse
stem:
A 9-month-old boy presents with a 24-hour history of right thigh swelling. His mother reports that he fell from a low couch. He is not yet walking or pulling to stand and has had no previous fractures. On examination, there is bruising over the thigh, mild swelling, and pain on movement. Imaging shows a spiral fracture of the right femoral shaft.

The infant also has a 2 cm bruise on the left buttock and a torn frenulum. There is no other history offered, no medical illness, and the mother appears anxious but engaged. The treating intern is unsure what to do next.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 90/56, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Thigh swelling, bruising over thigh and buttock, torn frenulum, no other injuries on initial inspection
data_table.Investigations: Plain radiograph right femur: spiral fracture mid-shaft; FBC, coags, LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the mother that accidental fractures are common in this age group and discharge with orthopaedic follow-up
Request a metabolic bone disease workup before initiating any safeguarding referral or specialist child protection assessment
Discuss the fracture with the family for further explanation and consider safeguarding only if no plausible account emerges
Notify child protection as mandated reporter and admit for skeletal survey, ophthalmology fundoscopy and child protection team consult
Apply a thomas splint, admit under orthopaedics for fracture management and arrange social work follow-up at discharge

stem:
A 3-week-old male infant is recalled to a tertiary paediatric centre after a positive newborn screening test for cystic fibrosis. He was born at term, was breastfed within the first hour and is now feeding well with appropriate weight gain. He has no respiratory symptoms, no steatorrhoea and no failure to thrive at this point. His parents are not known to each other to be carriers.

Genetic testing on the newborn screening dried blood spot shows two CFTR mutations: F508del and a class V splice-site mutation. The pulmonary nurse phones the on-call paediatric registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 42, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Alert, feeding well, no respiratory distress, no abdominal distension, normal anal sphincter tone
data_table.Investigations: Immunoreactive trypsinogen elevated x2 screens; CFTR genotype F508del and class V splice-site mutation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in confirming and initiating management?

options.text: Reassure parents that compound heterozygous mutations are usually mild and review with the general practitioner in 6 months
Arrange faecal elastase only and start pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy empirically without further confirmatory testing
Refer to the geneticist alone for counselling about carrier risk and defer all CF treatment until symptoms emerge later
Reassure that two mutations meet diagnostic criteria; commence azithromycin prophylaxis and salt supplementation immediately
Refer to the tertiary paediatric CF service for confirmatory sweat chloride testing, formal multidisciplinary review and structured surveillance

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to a general practitioner by her mother with 6 weeks of progressive patchy hair loss on the scalp. The child attends a primary school where several other children have similar findings. On examination there is a 3 by 4 cm area of broken hair shafts, mild scaling, and a slightly tender posterior occipital lymph node.

There is no kerion formation, no honey-coloured crusting, and no widespread inflammation. She is otherwise well, fully vaccinated and growing along the 50th centile. She has no known immunodeficiency or recent antibiotic use.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Patchy alopecia 3 by 4 cm with broken hairs and fine scale; tender occipital lymph node; no kerion
data_table.Investigations: Mycology skin scraping and plucked hair sample sent; KOH preparation pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Commence oral griseofulvin or terbinafine and add an antifungal shampoo to reduce household spread, awaiting mycology
Apply topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for 6 weeks and recommend avoiding sharing brushes and pillows in the household
Prescribe oral cefalexin for 10 days for likely bacterial superinfection of the scalp before any antifungal therapy
Recommend short-course oral prednisolone alongside topical betamethasone to suppress inflammation as initial measures
Reassure the family the condition is self-limiting and review in 8 weeks with no specific treatment beyond emollient

stem:
An 8-year-old girl is brought by her parents to a general practitioner with 6 weeks of progressively worsening headaches. The headaches initially occurred once a week and now occur daily. They are worse in the morning and on coughing or straining, and she has vomited (without nausea) on three mornings this week. She has been clumsier than usual on the netball court.

There is no fever, no neck stiffness and no rash. On examination she has a mild right-sided lower facial weakness and dysmetria of the right hand. Her family history includes migraine in her mother.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: Mild right facial weakness; right dysmetria; gait slightly wide-based; fundi reveal blurred disc margins
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence amitriptyline 10 mg nightly as migraine prophylaxis and review at the general practice clinic in 4 weeks
Refer urgently for same-day paediatric assessment with neuroimaging (preferably MRI) to evaluate for intracranial pathology
Order an outpatient MRI brain and review the imaging in 7 to 10 days as next available radiology appointment
Trial sumatriptan nasal spray during the next acute episode and review in the migraine clinic over coming weeks
Arrange lumbar puncture today before any imaging to measure opening pressure and exclude meningitis or pseudotumour cerebri

stem: A 14-month-old girl is brought to a regional emergency department 8 minutes after eating her first taste of peanut butter at home. Her mother describes immediate facial flushing and lip swelling, then audible wheeze and one episode of vomiting in the car. The child has eczema and a family history of asthma but no previous food reaction. She weighs 10 kg. On arrival she is distressed, has generalised urticaria, peri-oral oedema, and audible expiratory wheeze with mild intercostal recession. She is alert and crying.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 44, SpO2 94% room air, BP 80/45, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria; peri-oral oedema without tongue swelling; bilateral wheeze; CRT 3s; alert
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; allergy testing arranged out-patient after stabilisation

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Oral cetirizine 5 mg with planned clinical reassessment for any escalation in 30 minutes
Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as a bolus while preparing nebulised salbutamol therapy
Intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg of 1:1000 into the anterolateral mid-thigh and reassess promptly
Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.15 mg with a concurrent intravenous bolus of 20 mL/kg normal saline
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via mask with oxygen 6 L/min before any parenteral therapy

stem:
An 18-month-old girl is referred to a paediatric clinic by her general practitioner because her weight has crossed from the 50th centile at 6 months to below the 10th centile, while her height and head circumference have remained on the 25th centile. She walks well, says 10 words, and has reached her 18-month milestones. Her appetite has decreased and she now refuses bread, cereal, and pasta after several episodes of bloating.

Stools are bulky and pale 3 to 4 times per day. There is no history of vomiting, diarrhoeal illness, or recurrent infection. The family is well housed and food secure.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Thin child with mild abdominal distension; muscle bulk reduced in buttocks and thighs; no organomegaly; no rash; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart: weight crossed two major centiles down; height and head on track

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line investigation panel?

options.text: Coeliac screen with tissue transglutaminase IgA plus total IgA, FBC, ferritin, UEC, TSH, and urine culture
Bone age radiograph, insulin-like growth factor 1, growth hormone provocation testing, and karyotype
Urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to exclude an intracranial space-occupying lesion
Chromosomal microarray and Fragile X analysis as first-line for syndromic short stature
Referral to a paediatric dietitian for food diary and high-energy supplement plan without further testing

stem:
A 9-month-old previously well boy is brought to the emergency department with 12 hours of intermittent crying episodes during which he draws his knees to his chest and appears pale, followed by quiet drowsy periods. His mother reports one passage of stool that looked like raspberry jam this morning and two episodes of bilious vomiting. He has not fed since lunchtime.

On examination he is lethargic but rousable, with a sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant. There is no peritonitis. He weighs 9 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 36, SpO2 98% room air, BP 90/55, Temp 37.2
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable; CRT 3 s; soft abdomen with a sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass; no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Bedside USS: target sign in the right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous fluid resuscitation and proceed to image-guided air enema reduction with surgical standby
Plan urgent laparotomy as first-line management because of bilious vomiting and the abdominal mass
Administer ondansetron and observe in the short stay unit with serial abdominal examinations
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone for likely bacterial gastroenteritis and reassess in 6 hours
Perform a contrast meal and follow through study to confirm the diagnosis prior to definitive therapy

stem: A 4-day-old term boy is referred by the midwife after his mother noticed two episodes of green vomit overnight. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, passed meconium at 12 hours, and had been breastfeeding well. On arrival to the neonatal review clinic he is alert and pink but mildly distressed. His abdomen is soft and minimally distended without peritonism. Capillary refill is 2 seconds and his vital signs are normal for age.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 48, SpO2 98% room air, Temp 36.8, BP 70/40
data_table.Examination: Alert and pink; mild abdominal distension; soft non-tender abdomen; normally placed anus; passing meconium
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas: pH 7.36, lactate 1.6; FBC and UEC normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain supine abdominal radiograph and observe with hourly abdominal examinations in the paediatric unit
Urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study to exclude malrotation with midgut volvulus
Trial of a thickened amino acid based formula and dietitian review for cow's milk protein allergy
Commence ondansetron and IV maintenance fluids and reassess in 12 hours in the short stay unit
Abdominal ultrasound to assess the superior mesenteric artery and vein relationship and bowel perfusion

stem:
An 11-year-old girl with a 2-year history of migraine without aura attends a paediatric review with her mother. Headaches occur 4 to 5 times per month, last 6 hours each, and force her to lie down in a dark room. She has missed 6 days of school in the last term. Her abortive regimen is paracetamol with ibuprofen, taken at headache onset, which only partially helps.

She uses no triptans. There are no red flags on history or examination. Her mother has migraine. She is well in herself and her growth and development are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 110/68, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Normal general and neurological examination; no papilloedema; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Not performed; headache diary kept by mother showing 4 to 5 attacks per month

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue paracetamol and ibuprofen for acute attacks and review with a headache diary in 6 months
Refer for urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before any prophylactic agent is started
Commence amitriptyline 25 mg nocte and titrate the dose at 4 week intervals as tolerated
Prescribe oral sumatriptan as routine PRN abortive therapy without any prophylactic medication
Commence pizotifen 0.5 mg nocte, optimise sleep, hydration, screen time, and review in 8 weeks

stem: A 5-year-old previously well girl is brought to the emergency department after her parents noticed widespread pinpoint red spots and bruising for 24 hours. Two weeks ago she had a self-limiting febrile viral illness. There has been no nose bleed, no mucosal bleeding, and no haematuria. She is otherwise well and meeting milestones. On examination she is afebrile and well-appearing with diffuse petechiae over her trunk and limbs, scattered bruises, and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Her platelet count is 8 x10^9/L with normal white cells, normal haemoglobin, and a normal blood film aside from large platelets.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 36.7, BP 100/62
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing; widespread petechiae and bruises; no mucosal bleeding; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 125, WCC 7.5, platelets 8 x10^9/L; blood film shows large platelets, otherwise normal; CRP 4

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.8 g/kg as a single dose to raise the platelet count rapidly
Start oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days with a planned haematology review at the end of the course
Perform an urgent bone marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude acute leukaemia before any therapy
Observe with bleeding precautions, avoid contact sports, and review the next day with platelet count and clinical assessment
Transfuse a single adult unit of pooled platelets to raise the count above 50 x10^9/L for safety

stem:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department 6 hours after falling from a horse onto his head. He vomited twice in transit and his Glasgow Coma Scale was 14 on arrival. Over the next 90 minutes his GCS has dropped to 11 with reduced verbal response and localising to pain. His right pupil is 4 mm and sluggish, while the left is 3 mm and reactive.

Blood pressure has risen from 110/65 to 140/55 and heart rate has fallen from 92 to 50. He has not yet been imaged. The retrieval team estimates 60 minutes to the nearest paediatric neurosurgical centre.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 50, RR 14 irregular, SpO2 97% on 6 L mask, BP 140/55, Temp 36.7
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5); right pupil 4 mm sluggish, left 3 mm reactive; localising to pain; no focal limb weakness yet
data_table.Investigations: CT head not yet performed; FBC, UEC, coags pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation, head-up 30 degrees, hypertonic saline 3 percent bolus, urgent CT head and neurosurgery transfer
Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude a treatable cause of altered conscious state before transfer
Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone and dexamethasone for likely bacterial meningitis after recent trauma
Hyperventilate to a target PaCO2 of 25 mmHg as the primary measure to lower intracranial pressure
Administer intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg via a peripheral line without securing the airway first

stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department 2 hours after his mother found him with an open bottle of her ferrous sulfate 325 mg tablets. She estimates 10 tablets may be missing, giving an exposure of approximately 65 mg/kg of elemental iron. He has vomited twice and passed one loose grey-coloured stool. He is alert and crying. He weighs 12 kg. An abdominal radiograph shows several radio-opaque tablets in the upper gastrointestinal tract.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, BP 100/65, Temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Alert and crying; mildly distressed; soft tender epigastrium; CRT 2 s; no shock
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray: tablets visible in stomach; serum iron and venous gas sent at 4 hours post ingestion; UEC, FBC, LFTs pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally as soon as airway is protected for gastrointestinal decontamination
Administer empirical intravenous deferoxamine 15 mg/kg/hour before serum iron results are available
Perform orogastric lavage with warm saline to clear the residual iron tablets from the stomach immediately
Discharge home with safety advice because vomiting is a sign of likely self-decontamination and recovery
Commence polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation and serum iron at 4 hours, with deferoxamine if iron is above 90 micromol/L

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to a paediatric clinic by his mother who has noticed a firm abdominal mass while bathing him over the last 2 weeks. She also reports irritability, weight loss, and easy bruising of the eyelids that she initially attributed to a fall. He has been febrile intermittently. On examination he is pale and miserable with a firm fixed left upper abdominal mass that crosses the midline, periorbital ecchymoses without trauma, and blanching subcutaneous nodules. His blood pressure is 100/65. Urinary catecholamines are elevated. An MIBG scan shows tracer avidity in the primary mass and in skull lesions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 100/65, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 37.6, weight 14 kg (50th centile previously, now 25th)
data_table.Examination: Pale and miserable; firm fixed left upper abdominal mass crossing midline; periorbital ecchymoses; blanching subcutaneous nodules
data_table.Investigations: Urinary catecholamines elevated; MIBG: tracer avidity in primary mass and skull lesions; FBC: pancytopenia

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Plan urgent nephrectomy as definitive management for the abdominal mass and submit specimen for histology
Commence oral corticosteroids as a trial for likely autoimmune cytopenia with consequent ecchymoses
Reassure the family that periorbital ecchymoses are likely traumatic and review again in 4 weeks
Refer urgently to paediatric oncology for tissue diagnosis, full staging and risk-adapted multidisciplinary management
Plan a renal biopsy under ultrasound guidance to confirm Wilms tumour before any further intervention

stem: A 7-year-old boy is referred to the paediatric emergency department with two weeks of polyuria, polydipsia, and 4 kg weight loss. Today he developed vomiting, abdominal pain, and laboured breathing. He weighs 22 kg. He is alert, oriented, with deep sighing respirations and acetone breath. He has not previously been diagnosed with diabetes and has no shock features clinically, though he is moderately dehydrated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 98% room air, BP 98/62, Temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Kussmaul breathing; dry mucous membranes; CRT 2s; alert (GCS 15); no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28.4 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L; venous pH 7.10, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, urea 9.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid management?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes then reassess for further boluses
Intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 10 mL/kg over 30 minutes then maintenance plus deficit replacement over 48 hours
Intravenous Hartmann solution 30 mL/kg over an hour with intravenous insulin started immediately at induction
Oral rehydration solution titrated to thirst with bedside ketone reassessment every two hours before any insulin
Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes given the venous pH below 7.15 with normal saline alongside

stem: A 2-year-old girl presents to a metropolitan emergency department at 02:00 with a 12-hour history of coryza and a barking cough. Over the last hour she has developed audible inspiratory stridor at rest and is visibly distressed. She weighs 14 kg and has no past medical history. Her vaccinations are up to date. She has not yet received any treatment in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148, RR 38, SpO2 95% room air, Temp 37.8
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest; suprasternal and intercostal recession; tracheal tug; agitated but rousable
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; no imaging or bloods required

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose with reassessment of stridor severity after 30 minutes
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with concurrent oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and 3 hours (RCH minimum) observation
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back to back with ipratropium 250 micrograms then admission to short-stay unit
Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg plus immediate ENT review with airway plan for theatre intubation
Humidified oxygen via head box with a 30 minute trial of mist therapy before any pharmacological treatment

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with a 3-day palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and lower limbs, intermittent crampy abdominal pain, and an acutely swollen painful left knee. He had a coryzal illness two weeks ago. Today his urinalysis shows 1+ blood and no protein. His blood pressure is normal and his renal function is preserved. The family lives 90 minutes from the nearest paediatric centre and asks whether they need to remain admitted. The diagnosis has been discussed with the family.

data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura on lower limbs and buttocks; tender left knee with effusion; soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 1+, protein nil; Cr 38 micromol/L; FBC normal; platelets 312 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan for renal involvement?

options.text: Urine dipstick and blood pressure measurement weekly for one month then monthly to 6 months and at 12 months
Renal ultrasound now followed by routine paediatrician review in 6 weeks with paired urea and electrolytes
Discharge with general practitioner urinalysis once at 4 weeks unless rash, joint, or abdominal symptoms recur
Empirical oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 2 weeks plus weekly urinalysis until rash resolves then discharge
Urgent paediatric nephrology referral and percutaneous renal biopsy within 2 weeks regardless of progression

stem: A 3-year-old girl presents to her general practice with 36 hours of left ear pain and fever to 38.4. She has had two previous self-limiting episodes of similar pain. She is otherwise well, eating and drinking, and clinically not toxic. Otoscopy shows a bulging, immobile, opaque red left tympanic membrane without perforation, with normal contralateral findings. She lives in metropolitan Sydney and has no chronic conditions. She is not from an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander background.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, Temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Left TM bulging, immobile, opaque, red; no perforation or discharge; right TM normal
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; no swabs or imaging

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4 hours plus oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days starting today
Analgesia alone with paracetamol or ibuprofen and parental review in 48 hours if there is no clinical improvement
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days and topical ciprofloxacin drops to the affected ear
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days with intranasal decongestants to reduce middle ear inflammation rapidly
Urgent ENT review and tympanocentesis to obtain middle ear fluid for microbiology and targeted therapy choice

stem: An 18-month-old previously well boy presents after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting 18 minutes. The seizure terminated with intramuscular midazolam given by paramedics. He has a temperature of 39.1 and rhinorrhoea. He has fully regained his baseline neurological status over the past 2 hours. He has had one previous brief simple febrile seizure 4 months ago. Examination today shows no focal neurology, soft fontanelle, no neck stiffness, and no rash. He is feeding and interactive on the ward.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, BP 92/56, Temp 39.1
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive; soft fontanelle; no neck stiffness; no rash; no focal neurology; clear chest
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.8 mmol/L; venous gas normal; FBC and UEC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate further investigation pathway?

options.text: Urgent CT brain followed by lumbar puncture and electroencephalogram performed during the same admission today
Identify and treat the febrile source, observe for several hours, and discharge with safety-net advice if returned to baseline
Lumbar puncture in all children under 24 months with any febrile seizure to exclude meningitis or encephalitis
Outpatient MRI brain plus electroencephalogram in 4 weeks and commence prophylactic sodium valproate today
Admit to paediatric ICU for continuous EEG monitoring and 48 hours of intravenous antiepileptic loading therapy

stem: A 5-month-old previously well infant is admitted with a 3-day history of coryza, cough, and progressively worsening work of breathing. She weighs 7 kg. Standard low-flow nasal oxygen at 2 L/min over the past 2 hours has been insufficient to keep saturations stable above 92 percent and feeds have stopped. She remains alert and the bedside nurse asks for your guidance on the next step. The respiratory consultant has been notified. She has no congenital heart disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 90% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, Temp 37.6
data_table.Examination: Moderate intercostal and subcostal recession; tracheal tug; widespread expiratory wheeze with bilateral crackles; alert but tiring
data_table.Investigations: Clinical diagnosis; CXR not required routinely; nasopharyngeal swab pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent 4-hourly with 100 percent oxygen via Hudson mask
Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back and reassess response after the third dose has been administered
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh and prepare for emergent intubation now
Start high-flow humidified nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min FiO2 titrated to keep saturations above 92 percent
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days and continue current oxygen support without further escalation

stem:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to your general practice with 8 months of infrequent, hard, painful bowel motions every 5 to 7 days, soiling episodes 3 days per week with overflow incontinence, and intermittent abdominal pain. On examination her abdomen is soft with a palpable suprapubic faecal mass and her bottom is fissured externally. Her growth is on the 50th centile.

There are no red flags for organic disease and her parents are anxious about a recent school review. Toilet training was uneventful and there has been no recent stressor.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 92/58, Temp 36.6, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Palpable suprapubic faecal mass; perianal fissure visible; normal lower limb neurology; normal sacral spine; thyroid clinically normal
data_table.Investigations: No further investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery now for outpatient anorectal manometry and possible Hirschsprung biopsy work-up
Recommend daily lactulose 5 mL after meals plus a high-fibre diet and weekly bowel diary review
Prescribe stimulant senna 7.5 mg daily indefinitely with no disimpaction phase or behavioural toileting plan
Schedule a sodium phosphate enema cycle weekly for 4 weeks in clinic before commencing oral therapy plans
Commence escalating macrogol disimpaction regimen over 3 to 7 days with maintenance dosing and behavioural toileting plan

subtopic_detail: Neonatal hypoglycaemia screening in infant of diabetic mother
stem: A term male infant has just been born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks to a mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes who was on a basal-bolus regimen requiring 76 units per day at term. Birth weight is 4380 g (above 90th centile). Apgars are 9 and 9 and the baby has fed briefly at the breast within 30 minutes of birth and is now asleep in skin-to-skin contact with mother. He is pink, well perfused, and asymptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 46, SpO2 98% in air, axillary T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Pink, alert when handled, normal tone, no jitteriness, no cyanosis, no respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed since delivery 35 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this infant's management?

options.text: Check a true blood glucose at 2 hours of age after the second feed, before further feeding, and act on a threshold of 2.6 mmol/L
Defer all glucose testing until 6 hours of age provided the baby remains asymptomatic and feeds three-hourly with no jitteriness
Check a true blood glucose immediately and again at 4 hours, treating any reading below 3.3 mmol/L with intravenous dextrose
Give 200 mg/kg of 40 percent buccal dextrose gel routinely at one hour of age regardless of the screening glucose value
Admit to special care nursery now for prophylactic 10 percent dextrose infusion at 60 mL/kg/day without further bedside glucose testing

subtopic_detail: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis diagnostic pathway
stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy presents with three days of progressively forceful non-bilious vomiting that now occurs after every breastfeed and reaches the foot of the cot. He remains hungry and feeds eagerly after vomiting. He has lost 200 g since birth and last wet his nappy 8 hours ago. His mother had similar surgery as an infant. On examination he is alert with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and you palpate a firm mobile mass in the right upper quadrant during a test feed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 38, SpO2 99% air, T 36.7, weight 3.9 kg
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, CRT 3s, no abdominal distension, visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis after test feed, palpable olive RUQ
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.52, HCO3 33 mmol/L, Cl 88 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, Na 134 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound measuring pyloric muscle thickness and channel length against accepted paediatric thresholds
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study with barium swallow looking for a string sign at the pylorus
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy under general anaesthesia to visualise the pyloric channel and exclude mucosal pathology
Plain abdominal radiograph in supine and erect projections to identify the caterpillar sign and dilated stomach
Repeat test feed observation over 24 hours of inpatient admission with serial weight checks before any imaging

stem:
A 9-month-old previously well girl presents with 14 hours of episodic inconsolable screaming and drawing knees up, occurring every 20 minutes between which she is pale and listless. She vomited twice (one episode bile-stained) and passed dark red jelly-like stool in the nappy two hours ago. She is hydrated and alert between episodes, with a tender sausage-shaped mass palpable in the right upper quadrant.

There is no peritonism and no distension. Ultrasound performed in the emergency department shows a target sign in the right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 144, RR 28, SpO2 99% air, BP 92/58, T 36.9, weight 8.5 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert between paroxysms, soft non-distended abdomen, palpable RUQ mass, no peritonism, redcurrant jelly stool on PR
data_table.Investigations: USS: target sign RUQ, no free fluid, normal blood flow on Doppler. FBC normal, electrolytes normal, lactate 1.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and metronidazole then re-evaluate in 4 hours to see whether the paroxysms settle
Immediate laparotomy with manual reduction in theatre without any prior attempt at radiological reduction in the department
Barium contrast enema reduction in the radiology department with the family in the room throughout the procedure
Bowel rest with nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluids for 24 hours awaiting spontaneous resolution before reimaging
Pneumatic (air contrast) reduction under fluoroscopic guidance with paediatric surgical team scrubbed for immediate laparotomy

subtopic_detail: Cystic fibrosis newborn screening positive workup
stem: A 4-week-old boy is referred by the state newborn bloodspot screening program. His day-3 immunoreactive trypsinogen was 122 micrograms per litre (well above the 99th centile cutoff of 99). Reflex molecular testing on the same bloodspot identified a single F508del CFTR variant. He was born at term, fed well from birth, and his parents are both healthy with no family history of cystic fibrosis. Examination today is unremarkable with appropriate weight gain.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 38, SpO2 99% air, T 36.7, weight 4.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Pink, well perfused, no respiratory distress, no nasal polyps, soft abdomen, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Newborn screen: IRT 122 micrograms/L (cutoff 99), single F508del heterozygote on reflex panel
data_table.Medications: Vitamin K at birth, breastfed exclusively

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in this infant's diagnostic workup?

options.text: Start oral pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy and fat-soluble vitamin supplementation empirically while awaiting further testing
