Full extended CFTR gene sequencing performed immediately, deferring all sweat chloride testing until the molecular results return
Reassure the parents that single-variant heterozygotes are healthy carriers and discharge without further testing
High-resolution chest computed tomography to assess for early bronchiectasis before any diagnostic biochemistry
Sweat chloride testing at a specialist cystic fibrosis centre using pilocarpine iontophoresis with paired bilateral collections

subtopic_detail: SUDI prevention safe sleep counselling for parents
stem: A 6-week-old healthy term infant attends with her parents for a routine immunisation visit. The parents are tired and report that the baby sleeps best on her tummy on the parental bed, swaddled with a soft cot bumper around her. The father smokes outside but not in the house. Mother breastfeeds at night and occasionally falls asleep with the baby on the couch. Both parents are well, the household has no siblings, and the family lives in a 2-bedroom apartment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 38, SpO2 99% air, T 36.6, weight 5.1 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Pink, well, normal tone, normal cardiorespiratory examination, no concerning features
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated today
data_table.Medications: Vitamin D 400 IU daily (breastfed); routine vaccines today

lead_in: Which counselling point will most reduce this infant's risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy?

options.text: Continue tummy sleeping but only on a firm mattress with a thin sheet and remove the cot bumper from the sleep surface
Advise sleeping with the baby in the parents' bed as breastfeeding is easier and direct contact reduces SUDI risk in young infants
Recommend the father quit smoking entirely as smoke residue on clothing is the most modifiable SUDI risk in this family
Place the baby on her back to sleep every sleep, on her own safe sleep surface in the parents' room for at least the first 6 months
Use a wedge or anti-roll positioner to keep the baby on her side during sleep as this is the safest alternative to back sleeping

subtopic_detail: Paediatric limp Kocher discrimination septic arthritis transient synovitis
stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with 36 hours of limp affecting the right leg. She had a coryzal illness one week ago. She is alert and walking but refuses to bear full weight on the right side. She is mildly distressed only when the right hip is examined; passive log roll provokes pain. There is no joint swelling or warmth, and no obvious limb deformity. She is tolerating oral fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99% air, BP 100/62, T 38.6, weight 16.8 kg
data_table.Examination: Restricted internal rotation right hip, pain with log roll, no effusion or warmth at knee or ankle, no spinal tenderness, distal neurovascular intact
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 28 mg/L, ESR 42 mm/h; X-ray hip and pelvis normal; bedside ultrasound shows 4 mm right hip effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia and review in 48 to 72 hours, presuming transient synovitis given the recent viral illness and the limited hip effusion
Trial 48 hours of bed rest with ibuprofen 10 mg/kg three times daily and reassess all Kocher criteria including repeat inflammatory markers
Request an urgent MRI of the right hip and spine before any joint aspiration or commencement of empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy
Commence empiric oral cefalexin and arrange outpatient orthopaedic review in the next available clinic within 1 week
Admit for urgent ultrasound-guided hip aspiration in theatre with paediatric orthopaedics and IV flucloxacillin after fluid sampling

subtopic_detail: Bacterial tracheitis recognition in croup that fails to respond to adrenaline
stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to ED with worsening 'croup'. He had 3 days of viral upper respiratory illness with mild barking cough, then today rapidly deteriorated with high fever, severe stridor at rest, copious thick yellow secretions and a hoarse voice. He has had no benefit from two doses of nebulised adrenaline (5 mL of 1:1000) given 30 minutes apart and 0.6 mg/kg oral dexamethasone given on arrival. He is now sitting forward, drooling, looking toxic and frightened. His parents have not refused any care.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, RR 44, SpO2 90% on 2 L/min nasal prongs, BP 96/56, T 39.5, weight 18 kg
data_table.Examination: Toxic-looking, sitting forward, biphasic stridor, suprasternal and intercostal recession, hoarse voice, no rash, no obvious foreign body, copious purulent secretions
data_table.Investigations: Not yet - prioritising airway
data_table.Medications: Two doses nebulised adrenaline, oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, paracetamol given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000 and a second dose of dexamethasone, then reassess in 30 minutes for response
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray to look for a thumb-print sign of epiglottitis or steeple sign of croup before any airway intervention
Perform an awake nasendoscopy at the bedside to inspect the supraglottis for swollen cherry-red epiglottis and exclude epiglottitis
Call anaesthesia, ENT and intensive care for theatre intubation, then send tracheal cultures and start intravenous flucloxacillin plus ceftriaxone
Administer high-flow nasal oxygen at 2 litres per kilogram per minute and observe for 1 hour to allow steroid effect before considering intubation

subtopic_detail: Paediatric sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis acute management
stem: An 8-year-old boy with homozygous HbSS sickle cell disease presents to ED with 6 hours of severe bilateral lower limb and back pain after a cold swimming session at school. His mother gave him paracetamol and ibuprofen at home with minimal effect. He has previously had three admissions for vaso-occlusive crises and is on regular hydroxycarbamide plus penicillin prophylaxis. He has no fever, cough or breathlessness. He scores his pain 9 of 10. He is alert and orientated, well perfused, with no focal neurology and clear chest examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, RR 24, SpO2 97% air, BP 108/64, T 36.8, weight 28 kg
data_table.Examination: Distressed with pain, tender thighs and lumbar region, no joint effusion, normal cardiorespiratory examination, no focal neurology, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (baseline 80), reticulocyte 8 percent, WCC 12.4 (baseline 10), platelets 360, CRP 6 mg/L; venous gas pH 7.39, lactate 1.4
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol and ibuprofen at home; usually hydroxycarbamide 20 mg/kg/day, phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg BD

lead_in: Within the first hour, what is the most appropriate analgesic and supportive plan?

options.text: Continue oral paracetamol and ibuprofen, then add oral oxycodone 0.1 mg/kg and reassess in 60 minutes after fluids and rest in a quiet bay
Intranasal fentanyl while siting an intravenous cannula, then commence intravenous morphine titration with maintenance fluids and frequent reassessment
Arrange urgent exchange transfusion through the haematology service to reduce HbS percentage and abort the vaso-occlusive crisis immediately
Bolus 20 mL/kg of 0.9 percent sodium chloride to suppress sickling and reassess pain after rapid fluid loading is complete
Administer intramuscular pethidine 1 mg/kg as a single dose to settle the pain rapidly while a cannula is being placed for fluids

subtopic_detail: Pertussis in young infant antibiotic choice
stem: A 5-week-old previously well girl presents with a 7-day history of coryza followed by paroxysms of coughing ending in cyanotic spells and post-tussive vomiting. She has had no inspiratory whoop. Her older brother had a persistent cough for several weeks. She has had no immunisations yet as she is approaching her 6-week vaccinations. She is feeding poorly between paroxysms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 92 percent room air during paroxysm, T 36.9, weight 4.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival haemorrhages, mild subcostal recession, otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WCC 26 with lymphocytosis 18; pertussis PCR sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?

options.text: Inhaled salbutamol via spacer every 4 hours and oral prednisolone for 3 days to reduce inflammation
Discharge home with reassurance as antibiotics do not alter the clinical course of pertussis
Admit and commence oral azithromycin 10 mg per kg daily for 5 days with cardiorespiratory monitoring
Oral erythromycin 12.5 mg per kg every 6 hours for 14 days under outpatient daily review
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg per kg every 6 hours as empirical lower respiratory cover

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with 2 weeks of nocturnal perianal itching that wakes him and his 9-year-old sister from sleep. His mother has seen small white moving threads at the anus in the early morning. The household includes both parents and the two children, all otherwise well with no abdominal pain or weight loss.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 92, normal growth
data_table.Examination: Perianal excoriation, no bleeding, abdominal examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Sticky-tape test confirmed Enterobius eggs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Hygiene measures alone without medication including hand washing, short nails and washed linen
Single dose ivermectin to the index child only with second dose given two weeks later in clinic
Three-day course of albendazole 400 mg daily to all household members in a single course
Single dose pyrantel pamoate 10 mg per kg to the index child only with hygiene measures alone
Single dose mebendazole 100 mg to all household members and repeat the same dose in 2 weeks

subtopic_detail: Primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis first-line management
stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought in because he has never had a consistent dry night. He wets 5 to 7 nights per week and has had occasional brief dry spells of up to 1 week. He has no daytime urinary symptoms, no constipation, normal growth, and develops typically. His father had nocturnal enuresis until age 9. The child finds the wetting upsetting and his mother asks about treatment options.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/60, HR 78, BMI 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Normal external genitalia, abdomen soft non-tender, normal lower limb neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose, protein and infection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Intranasal desmopressin 20 mcg at bedtime with strict fluid restriction from 2 hours before sleep
Enuresis alarm therapy with parental supervision for a minimum of 8 weeks
Continue toilet training reminders and reward chart only without alarm or pharmacological therapy
Imipramine 25 mg at bedtime as long-term pharmacological treatment for nightly wetting
Referral for urodynamic studies and renal tract ultrasound before considering any treatment

subtopic_detail: Allergic rhinitis with sleep disturbance treatment escalation
stem: A 9-year-old girl with seasonal allergic rhinitis presents in spring with persistent rhinorrhoea, nasal blockage and itchy eyes. She wakes most nights with mouth breathing and is excessively tired at school. She has been using oral cetirizine 10 mg daily for 3 weeks without much improvement and has no other medical history.

data_table.Examination: Pale boggy nasal mucosa, conjunctival injection, no postnasal cobblestoning, tonsils 2+ symmetric
data_table.Investigations: Not required for diagnosis
data_table.Medications: Cetirizine 10 mg PO daily for 3 weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Refer for sublingual immunotherapy as the next step before intensifying medical therapy further
Switch cetirizine to a sedating antihistamine such as promethazine for nightly use only
Add oral montelukast 5 mg nightly to the existing cetirizine for a 3-month treatment trial
Add regular intranasal corticosteroid spray to the cetirizine for at least 4 weeks
Commence a 5-day course of oral prednisolone 30 mg daily to break the cycle of symptoms

stem: A 4-month-old breastfed boy presents with 6 weeks of frequent effortless regurgitation after most feeds. He gains weight along the 50th centile, feeds eagerly, and is otherwise well. There is no projectile vomiting, no blood, no bile, no back-arching during feeds and no respiratory symptoms. His mother is exhausted by laundry and is asking whether medication will help.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 36, T 36.7, weight 7.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Alert, smiling, soft abdomen, no abdominal distension, hydrated
data_table.Investigations: None required

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch from breast to extensively hydrolysed formula and review the infant in 2 weeks' time
Commence oral omeprazole 1 mg per kg once daily for an 8-week empirical treatment trial
Commence regular oral ranitidine 4 mg per kg twice daily as antacid for symptom control in this infant
Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for upper endoscopy and pH study before any conservative measures
Parental reassurance and conservative measures including upright positioning after feeds

stem: A 9-year-old girl living in a remote Northern Territory community presents with a 24-hour sore throat, fever to 39.2 degrees Celsius and difficulty swallowing solids. She has tender anterior cervical lymph nodes, large exudative tonsils and no cough. Her family has a history of acute rheumatic fever in an older sibling. She has no known drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2, HR 108, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent
data_table.Examination: Bilateral exudative tonsils, tender anterior cervical nodes, no rash, no cough
data_table.Investigations: Throat swab taken for GAS culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic management while awaiting throat swab results?

options.text: Single dose oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg now followed by symptomatic care alone
Oral azithromycin 12 mg per kg daily for 5 days while awaiting the throat culture result
Single intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin 900 mg now with single follow-up review
Oral amoxicillin 25 mg per kg twice daily for 10 days starting today after sample collection
Watchful waiting with paracetamol for 48 hours before reconsidering antibiotic prescription

subtopic_detail: Tetralogy of Fallot hypercyanotic spell first-line manoeuvre
stem: An 8-month-old boy known to have unrepaired tetralogy of Fallot is brought to the emergency department after a 10-minute episode of inconsolable crying, then deep cyanosis. He is now distressed, deeply blue and his mother says his murmur has become quieter. Cardiac surgery is planned in 2 weeks. He has no fever and no recent infections.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 56, SpO2 62 percent on room air, T 36.9
data_table.Examination: Marked central cyanosis, soft systolic murmur (previously harsh), no respiratory distress signs out of proportion
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Administer intravenous adrenaline 10 mcg per kg to support cardiac output during the spell
Begin chest compressions and bag-mask ventilation as the first response to the deep cyanosis present
Commence inhaled nitric oxide via face mask to dilate the pulmonary vasculature immediately now
Provide intravenous furosemide 1 mg per kg to reduce preload and lung congestion in this child
Place the child in the knee-to-chest position and give high-flow oxygen via face mask

subtopic_detail: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia salt-wasting crisis in newborn
stem: A 12-day-old breastfed boy is brought in by his parents after 3 days of poor feeding, lethargy and weight loss. He was born at term following an uneventful pregnancy. Examination shows hyperpigmented scrotal skin, weight 8 percent below birth weight, and obvious dehydration. Newborn screening for CAH was sent 9 days ago and result is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 56, BP 64/38, T 36.4, SpO2 96 percent
data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, cool peripheries, normal male external genitalia with hyperpigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Na 121 mmol/L, K 6.9 mmol/L, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, urea 8.4, creatinine 78, VBG pH 7.28

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate resuscitation step?

options.text: Withhold steroid until ACTH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone results return to confirm CAH diagnosis
Oral fludrocortisone 50 mcg now and admit for observation pending the newborn screening result
Intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL per kg of 10 percent solution to stabilise the cardiac membrane
Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat plus 0.9 percent saline with 5 percent dextrose 20 mL per kg bolus
Intravenous 3 percent saline 5 mL per kg over 1 hour to rapidly correct the severe hyponatraemia

subtopic_detail: Down syndrome newborn cardiac screening pathway
stem: A term newborn male has clinical features of trisomy 21 on day 1: hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, single transverse palmar creases bilaterally and a flat nasal bridge. He is feeding well and pulse oximetry congenital heart disease screen is normal. His chromosomal microarray result is pending and the parents ask about cardiac assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 99 percent right hand and right foot, T 36.8
data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur audible at left sternal edge; femoral pulses palpable equally bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Pulse oximetry CHD screen normal; chromosomal microarray pending
data_table.Medications: Vitamin K and hepatitis B vaccine given at birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cardiac investigation plan?

options.text: Chest radiograph and 12-lead electrocardiograph in the first month with cardiology review later
Formal transthoracic echocardiogram performed within the first 4 to 6 weeks of life
Pulse oximetry CHD screen alone with no further imaging while infant remains asymptomatic clinically
Cardiac MRI under general anaesthetic as the screening investigation of choice within 6 weeks
Defer cardiac imaging until the murmur is louder or symptoms emerge later in infancy

subtopic_detail: Persistent neonatal anuria suggesting posterior urethral valves
stem: A 3-day-old term male newborn has not passed urine since hospital discharge 24 hours after delivery and now appears irritable. His abdomen is mildly distended with a palpable bladder. Antenatal ultrasound at 32 weeks reported bilateral hydronephrosis but the parents declined further follow-up scans. His mother is otherwise well and birth was uncomplicated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 52, T 36.7, weight 3.2 kg (down 9 percent from birth weight)
data_table.Examination: Palpable bladder to umbilicus, no abdominal mass, normal external genitalia, dribbling urine stream when expressed
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L, Na 132, K 6.4, bedside USS distended bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis, dilated posterior urethra

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Suprapubic aspirate of urine for culture and discharge home with outpatient nephrology review
Fluid challenge with normal saline 20 mL per kg then reassess for spontaneous voiding within 4 hours
Intravenous furosemide 1 mg per kg to promote urine output before any imaging is performed
Urgent micturating cystourethrogram first before any other intervention to confirm the diagnosis
Insert a small-bore urethral catheter and admit to neonatal unit with urology referral

subtopic_detail: Croup - severity assessment and initial therapy
stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 23:00 with a 24-hour history of coryza, low-grade fever and a barking cough that has become harsher overnight. He has audible inspiratory stridor at rest but is comfortable on his mother's lap. He drinks half a cup of water without difficulty and his colour is normal. There is no drooling or tripod posture. He is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.0, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 97 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, no tracheal tug, alert, well perfused
data_table.Investigations: Bedside clinical assessment only - no investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses and oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg in the emergency department
Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and admission for observation overnight on continuous saturation monitoring
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose and observation for until stridor at rest settles (typically 1-2 hours) with discharge if stridor settles at rest
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 immediately as the first intervention before any other treatment
Discharge home with advice and saline nasal drops alone given the child is feeding and is well perfused at presentation

stem: A 7-year-old boy is reviewed in clinic 2 weeks after diagnosis of IgA vasculitis. He presented with a palpable purpuric rash on his buttocks and lower limbs, periarticular swelling of both ankles and intermittent colicky abdominal pain. The rash and joint swelling have resolved and he is back at school. His mother has been doing weekly urinalysis as advised. The latest urinalysis dipstick today shows 2+ blood and 1+ protein.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 92, BP 122/78 on a 130 cm 25 kg boy (above 95th centile)
data_table.Examination: No rash, no joint swelling, abdomen soft and non-tender, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 2+ blood 1+ protein, urine ACR 80 mg/mmol (normal <2.5), serum creatinine 58, eGFR 88, albumin 36

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure and continue weekly home urinalysis only, expecting spontaneous resolution within the next 4 weeks because the rash has cleared
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days then taper, planning empirical immunosuppression for nephritis without specialist input first
Stop further urinalysis monitoring and discharge from clinic because the active rash and arthritis have resolved, with return advice for abdominal pain or new rash
Refer urgently to paediatric nephrology with paired urine albumin to creatinine ratio, blood pressure confirmation and review for possible renal biopsy and treatment
Commence enalapril for blood pressure control and arrange routine outpatient nephrology review in 6 to 8 weeks for further monitoring

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease - diagnosis and IVIG timing
stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought in by his parents on the 6th day of a high fever that has not responded to paracetamol. He is irritable and refusing to feed. On examination he has bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, a red cracked tongue, an inflamed pharynx without exudate, a polymorphous truncal rash, and a single tender 2 cm right cervical lymph node. His hands and feet are swollen and red. He is fully immunised and previously well.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6, HR 138, BP 100/60, RR 28, SpO2 98 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, swollen erythematous hands and feet, single right cervical node 2 cm
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18, neutrophils 14, CRP 168, platelets 540, ALT 76, urine 30 WBC per HPF, ESR 88, ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment after starting acute care assessment?

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for community-acquired bacterial sepsis pending blood culture and respiratory virus PCR results
Oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day in divided doses and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days as outpatient therapy with weekly clinic review
Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses after baseline echocardiography
Topical antiseptic mouthwash, oral analgesia and a 5-day course of oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg six-hourly for presumed cervical lymphadenitis with viral exanthem
Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg as a single pulse dose followed by infliximab 5 mg/kg infusion as first-line immunosuppressive therapy

stem: A 9-month-old previously well boy presents to the emergency department with 6 hours of intermittent episodes of inconsolable crying with drawing his legs up, followed by quiet pale periods. He has vomited twice in the last hour, and the most recent vomit was bile-stained. He passed a small amount of red jelly-like stool 30 minutes ago. He is normally fully breastfed and has had no fever today. His parents are anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 152, BP 90/56, RR 32, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Pale and quiet between episodes, abdomen soft, palpable sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass, no peritonism, normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118, WCC 11, U/E unremarkable, glucose 5.8, lactate 1.8, abdominal ultrasound shows target sign in right upper quadrant consistent with ileocolic intussusception

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of conservative management with bowel rest, intravenous fluids and nasogastric decompression for 24 hours in the paediatric ward with serial examinations
Immediate exploratory laparotomy and manual reduction with consideration of bowel resection if any necrotic segment is identified intraoperatively in theatre
Intravenous access, fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and image-guided air or contrast enema reduction in radiology with paediatric surgical standby
Oral rehydration with electrolyte solution at home and outpatient surgical clinic review in 48 hours if symptoms persist or worsen with appropriate return advice
Diagnostic gastroscopy and colonoscopy under anaesthesia to confirm the diagnosis and identify a pathological lead point before non-operative reduction is attempted

stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy is brought to the emergency department with a 1-week history of progressively worsening non-bilious vomiting after every feed that has become projectile. He is hungry between feeds but his weight has dropped 200 g over the past week. His mother has noted reduced wet nappies. The paediatric surgeon has confirmed pyloric stenosis on ultrasound and theatre is provisionally booked for the next morning.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 168, BP 78/46, RR 36, SpO2 99 percent
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken anterior fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, palpable olive in right epigastrium, visible gastric peristalsis after feed
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 2.8, Cl 88, HCO3 36, pH 7.52, BE +10, glucose 4.4, creatinine 36, ultrasound pyloric muscle thickness 5 mm length 20 mm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Place nasogastric tube on free drainage, withhold oral feeds, give intravenous 0.9 percent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus then 0.9 percent saline with 20 mmol/L potassium maintenance until biochemistry corrects
Transfer directly to theatre for immediate Ramstedt pyloromyotomy in the next available slot, since dehydration will be most efficiently corrected by relieving the obstruction first
Start a trial of small frequent feeds of thickened expressed breast milk in upright position before re-evaluating in 24 hours to see if symptoms improve with conservative measures
Administer intravenous ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg and observe for resolution of vomiting before deciding whether resuscitation or surgical pathway is the most appropriate option
Commence intravenous dextrose 10 percent at maintenance rate alone without sodium chloride to address ongoing hypoglycaemia and weight loss before surgery is performed

subtopic_detail: Cystic fibrosis newborn screening - positive result followup
stem: A 3-week-old well-appearing baby is brought in by her parents after they receive a phone call from the newborn screening program saying the test was positive for cystic fibrosis. The baby was term, weighed 3.4 kg at birth, has been gaining weight well on breastfeeding and is passing 6 wet nappies per day and stools 3 times per day. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. The parents are anxious and want to understand what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 142, RR 38, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Examination: Well, alert, normal tone, chest clear, abdomen soft, weight tracking 25th centile, no clubbing
data_table.Investigations: Newborn screening IRT 240 ng/mL (above 99th centile cut-off), CFTR gene panel pending, no symptoms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family and arrange repeat blood spot newborn screening in 4 weeks if the baby remains well, given the positive screening test result on the initial sample today
Commence empirical pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy at 2000 lipase units per kg per feed with weekly clinic monitoring while diagnostic confirmation is pending
Arrange an immediate plain chest x-ray to look for early lung disease and barium meal to exclude meconium ileus given the positive newborn screening test result
Refer urgently to the local paediatric cystic fibrosis centre for diagnostic sweat chloride test and full CFTR mutation analysis with multidisciplinary team review
Send a faecal elastase sample and stool fat estimation now to evaluate for pancreatic insufficiency before confirming the cystic fibrosis diagnosis with further specialist tests

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis - admission criteria and supportive management
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old, ex-37-week infant in ED with 3 days of coryza progressing to noisy breathing and reduced feeding. The parents report wet nappies have halved and the last feed was 80 mL of formula 5 hours ago, taken with several pauses for breath. The infant is alert when handled but tires. The mother smoked in pregnancy and there are no siblings.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 162, RR 62, SpO2 93% in room air, BP 88/52, weight 6.3 kg
data_table.Examination: Mild tracheal tug and subcostal recession, fine bilateral crackles with scattered wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, anterior fontanelle flat
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate positive for RSV, capillary blood gas pH 7.35 pCO2 45 HCO3 22, blood glucose 4.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with reassessment in 20 minutes to determine whether bronchodilator therapy should continue regularly
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days alongside supportive care, given the wheeze component and family history of maternal smoking exposure
Admit for observation with low-flow nasal cannula oxygen, nasogastric or small-volume oral feeds, and minimal handling with routine reassessment of work of breathing
Commence intravenous amoxicillin and benzylpenicillin empirically while awaiting blood culture results, treating possible bacterial co-infection causing the respiratory distress
Discharge home with parental advice on small frequent feeds, nasal saline drops, and return immediately for any apnoea, cyanosis or worsening work of breathing observed

stem: You are the rural ED registrar called urgently to a 3-year-old brought in by ambulance with 6 hours of fever, irritability and a new spreading purpuric rash on the trunk and limbs. The child cries when handled and is mottled peripherally. The nearest tertiary paediatric hospital is 2 hours by retrieval helicopter. The parents report no prior immunisations because of religious objection. You have already secured intraosseous access in the right tibia.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4, HR 178, RR 44, SpO2 96%, BP 78/40, capillary refill 4 seconds, weight 14 kg
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching purpuric lesions on trunk, thighs and forearms, neck stiffness present, Kernig sign positive, GCS 13
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 3.6, lactate 4.1, awaiting bloods, no LP performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture for cell count and culture before any antibiotic dose to maximise yield, then commence intravenous ceftriaxone after sample collection
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg now, give a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus reassessing after each, and activate paediatric retrieval immediately for transfer
Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin 1.2 g now while awaiting transfer team, withhold further fluid until blood pressure trend confirms the need for resuscitation
Commence intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg first to reduce neurological sequelae and then begin antibiotic therapy after the steroid dose has been administered
Take blood cultures and meningococcal PCR before any antibiotic to preserve microbiological diagnosis, then start ceftriaxone once samples have left the bedside

subtopic_detail: Pyloric stenosis - acid-base disturbance and pre-operative resuscitation
stem: You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 5-week-old male, the first-born of consanguineous parents, referred from the GP with 2 weeks of progressive non-bilious vomiting now described as forceful and projectile after every feed. The mother is anxious because feeds are taken hungrily yet weight has fallen below the 3rd centile. There is a palpable olive in the right upper quadrant after a test feed. He has not passed urine for 8 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 168, RR 40, SpO2 99%, BP 78/45, weight 3.9 kg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, visible left to right gastric peristalsis, anterior fontanelle depressed
data_table.Investigations: Na 132, K 3.0, Cl 88, HCO3 34, urea 9.8, creatinine 48, venous pH 7.52 pCO2 50, ultrasound pyloric muscle 4.5 mm thickness 18 mm length

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management before surgical referral for pyloromyotomy?

options.text: Proceed immediately to theatre for Ramstedt pyloromyotomy under general anaesthesia, correcting the electrolytes intraoperatively to avoid further delay to surgical cure
Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of 4% albumin to restore intravascular volume rapidly then transition to half-normal saline with added potassium and dextrose for ongoing maintenance
Commence intravenous Hartmann solution at 150 mL/kg/day with no potassium supplementation because the metabolic alkalosis will worsen with chloride poor crystalloid
Insert a nasogastric tube on free drainage and restrict all fluid until vomiting settles to prevent further chloride loss and to allow spontaneous biochemical correction
Commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose at maintenance and add potassium chloride only after a urine output of 1 mL/kg/hour is documented

subtopic_detail: Supraventricular tachycardia in infancy - acute termination
stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to the resuscitation bay for a 6-week-old breastfed infant brought in by ambulance with 4 hours of poor feeding, sweating during feeds and pallor. The infant was term, no antenatal concerns and immunisations up to date for age. The infant is alert but mottled. Cardiac monitoring shows a narrow complex tachycardia with no visible P waves and a fixed rate that does not vary with handling. IV access has been secured in an antecubital vein.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 280, RR 60, SpO2 95%, BP 72/40, capillary refill 4 seconds, weight 4.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Pale, peripherally cool to mid-forearm, hepatomegaly 2 cm, no murmur audible at this rate, bilateral fine crackles at lung bases
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead ECG narrow QRS at 280, no discernible P waves, axis normal; bedside glucose 4.0; venous gas pH 7.28 lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a bag of crushed ice and water firmly to the central face for 15 to 30 seconds while continuous rhythm monitoring is observed for sinus rhythm restoration
Administer intravenous adenosine 0.1 mg/kg as a rapid push followed by a saline flush, with continuous rhythm strip and defibrillator pads on the chest ready
Synchronised DC cardioversion at 1 joule per kilogram under brief procedural sedation given the prolonged tachycardia and early signs of cardiogenic shock with poor perfusion
Administer intravenous verapamil 0.1 mg/kg slow push with continuous ECG monitoring to slow conduction through the atrioventricular node and restore sinus rhythm
Commence intravenous amiodarone loading at 5 mg/kg over 30 minutes with continuous monitoring while preparing for transfer to a paediatric cardiac centre

subtopic_detail: Suspected non-accidental injury - infant fracture work-up
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old infant brought in by mother and her new partner for irritability and reluctance to use the right arm since this morning. The mother reports the infant rolled off the change table 24 hours ago but acted normally afterwards. The partner is the primary daytime carer. Child protection records show no prior notifications. X-ray of the right arm shows a spiral fracture of the midshaft humerus. The infant is not yet rolling on developmental assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 150, RR 36, SpO2 99%, BP 86/52, weight 6.8 kg
data_table.Examination: Inconsolable when right arm handled, bruising over right upper arm and posterior thorax, small healing bruise on left cheek, fundoscopy not yet performed, anterior fontanelle soft, alert
data_table.Investigations: Right humerus spiral fracture midshaft, FBE and coagulation studies pending, CRP normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a collar and cuff immobilisation, prescribe regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, and discharge home with orthopaedic outpatient review and safety net advice
Arrange urgent bone profile including alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone, and refer for genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta before notifying authorities
Apply a back slab for analgesia, take repeated histories from each parent separately to clarify the mechanism, then decide on imaging based on consistency of stories
Admit the infant under paediatrics for a full skeletal survey, head CT or MRI, ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages, and mandatory notification to child protection
Discuss with parents the differential of accidental injury and arrange community child health nurse follow-up within 48 hours, deferring notification pending nurse review

subtopic_detail: Periorbital versus orbital cellulitis - imaging and admission
stem: You are the paediatric ED registrar assessing a 6-year-old with 3 days of right eyelid swelling and pain. The mother reports a recent upper respiratory infection. The child now refuses to open the right eye fully. On examination there is marked eyelid oedema with erythema, the eye appears proptosed by 3 mm compared with the left, and the child complains of pain on attempted upgaze with restricted abduction. The pupil is mid-sized and reactive but vision testing is difficult through swelling.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 99%, BP 102/64, weight 22 kg
data_table.Examination: Right eyelid erythema and oedema, proptosis, restricted abduction with pain on upgaze, conjunctival chemosis, sinus tenderness over right maxilla
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 138, blood culture taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home on oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg four times daily with ophthalmology outpatient review the following day given the absence of complete ophthalmoplegia in this child
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six hourly alone, with CT orbits and sinuses only if there is no clinical improvement after 48 hours of monotherapy
Admit for urgent contrast CT of orbits and paranasal sinuses, commence intravenous ceftriaxone with flucloxacillin or vancomycin, and request ENT and ophthalmology review
Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy with ophthalmology review in the morning, repeat clinical examination in 4 hours, and arrange imaging only if vision deteriorates
Apply warm compresses, commence oral amoxicillin clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily, and arrange paediatric outpatient review within 24 hours with safety net advice

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler - management and counselling
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing an 18-month-old whose mother has noticed pallor and reduced energy for play over 6 weeks. Diet history reveals 900 mL of cow's milk daily taken from a bottle, limited intake of solids, and a strong preference for white bread and pasta. Birth history was unremarkable at term. Growth parameters are tracking along the 25th centile. Developmental milestones are age-appropriate. There is no history of pica or melaena. Family migrated from Eritrea 2 years ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7, HR 124, RR 26, SpO2 99%, BP 92/56, weight 11 kg
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, no jaundice, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no koilonychia, cardiovascular examination normal with no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84, MCV 62, MCH 18, reticulocyte count 1.0%, ferritin 7, iron 4, transferrin saturation 6%, lead level pending, faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent paediatric haematology referral for haemoglobin electrophoresis and bone marrow examination given the markedly low MCV and migration history from northeast Africa
Admit for intravenous ferric carboxymaltose infusion as oral absorption is unreliable in toddlers and intravenous therapy guarantees full repletion of iron stores in a single dose
Commence oral ferrous sulfate elixir 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily and counsel to reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL with iron rich solids and vitamin C sources
Commence oral iron polymaltose 6 mg/kg of elemental iron three times daily with each meal for 12 weeks and review only after completion of the prescribed full course
Transfuse one unit of packed red cells with furosemide cover, repeat full blood count after 24 hours, and commence oral iron supplementation once haemoglobin is above 100

subtopic_detail: New presentation type 1 diabetes with DKA - initial fluid plan
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-year-old girl brought to ED with 5 days of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss and 12 hours of abdominal pain and vomiting. There is no past medical history. She is rousable but drowsy. The school nurse noticed her breath smelled fruity yesterday. There is no family history of diabetes. She has had no recent illness apart from this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5, HR 134, RR 32 with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99%, BP 96/58, weight 28 kg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, abdomen soft with mild generalised tenderness, GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 28, ketones 6.2, venous gas pH 7.05 HCO3 6 pCO2 18, Na 132 K 5.4 Cl 100 urea 9.2 creatinine 88, urine ketones 4+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan over the first hour?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride as a rapid bolus over 15 minutes then commence insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour with hourly neurological observations recorded

Give 10 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 to 60 minutes then continue maintenance plus deficit replacement at a calculated rate, deferring insulin infusion until 1 hour of fluids has been delivered
Commence intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 1 hour given the severe acidosis with pH 7.05, then begin sodium chloride maintenance and insulin infusion concurrently
Commence Hartmann solution at 1.5 times maintenance with insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour started immediately to halt ongoing ketogenesis without further delay to glycaemic control
Give 30 mL/kg of 0.45% sodium chloride over 1 hour with added potassium 40 mmol/L from the outset, then halve the rate and start insulin once acidosis begins to resolve

stem: You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 60-hour-old term baby boy in the postnatal ward. Mother is blood group O Rh positive, baby is A Rh positive. Direct antiglobulin test is positive. The baby is breastfed but feeding has been hesitant. The midwives are concerned about increasing yellow tinge. The baby was born by uneventful vaginal birth at 39+5 weeks and weighed 3.4 kg. There is no perinatal infection risk. The mother is otherwise well.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 99%, weight 3.25 kg (down 4.4% from birth)
data_table.Examination: Visibly jaundiced to chest, alert and responsive to handling, no hepatosplenomegaly, anterior fontanelle soft, primitive reflexes intact
data_table.Investigations: Total SBR 320 micromol/L, conjugated 10 micromol/L, Hb 158, reticulocytes 5%, blood group A Rh positive DAT positive (anti-A)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue exclusive breastfeeding with lactation support and repeat SBR in 12 hours, no phototherapy required as the value is below standard term thresholds for this age range
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg as first-line therapy to reduce antibody-mediated red cell destruction and avoid the need for phototherapy or further escalation
Arrange immediate exchange transfusion with double-volume calculation through an umbilical venous catheter to remove bilirubin and antibody-coated red cells without delay
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and switch to expressed formula to confirm breast milk jaundice as the cause, then reintroduce breastfeeding once SBR has begun to fall
Commence intensive phototherapy with light source above and below, ensure adequate fluid intake by feeding or formula top-up if needed, and repeat SBR in 4 to 6 hours

subtopic_detail: Acute asthma escalation after intravenous magnesium
stem: A 9-year-old boy with acute severe asthma is still unable to speak in sentences 30 minutes after intravenous magnesium sulfate, despite continuous nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium and intravenous hydrocortisone. He weighs 30 kg. The intensive care registrar is on the way.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 40, SpO2 92 percent on 8 L/min oxygen
data_table.Examination: Marked recession, globally reduced air entry, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous salbutamol 15 micrograms per kilogram over 10 minutes
Intravenous aminophylline 10 milligrams per kilogram over 60 minutes
Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms per kilogram to the thigh
Non-invasive ventilation using bilevel positive airway pressure now
Intravenous ketamine 1 milligram per kilogram before rapid sequence

stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 10-month-old boy at a follow-up visit two weeks after his first hospital admission for viral wheeze. His mother says the cough has resolved but he still has occasional noisy breathing when he gets a cold. There is no family history of atopy and he has no eczema. His father, who has well-controlled adult asthma, is asking whether the baby should start a preventer to stop further admissions.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 120 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 99% on room air, T 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, normal work of breathing, clear chest, no eczema, growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Discharge summary: confirmed RSV positive, responded to oxygen and supportive care, no salbutamol response documented

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management advice?

options.text: Start a daily low-dose inhaled budesonide preventer via spacer for the next twelve weeks
Refer urgently to a paediatric respiratory physician for cystic fibrosis sweat testing
Prescribe a montelukast 4 mg granule sachet nightly during the winter respiratory virus season
Trial regular salbutamol 100 micrograms twice daily via spacer through the winter period
Reassure the family, continue supportive care and review only if a further severe episode occurs

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to assess a 14-day-old term breastfed baby boy in the emergency department. He was born at 39 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth with a normal antenatal course and was discharged home day 2 with a normal newborn examination. Over the last 12 hours his mother reports poor feeding, decreased wet nappies and an episode of mottling. He has had no contact with unwell siblings.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188 bpm, RR 64, SpO2 96% on room air, axillary T 38.4°C, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, irritable on handling, mild jaundice, no rash, anterior fontanelle soft, no focal source
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pending; cultures from blood and urine taken; cerebrospinal fluid sample collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin at standard neonatal doses
Intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone at standard paediatric doses
Intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin at standard neonatal doses
Intravenous vancomycin and meropenem at standard paediatric doses
Intravenous amoxicillin and oral aciclovir at standard neonatal doses

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on a tertiary inpatient ward managing a 9-year-old girl admitted four hours ago with new-onset diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis. She received a 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus over 60 minutes and is now on a maintenance plus deficit infusion calculated for a 7% deficit replaced over 48 hours, alongside an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour.

Two hours into therapy the nurse calls you because the patient has developed a headache, has become increasingly drowsy and her heart rate has fallen from 130 to 78 bpm.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 bpm, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 132/88, T 36.8°C, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Pupils 4 mm equal and sluggishly reactive, no focal weakness, fundi not seen
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 14.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.20 (improved from 6.98), K 4.0 mmol/L, Na corrected 138 mmol/L, ketones 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion to 0.1 units/kg/hour and add intravenous dextrose 10%
Give intravenous mannitol 0.5 g/kg over 15 minutes and reduce fluid rate by one third
Urgently transfer for non-contrast CT brain to confirm cerebral oedema before treatment
Give a further 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus over 30 minutes for presumed hypovolaemia
Stop the insulin infusion and continue maintenance fluids only for the next hour

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in ED reviewing a 4-year-old boy who has refused to weight-bear since waking this morning. His mother reports a mild upper respiratory illness over the last week that resolved spontaneously. He has not taken any medications. There is no history of trauma. He is reluctant to allow examination of the right hip but shows no swelling or erythema. He has a low-grade temperature on triage of 38.1°C.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 bpm, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, T 38.1°C, BP 102/64
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation, painful log roll, full passive range only achievable under analgesia
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 38 mg/L, ESR 42 mm/h, hip ultrasound shows a 5 mm joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with simple analgesia, weight-bearing as tolerated and review by general practitioner in 48 to 72 hours
Admit for empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and ward reassessment in 24 hours without joint aspiration
Arrange urgent orthopaedic hip joint aspiration under image guidance for cell count, Gram stain and culture
Order outpatient magnetic resonance imaging of the right hip prior to any invasive procedure or admission
Prescribe oral ibuprofen with hourly observations and review in the short stay unit at 4 to 6 hours

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to ED at midnight to see a 5-day-old term boy with three episodes of green vomiting since this afternoon. He was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth and discharged home day 2 with normal newborn examination. He has been exclusively breastfed and had passed meconium within 24 hours of birth. He fed reluctantly today and his abdomen has become mildly distended over the last hour. He has not had a wet nappy for the last 5 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 60, SpO2 97% on room air, T 36.3°C, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Sleepy but rousable, mildly distended soft abdomen, no palpable mass, no peritonism, anal patency normal
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas: pH 7.28, lactate 2.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound looking specifically for the whirlpool sign of the mesenteric vessels
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study performed urgently within the next hour
Plain supine and erect abdominal radiographs to look for free air or obstruction
Sweat chloride testing arranged through the paediatric metabolic team in the morning
Contrast enema to exclude Hirschsprung disease as the cause of the obstructive symptoms

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a regional hospital reviewing a 6-month-old formula-fed boy admitted overnight with five days of viral gastroenteritis. The community nurse reports the family had been adding extra scoops of formula powder to the bottles to keep him fed during the illness. He has been increasingly lethargic since this morning. He weighs 7.0 kg and his pre-illness clinic weight one week ago was 7.5 kg. He has not had a wet nappy for 8 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 bpm, RR 36, SpO2 99% on room air, T 37.6°C, BP 80/52, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable, sunken eyes, doughy abdominal skin turgor, no rash, anterior fontanelle depressed
data_table.Investigations: Na 162 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 86 micromol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.28

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate fluid plan for the next 48 hours?

options.text: Replace the 7% fluid deficit with sodium chloride 0.9% plus 5% glucose over 48 hours with sodium fall not exceeding 0.5 mmol/L per hour
Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.45% then replace the deficit with the same fluid over 24 hours with electrolyte checks every 6 hours
Give a 20 mL/kg bolus of sodium chloride 0.9% then replace the deficit with 5% glucose over 24 hours with electrolyte checks every 6 hours
Administer oral rehydration solution at 10 mL/kg/hour and recheck sodium after 6 hours of trial of oral therapy
Replace the deficit with sodium chloride 0.9% plus 5% glucose over 12 hours and reassess electrolytes every hour during correction

stem: You are the on-call paediatric registrar called by the neonatal screening service about a 12-day-old infant whose newborn screen returned a markedly raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone. The baby has been feeding poorly for 24 hours with three episodes of vomiting and a reduced wet-nappy count. On examination external genitalia show clitoromegaly with partial labial fusion. The infant looks pale and mottled and has lost 12% of birth weight since discharge.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 192 bpm, RR 60, SpO2 96% on room air, T 36.3°C, BP 56/34, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, sunken anterior fontanelle, peripheral mottling, ambiguous genitalia, no palpable gonads, hyperpigmented areolae and scrotum-like rugae
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L, K 7.4 mmol/L, glucose 2.1 mmol/L, urea 9.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.22, 17-OHP markedly elevated on repeat

lead_in: Which combination of interventions should be initiated immediately?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 5 mg with oral fludrocortisone 50 micrograms and outpatient endocrinology phone review the next day
Intravenous dexamethasone 0.5 mg stat with 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.45% bolus and routine endocrinology review next day
Intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat with 10 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% plus 10% glucose bolus and paediatric endocrinology referral
Intravenous insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hour with calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg over 10 minutes for the hyperkalaemia
Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and intravenous immunoglobulin pending neonatal sepsis screening culture results

subtopic_detail: Hand foot and mouth disease counselling
stem: You are the GP seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother is worried she has chickenpox. Two days ago the child developed a low-grade fever and refused breakfast. This morning small grey-white blisters appeared on her palms, soles and the inside of her cheeks. Her older brother attends the same childcare centre. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and the girl is fully immunised including two doses of varicella vaccine. Mum asks when she can go back to childcare.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6°C, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Pinpoint vesicles on a non-erythematous base on hands, feet and buccal mucosa; trunk and face spared; alert and drinking small volumes
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding return to childcare?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg into the lateral thigh and observe response over 5 minutes
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg infused over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring in HDU
IV aminophylline 10 mg/kg load over 60 minutes on the general paediatric ward with telemetry only
Switch to high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min FiO2 0.5 and reassess at 30 minutes off bronchodilator
Switch corticosteroid route to IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg slow bolus and continue current nebulisers

subtopic_detail: Scarlet fever and rheumatic fever prevention
stem: You are the rural GP seeing a 7-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community presenting with two days of sore throat, fever and a rough sandpaper-like rash that started on his neck and spread to his trunk. He has a strawberry tongue and tender anterior cervical nodes. He has no penicillin allergy and is well enough to be managed as an outpatient with reliable follow up through the community clinic. His mother is happy to give oral medication.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous oropharynx with tonsillar exudate, palpable petechial rash with sandpaper texture sparing the face, strawberry tongue, no joint swelling, no carditis
data_table.Investigations: Rapid throat swab unavailable; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for an abbreviated five-day course
Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg twice daily for a seven-day course with supportive care
Symptomatic care only with paracetamol and clinic review in 48 hours if not better
Oral roxithromycin 4 mg/kg twice daily for ten days with topical throat lozenges
Oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for a full ten-day course

stem: You are the paediatric outpatient registrar reviewing a 14-month-old boy referred by his GP for bow legs and delayed walking. He was exclusively breastfed until 12 months and was not given vitamin D supplements. He spends most of his day indoors and his mother veils for cultural reasons. The family lives in Melbourne and the child has darkly pigmented skin. He has no chronic illnesses, no diarrhoea, and his diet is now mostly cow's milk with very little meat or fortified cereal.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7°C, HR 112, RR 24, weight on 25th centile, length on 10th centile
data_table.Examination: Frontal bossing, wrist widening, costochondral beading, valgus deformity of the lower limbs, hypotonia, no fractures
data_table.Investigations: Calcium 1.95 mmol/L, phosphate 0.7 mmol/L, ALP 1200 U/L, 25-OH vitamin D 18 nmol/L, PTH elevated, wrist X-ray: cupping and fraying of distal radius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral colecalciferol 1000 IU daily for three months without calcium supplementation
Oral colecalciferol 3000 IU daily for 12 weeks plus elemental calcium 500 mg daily
Refer to orthopaedics for surgical correction of genu varum before further medical workup
Single oral stoss dose of 300000 IU colecalciferol with bloods rechecked at two weeks
Intravenous calcium gluconate 0.5 mL/kg over 10 minutes and admit for cardiac monitoring

stem: You are the GP seeing a 4-month-old formula-fed boy whose parents are worried about ongoing crying, regurgitation and intermittent loose mucousy stools, occasionally with streaks of fresh blood. Symptoms began at 6 weeks, around the time he switched from breast to standard cow milk formula. He has mild eczema on the cheeks. He is alert, playful and feeding well, but weight gain has slowed from the 50th centile to the 15th centile over six weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9°C, HR 130, RR 32, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, well-hydrated, mild facial eczema, soft non-tender abdomen, normal anal tone, no anal fissure
data_table.Investigations: Faecal occult blood positive, FBC normal, no eosinophilia, no skin prick or specific IgE testing performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Switch to a lactose-free cow milk based formula and review symptoms in four weeks
Refer for specific IgE testing to cow milk protein before any change of formula trial
Switch to a soy-based infant formula and review symptoms in two weeks at the clinic
Thicken current formula and start omeprazole 1 mg/kg once daily before any formula change
Trial extensively hydrolysed casein formula for two to four weeks with clinical reassessment

stem: You are the GP reviewing a 7-day-old term baby boy with three days of bilateral sticky eyes and increasing eyelid swelling. He was born by spontaneous vaginal delivery to a 19-year-old mother whose antenatal STI screening was incomplete. The baby is feeding and gaining weight well, has no fever and no respiratory distress. Examination shows marked tarsal injection with mucopurulent discharge and mild eyelid oedema.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9°C, HR 140, RR 44, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral mucopurulent conjunctival discharge, no corneal involvement on fluorescein, no preauricular nodes, clear chest
data_table.Investigations: Eye swab for chlamydia PCR and bacterial culture obtained

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial therapy while results are pending?

options.text: Saline eye toilet four times daily and clinical review in 48 hours if not improving
Single intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg dose with saline eye toilet four times daily
Topical chloramphenicol drops six times daily for seven days with saline eye toilet
Oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg as a single dose with saline eye toilet four times daily
Oral erythromycin 50 mg/kg per day in four divided doses for a total of 14 days

stem: You are the rural GP seeing a 2-year-old girl who pulled a cup of freshly boiled tea onto her chest 30 minutes ago. The mother removed wet clothing and ran cool tap water for 20 minutes before driving in. The child is alert and crying intermittently but consolable. Examination shows a moist erythematous area with intact blisters across the anterior chest and right anterolateral abdomen. There is no facial, perineal or circumferential involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 130, RR 26, SpO2 99% on room air, cap refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Estimated 6% total body surface area partial-thickness scald to anterior chest and right flank, blistered with serous fluid, very painful to touch, no charring, no inhalational injury signs
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated in the field

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV crystalloid by Parkland formula at 4 mL/kg per percent TBSA over the first 24 hours
Burst blisters with a sterile needle, dress with paraffin gauze, observe in primary care
Cling film cover, intranasal fentanyl 1.5 micrograms/kg, urgent paediatric burns transfer
Continue cool running water for a further 30 minutes and reassess depth and area after
Silver sulfadiazine cream, non-adherent dressing, oral paracetamol, review the next day

stem: You are the ED registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl with 24 hours of profuse non-bilious vomiting and four watery stools over 12 hours. She has refused fluids for the last three hours and is tearful but consolable. Mum has been trying small sips of oral rehydration solution without success. She has no chronic illness, no surgical scars, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Capillary refill is two seconds and mucous membranes are slightly dry.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4°C, HR 132, RR 26, BP 96/60, SpO2 99% on room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild dryness of mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds, soft abdomen, no peritonism, normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside ketones 1.6 mmol/L, BSL 4.4 mmol/L; UEC not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert IV line and commence a 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes now
Nasogastric rehydration at 100 mL/kg oral rehydration solution given over four hours
Send stool for viral PCR and bacterial culture before any further symptomatic treatment
Single oral ondansetron 2 mg wafer followed by 30 minutes of patient oral rehydration
Oral loperamide 50 micrograms/kg with each loose stool and discharge home with review

stem: You are the GP seeing the parents of a 3-year-old boy who for the last 6 weeks has woken about 90 minutes after sleep onset screaming, sweating, with dilated pupils and inconsolability. The episodes last 5 to 10 minutes, after which he settles into sleep. The next morning he has no memory of the event. He is meeting all developmental milestones, attends day care without concerns, and family history is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal between episodes
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, growth on the 50th centile, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated based on history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure parents, sleep hygiene advice, scheduled awakening 15 minutes before the usual time
Refer to child psychiatry for assessment of an underlying primary anxiety disorder driver
Sleep-deprived EEG to exclude frontal lobe nocturnal seizures before any other treatment
Commence low-dose melatonin 1 mg at bedtime and review clinical effect in four weeks' time
Prescribe oral clonazepam 0.05 mg/kg at bedtime for four weeks with monthly clinic review

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with two days of dark cola-coloured urine and puffy eyes on waking. Two weeks ago he had impetigo on his legs that resolved with topical mupirocin. He has had a brief headache today but no seizures or visual changes. He is otherwise well, normotensive in the GP rooms (BP 105/65), and his urine dipstick shows 3+ blood and 1+ protein.

Bloods show normal urea and creatinine but low C3, normal C4, and a positive ASOT. There is no rash, no joint pain and no oliguria.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 118/78 in clinic on repeat
data_table.Examination: Mild periorbital oedema, no peripheral oedema, no rash, chest clear, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ blood 1+ protein, urine microscopy red cell casts, Cr 50 micromol/L, urea 5 mmol/L, C3 0.4 g/L (low), C4 0.2 g/L (normal), ASOT positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Arrange urgent renal biopsy to define the histological subtype before any other management
Admit for blood pressure monitoring with salt restriction and short-acting nifedipine if needed
Reassure and discharge home on no specific therapy with weekly GP review for the next six weeks
Commence high-dose prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for four weeks and outpatient nephrology review
Commence oral phenoxymethylpenicillin to eradicate residual streptococcal carriage at home

stem: You are the paediatric registrar consulted about a 14-year-old girl with six weeks of daily holocephalic headache that is worse on waking and on coughing. She has had two episodes of transient visual obscurations. Her BMI is 32. She started oral isotretinoin two months ago for severe acne. There is no fever, neck stiffness, focal neurology or recent head injury. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema and visual fields show enlarged blind spots.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no focal neurology, fundoscopy bilateral disc swelling, no nuchal rigidity
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and MR venogram: no mass, no venous sinus thrombosis, slit-like ventricles; lumbar puncture opening pressure 32 cm H2O lateral decubitus; CSF cells nil, protein 0.3 g/L, glucose normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Halve the isotretinoin dose and add propranolol 20 mg twice daily for migraine prophylaxis
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and ophthalmology review with perimetry in two weeks
Cease isotretinoin, start acetazolamide 500 mg twice daily, refer for serial automated perimetry
Arrange therapeutic lumbar punctures every 48 hours to maintain a low CSF opening pressure
Urgent neurosurgical referral for ventriculoperitoneal shunt insertion before any other therapy

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 13-year-old boy with three months of recurrent right-sided unilateral epistaxis, often requiring ED visits with packing. The episodes have become more frequent and are accompanied by progressive right-sided nasal obstruction. He has no easy bruising, no menorrhagia equivalent in family, and his bleeding screen at the last admission was normal. On anterior rhinoscopy you can see a smooth, lobulated, vascular-looking mass behind the right middle turbinate. He has no other red-flag symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Smooth lobulated reddish-purple mass posterior to right middle turbinate, no neck lymphadenopathy, no cranial nerve deficits, no proptosis
data_table.Investigations: FBC and coagulation screen normal; nasal endoscopy as described

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: In-office biopsy through the nasal cavity for histological diagnosis prior to any imaging
Repeat full blood count and coagulation screen in two weeks before further investigation
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the nasopharynx and skull base before any tissue biopsy is taken
Plain X-ray of the post-nasal space to estimate soft-tissue density before any cross-section
Empirical course of intranasal mometasone for six weeks before reimaging or specialist review

stem: You are the paediatric haematology registrar reviewing an 8-month-old boy of Greek heritage referred for progressive pallor, hepatosplenomegaly and faltering growth from 4 months of age. Newborn screening detected an elevated HbF and follow-up parental studies showed both parents to be beta-thalassaemia trait carriers. Confirmatory testing in the baby has shown two beta zero mutations on molecular genetic testing. He is now feeding poorly, listless and has hepatosplenomegaly extending 4 cm below the costal margins.

data_table.Examination: Marked pallor, mild scleral icterus, hepatomegaly 4 cm, splenomegaly 4 cm, frontal bossing, growth dropping across centiles
data_table.Investigations: Hb 58 g/L, MCV 62 fL, reticulocytes 10%, HbF 90% on HPLC, HbA absent, ferritin 80 micrograms/L, LDH elevated, bilirubin 35 micromol/L (unconjugated)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence hydroxycarbamide 15 mg/kg daily to induce fetal haemoglobin and avoid regular transfusion
Commence oral folic acid 5 mg daily and review in six weeks before considering any transfusion
Defer transfusion until haemoglobin falls below 50 g/L to limit cumulative iron loading risk
Start regular transfusion targeting pre-transfusion Hb 95 to 105 g/L; chelate when ferritin rises
Refer immediately for splenectomy as the primary measure to reduce transfusion requirements

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-year-old girl whose teacher and parents have noticed dozens of episodes per day where she stops, stares, blinks rapidly and is unresponsive for 5 to 10 seconds, then resumes activity. She has had no convulsive seizures, no postictal phase, and her development is normal. Hyperventilation in clinic for 3 minutes triggers a typical event. She has no family history of epilepsy and no behavioural concerns. The EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave with normal background.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, normal development
data_table.Investigations: EEG: 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave provoked by hyperventilation, normal awake and sleep background; MRI brain not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line medication?

options.text: Carbamazepine titrated to 15 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
Lamotrigine titrated slowly over six weeks to 5 mg/kg per day as first-line monotherapy
Sodium valproate titrated to 20 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
Levetiracetam titrated to 40 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy
Ethosuximide titrated to 15 to 40 mg/kg per day in two divided doses as first-line monotherapy

stem: You are the GP seeing a 4-year-old boy with three weeks of persistent night pain in both legs, increasing pallor and easy bruising. His mother brought him today because he is now refusing to walk in the mornings, and she noticed petechiae on his shins. He has had two low-grade fevers over the last week. There is no recent trauma, no joint swelling and no rash beyond the petechiae. He is otherwise alert and engages with you in clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4°C, HR 130, RR 24, SpO2 99% on room air, BP 95/58
data_table.Examination: Pallor, scattered petechiae on shins, palpable cervical and inguinal lymph nodes 1.5 cm, hepatomegaly 3 cm below costal margin, no joint swelling, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: Hb 70 g/L, WCC 24 x10^9/L with 70% blasts on film, platelets 18 x10^9/L, neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L, LDH 1800 U/L, urate 0.55 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for suspected septic arthritis of the lower limbs before further workup
Commence empirical oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily and outpatient haematology in two weeks
Request outpatient FBC and bone biochemistry in one week with GP review of the results
Same-day paediatric oncology contact and direct transfer for tumour-lysis prophylaxis and marrow
Commence oral ibuprofen for presumed growing pains and arrange GP review in one week

stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to see a 24-hour-old term boy whose mother had an antenatal anomaly scan showing bilateral hydronephrosis and oligohydramnios in the third trimester. He has so far passed only a few drops of urine; the midwife reports a palpable distended bladder. He has mild respiratory distress on room air. There is no antenatal MRI; he was delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery in a regional centre with a paediatric service and access to telehealth subspecialty advice.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 160, RR 64, SpO2 95% on room air
data_table.Examination: Distended bladder palpable to umbilicus, weak urinary stream when bladder pressed, no abdominal masses, no respiratory crackles
data_table.Investigations: Bedside bladder US confirms gross bladder distension and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis; Cr 110 micromol/L, K 5.4 mmol/L, urine output last 12 h 0.5 mL/kg/h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Pass a 6 Fr feeding tube to drain the bladder and arrange urgent paediatric urology transfer
Defer any intervention and recheck serum creatinine and bladder volume in 24 hours time
Commence IV furosemide 1 mg/kg now to maximise urine output before any catheter placement
Insert a 10 Fr Foley balloon catheter to maintain continuous drainage during transport in retrieval
Perform a single suprapubic aspiration only and discharge to outpatient urology follow up

stem: You are the GP responding to a code-blue call at a community health centre. A 9-month-old girl was being fed grated apple and is now in obvious respiratory distress with an ineffective weak cough, marked stridor and central cyanosis. She has been unable to vocalise for 20 seconds. A nurse is supporting her in a head-down prone position on the resuscitator's forearm. She has no known allergies and is fully immunised. There are no signs of trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70 bpm, falling, SpO2 70%, RR ineffective, central cyanosis
data_table.Examination: Unable to cry or cough, marked indrawing, decreased air entry bilaterally, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Not applicable in the acute setting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate manoeuvre?

options.text: Perform a finger sweep across the oropharynx to remove any directly visualised foreign body
Commence chest compressions at the 30:2 ratio immediately because the heart rate is below 80
Perform five abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre) just above the umbilicus in seated infant
Deliver up to five firm back blows between the scapulae in a head-down prone position
Administer 100% oxygen via tight-fitting non-rebreather mask and observe for spontaneous relief

stem: You are the neonatology fellow planning autumn discharge for an ex-29-week preterm girl, now 6 months corrected age and 4.8 kg, with established bronchopulmonary dysplasia requiring 0.25 L/min home oxygen at discharge. Her family lives in regional Victoria. RSV season is about to start in 4 weeks. Her older brother attends day care and the family includes a 2-year-old cousin sharing the household. Her mother asks what can be done to reduce her risk of severe bronchiolitis this season.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7°C, HR 130, RR 48 on 0.25 L/min via nasal prongs, SpO2 95%
data_table.Examination: Weight 4.8 kg (3rd centile), mild intercostal recession, scattered fine inspiratory crackles, no acute respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: Maternal antenatal RSV vaccination was not given (vaccine eligibility had not been reached before delivery), most recent chest X-ray: chronic interstitial changes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prevention strategy?

options.text: Commence oral montelukast 4 mg nightly to reduce post-bronchiolitis wheeze across the season
Administer monthly intramuscular palivizumab for the duration of the local RSV season
Single weight-based intramuscular nirsevimab dose before the start of the RSV season
