Standard hygiene and exposure-avoidance advice without any specific RSV pharmacoprophylaxis
Vaccinate the infant with the maternal recombinant RSV vaccine RSVpreF intramuscular dose

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in toddler with excessive cow milk intake
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 22-month-old boy whose mother reports he tires easily on walks and is increasingly pale. He drinks about 750 mL of full-cream cow milk a day from a bottle and refuses meat, eggs and fortified cereal. He was exclusively breastfed until 10 months. Vaccinations are up to date. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has no overt bleeding, no jaundice and no chronic illness. The blood film shows microcytic hypochromic red cells with anisocytosis.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 116, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, weight on 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival and palmar pallor; cardiovascular and abdominal examination otherwise normal; no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 64 fL, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, CRP 2 mg/L, reticulocytes low

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Trial a multivitamin syrup for six weeks before considering targeted iron treatment
Refer to paediatric haematology for an inpatient intravenous iron infusion
Oral elemental iron 3 mg/kg once daily and restrict cow milk to under 500 mL daily
Send haemoglobin electrophoresis to exclude thalassaemia before commencing treatment
Increase dietary iron alone and recheck the full blood count in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Atopic eczema stepped care in a toddler
stem: You are the GP seeing a 2-year-old girl with a 6-week history of dry itchy red flexural rashes at the antecubital and popliteal fossae, worse overnight and disturbing sleep. Her mother applies sorbolene cream twice a day. She has no infection signs and no oozing. Family history includes parental hay fever. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Vaccinations are up to date. There is no relevant medication history.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Lichenified erythematous plaques at flexures with excoriations; no honey-crust, no vesicles, no fever
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Continue sorbolene only and review again in eight weeks without active treatment
Apply hydrocortisone 1% to the flexures twice daily plus a thick emollient liberally
Commence oral prednisolone for 7 days alongside the existing sorbolene moisturiser
Start a daily non-sedating antihistamine without any change to topical treatment
Refer urgently to dermatology for ciclosporin without a trial of topical steroid first

subtopic_detail: Catch-up schedule for a partially vaccinated arrival
stem: You are the GP seeing a 14-month-old boy newly arrived from overseas. His written records confirm three doses of DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB at 2, 4 and 6 months, but no further immunisations. He is well, has no immunocompromise and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Mother asks what vaccines he should receive today to bring him up to schedule. Routine 12-month and 18-month doses are otherwise outstanding.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.5 °C, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well thriving toddler; growth on 50th centile; cardiovascular and respiratory unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Not required prior to catch-up immunisation

lead_in: Which combination of vaccines should be administered today?

options.text: DTPa-IPV booster only today and defer all other vaccines to the next scheduled visit
Defer immunisation until serology confirms current measles and varicella immune status
Hepatitis A vaccine and varicella vaccine only today and review again in four weeks
MMR plus meningococcal ACWY plus pneumococcal 13-valent at this visit using catch-up
Restart the schedule from infancy doses including DTPa, polio and hepatitis B today

subtopic_detail: Discrimination of ITP from HSP in school-age child with petechiae
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 5-year-old girl with two days of widespread bruising and mucosal bleeding from the gums. She had a viral upper respiratory illness two weeks ago. She has no fever, no joint swelling, no abdominal pain and no rash on the buttocks or legs. Examination shows scattered petechiae across the trunk and limbs with wet purpura on the buccal mucosa. Liver and spleen are not palpable. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 110, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, BP 100/64
data_table.Examination: Wet purpura on buccal mucosa, scattered petechiae trunk and limbs; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L, WCC 7.4, platelets 8 x10^9/L, blood film normal red and white cells, large platelets

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit and treat with intravenous immunoglobulin plus close inpatient bleeding observation
Discharge home with planned platelet recheck in one week and oral tranexamic acid
Commence oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day and review again in clinic in seven days
Order an urgent bone marrow aspirate prior to starting any specific drug therapy
Transfuse one adult unit of platelets immediately and admit for routine observation only

subtopic_detail: Undescended testis referral timing in a 9-month-old
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 9-month-old boy at his routine check. His mother says the right testis has never been visible in the scrotum. On examination, the right testis is palpable high in the inguinal canal and cannot be manipulated into the scrotum. The left testis is normally positioned. He was born at term and is otherwise well, with no abnormal genitalia, no hernia and no syndromic features. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6 °C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right testis high in inguinal canal, non-retractable; left testis normal; phallus normal; no inguinal hernia
data_table.Investigations: Imaging not indicated; karyotype not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Reassure parents and review the testicular position again at his 24-month visit
Refer to paediatric surgery so that orchidopexy can be planned before 18 months of age
Arrange a scrotal and inguinal ultrasound to confirm the position prior to any referral
Commence intramuscular human chorionic gonadotropin to encourage descent before surgery
Send karyotype and androgen receptor studies before deciding on any specific surgery

subtopic_detail: Timing of the switch from anti-inflammatory to antiplatelet aspirin after defervescence in Kawasaki disease
stem: A 3-year-old girl was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin for Kawasaki disease three days ago and has now been afebrile for 48 hours. She takes aspirin 30 mg/kg per day in four divided doses.

data_table.Examination: Well; rash resolved; early peeling of the fingertips
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiography at diagnosis showed normal coronary arteries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to her aspirin?

options.text: Reduce to 3 to 5 mg/kg once daily and continue it for six weeks
Continue 30 mg/kg per day in four divided doses for six more weeks
Stop aspirin now and review it after the next echocardiogram
Reduce to 3 to 5 mg/kg once daily and stop it after two weeks
Change to clopidogrel 1 mg/kg once daily in place of aspirin

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent cyanotic neonatal cardiac lesion presentation
stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to the postnatal ward at hour 36 of life. A term male is increasingly cyanosed and lethargic. He passed initial pulse oximetry screening. He now has central cyanosis, weak pulses in all four limbs and a hyperdynamic precordium without murmur. Pre-ductal SpO2 is 65% and post-ductal SpO2 is 64% in air, unchanged on 100% oxygen for 10 minutes. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.18, lactate 7.2 mmol/L, base excess -12, normal glucose.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.4 °C, HR 178, RR 70, SpO2 65% pre-ductal, 64% post-ductal, BP 56/34 mean 41
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, weak pulses all four limbs, no murmur, hepatomegaly 2 cm; no respiratory distress
data_table.Investigations: ECG normal QRS axis; CXR mildly enlarged cardiac silhouette, oligaemic lung fields

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 10 nanograms/kg/min and call cardiology
Increase FiO2 to 100% by nasal high flow and admit to special care nursery for monitoring
Treat for presumed early-onset sepsis with intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin only
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct the lactic acidosis
Commence dobutamine 5 micrograms/kg/min as inotropic support before any other measure

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a metropolitan tertiary centre admitting a 13-year-old girl with severe restrictive eating disorder who has not eaten for 10 days and has lost 14 kg over 6 months. She is alert but profoundly fatigued. She weighs 32 kg with a height of 158 cm (BMI 12.8 kg/m2). She has bradycardia and hypothermia. The dietitian asks for your prescription before commencing feeding via nasogastric tube.

The team plans to use a polymeric formula at 20 kcal/kg/day initially. Her admission electrolytes are at the lower end of normal but no oral or intravenous supplementation has yet been given.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 38 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg, Temp 35.4 degrees C, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Severe wasting, lanugo, cold peripheries, normal capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Phosphate 0.84 mmol/L, magnesium 0.72 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, ALT 92 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention before commencing enteral feeds?

options.text: Withhold all feeds for 48 hours while correcting electrolytes intravenously and observing on a cardiac monitor
Administer intravenous thiamine 100 mg followed by oral phosphate and magnesium supplementation, then start feeds
Commence enteral feeds at 40 kcal/kg/day immediately to address weight loss and reassess electrolytes daily
Give a single intravenous bolus of dextrose 10% 5 mL/kg to raise glucose before nasogastric feeding commences
Commence intravenous parenteral nutrition rather than enteral feeds to reduce the refeeding metabolic shift

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called urgently to the special care nursery. A 3-day-old term male infant has become progressively lethargic with poor feeding over 18 hours and now has tachypnoea without respiratory distress and intermittent posturing. He was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy. He fed eagerly for the first 36 hours then deteriorated. Birth weight was 3380 g. A septic screen has been sent and cultures are pending. The mother had a sister who died in the neonatal period of unknown cause.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 78, Temp 36.6 degrees C, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, intermittent extensor posturing, mild hepatomegaly, anterior fontanelle full
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.49, pCO2 22 mmHg, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, lactate 1.8 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, ammonia 420 micromol/L, ALT 38 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Stop protein-containing feeds, commence intravenous dextrose with intralipid, and arrange urgent haemodialysis
Increase enteral feeds with a high-protein neonatal formula to support growth and metabolic recovery
Commence intravenous aciclovir for presumed neonatal herpes encephalitis and await CSF results
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct acidosis and continue current feeds
Commence phenobarbital for presumed neonatal seizures and observe in the nursery overnight

stem:
You are the emergency registrar at a regional Queensland hospital during a 41 degrees C heatwave. A 15-year-old boy is brought in by ambulance after collapsing 90 minutes into a school cross-country event. He has been confused since collapse. He is now obtunded with hot dry skin despite cold packs applied in transit. Bystander first-aid included spraying him with water and fanning.

He has no known medical conditions. Weight is 60 kg. Estimated time since collapse is 35 minutes. Core (rectal) temperature has been recorded as 41.6 degrees C.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, RR 32, Temp 41.6 degrees C rectal, SpO2 95% room air
data_table.Examination: GCS 9 (E2 V3 M4), hot skin, capillary refill 4 seconds, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, creatinine 158 micromol/L, CK 12500 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate cooling strategy?

options.text: Iced gastric lavage via nasogastric tube as the primary cooling strategy in the resuscitation cubicle
Tepid sponging with continuous fanning while administering intravenous paracetamol 1 g and dantrolene
Cold-water immersion to bring core temperature to 39 degrees C as rapidly as possible while supporting airway and circulation
Cooled intravenous saline 30 mL/kg over 30 minutes as the primary cooling method with target normothermia
Defer aggressive cooling until intubation is performed and central venous access is established

stem: You are the emergency department resident assessing a 4-month-old boy brought in with a 3-day coryzal illness and worsening cough. He has taken only half his usual feeds for the last 12 hours and has not had a wet nappy for 8 hours. He was born at term with no comorbidities. His 3-year-old sister had a cold last week. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. No vaccines are overdue.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 168, RR 62, SpO2 92% room air
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, fine crackles bilaterally with wheeze, mild head bobbing, alert and tracking carers
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab pending; routine bloods and chest x-ray not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via mask with reassessment of respiratory work in 20 minutes after the dose
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose with planned review in the department in 4 hours from administration
Admit to the paediatric ward for standard low-flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 at least 90% with nasogastric feeding
Commence humidified nasal high-flow oxygen at 2 L/kg/min immediately as the initial respiratory support before any low-flow trial
Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin and ceftriaxone with admission for monitoring of presumed bacterial co-infection in this infant

stem: You are the after-hours emergency department registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy brought in with one day of coryza and a barking cough that started this evening. He has stridor audible at rest and mild intercostal recession but is interactive, smiling at his parents and has good colour. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. There are no immunisation gaps and no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 130, RR 36, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor at rest with mild intercostal recession, no cyanosis, no agitation, alert and interactive
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg via mask and reassess respiratory effort in 20 minutes
Nebulised adrenaline 0.5 mL/kg of 1 in 1000 and prepare for paediatric intubation
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg now and admit for intravenous antibiotic therapy
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose and observe in the department for 4 hours
Endotracheal intubation in theatre with ENT and anaesthetics teams on standby

stem: You are the GP reviewing an 18-month-old girl brought in by her mother with a 2-day history of fever and irritability, now refusing to lie flat and tugging at both ears. She is otherwise well, immunisations are up to date, and the family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. She has no eczema, no rash, and no recorded penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 150, RR 30, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes red and bulging with absent light reflex; neck supple; chest clear; no rash; no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days plus paracetamol for analgesia
Watchful waiting with paracetamol and review by phone in 48 hours if no improvement
Topical chloramphenicol ear drops for both ears with daily fluids and analgesia
Oral pseudoephedrine for 7 days with paracetamol and ibuprofen alternating for pain
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for 3 days with delayed antibiotic prescription if needed

stem: You are the GP seeing a 3-year-old girl brought by her mother with a 3-month history of hard infrequent stools every 5 to 7 days, soiling episodes and stool withholding posture during the day. There are no red flags: no blood per rectum, no abdominal distension, normal growth, normal back and anus on examination, and no delayed meconium at birth. The family is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Normal for age
data_table.Examination: Soft palpable faecal mass in the left lower quadrant; normal anus and back; normal lower limb neurology; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Lactulose 1 mL/kg twice daily as the sole pharmacological treatment for 2 weeks
Macrogol 3350 with electrolytes disimpaction regimen followed by daily maintenance dosing
Daily oral senna alone with dietary fibre advice and toilet sitting after meals
Refer to paediatric surgery for examination under anaesthetic and inpatient bowel washout
Daily PR phosphate enemas for one week and then dietary fibre advice alone

subtopic_detail: Household pertussis chemoprophylaxis with infant under 6 months
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 32-year-old mother with 3 weeks of paroxysmal cough and post-tussive vomiting. Pertussis PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab is positive. She lives with her 6-week-old infant who received the 6-week DTPa-IPV-Hib-HepB dose 3 days ago, a healthy 4-year-old who is up to date with vaccines, and her partner who had Tdap 12 years ago. None are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Mother: HR 76, BP 118/74, SpO2 98% room air; infant examined separately and well
data_table.Examination: Mother coughs intermittently during consultation; infant is feeding well with no apnoea, no cough and no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Maternal pertussis PCR positive; infant pertussis PCR not yet sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate post-exposure plan for the household?

options.text: Treat the mother with azithromycin and provide red flag advice only to the other household members
Vaccinate the 6-week-old with an accelerated DTPa dose and the adults with Tdap boosters
Test the 4-year-old and partner with PCR first and treat only those who return a positive result
Defer chemoprophylaxis pending the public health unit's instructions on close contacts
Give azithromycin chemoprophylaxis to the infant, sibling and adults alongside treating the mother

stem: You are the GP in a regional clinic seeing a 14-year-old girl brought urgently by her mother. She is drowsy after 8 hours of fever, severe headache and one episode of vomiting. In the last 30 minutes a non-blanching petechial rash has appeared on her trunk and limbs. The nearest emergency department is 90 minutes away by road. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. She has no documented antibiotic allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 130, RR 28, BP 92/56, SpO2 96% room air, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching petechial rash on trunk and limbs; warm peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds; mild neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L; lactate not available; venous access not yet established

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action in your clinic?

options.text: Administer intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg now and arrange urgent retrieval transfer
Wait for paramedic arrival to gain intravenous access before any antibiotic is given
Give intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and arrange retrieval transfer without antibiotic
Prescribe oral ciprofloxacin chemoprophylaxis to the family and transfer the patient
Transfer the patient to hospital without any antibiotic to avoid blood culture contamination

subtopic_detail: Episodic viral wheeze in preschooler without maintenance ICS
stem: You are the GP reviewing a 2-year-old boy whose mother reports this is his fourth wheeze episode this winter, each triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection. Between episodes he is symptom-free, has no nocturnal cough and no exercise limitation. He has no eczema, no allergic rhinitis and no family history of atopy. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has had no oral steroid courses to date.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 °C, HR 130, RR 36, SpO2 96% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild expiratory wheeze bilaterally with minimal recession; alert and feeding well; no nasal flare; symmetric air entry
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry not feasible at this age; chest x-ray not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Commence daily inhaled fluticasone 100 microgram twice daily via spacer for 12 weeks
Add daily oral montelukast and continue salbutamol as needed for symptom relief
Salbutamol via spacer as needed during episodes without maintenance inhaled corticosteroid
Refer for allergy skin prick testing before any decision on inhaled treatment is made
Prescribe a 5-day course of oral prednisolone now and review again in 4 weeks

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis of the hip discrimination from transient synovitis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old boy with 2 days of right hip pain, refusal to weight bear and progressive limp. He has had a low-grade temperature and looks unwell at triage. He has no recent trauma, no preceding viral illness and no rash. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 °C, HR 132, RR 24, BP 100/60, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Refusal to weight bear, hip held in flexion and external rotation, severe pain on log-roll and any internal rotation; no rash, no other joint involvement
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 95 mg/L, ESR 52 mm/h, blood culture pending; hip ultrasound shows joint effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with oral cefalexin and review in primary care in 48 hours if not better
Repeat ultrasound in 24 hours and start treatment only if the effusion has grown
Trial of weight bearing with regular ibuprofen and outpatient orthopaedic review
Start intravenous flucloxacillin without joint aspiration and reassess in 24 hours
Urgent hip aspiration in theatre with washout and empirical intravenous flucloxacillin

stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing an 11-year-old girl with four weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. She has had no vomiting and is alert and well perfused. Her family has no history of diabetes. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Her mother is keen to take her home if it is safe.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 92, BP 110/68, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well perfused, no acetone breath, no Kussmaul breathing, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: BSL 22 mmol/L, capillary ketones 1.4 mmol/L, venous pH 7.36, HCO3 22 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 58 micromol/L, HbA1c 11.6%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% saline and commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hour with hourly capillary glucose monitoring
Admit for intravenous maintenance fluids and oral fluids only with insulin deferred until capillary ketones have cleared below 0.6 mmol/L
Admit under the paediatric diabetes team for subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin initiation, structured education and a written sick-day plan before discharge
Discharge on metformin 500 mg twice daily with outpatient paediatric endocrinology review and home glucose monitoring within one week
Start subcutaneous long-acting insulin glargine alone with discharge home and outpatient diabetes review arranged for 48 hours later

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 22-month-old boy whose parents are concerned that he is pale and tires easily. He drinks around 900 mL of cow's milk daily, refuses meat and prefers crackers. He was born at term and is otherwise well. There is no history of jaundice, dark urine or recent infection. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 116, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no scleral icterus, no hepatosplenomegaly, soft systolic flow murmur
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 64 fL, MCH 19 pg, RDW 17.5%, platelets 480 x10^9/L, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, CRP 3 mg/L, reticulocyte count 0.7%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange transfusion of packed red cells in the paediatric day unit and refer to paediatric haematology for further evaluation
Start oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily, reduce cow's milk to under 500 mL/day and review with full blood count in 4 weeks
Order haemoglobin electrophoresis, direct antiglobulin test and serum lactate dehydrogenase before starting any treatment to exclude haemoglobinopathy
Refer for an intravenous iron infusion in the outpatient setting now and continue current dietary intake while awaiting the appointment
Reassure the family that the findings reflect a physiological dietary phase and review in three months without starting any pharmacological treatment

subtopic_detail: Moderate atopic eczema flare topical step-up
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 3-year-old girl with a one-week flare of itchy, weeping eczema on her cheeks and antecubital fossae. She has been using a daily soap substitute and 1% hydrocortisone for two weeks without improvement. There is no honey-coloured crust, no fever and no spreading erythema. She is otherwise well and has no allergies. The parents are reluctant to use stronger topical steroids.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Erythematous, weeping eczema on face and flexures, lichenification at popliteal fossae, no pustules or crusting, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Continue 1% hydrocortisone twice daily indefinitely with daily bleach baths and refer to a paediatric dermatologist for biologic therapy assessment
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for five days and review in clinic at the end of the course before tapering the dose
Commence oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily empirically for ten days and continue current topical regimen unchanged
Step up to methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% ointment once daily for two weeks, continue emollients and soap substitutes and review at the end of the course
Trial topical pimecrolimus 1% cream twice daily without any topical corticosteroid for a fortnight and review the response in clinic at that point

subtopic_detail: Urinary tract infection empirical antibiotic in a young child
stem: You are the emergency department registrar assessing a 14-month-old girl with 2 days of fever and irritability. She is feeding poorly but is alert and tracking carers. There is no cough, coryza or rash. She has no allergies and has had no recent antibiotics. A clean-catch urine sample has been collected. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.2 °C, HR 158, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, clear chest, soft abdomen, no rash, ears and throat normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: leucocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood trace, protein 1+. Urine microscopy and culture pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical management while awaiting urine culture?

options.text: Start oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 7 days while awaiting culture and review at the end of the course with the GP
Admit for intravenous gentamicin pending the urine culture result and reassess for an oral switch at 48 hours of treatment
Start oral trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole at standard paediatric dosing for 7 days and arrange follow-up with the GP at the end of the course
Start oral amoxicillin alone at standard paediatric dosing for 5 days with planned follow-up with the GP at the end of the antibiotic course
Reassure the family and arrange a repeat urine specimen at the GP in 48 hours with antibiotics deferred until microscopy and culture return positive results

subtopic_detail: Henoch-Schoenlein purpura with abdominal pain and normal renal function
stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 6-year-old boy who has had a non-blanching palpable purpuric rash over his buttocks and lower legs for five days. He now has colicky periumbilical pain and one episode of bile-stained vomiting. He has had a cold two weeks before this presentation. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. He has no oedema and is passing normal urine volumes.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 110, BP 102/64, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and lower limbs, swollen tender ankles, soft abdomen with periumbilical tenderness, no peritonism, no scrotal swelling
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: blood 2+, protein 1+, no nitrites or leucocytes. Urine protein:creatinine 32 mg/mmol. Creatinine 32 micromol/L, albumin 38 g/L. FBC and CRP normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows thickened proximal small bowel without intussusception.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for emergent laparotomy because of bile-stained vomiting and abdominal pain in a child with palpable purpura
Start intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for three days and admit to the paediatric intensive care unit for monitoring
Reassure the family that this is a self-limiting illness and discharge home with simple analgesia and outpatient follow-up arranged in six weeks
Initiate oral cyclophosphamide and azathioprine in conjunction with prednisolone and refer to paediatric nephrology for outpatient review within one week
Admit for analgesia, intravenous fluids and oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for two weeks with weekly urinalysis and blood pressure monitoring for six months

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease treatment within ten days of fever onset
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old boy on day 6 of fever above 39 °C. He has a polymorphous truncal rash, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a strawberry tongue and a unilateral cervical lymph node measuring 1.7 cm. His hands and feet are erythematous and swollen. He has had no diarrhoea and his immunisations are current. Throat swab for group A streptococcus is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 156, BP 95/58, RR 26, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Polymorphous rash, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, 1.7 cm right cervical node, swollen hands and feet, no peeling yet
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, platelets 540 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 92 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urinalysis: sterile pyuria. Throat swab negative. Echocardiogram requested.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin 50 mg/kg daily for ten days and review for clinical response and rash resolution at the end of the antibiotic course
Reassure the family that this is likely a viral exanthem with reactive cervical lymphadenitis and discharge home with simple antipyretic advice and review
Order an echocardiogram first and defer all systemic treatment until coronary artery dimensions are formally confirmed by the paediatric cardiology service
Admit for intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily, with echocardiography arranged within the admission
Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily monotherapy and arrange outpatient paediatric rheumatology follow-up within five working days of presentation

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice with ABO incompatibility and phototherapy threshold
stem: You are the neonatal resident reviewing a 38-hour-old term boy who appears jaundiced down to his upper thighs. He was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery to a healthy mother whose blood group is O Rh-positive. The baby's blood group is A Rh-positive. He is breastfeeding 3 to 4 hourly with good attachment. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 138, RR 46, SpO2 98% room air, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, vigorous suck, well perfused, jaundiced to upper thighs, no scalp haematoma, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 305 micromol/L (conjugated 12 micromol/L), Hb 158 g/L, reticulocytes 5%, direct antiglobulin test weakly positive, blood group A Rh-positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue routine breastfeeding without phototherapy or specific intervention and arrange a community midwife review at 72 hours of life for jaundice
Switch the infant to formula feeding for 24 hours, withhold breastfeeding and reassess the bilirubin trend after one full day of replacement feeds only
Commence intensive phototherapy, continue breastfeeding with supplementation if intake is inadequate and recheck bilirubin and haematocrit in 4 to 6 hours
Arrange immediate double-volume exchange transfusion in the neonatal intensive care unit as the initial intervention for haemolytic neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia
Administer a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg now and recheck the total bilirubin in six hours before deciding on additional phototherapy

subtopic_detail: Simple febrile convulsion in a toddler
stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 22-month-old boy who had a single 90 second generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home during a fever from a viral upper respiratory illness. He is now fully alert, feeding and interacting normally. He has had no previous seizures and his development is age appropriate. His older sister had two similar episodes as a toddler. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 °C, HR 140, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, no neck stiffness, no rash, ENT shows red bulging tympanic membranes bilaterally, soft abdomen, normal neurological exam
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L; no further investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent outpatient electroencephalogram and brain MRI within two weeks and refer to the paediatric neurology clinic
Discharge home with parental education on febrile convulsion recurrence, fever management and clear ambulance call criteria for prolonged events
Commence regular oral sodium valproate prophylaxis 10 mg/kg twice daily for six months given the positive family history and review in clinic
Admit overnight for cardiorespiratory monitoring and intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg pending blood culture and lumbar puncture results
Prescribe rectal diazepam 5 mg for the parents to administer at the onset of every future fever to prevent recurrence and review in clinic

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media in a toddler
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 20-month-old non-Aboriginal girl with 24 hours of fever, irritability and ear pulling. She has had no previous ear infections and immunisations are up to date. She has no penicillin allergy. There is no ear discharge and she has been drinking but not eating. The parents are keen to avoid unnecessary medications.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7 °C, HR 138, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous with loss of light reflex, left tympanic membrane normal, no mastoid tenderness, oropharynx unremarkable, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for five days and arrange review if symptoms worsen or persist beyond 48 hours
Arrange watchful waiting with paracetamol and ibuprofen analgesia for 48 hours before deciding whether to commence antibiotic therapy
Prescribe oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily for seven days as a broader-spectrum alternative given the bulging tympanic membrane
Refer urgently to the emergency department for intravenous benzylpenicillin and ENT review to exclude evolving mastoiditis given the high fever
Prescribe topical ciprofloxacin ear drops twice daily for seven days plus oral paracetamol and ibuprofen for analgesia at home

stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 10-week-old non-Aboriginal infant brought in by ambulance with three days of coryza and worsening cough. He is breastfeeding only every five hours instead of every three. He has had no apnoeas reported by the parents. His older sibling has the same illness. Birth was at term and there is no congenital cardiac history.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 158, RR 62, SpO2 92% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, audible wheeze, widespread fine crackles, capillary refill 2 seconds, normal fontanelle, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate respiratory syncytial virus positive; chest x-ray not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with parental education on feeding cues and warning signs and arrange general practice review the following morning
Admit for nasogastric or intravenous hydration with supplemental oxygen titrated to maintain saturations above 92% and ongoing observation
Trial inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess after 20 minutes before deciding on further management of his work of breathing
Administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg now and arrange a chest x-ray to assess for bacterial complication before deciding on admission
Start empiric oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for five days to cover bacterial superinfection and arrange paediatric clinic review in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Chronic functional constipation in a school-aged child
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with six months of hard stools every five to seven days associated with abdominal pain and recent soiling episodes at school. He has no rectal bleeding, no weight loss and growth tracks along the 50th centile. There is no family history of inflammatory bowel disease. He drinks little water and has a fussy diet. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa, normal perianal inspection, anal wink present, normal lower limb tone and reflexes
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange abdominal x-ray and serum coeliac antibodies and refer to paediatric gastroenterology before starting any laxative therapy
Commence oral macrogol 3350 disimpaction over three days followed by maintenance dosing, with toileting program and dietary advice
Prescribe a sodium phosphate enema in clinic now and review for further enemas if the impaction does not clear within 48 hours of disimpaction
Trial dietary fibre supplementation and increased oral fluids alone for four weeks without pharmacological laxatives before reassessment in clinic
Start oral senna 7.5 mg nightly as monotherapy and review in two weeks to assess soiling frequency and frequency of bowel motions

subtopic_detail: Severe croup with stridor at rest
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old boy with two days of barking cough and worsening stridor for the last three hours. He has biphasic stridor at rest and obvious sternal recession. He is anxious and clinging to his mother but maintains eye contact. He has no drooling and is fully immunised. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.1 °C, HR 152, RR 44, SpO2 94% room air
data_table.Examination: Loud biphasic stridor at rest, marked sternal and intercostal recession, hoarse voice, no drooling, no trismus, chest air entry reduced bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Bedside observation only; no investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mg in 5 mL saline plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe for at least four hours
Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose and discharge home with parental education about returning if stridor recurs at rest
Arrange urgent lateral neck x-ray and intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg pending findings before deciding on airway management with anaesthetics
Trial inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer and reassess after 20 minutes before deciding whether to administer corticosteroid therapy
Intubate immediately in the resuscitation bay with rapid sequence induction and admit to paediatric intensive care for ongoing ventilatory support

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old non-Aboriginal boy with a one-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and three days of vomiting. He has lost 3 kg and is breathing deeply at rest. He has not previously been diagnosed with diabetes. He is alert and oriented, capillary refill is three seconds and mucous membranes are dry. His weight today is 25 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0 °C, HR 132, BP 102/64, RR 30, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Deep Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, GCS 15, soft non-tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: BSL 26 mmol/L, capillary ketones 5.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.18, HCO3 9 mmol/L, Na 132 mmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, urea 9.1 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, corrected sodium 136 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid prescription for the first hour?

options.text: 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 60 minutes followed by deficit plus maintenance calculated over 48 hours with potassium added
20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus over 20 minutes repeated until perfusion improves followed by maintenance fluids at twice the normal rate
Commence intravenous 8.4% sodium bicarbonate infusion at 2 mmol/kg over the first hour to correct the acidosis before fluids and insulin
Start intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately and withhold all crystalloid fluids until the blood glucose has fallen below 14 mmol/L
Give 5% dextrose in 0.45% sodium chloride at twice maintenance rate immediately to provide glucose substrate and prevent further ketogenesis before insulin

subtopic_detail: Unexplained bruising in a non-mobile infant
stem: You are the paediatric resident reviewing a 5-month-old non-Aboriginal infant brought to the emergency department by her mother for unsettled crying. She is not yet rolling. While undressing her you notice two purple bruises over the left mandible and one over the right pinna. Her mother says she has not noticed them and gives no clear mechanism. The child is otherwise alert and feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 100% room air
data_table.Examination: Two 1 cm purple bruises over left mandible, one over right pinna, anterior fontanelle soft, no torn frenulum, no skeletal tenderness, normal neurological exam
data_table.Investigations: FBE, coagulation studies, LFTs and lipase pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for skeletal survey, head CT, ophthalmology review for retinal haemorrhages, and immediate child protection notification to the relevant state authority
Discharge home with safety netting advice once coagulation studies return normal, and arrange general practitioner review in 48 hours for ongoing assessment
Reassure the mother that bruising in this distribution is common in infants and arrange paediatric outpatient review within one week for reassessment
Request a urine drug screen and a metabolic bone disease panel to exclude inherited causes before notifying any external agencies of suspected harm
Refer to the social work team for community follow-up only and arrange return for repeat examination in two weeks if any further bruises appear at home

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old non-Aboriginal infant brought in by his parents for tactile fever and reduced feeding for 12 hours. He was born at term, breastfed and previously well. He has no rash and no cough. His mother had a negative group B Streptococcus screen at 36 weeks and labour was uncomplicated. He has not received any antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 °C rectal, HR 168, RR 52, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Examination: Pink, perfused, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no rash, normal tone, no focus of infection identified on full undressed examination
data_table.Investigations: Pending - FBE, blood culture, urine via catheter, lumbar puncture, CRP, viral PCR

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home on oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily with general practice review in 24 hours and clear advice about returning for warning signs
Admit for full septic screen including lumbar puncture and commence intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending culture results
Perform urinalysis and chest x-ray only, and observe for four hours in the short stay unit before deciding on antibiotics if no source is identified
Admit for observation without antibiotics until blood culture or urine culture results are available, given that the infant currently looks well clinically
Start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg monotherapy and admit for observation without performing a lumbar puncture in a well-appearing infant

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease recognition and IVIG window
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old non-Aboriginal boy on day 6 of fever. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked red lips with a strawberry tongue, a polymorphous truncal rash, and a single left cervical lymph node measuring 17 mm. His hands and feet are swollen and erythematous. He is irritable but not septic. His mother is asking when his fever will resolve.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1 °C, HR 158, RR 32, SpO2 98% room air, BP 95/55 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, fissured lips, indurated palms and soles, polymorphous trunk rash, one left cervical node 17 mm, no meningism, chest clear, no murmur, soft abdomen
data_table.Investigations: WCC 17.5 x10^9/L (neutrophils 13.2), platelets 555 x10^9/L, CRP 145 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 92 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urinalysis 25 WBC/HPF sterile, throat swab negative for group A strep

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial cervical lymphadenitis with systemic features and review cultures at 48 hours
Admit, commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours and oral aspirin, and arrange a baseline transthoracic echocardiogram
Send paired viral PCR including adenovirus and measles, withhold treatment, and review in 48 hours once the viral panel results have been formally reported
Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as initial monotherapy and review in the general paediatric clinic within three days
Reassure that this is viral exanthem with reactive adenopathy, prescribe regular paracetamol and oral fluids, and review in primary care in 48 hours if not improving

stem: You are the special care nursery resident reviewing a 60-hour-old term non-Aboriginal infant born at 39+2 weeks by uncomplicated vaginal birth. The midwives noted yellow sclerae and the transcutaneous bilirubinometer reads above the screening threshold. The mother is blood group O Rh-positive; cord blood was not sent. The baby is breastfeeding 6 times in 24 hours and has lost 7% of birth weight. There is no cephalohaematoma and no family history of haemolytic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 144, RR 46, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, jaundice to mid-thigh, no plethora, no hepatosplenomegaly, normal tone and Moro, suck coordinated
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin 320 micromol/L (gestation-and-age threshold for phototherapy 290; exchange 430), conjugated fraction 6 micromol/L, FBC Hb 175 g/L reticulocytes 4%, blood group O Rh-positive, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion under intensive care given the rising bilirubin trajectory and risk of acute bilirubin encephalopathy
Withhold phototherapy, supplement with formula top-ups of 30 mL every three hours, and repeat the bilirubin in 12 hours before deciding treatment
Commence intensive phototherapy, continue frequent breastfeeding with lactation support, and repeat serum bilirubin in 6 hours to confirm a downward trend
Commence intravenous immunoglobulin infusion to slow ongoing haemolysis and arrange transfer to the neonatal intensive care nursery for cardiorespiratory monitoring
Discharge home with parental education on jaundice warning signs and arrange routine community midwife review at 5 days of life for a repeat bilirubin

subtopic_detail: Paediatric anaphylaxis intramuscular adrenaline dose band
stem: You are the emergency department resident called to a 4-year-old non-Aboriginal boy who collapsed at a family meal where he was unknowingly given cashew. Within 10 minutes he developed urticaria, lip swelling and audible wheeze. He has known anaphylaxis to peanut. His EpiPen Jr was administered by his father 3 minutes before arrival. On arrival he remains wheezy with a hoarse cry and is sleepy but rousable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 156, RR 36, SpO2 90% room air rising to 96% on 8 L/min via face mask, BP 78/40 mmHg, weight estimated 16 kg by Broselow tape
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, marked lip and tongue swelling, audible stridor and biphasic wheeze, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 13 (eyes 3, verbal 4, motor 6)
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.6 mmol/L; no further investigations yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intramuscular promethazine 0.5 mg/kg, give nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000, and arrange urgent ENT review for the stridor
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.30 mL into the lateral thigh, give 200 mg hydrocortisone IV, and continue 8 L oxygen via face mask
Administer intravenous adrenaline 10 micrograms/kg bolus once intravenous access is established, sit him upright and prepare nebulised salbutamol
Administer intramuscular adrenaline 1:1000 at 0.15 mL into the lateral thigh, lay him flat with legs elevated, and prepare a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus
Withhold further adrenaline as one dose has been given, administer nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back-to-back, and reassess after the bronchodilator has been delivered

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old non-Aboriginal infant with a 9-day history of coryza now followed by 3 days of paroxysmal coughing spells ending in cyanosis and post-tussive vomiting. There is no inspiratory whoop. He has had one apnoeic episode of 25 seconds witnessed by his mother. His older brother had a bronchitic illness 3 weeks ago. The mother declined pertussis vaccination in pregnancy; the infant has not yet received his 6-week immunisations. The household includes a 28-week pregnant aunt.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 168, RR 56 between coughs, SpO2 91% room air, 96% on 1 L nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Alert between coughs, mild subcostal recession, chest clear between paroxysms, no focal crackles or wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: WCC 32 x10^9/L with absolute lymphocytosis 22 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, chest X-ray clear, nasopharyngeal PCR pending for Bordetella pertussis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with reassurance pending the nasopharyngeal PCR result, withhold antibiotics until the test confirms a positive result, and review in 48 hours in the general paediatric clinic
Discharge home on oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days with parental education on cough monitoring and ambulance criteria for cyanotic episodes
Admit, commence oral erythromycin ethyl succinate 40 mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses for 7 days, and continue intravenous fluid maintenance until feeding improves
Admit, commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours, and arrange a lumbar puncture to exclude bacterial meningitis as a cause of the apnoea
Admit to a monitored bed, commence oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily for 5 days, and arrange household contact post-exposure prophylaxis through public health

subtopic_detail: Reye-like syndrome in a child given aspirin during varicella
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-year-old non-Aboriginal girl admitted with 24 hours of incessant vomiting, irritability and increasing somnolence. Five days earlier she developed a vesicular rash that her grandmother managed with regular oral aspirin 300 mg every 4 hours obtained from an overseas pharmacy. She has no other medical conditions and her immunisations are otherwise up to date. There is no fever, no diarrhoea and no recent travel. Her mother brought her in because she became confused and combative an hour ago.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 132, RR 28 with intermittent yawning, SpO2 98% room air, BP 108/60 mmHg, capillary glucose 3.2 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Crusted varicella lesions on trunk and scalp, GCS 11 (eyes 2, verbal 4, motor 5) with hyperreflexia and brisk plantars, no neck stiffness, no focal deficit, liver edge palpable 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: ALT 1180 U/L, AST 1420 U/L, ammonia 165 micromol/L (normal under 50), INR 2.4, bilirubin 22 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, paracetamol level not detected, salicylate 1.8 mmol/L, CT brain shows diffuse cerebral oedema without focal lesion

lead_in: What is the single best initial intervention?

options.text: Administer N-acetylcysteine 150 mg/kg loading dose, withhold dextrose to avoid hyperglycaemia, and transfer to a ward bed for further serial liver function monitoring
Cease aspirin, escalate to paediatric intensive care for intracranial pressure management with intravenous 10% dextrose, hypertonic saline and head-of-bed elevation
Commence intravenous aciclovir 500 mg/m2 every 8 hours and intravenous ceftriaxone, perform a lumbar puncture once cerebral imaging is clear, and admit to the ward
Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg via nasogastric tube, give sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to alkalinise the urine, and arrange transfer for haemodialysis of salicylate
Withhold all medications, observe in the short stay unit overnight, and arrange a metabolic screen including urine organic acids before deciding further management

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old non-Aboriginal boy 2 weeks after admission for Henoch-Schonlein purpura with palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs and severe abdominal pain that resolved on a short steroid course. His joint swelling and skin lesions have resolved. He is otherwise well and eating normally. His parents want to know what follow-up is needed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 96, RR 20, BP 108/68 mmHg (above the 95th centile for height and age)
data_table.Examination: Fading post-inflammatory pigmentation on buttocks and lower legs, no active purpura, no joint swelling, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 2+ protein 1+, urine protein:creatinine ratio 38 mg/mmol (normal under 20), serum creatinine 38 micromol/L, albumin 36 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents, plan routine urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for 12 months, and refer to paediatric nephrology for ongoing assessment
Discharge to primary care with no further follow-up given the rash has resolved and the patient is otherwise clinically well at this stage
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and arrange urgent renal biopsy on the inpatient ward to confirm the diagnosis and grade severity
Arrange a routine review in 6 months and rely on parental observation for blood pressure changes or new rash with no scheduled urinalysis testing in the interim
Commence amlodipine 2.5 mg daily for the elevated blood pressure and review the urinalysis result in 6 weeks at the general practice clinic for further plan

subtopic_detail: Acute gastroenteritis in a toddler with mild dehydration
stem: You are the paediatric emergency resident reviewing a 14-month-old non-Aboriginal girl with 36 hours of watery non-bloody diarrhoea and three episodes of vomiting earlier in the day. She has been refusing breastfeeds but accepts sips of water. She lives at home with vaccinated siblings, attended childcare in the last week, and had her rotavirus immunisations on schedule. She is alert, plays in mother's lap and has cried tears during examination. Her parents are worried about her not eating solids.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, capillary refill 2 seconds, weight 9.2 kg (down from 9.7 kg one week ago at the child health nurse visit)
data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, mucous membranes mildly dry, eyes not sunken, anterior fontanelle closed, abdomen soft non-tender, bowel sounds active, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.4 mmol/L, urinalysis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer single-dose ondansetron 2 mg orally, observe for 30 minutes, then commence oral rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for the first hour
Insert a peripheral cannula and commence intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose at maintenance plus deficit replacement over 24 hours
Commence oral rehydration solution at 50 mL/kg over 4 hours given in 5 mL aliquots every 5 minutes, continue breastfeeding, and review at 4 hours
Insert a nasogastric tube and commence rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours given the failure of breastfeeding and the recent weight loss noted
Prescribe loperamide 0.2 mg/kg as a single dose to reduce stool losses and discharge home with parental advice to push high-sugar fluids such as apple juice

subtopic_detail: Positive newborn screen with raised immunoreactive trypsinogen
stem: You are the paediatric registrar at the regional CF service called by a community midwife about a 12-day-old non-Aboriginal infant whose newborn screening card returned a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen with two CFTR mutations identified on the second-tier panel. The infant is asymptomatic, breastfeeding well and has regained birth weight. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. The parents have just been told there is a problem with the screening test and are anxious.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well-perfused, chest clear, abdomen soft with normal stools, no nasal polyps, no failure to thrive
data_table.Investigations: Newborn screening IRT raised, CFTR genotype Phe508del / G551D, confirmatory tests not yet performed

lead_in: What is the single best next step?

options.text: Refer to the general paediatric clinic in 6 weeks for routine review, with no specific cystic fibrosis testing planned until symptoms appear or weight gain falters in early infancy
Reassure the parents that the raised immunoreactive trypsinogen is a common false positive and arrange a repeat newborn screening card in 4 weeks before further action
Commence pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy 2000 units lipase per 120 mL feed and arrange a chest X-ray plus high-resolution CT within the week to assess for bronchiectasis
Arrange urgent referral to the tertiary paediatric cystic fibrosis clinic for sweat chloride testing and structured family counselling within 1 week
Initiate oral azithromycin 5 mg/kg three times weekly for prophylaxis against Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation and order nasal swab surveillance every 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis severity and respiratory support escalation
stem: You are the paediatric resident on the inpatient ward reviewing a 7-week-old term infant on day 4 of a coryzal illness. He is breastfeeding only 40% of usual volumes and has had two episodes of brief apnoea overnight without colour change. He has no risk factors for chronic lung disease and is fully immunised for age. The night nursing team have escalated because of increasing work of breathing despite low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6 °C, HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 92% on 1 L nasal prongs, BP 78/48 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, tracheal tug, widespread fine inspiratory crackles, mild expiratory wheeze, alert but tiring, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for RSV, capillary blood gas pH 7.31, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, no chest radiograph performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min titrated to SpO2 at least 90%, start nasogastric feeds, and reassess after 2 hours before escalation
Commence inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes plus nebulised hypertonic saline 3% three times daily to reduce mucus plugging
Switch directly to humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 titrated to SpO2 above 92% without a low-flow trial first
Arrange immediate rapid sequence intubation and ventilation in PICU given the apnoeic episodes and the rising capillary blood gas carbon dioxide
Commence humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and liaise with paediatric retrieval and intensive care services immediately on arrival

subtopic_detail: Moderate-severe croup nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone
stem: You are the emergency department registrar reviewing a 16-month-old non-Aboriginal boy brought in at 02:00 with a 24-hour history of barking cough, hoarse voice and noisy breathing. He has stridor at rest and moderate sternal recession but remains pink in air. His mother says he has had similar but milder episodes twice before that settled at home. He is fully immunised and has no chronic conditions.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 °C, HR 158, RR 42, SpO2 96% room air, BP 92/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate sternal and intercostal recession, hoarse cry, alert and consolable on mother's lap, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed; bedside Westley croup score 6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg as a single dose, give paracetamol for fever and discharge home with safety-net advice if symptoms have settled within four hours of observation
Commence nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back, add ipratropium bromide and reassess in 30 minutes for response to bronchodilator therapy and need for paediatric admission

Administer nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with oxygen and concurrent oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, then observe in the department for 3 hours (RCH minimum) with attention to recurrence of stridor at rest
Take lateral neck radiograph and arrange urgent ENT review for direct laryngoscopy in theatre because of recurrent stridor and possible foreign body or epiglottitis given his age and presentation

Provide humidified oxygen via face mask, position on parent's lap and reassess every 15 minutes for spontaneous improvement before considering any pharmacological intervention or admission to the ward

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 5-month-old girl who has been admitted with her first febrile urinary tract infection. She responded to intravenous cefotaxime within 24 hours, defervesced and is now feeding well; there are no atypical features. Urine culture grew Escherichia coli sensitive to cefalexin and trimethoprim. Antenatal anomaly scans were complete and normal, and her parents have no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9 °C, HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, BP 88/52 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, soft non-tender abdomen, no palpable bladder or flank mass, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Mid-stream clean catch urine: leucocytes 250/microL, nitrites positive, culture E. coli over 100 x10^6 CFU/L cefotaxime sensitive; FBC, UEC and CRP within paediatric reference ranges after treatment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan from here?

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound during this admission and a micturating cystourethrogram if hydronephrosis or scarring is demonstrated on the scan
No additional imaging is required after this typical first urinary tract infection; counsel the family on prompt presentation for any future febrile illness
Arrange a DMSA renogram within 4 weeks and a micturating cystourethrogram for all infants under 12 months after a first febrile urinary tract infection regardless of severity
Arrange computed tomography of the urinary tract during this admission to exclude calculus and complex anomaly given the young age of the infant and high colony count
Commence long-term low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis at 2 mg/kg nocte and defer renal tract imaging until age 2 years unless a further breakthrough urinary tract infection develops

subtopic_detail: Suspected meningococcal sepsis lumbar puncture timing
stem: You are the night paediatric registrar at a tertiary children's hospital. A 22-month-old non-Aboriginal boy has been transferred by retrieval after 8 hours of fever and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash on the trunk and limbs. He was alert in the field but is now drowsy, with rising oxygen requirements and prolonged capillary refill despite 40 mL/kg of crystalloid given pre-transfer. The retrieval team has commenced ceftriaxone empirically and asks what investigation pathway you want pursued on arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 °C, HR 188, RR 48, SpO2 92% on 6 L Hudson, BP 78/40 mmHg, capillary refill 5 seconds, GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Examination: Non-blanching purpuric rash on trunk and limbs with new lesions in the last hour, mottled peripheries, cool extremities, no neck stiffness, fontanelle closed, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Venous gas pH 7.18, lactate 6.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.2 mmol/L, FBC WCC 22 x10^9/L platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L, CRP 220 mg/L, blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for lumbar puncture?

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture in the emergency department before any further fluid resuscitation to obtain cerebrospinal fluid before any further antibiotic doses alter culture yield and direct narrow-spectrum therapy

Perform lumbar puncture immediately after intubation and a second bolus of crystalloid, sending samples for cell count culture and meningococcal polymerase chain reaction before any further antibiotic doses

Defer lumbar puncture for at least 24 hours and arrange a non-contrast computed tomography of the brain before any lumbar puncture is attempted, irrespective of haemodynamic and coagulation status at that point

Defer lumbar puncture, continue empirical ceftriaxone, send blood for meningococcal polymerase chain reaction and serology and consider lumbar puncture later only once shock coagulopathy and rapidly evolving rash have resolved

Defer lumbar puncture but discontinue ceftriaxone, switch to vancomycin and aciclovir empirically and recommence ceftriaxone only after blood polymerase chain reaction and culture results are available within 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Suspected non-accidental injury workup in an infant
stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4-month-old non-Aboriginal infant brought in by his father for being unsettled. On examination the child has a spiral fracture of the left humerus, multiple bruises of varying ages on the trunk and back and a small frenular tear. The father's explanation is that the baby rolled off the lounge yesterday and was crying intermittently. The infant is otherwise developmentally appropriate and feeds normally. He is medically stable and analgesia has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 148, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air, BP 86/50 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Spiral fracture left humerus on radiograph, three trunk bruises of varying ages, frenular tear, no external head injury or seizure activity, anterior fontanelle soft, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFT, coagulation profile within paediatric reference ranges, left humerus radiograph confirms spiral fracture, no other imaging performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate investigation pathway?

options.text: Admit for analgesia and arrange a full skeletal survey, fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist, non-contrast head computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging and make a mandatory report to the child protection authority
Splint the humeral fracture, organise outpatient orthopaedic follow-up within 1 week and discharge home with social work liaison through the general paediatric clinic the following morning

Arrange a head computed tomography scan only, defer skeletal survey and ophthalmology until the family have given informed consent and discuss further investigation with the consultant paediatrician in the morning

Send extensive bone profile vitamin D and copper studies before any skeletal survey to first exclude metabolic bone disease as a cause of the spiral fracture, then reconsider child protection reporting in 48 hours

Arrange a full skeletal survey now but defer fundoscopy and head imaging until the infant develops neurological signs such as seizures, vomiting, lethargy or focal weakness on serial paediatric review

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid management at presentation
stem: You are the paediatric registrar receiving a 9-year-old non-Aboriginal girl with a 3-week history of polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss. She has been brought in by her parents after a day of vomiting and increasing drowsiness. She is breathing deeply with a fruity odour to her breath and is moderately dehydrated. There is no clinical evidence of cerebral oedema. Her weight today is 28 kg. The endocrinology consultant has confirmed first-presentation type 1 diabetes complicated by DKA and asks you to write up the initial fluid plan.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 132, RR 32 deep Kussmaul, SpO2 99% room air, BP 102/64 mmHg, GCS 14, capillary refill 3 seconds, weight 28 kg
data_table.Examination: Reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, mild acetone breath, alert and orientated, no focal neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: BSL 28.4 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, venous gas pH 7.10 pCO2 19 mmHg HCO3 6 mmol/L base excess minus 22, Na 132 corrected 137 mmol/L, K 4.5 mmol/L, urea 9.0 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan?

options.text: Bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 15 minutes and immediately commence an intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour with hourly neurological observations and electrolyte checks
Give 0.45% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose at maintenance plus 10% deficit replacement over 24 hours and commence intravenous insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour at the same time as fluids start

Give 10 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride over 30 minutes, then commence 0.9% sodium chloride with 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance plus 5-7% deficit over 48 hours and start insulin at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour after 1 hour

Give 20 mL/kg of Hartmann's compound sodium lactate over 60 minutes followed by maintenance fluids without potassium and review for insulin commencement when the venous gas has normalised on subsequent venous blood gas

Give 8.4% sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes to correct the acidosis before commencing any insulin infusion and use total body water deficit calculation to dictate replacement rate over 12 hours

subtopic_detail: Suspected airway foreign body in a toddler
stem: You are the paediatric emergency registrar reviewing an 18-month-old non-Aboriginal boy brought in with sudden onset of coughing and stridor while playing in the lounge room. His grandmother thinks he may have put a peanut in his mouth shortly before the episode. He is now alert, breathing spontaneously and stable but has persistent inspiratory stridor and intermittent coughing. There is no cyanosis and he is maintaining oxygen saturation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 142, RR 36, SpO2 96% room air, BP 92/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Awake, alert and consolable on mother's lap, intermittent strong cough, audible inspiratory stridor at rest, mild subcostal recession, breath sounds slightly reduced on right, no drooling, no tripod posture
data_table.Investigations: No imaging yet performed; bedside cardiorespiratory monitoring in place

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts immediately because the persistent inspiratory stridor confirms complete airway obstruction warranting basic life support manoeuvres before any expert airway help arrives

Administer nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL and oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg for presumed viral croup and observe in the short stay unit for 4 hours before any specialist referral or further investigation
Arrange an inspiratory and expiratory chest radiograph and review again only after the imaging is reported by a paediatric radiologist before deciding whether ENT or theatre referral is required

Commence direct laryngoscopy in the emergency department to retrieve the suspected peanut promptly under topical anaesthesia rather than transfer the child to the operating theatre with anaesthetic and ENT support

Keep the child calm in the parent's arms with supplemental oxygen as tolerated, fast for theatre, contact ENT and anaesthetics urgently for rigid bronchoscopy and avoid distressing procedures or instrumentation

subtopic_detail: Faltering growth in an exclusively breastfed infant
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 5-month-old exclusively breastfed non-Aboriginal infant whose weight has dropped from the 50th centile at birth to below the 3rd centile today, crossing two major centile lines over 8 weeks. His mother describes good attachment with feeds approximately every 3 hours but reports that he has slow weight gain at recent maternal child health nurse visits. There are no concerning features in the history and developmental milestones are appropriate for age.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air, BP 86/52 mmHg, weight 5.2 kg
data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, normal tone and posture, soft anterior fontanelle, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiac and respiratory examination, abdomen soft non-tender with no organomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart shows downward crossing of 2 centile lines over 8 weeks, no bloods or imaging performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange admission for nasogastric supplemental feeds while a paediatric metabolic workup including amino acids, acylcarnitine profile and very long chain fatty acids is performed and reviewed by metabolic specialists

Arrange a structured feeding history and observed feed with lactation support, a stool history for malabsorption, a focused examination and baseline investigations including FBC iron studies UEC LFT TFT urinalysis and coeliac serology

Refer immediately to a paediatric gastroenterologist for an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, jejunal biopsy and stool elastase to evaluate for malabsorption due to coeliac disease, cystic fibrosis or eosinophilic enteropathy

Recommend immediate introduction of cow's milk formula every 3 hours alongside continued breastfeeding and review weight gain in 2 weeks regardless of the maternal preference for exclusive breastfeeding

Reassure the mother that the centile chart drop reflects genetic potential and adequate exclusive breastfeeding and arrange a routine weight review at the maternal child health nurse appointment in 4 weeks' time

subtopic_detail: Functional chronic constipation Movicol disimpaction and maintenance
stem: You are the GP registrar reviewing a 4-year-old non-Aboriginal girl with a 14-month history of infrequent painful bowel motions, with stool frequency of 1 to 2 per week, frequent staining of underwear with small amounts of liquid stool between hard motions, and observed stool-withholding behaviour. There is a 6-month history of intermittent abdominal pain. She has met all developmental milestones, is fully toilet trained for urine, and has no symptoms of urinary tract infection. Examination shows a palpable suprapubic mass consistent with faecal loading, normal anal position and tone, no sacral dimple, and normal lower limb neurology.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 °C, HR 104, BP not routinely measured at age 4, weight 17 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Palpable suprapubic faecal mass, normal anal exam, no anal fissures, normal perineum and sacrum, normal lower limb neurology
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging required for diagnosis of functional constipation

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase dietary fibre to 18 grams daily through fruit, vegetables and wholegrains, encourage 1.5 litres of fluid intake per day, and reassess at 4 weeks before considering any pharmacological intervention or specific oral stool-softening therapy
