Refer urgently to paediatric gastroenterology for anorectal manometry and rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung's disease given the duration of symptoms and presence of overflow soiling at the age of presentation

Administer paraffin oil 5 mL orally twice daily and arrange daily glycerine suppositories for 7 days followed by ongoing rectal interventions if dietary modifications fail to soften stool after this initial disimpaction phase of intensive treatment

Disimpact with high-dose polyethylene glycol 3350 with electrolytes (Movicol Junior) 4 sachets daily, increasing to 8 sachets daily as needed for 3 to 7 days until impaction clears, then transition to maintenance Movicol 1 to 2 sachets daily with toileting routines and parent education

Prescribe lactulose 5 mL twice daily for 3 months as the only intervention required for functional childhood constipation alongside oral fluid encouragement and gradual increase in dietary fibre over the next month

subtopic_detail: Henoch-Schonlein purpura with renal involvement and timing of follow-up
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-year-old boy in the emergency department with a 5-day history of a palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and lower limbs, intermittent colicky abdominal pain for 3 days, and now a swollen painful right ankle. He has been previously well, fully immunised, no recent medication, and had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago.

He is haemodynamically stable. On examination there is a typical non-blanching palpable purpuric rash on the lower limbs and buttocks, a swollen tender right ankle, mild abdominal tenderness without peritonism, and normal genitalia.

data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura buttocks/lower limbs, right ankle swollen tender, abdomen mildly tender, no peritonism, normal scrotum
data_table.Investigations: FBC: WBC 9.4, Hb 124, plt 320; UEC normal; urinalysis: blood 2+, protein 1+, no casts; urinary albumin-creatinine ratio 18 mg/mmol; BP 102/64

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Admit for IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days then oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks and arrange urgent renal biopsy because of the proteinuria and microscopic haematuria at presentation

Discharge home with simple analgesia, supportive care, and a structured follow-up schedule of weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for 2 months and then 3-monthly checks for 12 months to detect delayed HSP nephritis

Admit for observation with intravenous cefotaxime 50 mg/kg every 8 hours empirically until a complete septic workup including blood cultures, CSF and lumbar puncture confirms or excludes meningococcal sepsis

Admit for monitoring and arrange abdominal ultrasound urgently to exclude intussusception given the abdominal pain, before reassessment to determine outpatient management at the end of the admission period

Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 14 days for arthralgia and abdominal pain without altering renal follow-up plan, on the basis that early steroids prevent progression to chronic HSP nephritis

subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice phototherapy threshold and risk-factor adjustment
stem:
You are the paediatric resident in the postnatal ward reviewing a 3-day-old term female neonate (40+2 weeks at birth, birthweight 3350 g) brought to the special care nursery because of yellowing of the skin extending to the trunk. She is breastfeeding 8 times per day, has wet nappies and is alert and active. Born by uncomplicated SVD. Mother's blood group A positive, infant's blood group B positive, direct Coombs negative.

Total serum bilirubin taken at 72 hours of age is 290 micromol/L (unconjugated 282), conjugated 8. The mother is Rh negative and received antenatal anti-D appropriately.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8 °C, HR 142, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice cephalocaudally to the chest, alert and active, normal tone, no cephalohaematoma or bruising, normal cardiac and respiratory exam
data_table.Investigations: TSB 290 micromol/L at 72 hours, conjugated 8, unconjugated 282, Hb 168 g/L, reticulocytes 4%, Coombs negative, blood group B+, maternal A+

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure mother that the bilirubin level is below the phototherapy threshold for a term well infant at 72 hours, advise on continued breastfeeding 8 to 12 times a day and arrange repeat bilirubin level at 96 hours

Arrange urgent exchange transfusion because the bilirubin level of 290 micromol/L is in the kernicterus risk zone in a 72-hour-old infant and immediate dual-volume exchange transfusion is mandated to prevent neurological injury

Investigate further with thyroid function, urine for reducing substances and G6PD screen given the elevated bilirubin and risk of metabolic causes before starting phototherapy because the level is unusual for breastfeeding-related jaundice

Administer intravenous immunoglobulin 1 g/kg over 4 hours because of the presence of ABO blood group setoff between mother (A) and infant (B) and the rising bilirubin trajectory, before considering phototherapy

Commence intensive (multi-light) phototherapy with monitoring of bilirubin in 6 hours, support continued breastfeeding with potential top-ups if hydration is suboptimal, and review for risk factors that would lower the threshold

subtopic_detail: Preschool viral-induced wheeze first-line bronchodilator and steroid evidence
stem: You are the emergency department paediatric registrar reviewing an 18-month-old boy with the third episode in 6 months of wheeze, cough and increased work of breathing during a coryzal illness. He responded to salbutamol via spacer at home this morning but has worsened over the day with persistent wheeze and tachypnoea. His first wheeze episode was at 8 months. There is no atopic history (no eczema, no food allergy), no parental asthma, and no inhaled smoke exposure. He has met all developmental milestones and growth is on the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4 °C, HR 152, RR 48, SpO2 92% room air, BP not routine
data_table.Examination: Moderate work of breathing with subcostal recession, audible expiratory wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, air entry symmetrical with widespread polyphonic wheeze, alert, mildly distressed
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or chest X-ray indicated routinely; NPS not required

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Administer back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses with high-flow oxygen, add nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms every 20 minutes and arrange admission for IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg every 6 hours

Discharge home with an oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days, salbutamol via spacer 6 puffs every 4 hours as required, with safety-net advice and review at 24 hours by GP for ongoing management of the acute episode

Administer salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for 3 doses with oxygen to maintain SpO2 above 94%, give oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg as a single dose, and reassess after the third salbutamol round before deciding admission

Commence inhaled fluticasone propionate 100 micrograms twice daily as a preventer from today given the recurrent wheeze episodes and review symptom control in 4 weeks before adjusting therapy or stepping up to combination inhaler

Administer nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with oxygen as is given for moderate-severe croup, on the basis that the wheeze could reflect upper airway involvement that has been mislabelled as lower airway disease

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in infant of diabetic mother
stem: You are the paediatric registrar on the postnatal ward reviewing a 2-hour-old term male infant born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39+2 weeks weighing 4.3 kg to a woman with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes. He had skin-to-skin contact and an attempt at breastfeeding at one hour of age but latched only briefly. The midwife performed a routine pre-feed blood glucose at 2 hours which is 1.8 mmol/L on a calibrated cot-side meter. The infant is alert, pink, breathing at 48/min with no recession, and has a normal cardiovascular and neurological examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 48, SpO2 97% in air, T 36.9 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Vigorous, well-perfused, normal tone and reflexes, anterior fontanelle soft, no jitteriness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside BGL 1.8 mmol/L (laboratory confirmation pending)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure the mother that this glucose is a normal physiological postnatal nadir in an infant of a diabetic mother and arrange a routine recheck only with the next scheduled three-hourly feed in approximately one hour

Transfer the infant to the special care nursery immediately for insertion of a peripheral intravenous cannula and commencement of 10% dextrose at 60 mL/kg/day with hourly capillary glucose monitoring until two consecutive readings exceed 2.6 mmol/L

Administer 200 mg/kg of 40% dextrose gel to the buccal mucosa now without offering an oral feed and recheck the capillary blood glucose 30 minutes later before deciding on any further escalation of management or further dextrose

Encourage an immediate breastfeed or expressed-breast-milk top-up of 5 mL/kg and recheck the blood glucose 30 minutes after the feed before considering buccal dextrose gel or intravenous glucose escalation

Send a critical sample for plasma glucose, insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids before any intervention because the most likely cause is congenital hyperinsulinism rather than transitional neonatal hypoglycaemia

subtopic_detail: Moderate croup with stridor at rest and mild recession
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 22-month-old boy brought in by his mother at 0200 with a 1-day history of coryza followed by a sudden barking cough and noisy breathing on waking from sleep. He is upset and crying intermittently. On examination he has audible inspiratory stridor at rest, mild suprasternal and intercostal recession but no tracheal tug, and is well perfused with a respiratory rate of 36 and oxygen saturations of 97% in air. He has not had previous croup episodes and has no congenital airway concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degrees C, HR 138, RR 36, SpO2 97% in air, CRT 1 second
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest, mild recession, voice hoarse but cry strong, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Nil performed (clinical diagnosis)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone now and observe the child for at least four hours after the dose to assess clinical response before considering discharge home with a written croup advice sheet for the family

Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 via mask immediately and arrange for paediatric high-dependency admission with continuous monitoring for at least 24 hours regardless of the response to the initial nebulised dose

Take a nasopharyngeal aspirate for respiratory viral PCR, perform a lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray to look for the steeple sign and withhold any pharmacological treatment until imaging and laboratory results have returned

Administer high-flow humidified oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min and a single intramuscular dose of 50 mg/kg ceftriaxone empirically pending the result of a paired blood culture and full blood count

Discharge home immediately with written advice on steam-bath therapy and indications to return, without any pharmacological intervention because the child is comfortably saturating well and the stridor will likely settle overnight

subtopic_detail: Febrile infant under 3 months with possible UTI
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan tertiary emergency department reviewing a 7-week-old previously well term male infant brought in by his parents with a 12-hour history of poor feeding, fussiness and a measured rectal temperature of 38.6 degrees C at home. On examination he is irritable but consolable, well perfused with a capillary refill of under 2 seconds, has a soft fontanelle and no focal source of infection on full examination including ENT, chest, abdomen and skin. He has had no recent antibiotics and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4 degrees C, HR 168, RR 48, SpO2 99% air, CRT under 2 sec
data_table.Examination: Irritable but consolable, no rash, fontanelle soft, no meningism, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Bedside cap gas: pH 7.38, BE -1, lactate 1.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent renal tract ultrasound and a micturating cystourethrogram before starting any antibiotic therapy because vesicoureteric reflux is the most likely underlying diagnosis in a male infant with fever

Collect a clean-catch bag urine specimen for microscopy and culture and discharge home on oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily with a planned review by the general practitioner within 24 hours of presentation

Reassure the parents that the child is well appearing with a normal lactate and observation alone in the emergency department for 4 hours with paracetamol is sufficient before discharge home without antibiotics or urine collection

Send urine collected by clean catch only for dipstick analysis and start oral amoxicillin clavulanate if the dipstick is positive for leucocyte esterase or nitrites, deferring blood tests unless the child clinically deteriorates

Obtain a catheter or suprapubic aspirate urine sample plus blood culture and full septic workup including lumbar puncture, then commence intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin pending results in a paediatric inpatient setting

subtopic_detail: Paediatric anaphylaxis dose, route and observation
stem: You are the paediatric registrar in a busy emergency department called to triage to assess a 6-year-old girl who developed lip swelling, generalised urticaria and a hoarse voice within 10 minutes of eating a cashew from a snack bag at her brother's birthday party 25 minutes ago. She has a history of mild asthma controlled with a salbutamol inhaler used twice in the last year, no known allergies and no chronic medication. On arrival she is anxious, has audible inspiratory stridor, wheeze on auscultation, widespread urticaria and is centrally well perfused.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 36, SpO2 94% in air, BP 92/56 mmHg, T 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Audible stridor, bilateral wheeze, widespread urticaria, mild peri-orbital oedema, alert
data_table.Investigations: Bedside observations as above; weight estimated at 22 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Administer 10 mg of intramuscular promethazine and 200 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone as first-line therapy and observe for two hours of clinical improvement before re-evaluating the need for further pharmacological treatment

Give intravenous adrenaline 1 mcg/kg as a slow push followed by a continuous infusion at 0.05 mcg/kg/min, intubate immediately for the stridor and admit her directly to the paediatric intensive care unit for ongoing airway management

Administer 0.3 mg of 1:1000 adrenaline by intramuscular injection into the mid anterolateral thigh now, lay her supine with legs elevated, give high-flow oxygen and observe for at least 4 hours after symptoms resolve before considering discharge

Give 10 puffs of inhaled salbutamol via spacer and 5 mL nebulised adrenaline 1:1000, then reassess in 15 minutes and only proceed to intramuscular adrenaline if wheeze and stridor have not resolved with these inhaled therapies

Administer an immediate 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride intravenously and observe blood pressure response before deciding whether intramuscular adrenaline is required, given that the systolic blood pressure remains above 90 mmHg

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease meeting full criteria at day 6
stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 3-year-old boy who has been febrile for six days with temperatures above 39 degrees C unresponsive to paracetamol. His parents describe a polymorphous truncal rash since day three, red cracked lips since day four and bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection that started yesterday. On examination today he has a tender 2 cm right cervical lymph node, swollen erythematous palms and soles, and pronounced strawberry tongue. He is irritable but well perfused and has no source of bacterial infection on workup.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.4 degrees C, HR 152, RR 30, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 98%
data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, dry fissured lips, strawberry tongue, polymorphous truncal rash, oedema of hands and feet, single 2 cm right cervical node
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.2 x10^9/L (neutrophils 12.5), Hb 102 g/L, platelets 462 x10^9/L, CRP 168 mg/L, ALT 92 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, sterile pyuria on urinalysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Defer all definitive treatment until day 10 of fever to allow further inflammatory markers, echocardiogram and rheumatology consultation to confirm the diagnosis before committing the child to systemic immunoglobulin therapy and antiplatelet therapy

Treat empirically with intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and toxic shock pending blood culture results, with serial daily examination for any new desquamation or hypotension over the coming 48 hours of admission

Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours plus oral aspirin 30 to 50 mg/kg/day in four divided doses, and arrange an inpatient baseline transthoracic echocardiogram to assess for coronary artery aneurysms during this admission

Commence high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg pulse for 3 days as initial monotherapy without intravenous immunoglobulin and review the need for adjunctive aspirin once the inflammatory markers begin to fall on serial testing

Start oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg/day alone without intravenous immunoglobulin and arrange outpatient transthoracic echocardiogram in 6 to 8 weeks because the platelet count is already markedly elevated suggesting late convalescent phase

subtopic_detail: Pancytopenia with circulating blasts in a child
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old girl referred from her GP with a 3-week history of progressive pallor, recurrent low-grade fevers, easy bruising on her shins and a new petechial rash on her trunk noticed by her mother yesterday. She has been more tired than usual at preschool and has refused to walk to the car last week, complaining of left thigh ache. On examination she is pale, has scattered petechiae and small ecchymoses, a soft 3 cm spleen tip palpable, and mild bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8 degrees C, HR 122, RR 24, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, scattered petechiae and bruises, soft spleen tip 3 cm, no hepatomegaly, no testicular masses, no neurological signs
data_table.Investigations: Hb 64 g/L, MCV 84 fL, WCC 28.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 0.6, blasts 22.0 x10^9/L), platelets 22 x10^9/L, LDH 1820 U/L, urate 0.48 mmol/L, K 4.4, phosphate 1.62, calcium corrected 2.18

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent CT abdomen and pelvis to confirm splenomegaly and exclude an intra-abdominal lymphoma mass, plus a peripheral lymph node excisional biopsy for histopathology before considering systemic chemotherapy or transfer

Admit to a regional paediatric ward for transfusion of one adult unit of packed red blood cells and one adult therapeutic dose of platelets, then refer to the haematology outpatient clinic for a bone marrow biopsy within the next two weeks

Start empirical intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin for presumed febrile neutropenia and oral fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis, and arrange a CT chest abdomen and pelvis to look for a sanctuary site of infection or occult abscess

Transfer urgently to a tertiary paediatric oncology unit for bone marrow aspirate and trephine plus immunophenotyping and cytogenetics, and commence intravenous hyperhydration with allopurinol or rasburicase for tumour lysis prophylaxis en route

Send blood for Epstein Barr virus, cytomegalovirus and parvovirus B19 serology and a peripheral blood film for atypical lymphocytes, and review again in 48 hours once infective causes of pancytopenia have been excluded by these results

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis with significant proteinuria requiring biopsy decision
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-year-old boy who was diagnosed in your clinic five weeks ago with IgA vasculitis based on a palpable purpuric rash over his lower limbs and buttocks, bilateral ankle arthralgia and intermittent peri-umbilical pain. The rash has now resolved. You arranged weekly urine dipstick and blood pressure at his GP. Today his GP rings because his urinalysis shows 3+ protein with 2+ blood and his blood pressure is 130/86 mmHg seated. He looks well, is afebrile and has no oedema on examination today in your clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 130/86 mmHg (above the 95th centile for age, sex, height), HR 84, T 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Faded post-inflammatory pigmentation on lower limbs, no fresh purpura, no oedema, abdomen soft, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 220 mg/mmol, urine RBC 60/high power field, dysmorphic, Hb 124 g/L, creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR 95, albumin 36 g/L, complement C3 and C4 normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Reassure that microscopic haematuria and mild proteinuria are expected after Henoch-Schonlein purpura and may persist for over a year without need for intervention, and continue weekly urinalysis monitoring with the general practitioner

Refer to a paediatric nephrologist for an urgent renal biopsy and consideration of oral prednisolone or pulse methylprednisolone with adjunctive ACE inhibitor and blood pressure control as guided by biopsy ISKDC class

Start a 4-week course of oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg/day without nephrology referral and aim to taper over a further 4 weeks while continuing community-based monitoring of urinalysis and blood pressure throughout the taper

Commence oral cyclophosphamide and mycophenolate mofetil empirically as combination therapy and arrange repeat urine protein creatinine ratio in 4 weeks to demonstrate biochemical response before deciding on need for renal biopsy

Test antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-GBM antibody and serum cryoglobulins urgently and treat as ANCA-associated small vessel vasculitis with plasma exchange and rituximab pending these confirmatory serological results

subtopic_detail: Mitochondrial disease presenting as developmental regression with lactic acidosis
stem: You are the paediatric registrar consulted on a 16-month-old boy admitted with two days of vomiting and decreased oral intake after a febrile illness. He was born at term, breastfed and weaned uneventfully but his parents now describe loss of words he previously had, loss of ability to walk in the last month and intermittent eye movement abnormalities. On examination he is thin but not dehydrated, has truncal hypotonia, brisk reflexes, an upgoing right plantar response and a left ptosis. There is no organomegaly. He has had no surgeries and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Examination: Hypotonia, brisk reflexes, left ptosis, intermittent dysconjugate eye movements, no organomegaly, weight on 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.28, lactate 6.8 mmol/L, glucose 4.0, K 3.8, Na 136, anion gap 22; CK 220 U/L; LFTs ALT 78 AST 102; ammonia 92 micromol/L; MRI brain shows symmetric bilateral basal ganglia and brainstem T2 hyperintensities

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send blood and urine for very-long-chain fatty acids and white-cell enzyme analysis for late-infantile metachromatic leukodystrophy, and discharge home pending results because the child is haemodynamically stable and feeding adequately

Treat empirically as autoimmune encephalitis with intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day for 5 days followed by intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg, and arrange anti-NMDA and anti-MOG antibody testing on serum and cerebrospinal fluid

Manage as severe gastroenteritis with intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% at 1.5 times maintenance plus ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg orally and continue ad lib oral feeding once vomiting subsides without further metabolic workup or imaging review

Start sodium valproate orally as empirical treatment for suspected refractory partial seizures presenting as dysconjugate eye movements, and arrange outpatient electroencephalography with sleep deprivation within the next fortnight

Refer urgently to a metabolic genetics service for whole-exome sequencing and mitochondrial DNA testing, commence high-dose riboflavin, thiamine and coenzyme Q10 cofactor therapy, and avoid sodium valproate, metformin and aminoglycosides during admission

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department reviewing a 5-month-old previously well term girl on day 3 of coryza, cough and fast breathing. She is taking around 60% of her usual breastfeed volumes, has not vomited, and her last wet nappy was 3 hours ago. Initial observations showed mild subcostal recession with SpO2 92% in air; after suction of clear nasal secretions and a 90 mL breastfeed she is alert, smiling, with no recession at rest and SpO2 of 95% in air for 30 minutes.

The mother is calm, has a working car, lives 25 minutes from the hospital, has a clear plan to seek review, and there is good GP follow-up the next morning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 44, SpO2 95% in air (after suction and feed), T 37.6 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mild wheeze with prolonged expiration, no chest wall recession at rest, good air entry, no focal crackles, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: Bedside nasopharyngeal aspirate viral PCR pending; no other investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Admit her for a chest x-ray and intravenous benzylpenicillin until viral nasopharyngeal aspirate PCR results return, given the fever and the possibility of an early bacterial lower respiratory tract co-infection
Discharge home with a written bronchiolitis action plan, simple analgesia for fever, advice on feed volumes and red-flag symptoms, and review by her general practitioner within 24 hours

Admit her to the paediatric ward for nasogastric feeding at two-thirds maintenance and continuous pulse oximetry monitoring for at least 24 hours regardless of her current observations and ongoing feeding
Discharge her home only after a 4-hour high-flow nasal cannula trial at 2 L/kg/min in the ED short stay unit to confirm she does not develop any escalating oxygen requirement before going home
Admit her for a trial of nebulised hypertonic 3% saline every 6 hours and a single inhaled salbutamol challenge to assess for any bronchodilator-responsive component of her wheeze before discharge

stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 26-month-old non-Aboriginal boy with no significant past history brought in by his mother after 24 hours of irritability, ear-tugging and fever to 38.6 degrees C. He is otherwise feeding reasonably, drinking, has been playing intermittently between paracetamol doses and has had no vomiting. He is fully immunised including 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, attends day care 3 days per week and has had no previous ear infections.

Otoscopy shows a bulging, opaque right tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks and no perforation or discharge; the left ear is normal. There is no mastoid tenderness, neck stiffness, facial weakness, or coexisting bacterial focus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR 28, SpO2 99% in air, T 38.6 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Right TM bulging and opaque with loss of light reflex; left TM normal; no mastoid swelling; oropharynx mildly erythematous; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management of his ear?

options.text: Provide regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, written safety-net advice, and arrange routine review at 48 hours with antibiotics only if symptoms have worsened or have not improved at that review point
Commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days and refer urgently to ear, nose and throat outpatients for a discussion of grommet insertion if any further episodes occur
Commence oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days now and review only if he develops persistent fever, ear discharge or new symptoms over the next week of treatment

Arrange same-day ENT outpatient review and tympanocentesis for microbiological sampling and an audiology assessment before any decision is made about whether antibiotics or analgesia alone is most appropriate
Refer him to the local emergency department for intravenous ceftriaxone, blood cultures and a lumbar puncture given the fever, irritability and unilateral bulging tympanic membrane on otoscopy today

stem:
You are the paediatric ED registrar reviewing a 7-year-old boy with a known diagnosis of mild persistent asthma on a low-dose inhaled fluticasone preventer who presented with a 6-hour exacerbation triggered by an upper respiratory infection. On arrival he had moderate work of breathing with tracheal tug and SpO2 of 93% in air. He has received salbutamol 12 puffs by spacer at 20-minute intervals for three doses, ipratropium 8 puffs by spacer for three doses, and a single oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg dose 2 hours ago.

He is now alert, talking in full sentences, with no recession, has just eaten and drunk, and is keen to go home; his salbutamol interval has been stretched to 3-hourly with no return of recession.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 97% in air, T 37.4 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mild scattered wheeze at end-expiration, no recession, full air entry bilaterally, no chest pain, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: No imaging or bloods required; salbutamol response sustained at 3-hourly dosing across two cycles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue 1-hourly salbutamol by spacer for a further 6 hours in the short stay unit and only consider discharge once the salbutamol interval can be stretched to at least every 6 hours during the day
Add a single oral montelukast 5 mg dose now, then a 5-day course at home in addition to his existing preventer, and discharge once 4 hours have elapsed from the last salbutamol given today
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes and admit him to the paediatric high-dependency unit for ongoing monitoring of his magnesium level and his cardiac rhythm overnight

Admit him to the paediatric ward for continuous pulse oximetry overnight and a 24-hour observation period before stepping down salbutamol given the duration of the symptoms and the upper respiratory tract trigger
Discharge home with a written asthma action plan, oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for a further 2 days, ongoing inhaled fluticasone preventer, and review by his GP within 48 to 72 hours of discharge

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 22-month-old developmentally normal girl 90 minutes after a single 2-minute generalised tonic-clonic seizure that occurred at home during the rapid rise of a viral upper respiratory illness. The seizure self-terminated before paramedics arrived; she had a brief postictal drowsiness, then woke spontaneously and is now alert, smiling, playing and breastfeeding well. Examination identifies an obvious viral source with clear coryza and erythematous pharynx and reveals no focal neurological signs, no neck stiffness, no rash, and no significant past medical or family history other than a maternal aunt who had two febrile seizures in childhood with normal subsequent development.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, RR 26, SpO2 99% in air, T 39.1 degrees C (after one dose of paracetamol), capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, age-appropriate interaction, normal tone and reflexes, normal cranial nerves, soft anterior fontanelle, no rash, no neck stiffness, clear viral coryza
data_table.Investigations: No bloods, lumbar puncture, imaging or EEG performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid microscopy, glucose and protein, blood cultures and commence empirical intravenous benzylpenicillin and ceftriaxone given the height of the fever today
Admit her overnight for a 24-hour continuous video electroencephalogram and a paediatric neurology consultation to exclude an underlying focal epilepsy syndrome before discharging her home tomorrow
Reassure the parents, give written advice on febrile seizure recurrence and basic first-aid recovery position management, discuss antipyretic use for comfort, and discharge home with GP follow-up

Commence regular sodium valproate as a maintenance anti-seizure medication for the next 6 months given the family history of febrile seizures in a first-degree relative and the height of the documented fever
Arrange a non-contrast CT brain scan today, an outpatient electroencephalogram within a week and outpatient paediatric neurology review before any decision is made about discharge home this afternoon

subtopic_detail: Intussusception recognition and air enema indication
stem:
You are the paediatric surgical registrar called to ED to review an 11-month-old boy with 18 hours of intermittent severe screaming attacks, drawing his knees up and going pale, each lasting 5 minutes and recurring every 20 to 30 minutes. He has vomited four times in the last 6 hours (now bilious), refused his last two feeds, and passed a small amount of dark blood mixed with mucus per rectum on the way to hospital.

On examination he is sleepy between episodes but rousable, has a soft non-distended abdomen with a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant, and his peripheries are well perfused. He has had no surgery or foreign-body ingestion.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 156, RR 36, SpO2 98% in air, T 37.2 degrees C, BP 96/58, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Sleepy between episodes, mildly dehydrated, abdomen soft with right upper quadrant sausage mass, no peritonism, blood-stained mucus on PR
data_table.Investigations: Urgent abdominal ultrasound shows a target sign 3.5 cm diameter at the ileocolic junction, no free fluid, no perforation; venous gas pH 7.34, lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit him for nil by mouth, intravenous maintenance fluids and serial abdominal examinations over the next 12 hours, repeating the ultrasound only if his symptoms have not spontaneously settled in that period

Insert an intravenous cannula, commence a 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% bolus, place a nasogastric tube on free drainage, give intravenous antibiotics and proceed to a radiologist-led air enema reduction with surgical standby

Transfer him directly to the operating theatre for an immediate diagnostic laparoscopy and manual reduction with possible bowel resection given the bilious vomiting and the blood per rectum noted on the way to hospital

Order a non-contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to confirm the ultrasound finding and exclude a lead point before proceeding with any decision about enema reduction or surgical referral

Give a stat dose of intramuscular morphine for the colicky pain and observe him in the short stay unit for 4 hours, expecting many ileocolic intussusceptions to reduce spontaneously without intervention

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan ED reviewing a non-ambulant 8-month-old boy brought in by his mother and her current partner. The history is that he 'rolled off the couch' onto a carpeted floor 4 hours ago. On examination you find a 2 cm fluctuant boggy swelling over the right parietal scalp, three small ovoid bruises over the left upper arm in a grip distribution, a torn upper labial frenulum, and a small healing burn on the dorsum of the left hand.

He is interactive but quiet; his fontanelle is soft. The partner cannot describe the incident in detail. The mother appears anxious. The infant has not previously been seen at this hospital and the family is not known to child protection services.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 38, SpO2 99% in air, T 36.8 degrees C, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Right parietal boggy swelling 2 cm, three ovoid bruises left upper arm with grip pattern, torn upper labial frenulum, healing dorsal hand burn 1 cm, no spinal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside neurological examination intact; no investigations performed at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit him for a non-contrast CT brain, a skeletal survey within 24 hours, dilated fundoscopy by ophthalmology, paediatric child protection team consultation, and notify the statutory child protection agency before discharge

Order a non-contrast CT brain only and discharge home with the mother once the scan is reported as normal, deferring the skeletal survey and child protection consultation to outpatient paediatric follow-up next week

Arrange social work involvement and a community child health nurse home visit within 7 days, and ask the mother to bring him back to ED only if he develops new bruises or any signs of head injury such as vomiting

Discharge him home with the mother after a discussion about home safety, provide written safety advice on supervised tummy time off raised surfaces, and arrange GP review within a week to recheck the scalp haematoma and the healing burn

Take a more detailed history from the mother and partner separately and re-examine in 4 hours; if the explanation reconciles with the injuries, discharge with GP follow-up, otherwise consider further investigation later

subtopic_detail: Mycoplasma pneumoniae atypical pneumonia in school-aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 9-year-old girl with 10 days of dry cough that has progressed to a paroxysmal cough productive of clear sputum and 4 days of fever to 38.5 degrees C, gradually worsening despite oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily prescribed by her GP on day 4. She has bilateral mild widespread crackles and scattered fine wheeze, no focal consolidation on examination, and is well perfused, alert and tolerating oral fluids.

Chest x-ray shows bilateral patchy peribronchial infiltrates without lobar consolidation or pleural effusion. Two of her classmates have had similar prolonged coughs recently and her dry cough has continued to disrupt her sleep at night.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100, RR 24, SpO2 96% in air, T 38.4 degrees C, BP 102/64, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mild bilateral crackles, scattered fine wheeze, no focal consolidation, no respiratory distress, no extrapulmonary rash, oropharynx clear
data_table.Investigations: CXR: bilateral patchy peribronchial infiltrates, no lobar consolidation, no effusion; WCC 9.5 x10^9/L, CRP 28 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in antimicrobial management?

options.text: Cease the amoxicillin and commence oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg on day 1 followed by 5 mg/kg daily for a further 4 days, with safety-net advice about return precautions and a planned GP review at 48 to 72 hours

Add oral doxycycline 2 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days in addition to her current amoxicillin to broaden cover to atypical pathogens while preserving pneumococcal cover until the cough resolves clinically

Stop antibiotics altogether and arrange a chest CT angiogram with intravenous contrast to exclude pulmonary embolism, foreign body or interstitial lung disease as the explanation for the persistent cough

Increase the oral amoxicillin to 45 mg/kg three times daily for a further 7 days to extend the bacterial cover for partially treated typical pneumococcal pneumonia given her improvement plateau and the recent classmate outbreaks
Admit her for intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg six-hourly for at least 48 hours and arrange a CT chest if she has not defervesced clinically by 48 hours into the intravenous treatment course

stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department reviewing a 2-year-old girl with a 12-hour history of harsh barking cough preceded by a coryzal prodrome. On assessment now, she has a barking cough, mild stridor only when distressed or crying, no stridor at rest, no chest wall recession, normal mental state, and is interactive with her parents while sitting on her mother's lap.

She has had no exposure to a foreign body, immunisations are up to date including Hib, and she has no past history of asthma or recurrent wheeze. Her older brother had viral croup two weeks ago. The Westley croup score is 1 and she has been observed for 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, BP 95/55
data_table.Examination: Barking cough on examination, no stridor at rest, no recession, alert and interactive, oropharynx unremarkable, chest auscultation clear, no drooling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 immediately followed by oral dexamethasone and observe in the short stay unit for at least four hours before reconsidering disposition with paediatric review
Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg now as a one-off and discharge home with written parental advice to return for stridor at rest, drooling, severe distress or any deterioration

Admit for nebulised budesonide every four hours and supplemental oxygen as required with paediatric inpatient observation overnight on the children's ward for serial respiratory assessment by the nursing staff

Reassure the family, provide humidified room air at home and paracetamol as required without corticosteroid, with no need for routine review unless the child develops obvious respiratory distress or worsening symptoms

Give intravenous dexamethasone and intramuscular ceftriaxone for possible bacterial tracheitis, then admit to the short stay unit overnight with ENT review and serial airway assessment given the persistent stridor on exertion

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease IVIG within 10 days plus high-dose aspirin
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy admitted on day 6 of persistent fever to 39.5 degrees not responding to paracetamol or ibuprofen. He has bilateral non-purulent bulbar conjunctival injection sparing the limbus, a strawberry tongue with cracked red lips, a polymorphous truncal rash that is not vesicular, a single right cervical lymph node measuring 1.8 cm, and early peri-ungual desquamation around the fingertips of the right hand noted today.

There has been no exposure to new medications. Echocardiography is being arranged for today and bloods are pending. He was previously well, fully immunised, with no travel and no sick contacts.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.5, HR 152, RR 30, BP 96/58, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, polymorphous trunk rash, right cervical node 1.8 cm, early fingertip desquamation, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.2, neutrophil 14, platelets 580, Hb 102, CRP 145, ESR 78, ALT 65, albumin 28, urine WCC 25 sterile, throat swab negative, ASOT not raised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 10-12 hours plus high-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day divided four times daily until afebrile then low-dose aspirin to follow-up echocardiography at 6 weeks for coronary artery assessment

High-dose aspirin 30 mg/kg/day divided four times daily as monotherapy and observation in hospital with daily echocardiography while monitoring for spontaneous defervescence prior to commencing intravenous immunoglobulin therapy

Intravenous methylprednisolone pulse 30 mg/kg daily for three days as first-line therapy for refractory Kawasaki disease with planned IVIG at 48 hours if no clinical response is observed and serial inflammatory marker measurement

Supportive care with paracetamol for fever, oral fluid encouragement and outpatient cardiology follow-up in four weeks with repeat echocardiography to assess for coronary changes and consideration of IVIG only if symptoms persist beyond 14 days

Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics with ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly for an occult bacterial focus and pending blood culture results before considering immunomodulatory therapy

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA initial fluid resuscitation without cerebral oedema
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department assessing an 8-year-old girl with new-onset type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting with two weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and 24 hours of vomiting and lethargy. She is alert (GCS 15), has dry mucous membranes, capillary refill of 3 seconds and is tachycardic but not shocked. Her weight today is 28 kg.

There are no focal neurological signs, the headache score is 0, and she has had no recent insulin (this is a new diagnosis). The PICU has been informed but admission to the children's ward is planned with one-hourly observation.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 130, BP 95/60, RR 22 with deep breathing, SpO2 99% room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, normal cardiovascular exam, deep sighing respirations, no focal neurology, weight 28 kg
data_table.Investigations: Capillary BSL 28.4, ketones 5.6, VBG pH 7.18 HCO3 9 pCO2 22, Na 134, K 5.0, urea 9.2, Cr 78, urine ketones ++++, HbA1c 11.8%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid plan?

options.text: Give 0.9 percent saline 10 mL/kg bolus over 60 minutes then commence calculated fluid as maintenance plus 5-7 percent dehydration replaced over 48 hours, and start IV insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour 1 hour after fluids begin

Give 0.9 percent saline 20 mL/kg bolus rapidly over 10-15 minutes followed by a second 20 mL/kg bolus if perfusion has not normalised, and commence IV insulin bolus 0.1 units/kg before transitioning to infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour

Commence IV 0.45 percent saline at twice maintenance without any initial bolus, and start IV insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately, with hourly capillary glucose and 2-hourly venous gas monitoring until acidosis resolves

Administer IV sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to correct the metabolic acidosis prior to other interventions, with 0.9 percent saline running concurrently and IV insulin commenced once the pH has improved above 7.20 on repeat gas

Commence IV 5 percent dextrose with potassium 40 mmol/L at maintenance rate from the outset to prevent hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia, with IV insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hour and target serum glucose between 6 and 10 mmol/L

subtopic_detail: Phototherapy threshold for late preterm infant at day 5 using age- and gestation-adjusted nomogram
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-day-old male infant born at 35 weeks and 1 day gestation by uncomplicated vaginal birth, now exclusively breastfed at home. He has had 9 percent weight loss from birth weight, dry mucous membranes and reduced wet nappies. He has visible jaundice extending to the lower legs. He is alert with normal tone. Mother's blood group is A positive (same as the baby), DCT is negative, and there is no family history of haemolytic disease, no bruising or cephalohaematoma. He had no jaundice on day-2 review by community midwife.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 148, RR 44, SpO2 99% room air, weight 2480 g (birth 2725 g, 9% loss)
data_table.Examination: Visible jaundice to lower legs, dry mucous membranes, alert, normal tone, no organomegaly, no cephalohaematoma or bruising, normal stool and urine output reported
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 280 micromol/L, direct 18, Hb 168, reticulocytes 3%, DCT negative, blood group A+ (same as mother), CRP <5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intensive phototherapy using overhead and underneath lights with infant naked except for nappy and eye protection, with feeding support to address lactation and 6-hourly serum bilirubin to monitor response and aim for cessation criteria

Arrange urgent double-volume exchange transfusion at the tertiary unit with planned admission to the neonatal intensive care unit and pre-procedure cross-match for two units of compatible blood from the transfusion service

Reassure the family that the jaundice is physiological breastfeeding jaundice given the normal DCT and absent haemolysis, encourage continued exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation and review in the community in 48 hours

Replace breastfeeding with formula feeds via cup feeding for 48 hours and recheck TSB at 24 hours without commencing phototherapy, as adequate caloric intake will usually resolve the bilirubin elevation without need for light therapy

Administer IV immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg over 4 hours and commence phototherapy concurrently, with serial TSB monitoring and DCT recheck within 24 hours to look for evidence of late-onset isoimmune haemolysis missed on initial testing

subtopic_detail: Repeat IM adrenaline at adult dose for school-age child with refractory anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with known peanut allergy who accidentally ate a peanut butter biscuit at a party 10 minutes ago. He has developed urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting once, a hoarse voice, audible expiratory wheeze, and a feeling of throat tightness. His parent administered his prescribed EpiPen Jr (150 mcg adrenaline) into the lateral thigh 5 minutes ago at home with no clear improvement before transfer.

On arrival in the resuscitation cubicle he remains distressed, tachypnoeic and his oxygen saturation has fallen on room air. Weight at his last GP visit was 24 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 140, RR 36, BP 92/56, SpO2 92% room air
data_table.Examination: Diffuse urticaria, lip and tongue swelling, hoarse voice, audible expiratory wheeze, mild intercostal recession, alert but distressed, weight 24 kg
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 5.6, ECG sinus tachycardia, no IV access yet established, allergy passport documents peanut as known allergen, prior adrenaline auto-injector at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Repeat the EpiPen Jr 150 mcg IM into the opposite lateral thigh, reassess in 5 minutes and consider escalation only if no response, while preparing intravenous access and high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask in the resuscitation bay

Administer 0.3 mL of 1:1000 adrenaline (300 mcg) IM into the mid-anterolateral thigh, apply high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask, position the patient supine with legs elevated, and obtain IV access for fluid resuscitation

Administer IV adrenaline 50 mcg bolus immediately under cardiac monitoring as the initial parenteral dose given the failure of the prehospital intramuscular dose to control the patient's airway and respiratory features

Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg via mask and IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg as primary therapy for the bronchospasm component, with adrenaline reserved as backup if there is no improvement over the next 10 minutes

Administer oral promethazine 10 mg and ranitidine 75 mg as combined H1 and H2 antihistamine therapy with reassessment after 20 minutes, plus consideration of a single dose of IM prednisolone 1 mg/kg as additional steroid

subtopic_detail: 3-monthly slit-lamp screening in ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA
stem: You are the paediatric rheumatology registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl with a 6-week history of intermittent painless right knee swelling and mild morning stiffness in the same joint. She has no fever, rash, mouth ulcers, weight loss, or systemic features. Examination shows a swollen non-tender right knee with reduced flexion, no other joints involved, and no enthesitis. Inflammatory markers are mildly elevated, ANA is positive at 1:320, RF and HLA-B27 are negative, and FBC is normal. Oligoarticular JIA has been diagnosed and an intra-articular triamcinolone injection has been planned. The family asks what additional screening their daughter requires.

data_table.Examination: Swollen non-tender right knee with reduced flexion, no other joints involved, no rash, no enthesitis, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: ANA 1:320 positive, RF negative, HLA-B27 negative, ESR 32, CRP 18, FBC normal, MRI knee shows synovitis with effusion, no slit-lamp examination done yet

lead_in: What additional screening should be recommended?

options.text: Annual review by an ophthalmologist with formal visual acuity testing and fundoscopy alone, with patient and family education to seek earlier review if any visual symptoms such as redness, pain, or photophobia occur in either eye

Testing for HLA-B27 has already been performed and was negative so further specific eye screening is not indicated, with reassurance that uveitis only complicates HLA-B27-positive enthesitis-related JIA

Six-monthly review by an orthopaedic surgeon for joint protection advice and assessment of leg-length discrepancy, with no requirement for additional eye review beyond standard school vision screening at age five

Three-monthly slit-lamp examination by an ophthalmologist to screen for chronic anterior uveitis, given that ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA in young girls is the highest-risk category and uveitis is typically asymptomatic until visual loss occurs

Reassure the family that screening for uveitis is only required if the patient develops symptoms of redness, pain or visual loss, given the low risk in oligoarticular JIA compared with polyarticular and systemic onset disease

subtopic_detail: Observation only for paediatric ITP without major bleeding
stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 5-year-old previously well girl referred by the GP with 5 days of widespread petechiae and easy bruising, and a viral URTI 2 weeks ago. Examination shows widespread petechiae and ecchymoses but no mucosal bleeding, no haematuria, no haematochezia, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy and no bony tenderness. She is alert, playing happily, and has had no head trauma. The blood film shows isolated thrombocytopenia with normal red and white cell morphology and no blasts. Acute immune thrombocytopenia is diagnosed.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.9, HR 102, BP 96/60, SpO2 99% room air, GCS 15
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and ecchymoses, no mucosal bleeding, no haematuria, no haematochezia, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no bony tenderness, playful
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 12, Hb 130, WCC 7.0 with normal differential, blood film isolated thrombocytopenia with no blasts, reticulocytes normal, coagulation profile normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Single dose of IVIG 0.8 g/kg over 6 hours as initial therapy because the platelet count is below 20 and the risk of intracranial haemorrhage is high enough to warrant first-line pharmacological intervention regardless of bleeding status

Oral prednisolone 4 mg/kg/day for 4 days as a first-line treatment for paediatric immune thrombocytopenia, with tapering over the subsequent week and repeat platelet count at 1 week to assess response to corticosteroid therapy

Bone marrow examination before any management decision is made in order to exclude acute lymphoblastic leukaemia presenting with isolated thrombocytopenia, with treatment guided by bone marrow findings and haematologist input

Single dose of intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg as inpatient therapy and admission for observation, with planned IVIG addition if no platelet response within 24 hours and haematology consultation for ongoing management

Observation only with no pharmacological treatment, written advice to avoid contact sport and NSAIDs, family education on signs of significant bleeding requiring re-presentation, and repeat platelet count by the GP in 1 week

subtopic_detail: Hand foot and mouth disease versus herpangina and HSV stomatitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-year-old previously well boy with 2 days of fever to 38.5 and refusal to eat due to mouth pain. Examination demonstrates multiple small grey-white vesicles on the palms of both hands (approximately 8 lesions), soles of both feet, and shallow ulcers on the buccal mucosa and tongue, with no rash on the trunk and no truncal vesicles.

His 5-year-old sister had a similar mild illness 1 week ago that resolved spontaneously. He is well-hydrated, alert, interactive with his parents, and there is no neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rash on the buttocks or perineum, and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 110, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Small grey-white vesicles on palms and soles (about 8 on hands), shallow oral ulcers on buccal mucosa and tongue, no truncal rash, mucous membranes moist, no lymphadenopathy, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: No bloods taken; bedside glucose 5.4; no swabs sent; family confirms no recent travel; immunisations including MMR up to date

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.text: Primary herpes simplex stomatitis with widespread painful vesicles and ulcers in the mouth, with oral aciclovir 80 mg/kg/day in divided doses for 5-7 days, paracetamol-based analgesia, and exclusion from childcare until oral lesions have crusted

Varicella zoster virus infection (chickenpox) with vesicular eruption progressing from face and trunk centrifugally, with supportive care, anti-pruritic management, and exclusion from childcare for at least 5 days after the rash has appeared

Hand foot and mouth disease caused by coxsackievirus A16 or enterovirus 71 with supportive care, adequate analgesia, oral fluid encouragement, and exclusion from childcare until vesicles have crusted (usually 7-10 days), with no antiviral therapy required

Herpangina from coxsackievirus group A presenting with isolated posterior pharyngeal vesicles and ulcers with high fever, with supportive analgesia and oral hydration, antiviral therapy is not warranted, and exclusion from school until resolution

Stevens-Johnson syndrome with mucocutaneous involvement requiring urgent admission, cessation of any culprit medication, fluid and electrolyte management, ophthalmology and dermatology input, and dermatology-directed biopsy of representative skin lesions

subtopic_detail: Moderate bronchiolitis HFNC and feeding strategy in infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old previously well term infant on day 3 of a coryzal illness now presenting with increased work of breathing and reduced feeds. He has had no apnoeas, is taking around 40% of his usual feed volumes, has had wet nappies 4 hours ago, and his older sibling is unwell with a viral upper respiratory tract infection.

He has no past wheeze, no atopy, no congenital heart disease and was not premature. Nasopharyngeal swab is pending. Trial of suctioning has provided only transient improvement and he remains in moderate respiratory distress on room air after observation in the ward over the last hour.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.6, HR 168, RR 64, SpO2 89% room air, BP 86/52
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring, scattered fine inspiratory crackles bilaterally, occasional expiratory wheeze, alert but irritable, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Nasal swab pending; VBG pH 7.34 pCO2 50 lactate 1.4; no chest X-ray done

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back and reassess in 20 minutes; if no improvement, give a single dose of oral prednisolone and admit overnight
Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90%, nasogastric feeds at two-thirds maintenance, and reassess after 2 hours
Administer intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg empirically, take blood cultures, perform a chest X-ray and observe overnight on the paediatric ward
Intubate and ventilate the infant urgently for impending respiratory failure given the venous blood gas pCO2 of 50 and persistent recessions despite suction
Discharge home on parent education for suctioning and paracetamol with return precautions for apnoeas, marked recession or feeding below half maintenance

subtopic_detail: Moderate acute asthma exacerbation salbutamol burst plus oral prednisolone
stem: You are the emergency department registrar assessing a 6-year-old girl with known mild persistent asthma who presents with 8 hours of progressive cough, wheeze and increased work of breathing following a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She normally uses a salbutamol pMDI with spacer as needed and a low-dose budesonide preventer with reasonable adherence. She has not had a preventer dose today. She last presented 6 months ago with an uncomplicated mild exacerbation managed at home. She is alert and speaks in short phrases between breaths.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.4, HR 132, RR 36, SpO2 93% room air, BP 100/62
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, widespread polyphonic wheeze, prolonged expiratory phase, no stridor, alert and oriented, peak flow not measurable due to distress
data_table.Investigations: No imaging or bloods performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Administer single nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms without salbutamol, observe for 20 minutes, then commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg if response is inadequate and admit the patient for inpatient observation overnight

Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 20 minutes immediately as first-line therapy, give intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and admit to the paediatric high-dependency unit for continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring overnight

Give salbutamol pMDI with spacer 6 puffs every 20 minutes for 3 doses with oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg, reassess after the third dose, and stretch salbutamol to 1-2 hourly if improving with disposition decision at four hours

Up-titrate her inhaled budesonide preventer to twice daily for two weeks, dispense a single dose of oral prednisolone for home use and discharge with safety netting and review by the general practitioner in seven days

Intubate and ventilate the patient electively now for impending respiratory failure given the speech limitation and respiratory rate, with rapid-sequence induction using ketamine in the resuscitation cubicle and transfer to PICU

subtopic_detail: Simple febrile seizure outpatient discharge after first event
stem: You are the paediatric registrar assessing an 18-month-old previously well boy who had a single generalised tonic-clonic convulsion lasting 2 minutes at home, followed by 15 minutes of drowsiness and now full recovery in the emergency department. He has a temperature of 38.7 degrees with clinical findings of an uncomplicated viral upper respiratory tract infection. He is fully immunised, has no developmental concerns, no family history of epilepsy, no prior seizures and no medication exposure. He is now alert, interactive, taking sips of fluid and his neurological examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air, BP 96/58
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, GCS 15, normal cranial nerves, normal tone power and reflexes, no neck stiffness, no rash, ENT consistent with viral URTI, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging performed; bedside glucose 5.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition and follow-up plan?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever relief, written first-aid febrile seizure advice, GP review within 48 hours and return precautions for any recurrent seizure, prolonged drowsiness or focal neurology

Perform a lumbar puncture, full blood examination, blood cultures and venous blood gas as routine workup, commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone for possible meningitis and admit the patient for observation overnight on the paediatric ward

Arrange an electroencephalogram in the next week, refer to the paediatric neurology outpatient clinic for ongoing follow-up and counsel the family about the elevated lifetime risk of developing childhood epilepsy after a febrile seizure

Arrange an urgent non-contrast computed tomography of the brain in the emergency department to rule out intracranial pathology before discharge, with paediatric neurology phone consultation prior to leaving the department for safety

Commence regular oral diazepam 0.5 mg/kg daily as prophylaxis to be continued for 6 months, with written instructions on use of buccal midazolam for any breakthrough seizure activity at home and review in 1 month

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media antibiotic threshold in child under 2 years
stem: You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 14-month-old girl with 36 hours of fever, fussiness, poor sleep and persistent ear-pulling on the right side. She is fully immunised including pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, has no previous episodes of acute otitis media, and has no chronic ear disease. There is no perforation visible. Her appetite is reduced but she is taking oral fluids and her nappies remain wet. Antibiotic susceptibility patterns in your local population are typical of community-acquired pneumococcus and Haemophilus influenzae.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6, HR 140, RR 28, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging, opaque and erythematous with loss of normal landmarks; left tympanic membrane normal; no mastoid tenderness or post-auricular swelling; oropharynx mildly erythematous

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Trial 48 hours of watchful waiting with paracetamol or ibuprofen analgesia and review in 48 hours by the general practitioner with antibiotics deferred unless the child deteriorates or remains symptomatic at the planned review

Prescribe oral cefaclor 10 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days with paracetamol or ibuprofen as required for fever and pain, and review in the general practice clinic in one week to confirm resolution and tympanic membrane normalisation

Refer urgently to ear nose and throat outpatients for myringotomy and grommet insertion given the bulging tympanic membrane with constitutional symptoms in a young child, and provide paracetamol as required while awaiting the appointment

Prescribe oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days with paracetamol or ibuprofen for analgesia, provide parental return advice for vomiting or deterioration, and follow up by the GP in one week

Prescribe ciprofloxacin otic drops 0.3% twice daily for 7 days with paracetamol or ibuprofen as required, advise warm compress to the affected ear and review in the general practice clinic in 48 hours for ongoing assessment

subtopic_detail: DKA cerebral oedema recognition and hypertonic saline management
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar managing an 8-year-old girl with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis who has been on her calculated rehydration and 0.05 unit/kg/hour insulin infusion for 4 hours. Her presenting pH was 7.05, glucose 32 mmol/L, ketones 5.8 mmol/L, and corrected sodium was 138 mmol/L. Two hours ago her glucose had fallen to 18 mmol/L and 5% dextrose was added to her fluids.

Over the last 30 minutes she has developed worsening headache, become more drowsy, and has had two episodes of vomiting. Her bedside glucose is now 14 mmol/L. Senior paediatric and intensive care support have been called.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 64 (was 110), RR 18, BP 138/86 (was 100/60), SpO2 99% room air, GCS now 12 (was 14)
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, irritable when roused, sluggish pupillary reactions, no focal neurology, no neck stiffness, mild Kussmaul breathing reduced
data_table.Investigations: Latest VBG: pH 7.18 HCO3 12 BE -10 lactate 1.6; glucose 14 mmol/L; ketones 3.4 mmol/L; Na 142 corrected, K 3.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion rate to 0.1 unit/kg/hour to accelerate ketone clearance and request urgent contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the brain to characterise the suspected cerebral oedema before further intervention

Give a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus over 15 minutes to address suspected hypovolaemia from intravascular depletion and continue the same insulin infusion rate while reassessing neurological status every 5 minutes

Intubate immediately in the paediatric resuscitation cubicle for airway protection given the falling GCS and use propofol induction with bag-mask ventilation to mild hyperventilation aiming for an end-tidal CO2 of 30

Continue current management unchanged and recheck the venous blood gas in 1 hour because the pH has improved from 7.05 to 7.18 and the glucose is approaching target range, treating the symptoms as evolving recovery

Administer 3% hypertonic saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes (or alternatively mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg over 20 minutes), reduce maintenance fluid rate by one-third, elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees and call intensive care for transfer

subtopic_detail: Non-accidental injury mandatory reporting and safety admission
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-month-old boy brought to the emergency department by his mother because he has stopped using his right leg. There is bruising on the medial thigh and the radiograph shows a transverse mid-shaft femoral fracture. His mother says he rolled off a low couch this morning, but a triage note states she earlier told the nurse he was kicked accidentally by his 3-year-old brother.

The infant is not yet rolling on developmental assessment and weighs on the 25th centile. The maternal partner has been demanding to take the family home before assessment is complete and is becoming increasingly agitated.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.0, HR 144, RR 36, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Distressed with passive movement of right leg, swelling and bruising of the right medial thigh, 1 cm bruise to the left flank, no other external injuries identified, anterior fontanelle soft, no scleral haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: Plain right femur radiograph: transverse mid-shaft femur fracture; FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation, calcium and CK pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Apply a Thomas splint, prescribe simple analgesia, refer to orthopaedics for outpatient closed reduction and follow-up, and discharge once the mother has signed an undertaking to attend the social work appointment next week with both parents

Admit the infant under paediatrics for safety and analgesia, notify the statutory child protection service and senior paediatrician immediately, arrange a skeletal survey within 24 hours and request hospital security if there is any attempt to remove the child

Request an urgent contrast computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to look for hidden visceral injury and a head computed tomography to exclude intracranial haemorrhage, and defer child protection notification pending those imaging results

Allow the family to leave the department with a follow-up paediatric appointment in 24 hours after a full ward discharge summary has been provided, after ensuring the orthopaedic plan is documented and analgesia has been prescribed for home use

Counsel the mother that this presentation is most likely accidental given the explanation of being kicked by a sibling, document the parents' account verbatim and discharge with primary health network referral for early childhood developmental support

subtopic_detail: Septic arthritis hip urgent joint aspiration and IV antibiotics
stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar assessing a 6-year-old boy with 36 hours of right hip pain, fever and refusal to weight-bear. He had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago that has fully resolved. The hip is held in slight flexion, external rotation and abduction with marked guarding on attempted passive internal rotation. He has had no recent trauma, no skin breakdown and no rash.

He has not had any episodes of haematuria or oliguria, and he is otherwise developmentally normal. Orthopaedics has been called for senior review and the operating theatre has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 130, RR 26, BP 102/64, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Right hip held in slight flexion external rotation, severe pain on attempted internal rotation, refuses to bear weight, no obvious effusion of the knee or ankle, no rash, mild right-sided inguinal tenderness, otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.6, neutrophils 14.2, CRP 92, ESR 56, blood cultures sent; hip ultrasound shows a significant right hip joint effusion compared to the left

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Commence oral ibuprofen and observe for 24 hours on the paediatric ward with rest and weight-bearing as tolerated, anticipating clinical resolution typical of transient synovitis of the hip following a recent viral illness

Arrange a contrast magnetic resonance imaging of the hip before any intervention to differentiate transient synovitis, septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, and commence empirical oral cefalexin while awaiting the scan and ward review

Take blood cultures, transfer to operating theatre for urgent hip arthrotomy with washout and synovial fluid microscopy and culture, and commence intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly empirically immediately after the cultures

Commence intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone empirically to provide broad cover including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and Kingella kingae, and admit under paediatric medicine for serial clinical review without aspiration

Trial intravenous ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg daily for 48 hours, reassess clinically and biochemically with repeat CRP and clinical examination at that point, and consider operative intervention only if no clinical or biochemical improvement

subtopic_detail: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis hydration and opioid analgesia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 8-year-old boy with known homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) on regular folate and hydroxycarbamide, brought by his mother with severe right thigh pain since this morning. He has had a similar episode 6 months ago that resolved with admission. His baseline haemoglobin is 78 g/L and he is fully immunised including pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib boosters.

He has no current fever, no respiratory symptoms, no chest pain and no neurological symptoms. He has not been swimming or had any trauma. He weighs 24 kg and has been able to drink only sips of fluid since the pain commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.1, HR 122, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, BP 108/68, pain score 8/10
data_table.Examination: Tender right thigh without erythema, swelling or restricted joint movement, chest clear, no focal neurology, no splenic enlargement
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76, retic 320, WCC 11.2, platelets 380, CRP 8, type and screen sent; chest X-ray clear; urine MCS pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluids at 1.5 times maintenance with regular paracetamol, ibuprofen and intravenous morphine bolus then patient-controlled analgesia, supplemental oxygen if SpO2 drops, screen for acute chest syndrome with serial respiratory assessment and continue hydroxycarbamide

Prescribe oral paracetamol and ibuprofen as required, encourage oral fluid intake and discharge home with general practice review in 24 hours and clear advice to return for any new fever, chest pain or breathing difficulty over the next week

Arrange urgent simple red cell transfusion of 10 mL/kg to a target haemoglobin of 100 g/L for all sickle cell vaso-occlusive crises on presentation, with prior cross-match using extended phenotyping for Rh and Kell antigens to minimise alloimmunisation

Commence intravenous ceftriaxone 80 mg/kg daily empirically for occult bacteraemia given the underlying functional asplenia and severe pain, with discharge planned at 48 hours if cultures are negative and the patient is clinically improved

Arrange urgent exchange transfusion with leucodepleted packed red cells in the high-dependency unit to reduce HbS percentage below 30, with a peripheral large-bore intravenous access and continuous cardiac monitoring during the procedure

subtopic_detail: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome recognition in failure to thrive with neutropenia and steatorrhoea
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy referred from primary care for failure to thrive (weight tracking just below the 3rd centile, height on the 5th centile), recurrent respiratory and middle-ear infections over the past 12 months, and three months of bulky pale offensive stools that float and stain the nappy. He was born at term without complications.

His parents are non-consanguineous of European ancestry. Sweat chloride testing performed twice at the regional centre has been normal at 22 and 18 mmol/L. He has no skin or hair changes, no organomegaly and no rash.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8, HR 110, RR 24, weight 10.4 kg, height 84 cm, BP 92/56
data_table.Examination: Mildly wasted appearance, mild abdominal distension, no organomegaly, no rash, normal cardiovascular and respiratory exam, normal external genitalia, no skeletal abnormalities on standard examination
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96, MCV 78, WCC 4.2 with neutrophils 0.4, platelets 240, faecal elastase 78 micrograms per gram (low), faecal fat increased, immunoglobulins normal, coeliac serology negative, IgA normal, two sweat chlorides normal (22 and 18)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation and management plan?

options.text: Repeat the sweat chloride test for a third time and proceed with empirical pancreatic enzyme replacement at 1000 lipase units per kilogram per meal and a high-energy formula, attributing the neutropenia to chronic inflammation while awaiting the repeat sweat result
