Commence intravenous pancreatic enzyme replacement, dietitian-led calorie supplementation, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor 5 micrograms per kilogram subcutaneously daily, and refer immediately to oncology for empiric bone marrow transplant workup pending DNA result

Arrange a duodenal biopsy under general anaesthesia given the steatorrhoea and growth failure, send for histology to confirm villous architecture, and commence a gluten-free trial despite negative coeliac serology in case of IgA-deficient coeliac disease as a unifying diagnosis

Request a skeletal survey, send SBDS gene testing for Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, refer to paediatric haematology, paediatric gastroenterology and a dietitian, commence oral pancreatic enzyme replacement and fat-soluble vitamins, and arrange neutropenia monitoring with infection precautions

Reassure that the constellation likely represents toddler diarrhoea and constitutional small stature, recommend daily faecal elastase repeat after a high-fat dietary trial, and review in 3 months in the general paediatrics clinic with weight and height plotted

stem: A 9-month-old infant is brought to a regional emergency department by his parents with 3 days of coryza and cough, and 24 hours of increasing work of breathing. He has taken half his usual feeds today and had no apnoea. He was born at 39 weeks and has no comorbidities. The nearest paediatric retrieval team is 90 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.6 degrees Celsius, HR 158, RR 62, SpO2 88% in room air, BP 92/58 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Moderate work of breathing with subcostal and intercostal recession, widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, alert and consolable

lead_in: Which is the single best initial respiratory intervention?

options.text: Commence low-flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min titrated to maintain SpO2 at least 90% and admit under paediatrics for monitoring
Commence humidified high-flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with FiO2 to target SpO2 92 to 96% as first-line respiratory support
Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg with oxygen and reassess in 20 minutes for any change in work of breathing
Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring in the resuscitation cubicle
Intubate, ventilate, and arrange urgent retrieval to a paediatric intensive care unit for further respiratory support

stem: A 4-year-old girl presents to her general practitioner with 4 months of infrequent, hard, painful bowel motions every 4 to 5 days. She withholds on the toilet and has occasional faecal soiling. There is no blood, no vomiting and her growth is on the 50th centile. Toilet training is otherwise complete. Coeliac serology and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with a palpable suprapubic faecal mass, normal anal position and tone, no anal fissure, normal lumbosacral spine
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac IgA tTG negative, TSH 2.4 mU/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Sodium phosphate enema with manual disimpaction under conscious sedation
Lactulose 5 mL orally twice daily as the sole maintenance therapy now
Oral macrogol 3350 with electrolytes daily in escalating disimpaction dose
Increased dietary fibre and fluid alongside daily toileting routine review
Anorectal manometry and paediatric surgery referral for suction biopsy

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 0200 with a 1-day history of coryza followed by 4 hours of a barking cough and noisy breathing. He is alert, drinking small sips, and pinker after being upset on triage. He has had no foreign body exposure and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.2 degrees Celsius, HR 140, RR 36, SpO2 96% in room air
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest, moderate suprasternal and intercostal recession, barking cough, no drooling, chest clear, alert

lead_in: What is the single best initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose; observe until stridor at rest settles and oral intake is adequate (typically 1-2 hours)
Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally with at least 3 hours of in-department observation
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose and arrange discharge home after consultant review and parent education
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 flat dose with at least 3 hours of post-adrenaline observation
Intubation in theatre with paediatric intensive care unit admission for ongoing airway and respiratory support after retrieval

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with 3 days of palpable purpura over his buttocks and lower legs, bilateral ankle swelling, and crampy peri-umbilical abdominal pain that has worsened in the last 12 hours. He has vomited twice this morning. His mother reports no haematemesis or melaena. He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.4 degrees Celsius, HR 110, RR 22, BP 102/64 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Palpable non-blanching purpura on extensor surfaces and buttocks, soft abdomen with peri-umbilical tenderness, no peritonism, no scrotal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick blood 1+ protein negative, FBC platelets 320, creatinine 38 micromol/L, faecal occult blood positive

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and general practitioner review in 48 hours
Arrange urgent contrast computed tomography of abdomen to exclude appendicitis
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and arrange general practitioner follow-up
Refer urgently to nephrology for renal biopsy and immunosuppression today
Admit for analgesia, oral hydration, surgical review and abdominal ultrasound

stem: A 3-year-old girl was admitted 36 hours ago with day-6 fever, polymorphous rash, bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. She received IVIG 2 g/kg and high-dose aspirin. She remains febrile to 39.1 degrees Celsius 36 hours after the IVIG infusion finished. Her echocardiogram performed today is normal. She has no allergies and the cardiology registrar has been notified.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.1 degrees Celsius, HR 150, RR 28, BP 90/52 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Persistent conjunctivitis and rash, irritable but consolable, no respiratory distress, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: CRP 95 mg/L (was 130 on admission), platelets 480, normal LFTs, blood culture pending and no growth at 24 hours

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer a second dose of IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours
Commence intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days
Start intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg as a single infusion
Escalate aspirin from anti-inflammatory to antiplatelet dose
Stop aspirin and start intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone

stem: A breastfeeding term newborn boy is reviewed at 48 hours of life for visible jaundice. The mother is blood group O Rh-positive and the baby is group A Rh-positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. The first total serum bilirubin at 30 hours of life was 280 micromol/L and has risen to 460 micromol/L at 48 hours despite intensive double phototherapy initiated 12 hours ago. He is feeding poorly but alert.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.9 degrees Celsius, HR 152, RR 48, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Alert and responsive, mild hypotonia, normal Moro reflex, no opisthotonus, no high-pitched cry
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 460 micromol/L, conjugated 12 micromol/L, haemoglobin 142 g/L, reticulocytes 6%, DAT positive, weight loss 7% from birth

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intensive double phototherapy and repeat bilirubin in 6 hours
Administer a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 0.5 g/kg only
Arrange double-volume exchange transfusion with cross-matched compatible blood
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours and supplement feeds with infant formula
Start oral phenobarbital 5 mg/kg daily to induce bilirubin conjugation

stem: An 8-month-old previously well boy was admitted 4 days ago with high fever and a clean-catch urine growing more than 100,000 colony-forming units per millilitre of Escherichia coli sensitive to gentamicin and cefalexin. He responded promptly to intravenous gentamicin and is afebrile on oral cefalexin to complete a 10-day course. His renal tract ultrasound performed yesterday is normal with no hydronephrosis. He is discharged tomorrow and feeding normally.

data_table.Examination: Afebrile, well, normal external genitalia, retractile foreskin, no abdominal mass, growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture E. coli more than 100,000 CFU/mL, CRP peak 110 mg/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, renal ultrasound normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: No further imaging required; outpatient paediatric review and parental education to present promptly with any future fever
Micturating cystourethrogram before discharge while still inpatient to assess for vesico-ureteric reflux severity
Magnetic resonance urography under general anaesthetic within the next month to characterise the renal tract structure
DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring after this first febrile UTI episode
Long-term low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis without any further imaging until a future symptomatic infection occurs

stem: A 15-year-old rugby player presents to the local clinic 24 hours after being tackled during a match. He had a 20-second loss of consciousness, brief retrograde amnesia and a headache. He has had no further headache since the morning of presentation, no vomiting, and his neurological examination today is normal. His parents ask when he can return to contact training. He had a previous concussion 8 months ago that resolved in 1 week.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 72, RR 14, BP 118/72 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 15, normal cranial nerves, normal coordination, normal tandem gait, no scalp haematoma
data_table.Investigations: SCAT5 symptom score 0 at rest

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate advice today?

options.text: Immediate return to non-contact training tomorrow if he stays asymptomatic
Permanent retirement from contact sport because of repeat concussion
Strict cognitive and physical rest for 4 weeks then resume contact
Computed tomography of the head before any return to activity
Begin a graded return-to-sport protocol with at least 24 hours per stage

stem: A 14-month-old girl presents to her general practitioner with 24 hours of fever to 39 degrees Celsius, irritability and bilateral ear pulling. She is feeding less well but is interactive between febrile episodes. Her vaccinations are up to date and she has had no prior ear infections. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.0 degrees Celsius, HR 144, RR 30, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes are bulging, opaque and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy; no otorrhoea; chest clear; throat unremarkable; no neck stiffness

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic management with regular paracetamol and review in 48 hours if not improving
Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg/dose once daily for 3 days as a single-dose option
Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 10 days as a high-dose course
Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 5 days with safety-net advice
Oral cefaclor 10 mg/kg/dose three times daily for 5 days as a cephalosporin alternative

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents to a metropolitan GP with 3 weeks of dry cough, now with paroxysms of coughing followed by an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. He is otherwise well between episodes. His mother is 32 weeks pregnant with her second child. A 6-week-old cousin lives in the same house. The child had three doses of pertussis-containing vaccine in infancy. NAAT swab returns positive for Bordetella pertussis.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 24, SpO2 98% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well between paroxysms; chest clear; no respiratory distress at rest

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step for the index child and the household?

options.text: Treat the index child with azithromycin and offer prophylaxis to all household contacts regardless of risk
Symptomatic management only as the index child is past the contagious period and no longer infectious
Treat the index child with amoxicillin and offer the same antibiotic to all household contacts
Treat the index child with azithromycin and provide household prophylaxis to high-risk contacts
Defer treatment and arrange paired pertussis serology before deciding on antibiotic prophylaxis

stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to a GP because his parents are worried he looks pale and has been a fussy eater. He drinks 800 mL of cow's milk daily and refuses red meat. He met motor milestones on time and is now running. There is no family history of haemoglobinopathy and he is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. Recent FBC and iron studies are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.7 degrees Celsius, HR 124, RR 24, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae; no jaundice; no hepatosplenomegaly; no lymphadenopathy; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 62 fL, MCH 19 pg, reticulocytes 0.6%, ferritin 6 microgram/L, transferrin saturation 5%, CRP 2 mg/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent haematology referral for bone marrow biopsy to exclude marrow failure as the cause
Commence oral ferrous sulfate 3 mg/kg of elemental iron once daily and reduce cow's milk to 500 mL/day
Request haemoglobin electrophoresis and defer treatment until thalassaemia trait has been excluded
Arrange an intravenous iron infusion in day surgery because oral iron is poorly tolerated in toddlers
Commence vitamin B12 and folate supplementation as the most likely cause of nutritional anaemia

subtopic_detail: Next step when an adequate oral macrogol disimpaction regimen has failed
stem: A 6-year-old boy with functional constipation has completed seven days of an escalating oral macrogol regimen to the maximum dose for his age, taken as prescribed. He still soils most days.

data_table.Examination: Palpable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa; normal perianal appearance; growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Nil indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Add an oral stimulant laxative such as senna to the macrogol
Stop the macrogol and start a daily lactulose preparation instead
Arrange a plain abdominal radiograph to quantify the faecal loading
Refer for a phosphate enema in the emergency department today
Halve the macrogol dose and add a scheduled toilet sitting routine

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to ED with a 5-day history of palpable purpuric rash over the buttocks and lower limbs, intermittent crampy abdominal pain and bilateral ankle pain. Today he has had two episodes of dark cola-coloured urine. He had a viral upper respiratory illness 2 weeks ago. His mother says urine output is reduced. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.1 degrees Celsius, HR 104, RR 22, BP 132/88 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and lower legs, abdomen soft with mild tenderness, no peritonism, ankles swollen but full range, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis 3+ blood, 2+ protein with red cell casts; urine protein-creatinine ratio 180 mg/mmol; creatinine 78 micromol/L; urea 9 mmol/L; platelets 380 x10^9/L; coags normal

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate disposition and initial management?

options.text: Discharge with paracetamol and outpatient urinalysis weekly because skin and joint signs predominate
Admit for blood pressure control, monitoring of renal function and paediatric nephrology consultation
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg in the emergency department and discharge with follow-up in a week
Request abdominal ultrasound to exclude intussusception then discharge if no lead point is identified
Commence empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for suspected post-infectious glomerulonephritis

stem: An 11-year-old girl presents to ED with 3 weeks of polyuria, polydipsia and 4 kg weight loss. She has no vomiting, abdominal pain or tachypnoea. She walks into the cubicle. A fingerprick capillary BSL is 22 mmol/L. You are deciding the initial inpatient plan as the paediatric registrar. Investigations are shown.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 96, RR 18, BP 108/64 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, mildly dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft, no Kussmaul breathing, no acetone on breath
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.35, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 1.6 mmol/L, BGL 22 mmol/L, Na 138 mmol/L, K 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 60 micromol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Admit and commence a subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin regimen with diabetes education and oral fluids
Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/h with 0.9% sodium chloride at maintenance rates
Administer a 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus then commence DKA protocol with two-bag system
Discharge after diabetes nurse contact and commence metformin pending outpatient endocrinology review
Trial oral rehydration in the short-stay unit and re-measure ketones at 4 hours before deciding on insulin

stem: A 2-year-old boy is recovering from his second culture-confirmed febrile UTI in 6 months, both with E. coli. His first UTI at 18 months was treated with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and he had a normal renal tract ultrasound at the time. Today he is afebrile after 24 hours of oral co-trimoxazole. His mother asks what additional imaging is needed.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.0 degrees Celsius, HR 110, RR 24, BP 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Well, abdomen soft non-tender, no renal angle tenderness, growth on 50th centile, no spinal anomaly

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: Commence long-term low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis and defer all imaging unless a further symptomatic infection occurs in the future
Arrange an urgent inpatient micturating cystourethrogram to assess for vesico-ureteric reflux before discharge from this admission
Repeat renal tract ultrasound and refer to paediatric nephrology for recurrent UTI; no routine DMSA scan in the RCH pathway
Arrange a contrast-enhanced CT KUB to characterise the renal cortex and to exclude any obstructive uropathy in this child
Arrange a DMSA scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring after this second febrile UTI episode

stem: A 2-day-old male term neonate is brought back to a regional hospital with poor feeding and cyanosis. He was born by uncomplicated NVD with Apgars 9 and 10 and discharged at 18 hours. His mother reports he has become progressively bluer over the morning, particularly with crying. Pre-ductal SpO2 is 78% and post-ductal SpO2 is 78%; both fail to rise above 85% in 100% oxygen by Hudson mask. Cardiac auscultation reveals a single second heart sound and no murmur. The paediatric retrieval team is 2 hours away.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 168, RR 60, SpO2 78% pre and post-ductal, BP 64/40 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Centrally cyanosed even on 100% oxygen, peripheries warm with brisk capillary refill, abdomen soft, liver edge 1 cm below costal margin, no audible murmur, single loud S2
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.30, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L, BSL 3.2 mmol/L; CXR shows narrow mediastinum with mildly increased pulmonary vascularity

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step before retrieval arrives?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion at 10 nanogram/kg/min and monitor for apnoea
Continue 100% oxygen via Hudson mask and arrange urgent transthoracic echocardiogram before any treatment
Intubate, ventilate with 100% oxygen and commence dopamine infusion at 10 microgram/kg/min
Commence intravenous adenosine 100 microgram/kg as a rapid bolus for suspected supraventricular tachycardia
Commence broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for sepsis and defer cardiac assessment until cultures return

stem: A 30-month-old boy is brought to his GP with 36 hours of right ear pain and fever to 38.6 degrees Celsius. He has been miserable but is feeding well and is alert between febrile episodes. He has had one prior episode of unilateral acute otitis media 8 months ago that resolved with observation. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and is fully immunised.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.6 degrees Celsius, HR 130, RR 26, SpO2 99% in room air
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous with reduced mobility on pneumatic otoscopy; no otorrhoea; left tympanic membrane normal; chest clear; throat unremarkable

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Symptomatic analgesia with regular paracetamol and review in 48 hours if not improving
Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days commenced immediately today
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days commenced now
Oral cefuroxime axetil 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days as a cephalosporin alternative
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as a single dose given the risk of mastoiditis

stem: An 18-month-old girl presents to her GP with a 2-day history of fever to 38.4 degrees Celsius, oral pain and a rash on her hands and feet. She is still drinking water and dilute juice but has refused solids for 24 hours. She attends family day care 3 days per week. Her vaccinations are up to date and she is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 99% in room air; wet nappies in last 4 hours
data_table.Examination: Multiple shallow grey ulcers on tongue and buccal mucosa; vesicles on palms and soles and around perioral skin; no neck stiffness; chest clear; abdomen soft

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days targeting herpes simplex replication
Symptomatic analgesia with paracetamol, oral fluids, and day care exclusion until blisters dry
Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days targeting bacterial pharyngitis as cause
Topical viscous lidocaine 2% to the oral ulcers four times daily as topical analgesia
Oral nystatin 100,000 units four times daily as antifungal mouth therapy for oral ulcers

stem: A 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of fever and reduced feeding. There are no respiratory symptoms and no rash. She is the first child of well parents, was born at term and has had no prior infections. She is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. A catheter specimen of urine shows leucocytes and nitrites with bacteria on microscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 39.4 degrees Celsius, HR 170, RR 40, SpO2 98% in room air, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Alert but irritable; anterior fontanelle soft; chest clear; abdomen soft with no mass; nappy area normal
data_table.Investigations: Catheter urine: leucocytes 4+, nitrites positive, bacteria 3+; bloods: WCC 18, CRP 75, creatinine 30; blood culture pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 4 mg/kg twice daily for 5 days at home with GP review in 48 hours
Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days as outpatient management today
Admit for IV gentamicin 7 mg/kg daily and IV benzylpenicillin while culture results return
Discharge with a single intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg and outpatient follow-up tomorrow
Discharge with oral amoxicillin and arrange an outpatient renal tract ultrasound next week

stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes at home in the setting of fever to 39.2 degrees Celsius. He has had 24 hours of cough and rhinorrhoea. He has no prior seizures and his development is normal. He is now alert though sleepy. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.8 degrees Celsius, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 99% in room air, capillary glucose 5.2
data_table.Examination: GCS 15, no focal neurology, anterior fontanelle closed and not bulging, no neck stiffness, no petechial rash, ENT normal, chest clear

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for lumbar puncture given age under 24 months and a seizure in the setting of fever
Commence daily prophylactic sodium valproate 20 mg/kg/day to prevent further febrile seizures
Arrange an outpatient EEG within 1 week to characterise the seizure type before discharge
Reassure the family, advise antipyretics for comfort, and provide written first-aid seizure advice
Prescribe buccal midazolam 0.3 mg/kg for parents to use if any future seizure exceeds 5 minutes

stem: A 5-year-old boy (20 kg) with known peanut allergy collapsed at a birthday party 15 minutes ago after eating a satay skewer. The ambulance crew gave intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg in the lateral thigh en route and again 5 minutes later on arrival in the emergency department. IV access has been established. He remains audibly stridorous with widespread urticaria.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 38, SpO2 90% on 8 L oxygen via mask, BP 65/35, HR 165, GCS 14
data_table.Examination: Audible inspiratory stridor and expiratory wheeze, generalised urticaria, perioral angioedema, cool peripheries, capillary refill 4 seconds
data_table.Medications: Two IM adrenaline 0.15 mg doses given 5 minutes apart; IV crystalloid 20 mL/kg bolus commenced

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Third intramuscular adrenaline 0.15 mg dose with a second IV crystalloid bolus of 20 mL/kg
IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg and oral cetirizine 5 mg as adjunct anti-inflammatory therapy
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg in 5 mL of saline for ongoing upper airway swelling and stridor
IM adrenaline 0.5 mg using the adult dose to overcome refractory severe symptoms
Commence IV adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min titrated and continue IV fluid resuscitation

stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the GP with 6 months of hard infrequent stools every 4 to 5 days and recent daily faecal soiling of his underwear. He has crampy abdominal pain that improves after stooling. He passed meconium at 18 hours of age, growth percentiles are appropriate for age and the lumbosacral spine is normal. He has been on lactulose 5 mL twice daily for 8 weeks without improvement.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with palpable suprapubic faecal mass; perianal inspection normal with no fissure or anteriorly displaced anus; normal lower limb tone, reflexes and gait
data_table.Investigations: Growth chart: height and weight tracking 50th centile; no plain abdominal x-ray performed

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence outpatient high-dose macrogol 3350 with electrolytes disimpaction regimen over 3 days
Refer to paediatric surgery for assessment for Hirschsprung disease and anorectal manometry
Admit for nasogastric polyethylene glycol lavage given outpatient laxative failure to date
Add a daily sodium picosulfate stimulant to current lactulose for ongoing chronic management
Order plain abdominal x-ray to confirm faecal loading before changing management today

subtopic_detail: Infantile spasms recognition and initial therapy
stem: A previously well 5-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with a 2-week history of recurrent brief episodes of sudden symmetric flexion of her head, arms and legs, occurring in clusters of 10 to 30 events shortly after waking. Her parents have captured several events on video. Over the same period her parents report loss of social smiling and reduced engagement compared with her baseline. She is afebrile and is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

data_table.Examination: Alert but quiet, no focal neurology, anterior fontanelle soft, head circumference 50th centile; no neurocutaneous stigmata on inspection of skin
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 4.8; videos reviewed show characteristic flexor spasms in clusters with brief crying after each cluster

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure parents that these are benign myoclonic jerks of infancy and require no investigation
Arrange urgent neurology referral and EEG within 24 to 48 hours and start oral prednisolone 40 mg daily
Trial oral phenobarbital 5 mg/kg daily and review response in clinic at 4 weeks
Order outpatient MRI brain at 4 weeks and review with results before treatment
Commence sodium valproate 20 mg/kg daily and review in 2 weeks for clinical response

subtopic_detail: Neonatal HSV central nervous system disease
stem: An 18-day-old term neonate is brought to the emergency department with 24 hours of lethargy, poor feeding, fever to 38.4 degrees Celsius and clusters of vesicles on the scalp at the site of a fetal scalp electrode. The mother had primary genital herpes at 36 weeks of gestation and was on suppressive aciclovir from 36 weeks. He was born by spontaneous vaginal birth.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 38.4 degrees Celsius, HR 180, RR 60, SpO2 96% in room air, capillary glucose 3.6
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, decreased tone, anterior fontanelle full but not bulging, scalp vesicles in clusters on a red base; chest clear; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Blood culture pending; CSF: WCC 50 (mononuclear), protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 2.4; CSF HSV-2 PCR positive; surface viral swabs pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: IV cefotaxime 50 mg/kg eight-hourly for 14 days as empirical bacterial meningitis cover only
Oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily for 14 days as outpatient management with review
IV aciclovir 20 mg/kg eight-hourly for 21 days with ophthalmology and neurology review
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and IV amoxicillin 50 mg/kg six-hourly for 10 days
IV ganciclovir 6 mg/kg twice daily for 21 days targeting cytomegalovirus disease

stem: A 9-month-old previously well infant is brought to a regional ED with 3 days of coryza and 1 day of increasing cough and noisy breathing. He has not been feeding well today and his nappies are dry over the past 8 hours. He has had no apnoeas reported by his mother and is alert when stimulated. He is not Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander and is up to date with vaccinations. His chest auscultation reveals widespread fine crackles and mild expiratory wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 37.6 degrees Celsius, HR 158, RR 64, SpO2 90% on room air, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Examination: Moderate intercostal and subcostal recession, nasal flaring; cool peripheries; chest with widespread crackles and wheeze; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care viral PCR positive for respiratory syncytial virus; capillary blood gas: pH 7.36, pCO2 42 mmHg, HCO3 22 mmol/L

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit, commence humidified low-flow nasal cannula oxygen to maintain SpO2 above 92 percent, support feeding with small frequent volumes or nasogastric feeds as needed, and reassess hourly
Admit for trial of nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes and intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg six hourly as the first-line therapy for moderate bronchiolitis in this child today
Discharge home with parental safety-net advice, oral paracetamol 15 mg/kg six hourly and review with the GP in 24 hours if symptoms have not improved at all by then with rest
Commence intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg once daily and order a chest X-ray as the first-line management for moderate bronchiolitis in this previously well 9-month-old infant today
Admit, commence humidified nasal cannula oxygen to keep SpO2 of at least 90 percent, support hydration with small frequent feeds or nasogastric top-ups, and reassess hourly

subtopic_detail: Suspected non-accidental injury in a non-mobile infant
stem: A 5-month-old girl is brought to ED by her mother after being noticed to have multiple bruises in different stages of healing. She is not yet rolling or crawling. Chest radiograph performed for an unrelated cough shows a healing posterior rib fracture. There is no documented family history of bleeding disorders or osteogenesis imperfecta. The history of injury offered is vague and changes between caregivers. Other siblings are unwell with no clear medical cause documented.

data_table.Vital signs: Temp 36.8 degrees Celsius, HR 132, SpO2 98% on room air
data_table.Examination: Multiple bruises over trunk and limbs in different stages of healing, frenal tear noted on upper lip examination, anterior fontanelle full
data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 2.6 g/L, ALT 28 U/L; calcium and ALP within reference range; CXR shows healing posterior rib fracture

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with verbal safety advice for the parents, with a GP review in 4 weeks for general well-child check and no further specialist or child protection involvement initiated at this time
Arrange GP follow-up in 6 weeks for review of the bruises and the healing rib fracture, with no specific paediatric or child protection involvement requested before that GP review
Treat the rib fracture conservatively with simple analgesia and discharge home with no further investigation, no consultation with child protection services, and no follow-up at any later date

Telephone parents to clarify the history of the injury and arrange a home visit by a community nurse in 24 hours, with no immediate inpatient workup, safeguarding referral or mandatory report submitted

Admit for full skeletal survey, fundoscopy, head imaging and coagulation profile to exclude mimics, plus urgent paediatric and child protection team consultations and a mandatory report to statutory services

subtopic_detail: Acute otitis media without severe features in a well child over 24 months
stem: A 26-month-old child presents with 24 hours of left ear pain and unsettled sleep, with a temperature of 38.2 degrees Celsius. He is feeding well and is alert. There is no history of recurrent ear infection and no perforation or otorrhoea. Father asks whether antibiotics are needed today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, RR 24, T 38.2, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Mildly bulging erythematous left tympanic membrane with intact light reflex; right ear normal; no mastoid tenderness; no rash

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days starting at this visit today
Oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 3 days starting at this visit today
Regular paracetamol with safety-netting and planned clinical review at 48 hours
Same-day ENT referral for myringotomy with grommet insertion under general anaesthetic
Topical ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops twice daily for 7 days with home review

subtopic_detail: Mild to moderate croup disposition and treatment selection
stem: A 2-year-old boy presents in the early hours of the morning with a 1 day coryzal illness followed by a sudden onset barking cough and noisy breathing. He has a mild intermittent inspiratory stridor at rest, mild chest wall recession on excitement, and settles when held by his mother. He is taking oral fluids. There are no drooling, dysphagia, or unvaccinated immunisation status concerns.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, RR 32, SpO2 97% room air, T 37.8
data_table.Examination: Hoarse voice, barking cough, mild inspiratory stridor at rest, mild recession on crying, equal air entry, no foreign body history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for suspected bacterial tracheitis with a chest X-ray to confirm
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL and admit to the paediatric high dependency unit overnight for continuous monitoring of airway
Single dose oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, observe until stridor at rest settles and oral intake is reliable, then discharge with safety-net advice
Cool mist humidification therapy and discharge home with parental reassurance and no medication for this distressing nocturnal symptom
Urgent ENT review with anaesthetic team on standby for fibreoptic laryngoscopy to exclude any structural airway pathology

subtopic_detail: Acute asthma exacerbation in a 5 year old: oral prednisolone course
stem: A 5-year-old girl with a known diagnosis of asthma presents with 2 days of cough and wheeze after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She has used her salbutamol metered dose inhaler with spacer 4 hourly at home without sustained relief. She is talking in short phrases, with mild intercostal recession. She has been given salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer in the department with a partial response.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 38, SpO2 94% room air, T 37.2
data_table.Examination: Bilateral expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase, mild subcostal recession, no cyanosis, alert

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in addition to ongoing bronchodilator therapy?

options.text: Nebulised ipratropium bromide 250 micrograms every 20 minutes for the first hour
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg as a single dose given over 20 minutes now
Inhaled fluticasone propionate 125 micrograms twice daily as preventer initiation
Empirical oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days as adjunctive cover
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg once daily for 3 days starting at this presentation

subtopic_detail: First febrile UTI in young girl: imaging algorithm
stem: An 18-month-old girl is admitted with a first episode of fever to 39 degrees Celsius and vomiting. A clean catch urine culture grows greater than 10 to the 8 colony forming units per litre of Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim. She responds to intravenous gentamicin with defervescence by 36 hours and switches to oral trimethoprim to complete a 7 day course. Family history is negative for renal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 30, T 38.4 on day 2, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Well perfused, soft non-tender abdomen, no flank mass, normal external genitalia
data_table.Investigations: CRP peak 96 mg/L, creatinine 28 micromol/L, urine culture E. coli >10^8 CFU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate further imaging plan after clinical recovery?

options.text: Urgent micturating cystourethrogram during the admission to exclude grade V vesicoureteric reflux
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks of the acute illness with further imaging guided by findings
DMSA renal scintigraphy at 6 weeks regardless of ultrasound findings to look for cortical scarring
Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to map the urinary tract
No imaging is required; arrange continuous low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis for 12 months

subtopic_detail: Functional constipation in a preschool child: disimpaction and maintenance
stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with a 4 month history of infrequent hard stools, with bowel actions every 4 to 5 days and visible straining. There is intermittent soiling between bowel actions. Toilet training started at 30 months without success. Abdominal examination reveals a palpable left iliac fossa mass that is faecal in character. Anal examination shows no fissures or perianal disease. There are no red flag features for organic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Apyrexial, HR 100, RR 22, BP 92/58
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa, normal external anus, no fissure, normal sacral spine
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated based on history and examination

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Plain abdominal radiograph today to quantify faecal loading and guide laxative dosing
Glycerol suppository now and review the family in 6 weeks without further laxative use
Disimpaction with oral macrogol over 3 to 7 days then a daily maintenance osmotic laxative
Referral to paediatric gastroenterology for rectal biopsy to exclude Hirschsprung disease
Increased dietary fibre and water intake alone with planned follow up in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Eczema herpeticum recognition in a child with atopic dermatitis
stem: A 4-year-old girl with moderate atopic dermatitis presents with a 36 hour history of a worsening rash on her face and neck, fevers, and pain on touching the lesions. Examination shows clustered punched-out monomorphic erosions with yellow crusting overlying eczematous skin on her cheeks, neck, and upper trunk. She has not used new topical products and is currently on mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment for flares.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 28, T 38.6, SpO2 99% room air
data_table.Examination: Clustered punched-out monomorphic erosions with crust on cheeks, neck, upper trunk; eczematous background; cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Skin swab for viral PCR taken at triage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous aciclovir with paediatric infectious diseases and ophthalmology involvement
Up-titrate topical mometasone furoate to twice daily across all involved sites for 7 days
Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg four times daily for impetiginised eczema as outpatient management
Wet wrap therapy with diluted topical steroid alone and review at the eczema clinic in 1 week
Oral valaciclovir 20 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days and discharge home with safety netting

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler with excess cow milk intake
stem: A 22-month-old boy is referred by his maternal child health nurse for pallor and decreased activity over the past 2 months. He drinks approximately 1 litre of full cream cow milk daily and is a fussy eater. Family is Australian-born without known haemoglobinopathy. He has tongue pallor and a soft systolic flow murmur. His parents are otherwise reassured by his behaviour and growth which is at the 25th centile for weight and 50th centile for height.

data_table.Examination: Pallor of tongue and conjunctivae, soft systolic flow murmur at left sternal edge, no organomegaly, no purpura
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 64 fL, MCH 19 pg, ferritin 8 micrograms/L, CRP 3 mg/L, WCC and platelets normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Intravenous iron carboxymaltose infusion today as first-line because oral iron is poorly tolerated
Oral elemental iron 3 to 6 mg/kg daily for 3 months and reduce cow milk to under 500 mL daily
Packed red cell transfusion of 10 mL/kg over 4 hours and admit for further evaluation
Haemoglobin electrophoresis and bone marrow biopsy now to exclude thalassaemia and aplasia
Increased dietary iron-rich foods alone with repeat full blood count in 3 months

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease beyond day 10 with persistent fever
stem: A 3-year-old boy is admitted on day 11 of illness with persistent fever to 39.5 degrees Celsius despite a 5 day course of empirical amoxicillin. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked lips, a polymorphous truncal rash, and unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy of 2.5 cm. There is no extremity desquamation yet. Echocardiography shows a left anterior descending coronary artery z-score of 2.6.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, cracked fissured lips, polymorphous trunk rash, 2.5 cm right cervical node, no rash desquamation
data_table.Investigations: CRP 168 mg/L, ESR 88 mm/h, ALT 78 U/L, platelets 612 x10^9/L, Hb 96 g/L, albumin 27 g/L, urine WCC raised, blood cultures negative; echo LAD z-score 2.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg single infusion plus oral aspirin 3 to 5 mg/kg daily
Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days as primary monotherapy
Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin 50 mg/kg six hourly for staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Subcutaneous infliximab loading dose 5 mg/kg today as primary refractory disease treatment
Symptomatic care with paracetamol and ibuprofen with echocardiography review in 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis with proteinuria: renal involvement assessment
stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with palpable purpura distributed over her buttocks and lower legs, with bilateral ankle swelling and intermittent colicky abdominal pain over the past 5 days. The rash followed a viral upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. She has not had macroscopic haematuria. Her parents ask about the next step in monitoring.

data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and extensor surfaces of lower legs, bilateral ankle synovitis, soft non-tender abdomen, no scrotal swelling, no neurology
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis dipstick blood 2+ protein 3+; urine protein creatinine ratio 280 mg/mmol; creatinine 52 micromol/L; albumin 32 g/L; platelets 320 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days followed by oral mycophenolate mofetil
Discharge with oral analgesia and review with the general practitioner in 2 weeks
Empirical oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg four times daily for 7 days as post-streptococcal cover
Admit for paediatric nephrology review and start oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg daily
Renal tract ultrasound today to exclude obstructive uropathy as the cause of proteinuria

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis failing high flow nasal cannula: escalation decision
stem: A 4-month-old former 38 week infant has been admitted with RSV bronchiolitis. She has been on humidified high flow nasal cannula oxygen 2 L/kg/min at FiO2 0.5 for the past 4 hours. She remains tachypnoeic with marked subcostal recessions, intermittent grunting, and rising work of breathing. Capillary blood gas shows pH 7.22, pCO2 70 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, lactate 1.4 mmol/L. She is becoming less responsive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 78 with intermittent apnoeas, SpO2 88% on HFNC FiO2 0.5, T 38.0
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession, intermittent grunting, head bobbing, drowsy, reduced air entry bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Capillary gas pH 7.22 pCO2 70 mmHg HCO3 25 mmol/L lactate 1.4 mmol/L; CXR hyperinflation without focal consolidation; RSV PCR positive

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Escalate to paediatric intensive care for non-invasive ventilation and intubation readiness
Trial nebulised hypertonic saline 3% every 4 hours to improve mucus clearance and oxygenation
Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and inhaled salbutamol 6 puffs via spacer hourly for 3 hours
Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for secondary bacterial pneumonia coverage
Continue current HFNC settings and observe for another 4 hours before considering escalation

subtopic_detail: Day 4 neonatal jaundice approaching exchange threshold
stem:
A term male infant on day 4 of life is brought to the special care nursery with progressive jaundice. He was born at 39 weeks by spontaneous vaginal delivery with a birth weight of 3.4 kg, now 3.1 kg. Mother is blood group O Rh positive and the infant is A Rh positive with a positive direct antiglobulin test. He is breastfeeding only with reduced wet nappies.

The serum bilirubin has risen by 11 micromol/L per hour over the past 6 hours and is now 460 micromol/L; the exchange threshold for this infant is 480 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 56, T 36.8, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Cephalad jaundice extending to soles, sleepy but rousable, mild dehydration, no neurological abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Total SBR 460 micromol/L (exchange threshold 480), conjugated 18 micromol/L, Hb 152 g/L, DAT positive, reticulocytes 8%, weight loss 9% from birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue single phototherapy with breastfeeding support and repeat bilirubin in 6 hours
Immediate single volume exchange transfusion without trial of intensive phototherapy first
Cease breastfeeding for 24 hours and switch to formula to exclude breast milk jaundice diagnosis
Intensive phototherapy on three sides with IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg and prepare for exchange
Phenobarbital 5 mg/kg twice daily to induce hepatic glucuronidation as bridging therapy

subtopic_detail: Complicated pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion management
stem: A 6-year-old boy was admitted 3 days ago with right lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia and started on intravenous benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg six hourly. He has had persistent fevers to 39 degrees Celsius, increasing right-sided chest pain, and rising oxygen requirement. Repeat chest radiograph shows a moderate right pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound shows 4 cm depth of fluid with internal septations.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142, RR 38, T 39.1, SpO2 92% on 2 L/min via nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Reduced air entry and stony dull percussion right base, splinting on inspiration, no shift of trachea
data_table.Investigations: CRP 220 mg/L, WCC 22 x10^9/L; ultrasound right effusion 4 cm depth with internal septations; blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Diagnostic pleural tap only with ongoing intravenous benzylpenicillin and no indwelling drain
Continue benzylpenicillin monotherapy and reassess clinical state in 48 hours without drainage
Refer to cardiothoracic surgery for primary video-assisted thoracoscopic decortication today
Switch to broader spectrum antibiotics with intrapleural fibrinolytic delivered chest drain
Oral switch to amoxicillin clavulanate 25 mg/kg three times daily and discharge home today

subtopic_detail: Pertussis treatment in a young unvaccinated infant
stem: A 7-week-old infant presents with three weeks of progressive cough, now with paroxysms and post-tussive vomiting and one brief cyanotic episode. The infant has had no scheduled vaccines because the family delayed the 6-week visit. The mother had a non-productive cough for 4 weeks during the third trimester and did not receive an antenatal pertussis booster. The infant is feeding two-thirds of normal volumes and has no apnoeic pauses on monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152, RR 44, T 37.2, SpO2 96% room air with brief desaturation to 88% during paroxysm
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession, chest clear between paroxysms, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal PCR positive for Bordetella pertussis; chest x-ray shows perihilar streakiness without focal consolidation; FBC WCC 28 with lymphocytosis 18

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate antimicrobial management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 30 mg/kg three times daily for 7 days as an outpatient with telephone review
Admit and start oral azithromycin 10 mg/kg once daily for 5 days plus household post-exposure prophylaxis
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 4 mg/kg twice daily for 14 days as an outpatient referral
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 4 hours plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 3 days
Discharge with safety-netting only; antibiotics offer no benefit after 21 days of cough in any age group

subtopic_detail: Measles recognition in an unvaccinated traveller-returned child
stem: A 4-year-old returns to the emergency department two days after presenting with fever and cough. She returned 10 days ago from a 6-week visit to family in Indonesia and has no record of MMR vaccination. Today her fever persists with a new descending maculopapular rash starting on the forehead. There is no contact with strawberry tongue, parotitis, or known varicella.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 26, T 39.4, SpO2 97% room air
data_table.Examination: Confluent erythematous maculopapular rash on face and upper trunk; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; white spots on buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars; pharynx mildly injected; chest clear; no joint swelling

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next public health action?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol, school exclusion for 5 days, and routine MMR catch-up at the general practitioner next week
Reassure parents the rash is roseola, advise antipyretics, and review at the general practitioner if persistent at 72 hours from rash onset
Admit for intravenous benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg every 6 hours assuming early scarlet fever pending throat swab confirmation
Isolate in a negative-pressure room, notify the public health unit by phone today, and send measles IgM with throat and urine PCR
Order varicella PCR from a vesicular fluid swab and start oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 5 days empirically

stem: A 14-month-old is brought for review because the parents have noticed an inward turning of the right eye when she looks at distant objects, present consistently for the past month. There is no family history of amblyopia. She was born at term and otherwise tracks objects normally at close range. Photographs show the asymmetry from 8 months of age.

data_table.Examination: Right convergent strabismus with corneal light reflex displaced to the lateral limbus on the right; red reflex symmetric and present bilaterally; no leukocoria; cover test reveals refixation movement of the right eye; visual fields by confrontation grossly intact

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that intermittent infantile strabismus typically resolves and review at the 18-month general practitioner check
Prescribe occlusion patching of the left eye for 2 hours daily for 8 weeks then arrange optometry review
Refer urgently to a paediatric ophthalmologist within 4 weeks for cycloplegic refraction and orthoptic assessment
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits before specialist referral is considered
Order a B-scan ultrasound of the right globe via the general practitioner pathway to exclude posterior segment pathology

stem: A 7-year-old is brought to the general practice with 2 weeks of scalp itch, and the mother has identified live head lice and eggs on combing. The child attends mainstream school and lives with two siblings without scalp itch. There is no recent overseas travel, no eczema, and the scalp is intact without bacterial superinfection.

data_table.Examination: Multiple eggs cemented to hair shafts within 1 cm of the scalp; two live lice identified on combing; no excoriation, no impetigo, no occipital lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Wet combing with conditioner every 4 days for 2 weeks until no live lice are seen on three consecutive combings
Topical permethrin 1% lotion applied to dry hair for 10 minutes then rinsed, repeated weekly for 6 weeks
Oral ivermectin 200 microgram per kilogram as a single dose with rinse-out repeat at 8 days
Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 4 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days to clear lice and prevent impetiginisation
Shave the head completely under general practitioner sedation and apply topical malathion 0.5% for 12 hours overnight

stem: An 11-month-old presents with 18 hours of episodic inconsolable crying lasting 10 minutes every hour, drawing up his legs and now lying lethargic between episodes. Today there was one stool with red mucoid blood. He vomited twice with the second containing bile-stained material. He had a recent viral illness 5 days ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 38, T 37.6, SpO2 98%, BP 86/52, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Lethargic but rousable; right upper quadrant sausage-shaped mass palpable; bowel sounds reduced; perianal inspection shows redcurrant material on the nappy
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care ultrasound by emergency consultant shows a target sign at the hepatic flexure with poor colour Doppler signal in the inner loop

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat clinical observation for 4 hours with oral rehydration before re-examining for ongoing concerns
Arrange an outpatient lower limb venous Doppler study and surgical clinic review the next morning before deciding on reduction
Proceed to laparoscopic exploration with manual reduction without further imaging or trial of pneumatic reduction
Transfuse 10 mL/kg packed red cells over 30 minutes for ongoing redcurrant rectal bleeding before imaging review
Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg balanced crystalloid and proceed to fluoroscopic air enema reduction with surgical and theatre standby

subtopic_detail: Pre-operative correction in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
stem: A 5-week-old first-born male presents with 2 weeks of progressively forceful non-bilious vomiting after every feed and visible peristalsis across the upper abdomen. He has lost 6% of his birth weight. An ultrasound by the on-call radiologist confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis with a pyloric muscle thickness of 4.2 mm and channel length of 18 mm. Paediatric surgery has accepted him for pyloromyotomy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158, RR 42, T 36.8, SpO2 99%, capillary refill 3 seconds, anterior fontanelle mildly depressed
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas pH 7.52, pCO2 50, HCO3 38, Na 132, K 3.0, Cl 92, glucose 4.1, creatinine 38

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step before theatre?

options.text: Proceed directly to theatre today as the procedure is brief and any electrolyte derangement will correct intraoperatively
Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus then maintenance with 4% dextrose and 0.18% sodium chloride until theatre
Resuscitate with sodium chloride 0.9% then maintenance sodium chloride 0.45% with 5% dextrose and potassium chloride 20 mmol/L before theatre
Replace the fluid deficit with oral electrolyte solution by feeding cup over 24 hours then proceed to surgery once tolerating feeds
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg slowly to partially correct the metabolic alkalosis before theatre transfer

subtopic_detail: Suspected inhaled foreign body in a toddler
stem: A 22-month-old presents 6 hours after a sudden coughing fit while eating peanuts during a family barbecue. The choking episode resolved spontaneously but he is now persistently coughing and his mother says his breathing sounds different. He has no preceding upper respiratory tract symptoms, no fevers, no eczema, and no prior wheeze.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, RR 42, T 37.0, SpO2 94% room air
data_table.Examination: Mild intercostal recession, unilateral monophonic wheeze right side, decreased air entry on the right, no stridor at rest, no drooling, no cyanosis
data_table.Investigations: Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation of the right lung with mediastinal shift to the left on expiratory film

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for three doses then reassess for viral-induced wheeze before further imaging
Arrange urgent rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia by the on-call paediatric otolaryngology service today
Perform five back blows and five chest thrusts now in the emergency department then observe in the short-stay unit
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days plus inhaled corticosteroid maintenance, with general practitioner review in 1 week
Discharge with safety-netting after a normal inspiratory chest x-ray report and return if symptoms worsen overnight

subtopic_detail: Salter-Harris distal tibial fracture in a child
stem: A 12-year-old presents 90 minutes after twisting her right ankle on a trampoline. She heard a pop and could not bear weight to walk to the car. There is no head strike, no other limb injury. She has a previously normal contralateral ankle and no bleeding disorder. The ankle is now swollen with localised tenderness over the medial malleolus.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, RR 16, T 36.6, BP 110/72, capillary refill less than 2 seconds in the toes, sensation intact
data_table.Examination: Marked swelling around the medial malleolus, point tenderness over the distal tibial physis, unable to bear weight for four steps in the department, neurovascular status intact distally
data_table.Investigations: Ankle radiograph shows a vertical fracture line through the distal tibial epiphysis extending into the physis without metaphyseal involvement; mortise widening 1 mm

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a removable below-knee splint, allow weight-bearing as tolerated, and arrange general practitioner review in 1 week without specialist referral
Apply a full below-knee fibreglass cast and discharge with crutches and orthopaedic outpatient appointment within 6 weeks
Discharge with a tubular bandage and crutches plus advice to return only if pain or swelling persists beyond 7 days
Apply a backslab and arrange same-day orthopaedic review for consideration of computed tomography and reduction of the intra-articular fracture
Arrange a magnetic resonance imaging scan of the ankle from the emergency department and review the patient in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome prophylaxis in high-risk ALL induction
stem: An 8-year-old has been diagnosed with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with a presenting white cell count of 88 x10^9/L and bulky cervical adenopathy. The paediatric oncology team plan induction chemotherapy commencing within 24 hours. Pre-chemotherapy bloods show baseline uric acid 0.62 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, potassium 4.6, phosphate 1.9 mmol/L, calcium 2.18 mmol/L, and lactate dehydrogenase 1450 U/L.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral 3 cm cervical lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly 4 cm below costal margin, splenomegaly 5 cm, no respiratory compromise, no tumour lysis-related arrhythmia
data_table.Investigations: G6PD assay pending and not yet returned from referral laboratory; weight 26 kg; eGFR estimated 76 mL/min/1.73 m2

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate tumour lysis prophylaxis to commence now?

options.text: Hyperhydrate at twice maintenance with isotonic crystalloid without potassium plus oral allopurinol 100 mg/m2 three times daily, holding rasburicase pending G6PD
Hyperhydrate at twice maintenance with isotonic crystalloid plus alkalinisation with intravenous sodium bicarbonate to maintain urine pH 7.0 to 7.5 throughout induction
Commence intravenous rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg once daily for 5 days now and proceed to chemotherapy induction the morning after the first dose
Restrict fluids to two-thirds maintenance to prevent volume overload and start oral allopurinol 100 mg/m2 once daily with daily renal function and electrolyte review
Initiate intermittent haemodialysis prophylactically from the start of chemotherapy to clear uric acid and prevent acute kidney injury during induction

stem: An 8-month-old previously well infant is brought to ED in winter with 3 days of coryza, cough and worsening work of breathing. He has been feeding only one-third of normal and his last wet nappy was 6 hours ago. He has had two doses of low-flow oxygen at 1 L/min but remains tachypnoeic with subcostal recession. His parents have not yet given him any nebulised medications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168, RR 68, SpO2 92% on 1 L/min nasal cannulae, T 38.0°C
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, bilateral wheeze and fine crackles, alert, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab: RSV positive; CXR not performed; cap gas pH 7.34 pCO2 48 mmHg HCO3 25

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase nasal cannula flow to 3 L/min and continue current observations with oral feeds
Administer nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for three doses and reassess
Give nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent over 15 minutes and reassess work of breathing
Commence intravenous dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg daily for 3 days and cease nasal oxygen
Commence high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min with continuous monitoring on ward

stem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the GP with 6 months of infrequent hard stools, soiling episodes most days and abdominal pain. She passes stool once every 4 to 5 days with straining and screaming. She started day-care 8 months ago and reduced fluid intake notably around that time. Her parents have tried prune juice and increased fibre without sustained improvement.

data_table.Vital signs: Weight 14 kg (50th centile), height 95 cm (50th centile), well-appearing afebrile child
data_table.Examination: Soft non-distended abdomen with palpable faecal mass in left iliac fossa; perianal exam: no fissures or anal abnormalities; growth following centile
data_table.Investigations: None at this stage; no red flags (no failure to thrive, no delayed meconium, normal spine and lower limb examination)

lead_in: Which management plan is most appropriate now?

options.text: Commence oral macrogol 3350 (Movicol Junior) escalating disimpaction regimen over 7 days
Continue dietary measures (increased fluid, fibre, pear/prune juice) and review in 4 weeks
Administer phosphate enemas daily for 3 days then commence oral lactulose maintenance
Refer for manual disimpaction under general anaesthetic and surgical opinion within a fortnight
Order anorectal manometry and barium enema to exclude underlying Hirschsprung disease today

stem: A 22-month-old boy is brought to ED at 2 am with a 6-hour history of barking cough and noisy breathing that started after a coryzal illness. He is alert and consolable in his mother's lap. His parents have given paracetamol 2 hours ago for fever. He has no previous admissions and no chronic respiratory conditions.

data_table.Examination: Audible stridor at rest, mild intercostal recession, no cyanosis; speaks in short sentences when settled; chest clear on auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; clinical diagnosis; Westley croup score 4 (moderate)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg every 20 minutes for 3 doses with continuous SpO2 monitoring
Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg with intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg as cover
Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL with ICU bed booked for likely escalation overnight
Single oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe for at least 2 hours in the department
Reassure parents, recommend cool mist humidifier at home and discharge with safety netting

stem: A 4-year-old non-Indigenous, otherwise well boy presents with 18 hours of right ear pain following a viral URTI. He has had no previous episodes of otitis media and is up to date with immunisations including 13vPCV. His parents are happy to follow a 'wait and see' approach if it is safe and want to know how to monitor him.

data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane: bulging, erythematous, no perforation, no discharge; left tympanic membrane normal; not toxic, alert, playful
data_table.Investigations: None indicated; clinical diagnosis of acute otitis media (right)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 15 mg/kg three times daily for 5 days plus regular analgesia at home
Intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for 3 days as a single short parenteral course
Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen and fill antibiotic script only if no improvement at 48 hours
Topical otic ciprofloxacin 0.3 percent drops twice daily for 7 days with no oral antibiotics
Refer urgently for myringotomy and grommet insertion within the next fortnight as outpatient

stem: A 10-week-old formula-fed infant is brought to the GP with 5 weeks of frequent posseting, recurrent crying with feeds and now 2 weeks of streaks of fresh blood in stools. The crying is worst during and after feeds. She is otherwise alert; weight gain has dropped from the 50th to the 25th centile. There is no family history of atopy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 36, T 36.7°C, well-perfused infant
data_table.Examination: Mild eczema on cheeks, abdomen soft non-distended, normal anal exam, mild fissure not seen; weight tracking off centile downwards
data_table.Investigations: Stool: blood streaks visible; no infection symptoms; clinical exam otherwise normal

lead_in: Which initial management strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Commence omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily and continue current formula with anti-reflux thickening
Switch to a soy-based infant formula for 4 weeks then reintroduce cow's milk gradually
Trial of extensively hydrolysed formula for 2 to 4 weeks with paediatric dietitian input
Refer urgently for paediatric colonoscopy to investigate the lower gastrointestinal bleeding now
Add probiotic Lactobacillus reuteri drops and review symptoms after 6 weeks of therapy

stem: A 5-week-old male infant is brought to ED with fever measured at 38.6 degrees Celsius at home and again on arrival. He was born at term by normal vaginal birth with no maternal GBS risk factors and has been feeding normally until today. He has fed less in the last 6 hours. He appears alert in the parents' arms but is mildly tachypnoeic without distress.

data_table.Examination: Alert, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft; no focal infection; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Not yet done; needs evaluation per RCH SBI guideline

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate plan?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol and safety-net advice with paediatric review in 24 hours
Take blood and urine cultures, lumbar puncture and commence IV benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin
Take blood cultures and CRP only and admit for 24 hours of observation without antibiotics
Perform urine bag sample only and commence oral amoxicillin awaiting outpatient review tomorrow
Administer intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg single dose and discharge home for review

stem: A 2-year-old boy is admitted with 6 days of fever to 39.5 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked red lips, an erythematous polymorphous trunk rash and induration of the hands but no significant cervical lymphadenopathy. Screening for streptococcal infection and respiratory viruses has been negative. The team is uncertain whether he meets criteria for definite Kawasaki disease.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, no exudate, polymorphous rash, dorsal hand induration; no cervical lymphadenopathy >= 1.5 cm
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, platelets 525 x10^9/L, WCC 16 (neutrophils 12), CRP 145 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/h, ALT 84 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urinalysis sterile pyuria; echo: small proximal LAD dilation (Z+2.1)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and reassess at 24 hours before further treatment
Administer IVIG 2 g/kg over 10 to 12 hours plus high-dose aspirin and arrange paediatric cardiology
Start oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily as primary therapy and withhold IVIG until day 10
Defer all treatment until thrombocytosis exceeds 600 x10^9/L and skin desquamation appears
Treat as scarlet fever with intravenous benzylpenicillin and reassess after 48 hours

stem: A 6-year-old girl with focal epilepsy on valproate is brought to ED actively seizing. Paramedics gave IM midazolam 5 mg en route at 8 minutes and IV midazolam 0.15 mg/kg on arrival at 18 minutes, but generalised tonic-clonic activity has continued. It is now 28 minutes of continuous seizure. The team is preparing the second-line agent.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, RR 32 (ongoing seizure), SpO2 93% on 6 L oxygen mask, T 37.2°C, BSL 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Ongoing generalised tonic-clonic activity, eyes deviated upwards, pupils 4 mm equal; secured airway, IV access x 2
data_table.Investigations: VBG: pH 7.22, pCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 19, lactate 5.8, Na 138, K 4.0, Mg 0.84, Ca 2.32

lead_in: Which second-line anticonvulsant is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading at 1 mg/kg/min with continuous cardiac monitoring
Additional intravenous midazolam 0.15 mg/kg bolus then continuous infusion at 0.1 mg/kg/h
Intravenous sodium valproate 40 mg/kg load over 10 minutes given her existing valproate use
Intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg loading dose over 5 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Rapid sequence intubation and propofol infusion as primary management without anticonvulsant loading

stem: A 9-year-old girl admitted with severe DKA (pH 7.05, BSL 32, ketones 5.6) was rehydrated with 0.9 percent sodium chloride at 5 mL/kg/h plus an insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/h. Five hours into treatment she develops new-onset confusion and a fronto-occipital headache. Her parents report she 'doesn't recognise them' and she has had one episode of vomiting in the last 30 minutes. The bedside nurse notes that her BP has risen from 110/64 to 138/86 and her heart rate has fallen from 124 to 78.

data_table.Examination: Pupils 3 mm equal reactive, no focal weakness, bilateral plantar flexion responses; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: BSL 14 mmol/L, ketones 3.2, pH 7.20 (improving), Na 140, K 4.1, corrected Na rising from 134 to 140

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Continue current fluid and insulin rates as her acidosis is improving and reassess in 30 minutes
Increase the insulin infusion rate to 0.1 unit/kg/h to reduce hyperglycaemia more aggressively
Halve the fluid rate, give hypertonic saline 3 percent 3 mL/kg over 10 minutes and elevate head
Administer sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg bolus to correct the residual acidosis quickly
Perform urgent CT brain before any intervention to confirm cerebral oedema is the cause now

stem: A 6-year-old boy is reviewed in clinic 3 weeks after diagnosis with Henoch-Schonlein purpura (now IgA vasculitis) following a URTI. He had palpable purpura over both lower limbs and buttocks plus right ankle arthritis. The rash and joint symptoms have resolved. He has no abdominal pain, no haematuria visible and his BP at this visit is 102/68. His parents ask what the follow-up plan should be.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/68 (50th centile for age and height), HR 88, T 36.5°C
data_table.Examination: Fading petechiae on lower legs, full range of joint movement, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis at diagnosis: 2+ blood, no protein; serum creatinine 38 micromol/L; albumin 38 g/L; today's urinalysis: 1+ blood, no protein

lead_in: Which monitoring plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Discharge from follow-up as rash has resolved and renal involvement appears self-limited
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks to prevent late nephritis as prophylaxis
Weekly urinalysis plus BP for 6 weeks then monthly for 6 months and nephrology referral if abnormal
Arrange immediate renal biopsy to assess crescentic disease prior to immunosuppressive therapy
Single urinalysis and BP check at 12 months as he is now asymptomatic and well-appearing

stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with 36 hours of right eye swelling that began after a URTI. The swelling has progressed and she now reports double vision when looking to the left. She has not been able to fully open the right eye since this morning. There is no history of trauma or insect bite. She is up to date with immunisations including Hib.

data_table.Examination: Right eye: marked periorbital erythema and oedema, proptosis 4 mm by exophthalmometer, painful restricted eye movements (failure to abduct), diplopia on left gaze; visual acuity 6/9 right, 6/6 left
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18 x10^9/L, neutrophils 14, CRP 168 mg/L; blood culture pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg three times daily with planned emergency department review in 24 hours
Topical chloramphenicol eye drops with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate twice daily for 5 days
Admit for urgent CT of orbits and sinuses and commence IV ceftriaxone plus flucloxacillin
Discharge home with daily GP review and structured safety-netting advice on deterioration
Perform emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis prior to any imaging or antibiotic

stem: A breastfed term male newborn (gestation 39+2 weeks, birthweight 3.4 kg) is reviewed on day 4 with visible jaundice noted by the midwife at home visit. He is feeding 8 times daily and producing 5 to 6 wet nappies. His mother is blood group O Rh-positive; cord blood and DAT are negative. He has had no previous transcutaneous bilirubin recorded. He is alert and feeding actively in the clinic.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.8°C, HR 138, RR 42; alert, well-perfused, weight 3.28 kg (-3.5 percent from birth)
data_table.Examination: Jaundice to chest and proximal limbs, soft fontanelle, no hepatosplenomegaly, no petechiae, normal Moro and tone
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin 320 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 8 micromol/L (well under 20 percent), Hb 168 g/L, retics 2.5 percent, blood film normal

lead_in: Which management is most appropriate?

options.text: Admit for phototherapy with continued breastfeeding and review bilirubin in 6 hours
Reassure parents and review with repeat transcutaneous bilirubin in 48 hours
Cease breastfeeding and switch to formula for 48 hours to confirm breast milk jaundice
Arrange urgent double-volume exchange transfusion as bilirubin exceeds the exchange threshold today
Commence oral phenobarbital 5 mg/kg/day to induce bilirubin conjugation enzymes safely

stem: You are the ED RMO seeing an 8-month-old infant brought in by her mother for worsening breathing. She has had 3 days of coryza and cough. Today the mother reports feeding has dropped to about 50% of usual volume and the last wet nappy was three hours ago. The infant is alert but distressed.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 62, SpO2 92% room air, HR 158, T 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Subcostal and intercostal recession, fine bilateral crackles, no wheeze, mucous membranes tacky
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for inpatient observation with supplemental oxygen as needed and paced nasogastric feeds
Trial inhaled salbutamol via spacer and formally reassess work of breathing after twenty minutes
Administer a single oral prednisolone dose and observe in the emergency department for one hour
