Discharge home with written safety netting and a planned GP review the following morning
Administer nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with a planned repeat dose at thirty minutes if needed

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 10-month-old boy admitted overnight with first febrile UTI. Urine grew E. coli sensitive to cefalexin. He responded to IV ceftriaxone within 24 hours and has been afebrile for 48 hours. He is now feeding well, hydrated, and ready for discharge on oral cefalexin to complete the course. The parents ask about follow-up imaging.

data_table.Examination: Well, no abdominal mass, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture E. coli sensitive to cefalexin; bedside renal tract ultrasound during admission was normal
data_table.Medications: Oral cefalexin to complete a total 10-day course

lead_in: What further imaging or investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: Arrange a DMSA scan at three months to assess for renal scarring after the first febrile UTI
Arrange a micturating cystourethrogram in the next four weeks to exclude vesicoureteric reflux
No further imaging is required as the renal tract ultrasound during admission was normal
Commence trimethoprim antibiotic prophylaxis until two years of age as routine secondary prevention
Repeat a urine culture at the end of the antibiotic course to confirm microbiological cure

stem: You are the PICU registrar caring for an 8-year-old girl 6 hours into treatment for severe diabetic ketoacidosis. She has received 10 mL/kg saline bolus and is on maintenance fluids with insulin infusion at 0.05 units/kg/hr. Her GCS was 15 on arrival. The nurse calls because the patient is now harder to rouse and complains of a headache, with her father noting she is unusually irritable when stimulated.

data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), pupils 3 mm reactive, no focal neurology, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18 (was 7.04), bicarbonate 14 (was 6), glucose 14 mmol/L, sodium 138, potassium 3.6
data_table.Medications: Insulin infusion 0.05 units/kg/hr; saline 0.9% with potassium replacement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch from saline to compound sodium lactate solution and continue the current insulin infusion rate while monitoring closely
Stop the insulin infusion entirely because hypoglycaemia is the most likely cause of the decreased conscious state in this clinical context
Increase the fluid replacement rate to correct presumed ongoing dehydration and add a further isotonic saline bolus over thirty minutes
Arrange an urgent CT brain before any treatment to confirm the diagnosis of cerebral oedema and exclude alternative intracranial pathology
Administer hypertonic saline or mannitol immediately and halve the maintenance fluid rate while obtaining urgent neuroimaging only after stabilisation

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-month-old boy with 6 days of fever, irritability, and limited oral intake. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, cracked lips, and BCG site erythema, with no rash, no lymphadenopathy, and no peripheral changes. He has been treated empirically with oral antibiotics by the GP without improvement.

data_table.Examination: Conjunctival injection without exudate, dry cracked lips, BCG site erythema, no rash, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: CRP 145 mg/L, ESR 78, platelets 540 x10^9/L, ALT 88, albumin 28, urine WCC raised without bacteriuria, sodium 132

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue supportive care and review tomorrow if no improvement, as classic criteria require five clinical features and have not yet been met
Arrange echocardiography and commence IVIG 2 g/kg with aspirin based on the supplementary laboratory criteria for incomplete disease
Change empiric antibiotics to IV ceftriaxone for occult bacterial sepsis after a full septic workup including lumbar puncture
Arrange outpatient rheumatology review next week and commence oral prednisolone empirically for systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Trial high-dose ibuprofen for presumed viral inflammation and reassess clinical features over the next forty-eight hours of observation

stem: You are the paediatric registrar called to ED to see a 4-month-old infant brought in with episodes of unusual pallor and apparent fatigue over 12 hours. The parents describe two episodes of inconsolable crying lasting around 10 minutes followed by limpness, with no fever or vomiting. The child has had one normal stool today.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 162, RR 44, T 36.9, SpO2 99%, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Examination: Pale, drowsy between episodes, abdomen soft with palpable fullness in right upper quadrant, normal genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.8, FBC and UEC pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: CT abdomen with intravenous contrast to fully characterise abdominal pathology and assess for an underlying lead point causing the presentation
Three-view abdominal radiograph series to assess for free air and characterise any bowel obstruction before further imaging is arranged
EEG to evaluate for atypical seizure activity given the recurrent episodes of decreased responsiveness reported by the parents over twelve hours
Urgent abdominal ultrasound to assess for a target sign with paediatric surgical consult booked in parallel
Lumbar puncture to exclude occult central nervous system infection causing the lethargy and unusual behaviour observed at home this morning

stem: You are the ED RMO managing a previously well 3-year-old girl presenting with 24 hours of fever and progressive lethargy. She has mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill, and cool peripheries. An IV line is in. The senior nurse is preparing fluids while you prepare to give broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178, BP 78/40, RR 42, SpO2 96% room air, T 39.6, capillary refill 5 seconds
data_table.Examination: Mottled cool peripheries, drowsy but rousable, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L, glucose 5.2, FBC and cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial fluid strategy?

options.text: Administer a 10 to 20 mL/kg bolus of balanced crystalloid over 5 to 10 minutes with reassessment after each bolus
Administer a 40 mL/kg bolus of normal saline over the first ten minutes prior to any reassessment of haemodynamics or perfusion markers
Start a peripheral noradrenaline infusion immediately as first-line haemodynamic support before any further crystalloid resuscitation is given
Commence packed red blood cell transfusion as initial volume resuscitation while awaiting the full blood count and group and screen results
Administer 5% albumin 20 mL/kg as the preferred crystalloid alternative for septic shock fluid resuscitation in paediatric practice

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 12-year-old girl in clinic after a third episode of syncope while swimming in cold water at school carnivals. Each episode involved sudden loss of consciousness with rapid recovery. Her ECG at rest shows a QTc of 488 ms calculated using the Bazett formula. Her paternal grandfather died suddenly aged 32 of unknown cause while swimming.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78 sinus, BP 108/64
data_table.Examination: Normal cardiovascular and neurological examination, no dysmorphism
data_table.Investigations: Resting ECG QTc 488 ms (Bazett), no arrhythmia on Holter; electrolytes including magnesium normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next management step?

options.text: Commence flecainide as antiarrhythmic prophylaxis pending genetic confirmation while continuing routine sport participation as tolerated by the patient
Commence metoprolol succinate at a paediatric dose and reassess in three months with repeat resting ECG to evaluate the effect on QTc and clinical symptoms
Implant a single-chamber ICD as primary prevention given the family history and three syncopal episodes despite a normal Holter recording
Commence a non-selective beta-blocker such as nadolol or propranolol with referral for genetic testing and family cascade screening
Reassure the family and arrange a tilt-table test to confirm vasovagal syncope as the likely diagnosis based on the recurrent self-limiting episodes

stem: You are the PICU registrar receiving a 6-day-old breastfed boy retrieved from a regional centre with progressive lethargy and refusal to feed since day 4. He has had two brief tonic-clonic events. The infant is now obtunded. Bedside glucose is 4.2 mmol/L. The retrieval team has sent off a metabolic screen and ammonia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188, RR 70, T 36.4, SpO2 98% on minimal oxygen
data_table.Examination: Obtunded, hypotonic, no focal neurology, no dysmorphic features, normal newborn examination at birth
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 4.2, lactate 1.8, venous pH 7.49, bicarbonate 22, ammonia 540 micromol/L, anion gap 14, urine ketones negative
data_table.Medications: Nil; standard newborn vitamin K and hepatitis B at birth

lead_in: Which finding most strongly directs initial management?

options.text: Hypoglycaemia requiring high-rate dextrose infusion at 8 mg/kg/min with concurrent insulin to facilitate intracellular potassium shift
Hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis and absent ketosis directing urgent referral for haemofiltration and a urea cycle defect pathway
Metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap and ketosis pointing toward organic acidaemia requiring sodium bicarbonate and biotin empirically
Raised lactate suggesting mitochondrial disease and requiring high-dose thiamine, riboflavin, and coenzyme Q10 prior to further imaging
Normal newborn examination history excluding inborn error of metabolism and directing toward neonatal sepsis pathway and empiric antibiotics

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 7-week-old previously well term male infant brought in by parents with 24 hours of fever, irritability, and reduced feeding (taking about half his usual volume). He has had no vomiting or diarrhoea. There is no rash, no recent travel, and immunisations are up to date. ED has obtained a catheter urine specimen which is positive for nitrites and leukocyte esterase. Bloods are back.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 178, RR 52, SpO2 98% RA, cap refill 2 s
data_table.Examination: Alert when held; wet nappies reduced; no rash; chest clear; abdomen soft, no mass; suprapubic non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4, neutrophils 13.2, Hb 110, CRP 84, Na 138, K 4.6, Cr 28; urine: nitrites +, leuk +++, blood +, microscopy WCC >100/mcL; blood and urine cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 25 mg/kg twice daily for 7 days with GP review within 48 hours arranged
Admit for IV gentamicin and IV benzylpenicillin with renal tract ultrasound during admission
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily and arrange micturating cystourethrogram during this admission
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 22.5 mg/kg three times daily with paediatric review in 24 hours
Discharge home awaiting urine culture sensitivities and start antibiotics if a pathogen grows

stem: You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 2-year-old girl in ED with a 1-day history of barking cough and stridor. She had a coryzal prodrome 2 days ago. At triage she had inspiratory stridor at rest with mild chest wall retractions, and was given a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg 30 minutes ago. On reassessment she now has inspiratory stridor at rest with marked sternal recession, looks distressed, and is reluctant to drink. She is afebrile.

data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest, marked sternal recession, mild tracheal tug, no drooling, no cyanosis, alert but distressed, air entry symmetrical with no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: No bloods or imaging needed at this stage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg (5 mL of 1:1000) with continued close monitoring in resuscitation bay
Repeat oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg now and reassess clinical severity in a further 60 minutes
Heated humidified oxygen by mask at 6 L/min and reassess clinical severity in 30 minutes
Urgent lateral neck radiograph to exclude foreign body or epiglottitis before further treatment
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg via spacer with budesonide and clinical reassessment in 30 minutes

stem: You are the paediatric registrar in ED at 02:30 reviewing a previously well 13-year-old boy with sudden onset severe left scrotal pain that woke him from sleep 4 hours ago. He has vomited twice. He denies trauma, dysuria, or recent illness. He has not previously been sexually active. The left testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie and exquisitely tender; the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left. The right side is unremarkable. Urinalysis is clear.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum erythematous, swollen, left testis high-riding with horizontal lie, exquisite tenderness, absent cremasteric reflex; right side normal; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: nil; FBC and EUC sent
data_table.Medications: Paracetamol 1 g PO 1 hour ago in ED

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent scrotal Doppler ultrasound to assess testicular blood flow before any surgical referral
Empirical oral ceftriaxone and doxycycline for presumed epididymo-orchitis with urology review
Immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum with bilateral orchidopexy by urology this hour
Attempt manual detorsion in ED rotating the left testis medially and admit for observation overnight
Admit under paediatrics for analgesia and elevation, with urology review on the morning round

stem: You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9-month-old boy with 6 days of fever to 39.5, marked irritability, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, and a polymorphous truncal rash. He has no cervical lymphadenopathy, no oral changes, and no extremity changes yet. Mucosal swabs and blood cultures are pending. Initial bloods show neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised CRP, mild anaemia, hyponatraemia, low albumin, and elevated ALT. Echocardiogram performed by paediatric cardiology shows borderline left anterior descending coronary dilation (Z score 2.3).

data_table.Examination: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection without exudate, polymorphous truncal rash, irritable; no lymphadenopathy, no oral or hand or foot changes
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19, neutrophils 14, Hb 96, plt 540, CRP 162, ESR 78, Na 130, ALT 88, albumin 28; urinalysis: sterile pyuria; echocardiogram: LAD Z score 2.3, no pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue supportive care and antipyretics; reassess at day 10 of fever to apply Kawasaki criteria
IV ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for empirical sepsis with paediatric infectious diseases consultation
IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg daily for 3 days as first-line treatment of incomplete Kawasaki
IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over 12 hours with high-dose oral aspirin 30 mg/kg/day divided
Oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily monotherapy and repeat echocardiogram in 7 days for review

stem: You are the neonatal registrar called to postnatal ward at 90 minutes of life to review a term male infant born by elective LSCS to a 32-year-old G2P1 with insulin-treated type 1 diabetes. Birth weight is 4350 g (>97th centile). Maternal HbA1c at 36 weeks was 7.4%. The infant was placed skin-to-skin and breastfed at 30 minutes. Routine BSL screening at 90 minutes is 1.6 mmol/L (taken before the second feed). The infant is alert with normal tone, no jitteriness, no apnoea, and a normal cry.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.7 (axillary), HR 142, RR 50, SpO2 98% RA
data_table.Examination: Term appearance, large for gestational age, alert, normal tone, no jitteriness, no apnoea, plethoric but not cyanotic
data_table.Investigations: Bedside BSL 1.6 mmol/L; cord gases at delivery normal; no further bloods yet
data_table.Medications: Vitamin K 1 mg IM at birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding only and recheck BSL prior to the next scheduled feed in 3 hours
Give a single bolus of 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg intravenously and continue routine ward observations afterwards
Commence intravenous 10% dextrose at 60 mL/kg/day infusion via cannula and admit to neonatal nursery
Administer intramuscular glucagon 100 mcg/kg single dose with continued breastfeeding and observation
Administer 40% buccal dextrose gel 200 mg/kg with immediate top-up feed and recheck BSL in 30 minutes

stem: You are the paediatric nephrology registrar reviewing an 8-year-old boy 6 weeks after a clinical diagnosis of Henoch-Schönlein purpura (palpable purpura, polyarthralgia, mild abdominal pain) which has otherwise resolved. He was managed conservatively at first presentation. Today his palpable purpura has cleared. Routine urinalysis shows persistent proteinuria and microscopic haematuria. Spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is 280 mg/mmol (heavily nephrotic range). Serum albumin is 22 g/L. eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73m2 (mildly reduced). He is normotensive. Complement and ANA are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/64 (50th centile for age and height), HR 88
data_table.Examination: Mild periorbital and ankle oedema, purpura resolved, abdomen soft, joints non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis: protein +++, blood ++; UPCR 280 mg/mmol; albumin 22 g/L; eGFR 78; C3 normal, C4 normal, ANA negative, anti-dsDNA negative; hep B/C and ASOT negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and recheck urinalysis and renal function in 6 months as HSP nephritis usually self-resolves
Empirical oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks then taper, without histological confirmation now
Renal biopsy now to grade nephritis severity and guide immunosuppressive therapy choice
Commence ACE inhibitor monotherapy (enalapril) with monthly urinalysis and BP monitoring at GP
Plasmapheresis with IV pulse methylprednisolone now and admit under nephrology for cyclophosphamide

stem: You are the paediatric oncology registrar reviewing a 3-year-old girl with a 3-week history of progressive abdominal distension, intermittent low-grade fever, weight loss, and bone pain in both legs causing limping. Examination shows a 10 cm firm abdominal mass crossing the midline. She has periorbital ecchymosis bilaterally. There is no haematuria. BP is 90th centile for age. Urinary VMA and HVA are markedly elevated. MIBG scan is being arranged. Bone marrow aspirate is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 108/68 (90th centile), HR 124, T 37.8, RR 24, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: 10 cm firm irregular abdominal mass crossing midline, bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), opsoclonus on prolonged ocular pursuit, tender shins bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Hb 84, plt 198, WCC 12, LDH 1240, urinary VMA and HVA markedly elevated; MRI abdomen: 10 cm adrenal mass crossing midline encasing aorta

lead_in: Which feature most strongly differentiates this presentation from Wilms tumour?

options.text: Presence of a firm palpable abdominal mass detected on routine paediatric abdominal examination today
Hypertension within the 90th centile range for age detected on routine ward observations today
Mass crossing the abdominal midline with encasement of the aorta on the most recent MRI scan
Bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) with opsoclonus and bone pain from skeletal metastasis
Markedly elevated urinary catecholamine metabolite levels (VMA and HVA) detected on urine testing

stem: You are the paediatric immunology registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy referred by GP with 8 documented episodes over the past 6 months of fever to 40, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis with negative throat swabs, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Episodes last 4 days at a time and recur every 3 to 4 weeks with clockwork regularity. Between episodes he is entirely well. Growth is on the 50th centile. Family history is negative for periodic fevers. Genetic testing for MEFV, TNFRSF1A, MVK, and NLRP3 has returned negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Between episodes: afebrile, normal vitals
data_table.Examination: During episode: aphthous stomatitis, exudative pharyngitis, tender cervical lymphadenopathy; between episodes: examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: During episode: CRP 120, neutrophilia, normal ferritin; between episodes: CRP <5, normal FBC; throat swabs negative on all episodes; genetic panel for FMF (MEFV), TRAPS (TNFRSF1A), HIDS (MVK), CAPS (NLRP3) all negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Empirical daily oral colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily as prophylaxis against further episodes of fever
Continuous oral cimetidine 20 mg/kg/day for 6 months as prophylaxis against further febrile attacks
Subcutaneous anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) 2 mg/kg daily during each acute febrile episode now
Urgent referral to ENT for tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy as definitive treatment of recurrent fever
Single oral dose of prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg at fever onset to abort each PFAPA episode promptly

subtopic_detail: Urea cycle disorder - hyperammonaemia emergency management
stem: A 3-day-old term male infant presents with progressive lethargy, poor feeding, and vomiting since yesterday. He was born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery at 39 weeks with a normal birth weight and was breastfeeding well until 36 hours ago. On examination he is tachypnoeic, hypotonic, and minimally responsive to stimulation. A generalised tonic seizure occurs during assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 170, RR 55, SpO2 97% on room air, Temp 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 480 micromol/L (ref <50), venous pH 7.52, pCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3 18 mmol/L, lactate 2.1 mmol/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, anion gap 12 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV sodium benzoate and phenylbutyrate with haemodialysis referral
IV dextrose 10% bolus with insulin infusion and bicarbonate correction
High-dose oral carnitine supplementation with dietary protein restriction
Emergent exchange transfusion with fresh frozen plasma replacement
IV biotin 10 mg loading dose with empiric thiamine and riboflavin

subtopic_detail: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn - iNO initiation
stem: A term neonate born through thick meconium-stained liquor develops progressive respiratory distress within the first 6 hours. Despite surfactant administration and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation with FiO2 1.0, hypoxaemia persists. Echocardiography confirms right-to-left shunting at the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale with a tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity consistent with suprasystemic pulmonary pressures. Structurally normal heart confirmed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 165, pre-ductal SpO2 82%, post-ductal SpO2 68%, MAP 42 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Oxygenation index 28, pH 7.28, pCO2 48 mmHg, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, chest X-ray showing bilateral patchy opacification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence IV milrinone infusion for right ventricular afterload reduction
Initiate inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm with serial oxygenation index monitoring
Arrange emergent venoarterial ECMO transfer without further medical therapy
Commence IV prostacyclin infusion with invasive haemodynamic monitoring
Switch to conventional ventilation with permissive hypercapnia strategy

subtopic_detail: Turner syndrome - initial cardiac and renal workup
stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred for short stature. She is tracking below the 1st centile for height with a height velocity of 3.5 cm/year. Her mid-parental height predicts the 35th centile. On examination she has a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, a low posterior hairline, and mild cubitus valgus. Karyotype confirms 45,X.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 105/65 mmHg (right arm), height 107 cm (<1st centile), weight 20 kg (10th centile)
data_table.Investigations: TSH 3.2 mIU/L (ref 0.5-5.0), free T4 14 pmol/L (ref 10-25), coeliac serology negative, IGF-1 low-normal for age

lead_in: Which investigation is the highest priority to arrange next?

options.text: Pelvic ultrasound to assess ovarian morphology and uterine presence
Growth hormone stimulation testing before considering GH therapy
Echocardiography to screen for bicuspid aortic valve and coarctation
Renal ultrasound to assess for horseshoe kidney and collecting system anomalies
Audiometry to screen for sensorineural and conductive hearing loss

subtopic_detail: Paediatric Crohn disease - exclusive enteral nutrition induction
stem: A 13-year-old boy presents with a 3-month history of abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhoea, weight loss of 4 kg, and fatigue. He has fallen from the 50th to the 15th centile for weight and has delayed Tanner stage II puberty. Ileocolonoscopy shows patchy, transmural inflammation with aphthous ulceration in the terminal ileum and ascending colon with skip lesions. Histology confirms non-caseating granulomas. His paediatric Crohn disease activity index score is moderate.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 105 g/L, platelets 450 x10^9/L, albumin 28 g/L, CRP 42 mg/L, ESR 38 mm/hr, faecal calprotectin 1200 microg/g, iron studies consistent with iron deficiency

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction therapy?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day weaning over 8 weeks
Azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day as monotherapy for induction
Infliximab induction with three loading doses at weeks 0, 2, and 6
Exclusive enteral nutrition with polymeric formula for 6 to 8 weeks
Oral mesalazine 50 mg/kg/day with folic acid supplementation

stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with his fourth episode of deep-seated infection in 18 months. Previous episodes include a hepatic abscess requiring drainage (Staphylococcus aureus), pneumonia with empyema (Aspergillus fumigatus), and perianal abscess (Serratia marcescens). His immunoglobulin levels, complement, and lymphocyte subsets are normal. HIV serology is negative.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 x10^9/L, lymphocytes 3.8 x10^9/L, platelets 380 x10^9/L, CRP 85 mg/L, IgG 8.2 g/L (normal), IgA 0.9 g/L (normal), IgM 1.1 g/L (normal)

lead_in: Which investigation will most likely confirm the underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Genetic testing for STAT3 gain-of-function mutation panel
Mannose-binding lectin level and complement functional assays
Lymphocyte proliferation assay to mitogens and antigens
Specific antibody response to pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine
Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry assay of neutrophil oxidative burst

stem: A 10-month-old boy presents with 6 days of fever up to 39.5 degrees C that has not responded to paracetamol and ibuprofen. He has bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection and cracked, erythematous lips. He has no rash, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and no extremity changes. He is irritable and refusing feeds. His older sibling had a viral upper respiratory tract infection last week.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 bpm, RR 36, Temp 39.2 degrees C, SpO2 99%
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (neutrophils 14.2), platelets 480 x10^9/L, CRP 142 mg/L, ESR 78 mm/hr, ALT 68 U/L, albumin 28 g/L, urine microscopy - sterile pyuria (WCC 42/hpf), echocardiogram - mild coronary artery dilation (right coronary artery Z-score +2.8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue supportive care and antipyretics as this is likely a prolonged viral illness given the household contact history
Administer IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion over 10-12 hours with high-dose aspirin 30-50 mg/kg/day in divided doses
Commence IV ceftriaxone for possible occult bacteraemia given the prolonged fever and elevated inflammatory markers
Observe for 48 more hours to see if additional clinical features develop to meet full Kawasaki criteria before treating
Commence oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day as primary treatment with low-dose aspirin and serial echocardiography monitoring

stem: A 5-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department by his mother with a swollen left thigh noticed during a nappy change. The mother states the infant has been unsettled for the past 2 days and she assumed he was teething. There is no reported history of trauma. The infant was born at term with no neonatal complications. He is not yet pulling to stand or cruising. X-ray of the left femur shows a spiral fracture of the mid-shaft. You also notice fading bruises on both ears.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 152 bpm, RR 38, Temp 37.0 degrees C, weight 7.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Examination: Left thigh swollen and tender to palpation, fading yellow-green bruises on bilateral ear pinnae, no other bruises, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, fundoscopy normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Apply a splint to the left thigh and discharge with outpatient orthopaedic follow-up in 1 week for the fracture
Reassure the mother that spiral femoral fractures are common in infants learning to roll and manage with a hip spica
Admit the infant, perform skeletal survey and bloods including FBC, coagulation, calcium, phosphate, and ALP, and notify the child protection team
Order genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta and defer child protection involvement until results are available
Contact police directly without involving the hospital child protection team, and arrange foster care before investigation

stem: A 3-day-old term male infant, birth weight 4.6 kg, born to a non-diabetic mother, has had persistent hypoglycaemia despite maximum enteral feeding and IV dextrose at 12 mg/kg/min. He was macrosomic at birth with no dysmorphic features. He has had 4 episodes of blood glucose below 2.0 mmol/L in the past 24 hours despite escalating IV dextrose. A critical sample was collected during a hypoglycaemic episode.

data_table.Investigations: Critical sample results - blood glucose 1.4 mmol/L, serum insulin 42 mIU/L (ref < 2 when glucose < 2.6), C-peptide 1.8 nmol/L (elevated), cortisol 420 nmol/L, growth hormone 18 mIU/L, ketones 0.1 mmol/L, free fatty acids 0.08 mmol/L (low), ammonia 32 micromol/L (ref < 50), lactate 1.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase IV dextrose concentration and rate to achieve glucose delivery of 15 mg/kg/min with continuous glucagon infusion
Commence oral hydrocortisone 5 mg/m2/day in three divided doses for suspected cortisol deficiency causing hypoglycaemia
Commence dietary management with cornstarch supplementation and frequent high-protein feeds to stabilise glucose
Commence diazoxide 5-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses with chlorothiazide, and refer to a paediatric endocrinologist for further evaluation
Arrange urgent pancreatic MRI and plan for near-total pancreatectomy given the severity of hypoglycaemia requiring high glucose

stem: A 12-day-old infant born at term presents to the emergency department with poor feeding, lethargy, and weight loss since birth (birth weight 3.4 kg, current weight 2.9 kg). The infant was born with ambiguous genitalia - apparent clitoromegaly with partially fused labioscrotal folds and a single perineal opening - but the family was told to wait for the newborn screening result. The newborn screening result is not yet available. The infant appears dehydrated and peripherally shut down with poor capillary refill.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 192 bpm, RR 52, Temp 36.2 degrees C, SpO2 97%, CRT 5 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L, potassium 8.2 mmol/L, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, venous pH 7.22, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L, ECG shows peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus, IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg for hypoglycaemia, and commence IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat with urgent endocrine consult
Commence IV insulin-dextrose infusion to correct the hyperkalaemia as the primary emergency treatment before any further investigation or workup
Oral sodium chloride supplementation and fludrocortisone, recheck electrolytes in 4 hours, and await newborn screening results before starting steroids
Arrange urgent karyotype and pelvic ultrasound to determine chromosomal sex before initiating any treatment for the presenting adrenal crisis
IV calcium gluconate 10% for cardiac stabilisation, IV 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg bolus, IV dextrose, IV hydrocortisone 25 mg stat, and send 17-OHP before steroid

subtopic_detail: Recurrent wheeze in toddler: ICS preventer threshold
stem: A 20-month-old boy presents for review after his third episode of wheeze in 6 months. Each episode was triggered by a viral upper respiratory infection and responded to salbutamol. Between episodes he is well with no nocturnal cough or exercise limitation. His mother has a diagnosis of asthma. He has no personal history of eczema or food allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 28, HR 120, SpO2 98% on room air, T 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Well-appearing, no wheeze currently, no eczema, growth on 50th centile for weight and length
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol MDI via spacer PRN during acute episodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence low-dose ICS via spacer for an 8-week trial period
Continue salbutamol PRN alone and reassess in another 3 months
Commence montelukast 4 mg nightly as first-line preventer
Refer for skin prick allergy testing before starting therapy
Commence high-dose ICS via spacer for a rapid 4-week trial

stem: A 15-year-old girl is admitted to a paediatric ward with a 4-month history of progressive weight loss. Her parents report she has been eating less than 500 kcal per day for the past 2 weeks. Her pre-morbid weight was 58 kg and current weight is 42 kg. She appears emaciated and lethargic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 48, BP 85/55 supine (postural drop 20 mmHg on standing), T 35.4 C, RR 14
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, K 3.1, PO4 0.62, Mg 0.68, Ca corrected 2.18, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, albumin 30 g/L, ECG: sinus bradycardia with prolonged QTc 470 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial nutritional approach?

options.text: Start nasogastric continuous feeds at full estimated requirements
Begin oral intake at 1200 kcal/day with prophylactic phosphate supplement
Start oral nutritional supplements at 2000 kcal/day with monitoring
Commence total parenteral nutrition via a central venous catheter
Commence enteral feeds at 500 kcal/day and increase over two weeks

stem: A 5-year-old boy is referred by his GP for evaluation of chronic snoring. His parents report nightly snoring with observed apnoeic pauses for the past 12 months. He has daytime mouth-breathing, hyperactivity at school, and bedwetting that had previously resolved. He has had 4 episodes of tonsillitis in the past year. His growth has plateaued, crossing from the 50th to the 25th centile for weight.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 90, RR 20, SpO2 97% awake, weight 17 kg (25th centile)
data_table.Examination: Grade 3+ tonsils bilaterally, adenoid facies, high-arched palate, no craniofacial abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Polysomnography: obstructive AHI 8.2 events/hour, SpO2 nadir 84%, ETCO2 peak 55 mmHg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Trial of intranasal mometasone and montelukast for 12 weeks
Commence nocturnal CPAP therapy and reassess in 6 months
Refer for adenotonsillectomy with post-operative monitoring plan
Repeat polysomnography in 6 months before deciding on surgery
Refer for tonsillectomy alone preserving the adenoid tissue

subtopic_detail: Infant GORD: red flags prompting investigation
stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed girl is brought to your clinic with frequent posseting after feeds. Her mother reports she arches her back during feeds, has episodes of irritability after lying flat, and has had two episodes of green-tinged vomiting in the past week. She was born at term via normal vaginal delivery with no neonatal complications.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 145, RR 38, T 36.9 C, weight 3.9 kg (birth weight 3.5 kg, now tracking below 10th centile)
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no palpable mass, mildly distended, normal bowel sounds, no bile staining on nappy
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Trial of 4-week omeprazole and review clinical response
24-hour oesophageal pH monitoring with impedance study
Abdominal ultrasound to assess the pylorus and gut anatomy
Urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast study within 24 hours
Reassurance with feeding advice and weight check in 2 weeks

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 6-month history of infrequent hard stools, passage every 4-5 days, and intermittent faecal soiling. His parents report that he withholds stool, crossing his legs and hiding behind furniture. He was previously toilet-trained at age 2.5 years. Dietary history reveals low fibre and fluid intake. There are no red flags for organic disease.

data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen with a palpable faecal mass in the left lower quadrant, normal anal position and tone, no perianal fissures
data_table.Investigations: Not required for clinical diagnosis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management approach?

options.text: Dietary modification with increased fibre and fluids alone
Daily lactulose 10 mL twice daily for ongoing maintenance
Phosphate enema followed by daily senna for 3 months
Abdominal X-ray to confirm impaction then plan treatment
Oral macrogol disimpaction regimen then daily macrogol maintenance

subtopic_detail: Paediatric Crohn disease: escalation after 5-ASA failure
stem: A 14-year-old boy with ileocolonic Crohn disease diagnosed 8 months ago returns with worsening abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea, and 3 kg weight loss over 6 weeks despite adherent mesalazine therapy. His linear growth has decelerated, crossing from the 50th to the 25th centile for height over the past year. He has no perianal disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 110/65, T 37.2 C, weight 45 kg (25th centile)
data_table.Investigations: CRP 42 mg/L, ESR 38, albumin 28 g/L, faecal calprotectin 1850 mcg/g, Hb 108 g/L, MCV 74 fL

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his management?

options.text: Commence exclusive enteral nutrition for 8 weeks as induction
Add prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day tapering course for 8 weeks
Start azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day as maintenance immunomodulator
Escalate mesalazine to maximum dose of 4 g daily with review
Start infliximab induction at 5 mg/kg intravenously now

stem: A male infant is born at 38 weeks gestation via emergency caesarean section for fetal distress. A left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia was diagnosed on antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks. At birth he is cyanotic and in respiratory distress. The left hemithorax has absent breath sounds and the abdomen is scaphoid. He is intubated in the delivery suite.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 160, SpO2 78% pre-ductal on FiO2 1.0, BP 45/28 (MAP 34)
data_table.Investigations: Pre-ductal ABG: pH 7.18, pCO2 62, pO2 42, BE -8, lactate 5.2 mmol/L
data_table.Examination: Intubated, left hemithorax dull to percussion with absent breath sounds, heart sounds displaced to the right, scaphoid abdomen

lead_in: What is the single most important initial intervention?

options.text: Immediate surgical repair of the diaphragmatic defect now
Insert a large-bore orogastric tube on continuous drainage
Commence inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm for pulmonary vasodilation
Insert a left intercostal chest drain to relieve pneumothorax
Commence bag-mask ventilation with high-pressure support

stem: A 2-day-old male infant born at 39 weeks to a mother on a methadone maintenance program (80 mg daily) is in the special care nursery for observation. He is breastfeeding but has developed high-pitched crying, tremors when disturbed, frequent sneezing, loose stools, and disrupted sleep cycles. Serial modified Finnegan scores over the past 12 hours have been 9, 11, and 12.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 172, RR 52, T 37.6 C, SpO2 98% RA
data_table.Examination: Jittery with increased tone, hyperactive Moro reflex, nasal stuffiness, mild excoriation from facial rubbing, no seizures
data_table.Feeding: Breastfeeding with supplementary expressed breast milk, intake adequate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Increase non-pharmacological care and rescore in 4 hours
Commence phenobarbital 20 mg/kg loading dose intravenously
Commence oral morphine using a symptom-based dosing protocol
Cease breastfeeding and commence a high-calorie formula
Transfer to NICU for continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring

subtopic_detail: Meconium ileus: investigation pathway for cystic fibrosis
stem: A 36-hour-old term neonate has not passed meconium and has developed progressive abdominal distension with bilious vomiting. There is no family history of cystic fibrosis. The newborn bloodspot screening (immunoreactive trypsinogen) result is pending. Antenatal ultrasound at 32 weeks showed echogenic bowel.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 155, RR 48, T 36.7 C, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Grossly distended abdomen, visible bowel loops, no hernia, rectum empty on gentle examination
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal X-ray: multiple dilated loops of small bowel, no air-fluid levels, ground-glass opacity in right lower quadrant, no distal gas in rectum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Insert a rectal tube and administer warm saline washouts
Arrange urgent laparotomy for small bowel obstruction now
Observe with IV fluids and await newborn screening results
Therapeutic water-soluble contrast enema under fluoroscopy
Commence oral N-acetylcysteine to dissolve the meconium plug

subtopic_detail: Central precocious puberty: GnRH agonist indication
stem: A 6-year-old girl is referred by her GP for breast development noticed by her mother 4 months ago. She has no history of adrenal disease or exposure to exogenous oestrogens. She is the tallest girl in her class but her mid-parental height prediction is 50th centile. There is no headache or visual disturbance.

data_table.Examination: Tanner breast stage 3, Tanner pubic hair stage 2, no axillary hair, no acne, height 128 cm (>97th centile for age), weight 27 kg (90th centile)
data_table.Investigations: Bone age X-ray: 9 years (chronological age 6.3 years), basal LH 1.8 IU/L, basal FSH 4.2 IU/L, oestradiol 120 pmol/L, pelvic ultrasound: uterine length 42 mm with endometrial echo, bilateral ovarian volumes 3.5 mL, MRI brain: normal pituitary and hypothalamus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure and monitor growth with 6-monthly bone age imaging
Commence cyproterone acetate to suppress androgen effects
Perform GnRH stimulation test before initiating any treatment
Commence letrozole to suppress peripheral oestrogen synthesis
Commence GnRH agonist therapy with 3-monthly depot injection

stem: A 3-week-old girl was diagnosed with congenital hypothyroidism on newborn bloodspot screening (elevated TSH) and commenced on levothyroxine 12 mcg/kg/day at day 10 of life. She was born at term with a birth weight of 3.4 kg. Her mother asks about the follow-up plan at a 2-week review appointment. She is feeding well and growing normally.

data_table.Investigations: Day 10 confirmatory: TSH 85 mIU/L (ref <10), free T4 6.2 pmol/L (ref 12-22). Today (day 24): TSH 18 mIU/L, free T4 22 pmol/L
data_table.Examination: Alert, no prolonged jaundice, anterior fontanelle normal, no goitre, normal tone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her thyroid replacement?

options.text: Increase levothyroxine dose and recheck TFTs in 2 weeks
Continue current dose as free T4 is now within normal range
Reduce levothyroxine as free T4 is at the upper reference limit
Order a thyroid scintigraphy scan before adjusting dosing
Cease levothyroxine and recheck TFTs in 4 weeks to confirm

subtopic_detail: Short stature: growth hormone stimulation test indication
stem: An 8-year-old boy is referred for short stature. His height is 116 cm (below 3rd centile) and his growth velocity over the past year has been 3.5 cm/year (normal >5 cm/year at this age). His mid-parental height prediction is 50th centile. He was born SGA at 2.4 kg but had adequate catch-up growth by age 2. He has no chronic illness, his diet is adequate, and he is prepubertal.

data_table.Investigations: FBC normal, ESR 4, coeliac serology negative, TFTs normal (TSH 2.1, fT4 16), IGF-1 78 ng/mL (low for age), bone age 6 years (delayed by 2 years)
data_table.Examination: Proportionate short stature, no dysmorphic features, no midline defects, Tanner stage 1

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: MRI of the pituitary gland and hypothalamus with contrast
Growth hormone stimulation test with two pharmacological agents
Karyotype analysis to exclude Turner syndrome or variant
Reassure that this represents constitutional delay of growth
Commence a 6-month trial of growth hormone without testing

subtopic_detail: Graves disease in adolescent: antithyroid drug choice
stem: A 13-year-old girl presents with a 3-month history of weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremor, and difficulty concentrating at school. Her mother noticed a neck swelling. She has no eye symptoms. There is no family history of autoimmune disease.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110 (sinus tachycardia), BP 130/60, T 37.2 C
data_table.Examination: Diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, fine tremor of outstretched hands, lid lag but no proptosis, brisk reflexes
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01 mIU/L (ref 0.5-5.0), free T4 58 pmol/L (ref 12-22), free T3 18.2 pmol/L (ref 3.5-6.5), TSH receptor antibodies strongly positive, FBC and LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily with LFT monitoring
Radioactive iodine ablation after 2 weeks of beta-blocker
Carbimazole 0.5 mg/kg/day plus propranolol for symptom relief
Referral for total thyroidectomy as definitive first treatment
Atenolol alone as initial therapy with thyroid monitoring weekly

subtopic_detail: Acute rheumatic fever: Australian Jones criteria modification
stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote Northern Territory community presents with fever, migratory polyarthralgia affecting his knees and ankles, and a new cardiac murmur. He had a sore throat 3 weeks ago that was not treated with antibiotics. He has no rash, no subcutaneous nodules, and no chorea.

data_table.Examination: Pan-systolic murmur grade 3/6 at the apex radiating to the axilla, tender swollen left knee and right ankle, no erythema marginatum, no subcutaneous nodules
data_table.Investigations: CRP 68 mg/L, ESR 55, ASO titre 480 IU/mL (ref <200), anti-DNase B 620 IU/mL (ref <300), throat swab: no group A streptococcus isolated, echocardiogram: moderate mitral regurgitation with anterior leaflet prolapse

lead_in: How many major Jones criteria does this child meet under the Australian modification?

options.text: One major criterion: carditis with mitral regurgitation only
One major and one minor only, insufficient for diagnosis
Three major criteria: carditis plus arthritis plus fever
Two major criteria: carditis and polyarthralgia under AU rules
Two major criteria: carditis and polyarthritis as per standard

subtopic_detail: Rheumatic heart disease: secondary prophylaxis duration
stem: A 12-year-old Aboriginal girl from a regional Queensland community had a confirmed episode of acute rheumatic fever at age 10 with mild carditis (mitral regurgitation on echocardiography). She has been on benzathine penicillin G injections every 28 days since diagnosis. Her most recent echocardiogram shows persistent mild mitral regurgitation. Her parents ask how long she needs to continue the injections.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: mild mitral regurgitation, no mitral stenosis, normal LV function
data_table.Medications: Benzathine penicillin G 900 mg (1.2 million units) IM every 28 days

lead_in: What is the recommended duration of secondary prophylaxis?

options.text: Continue for 5 years from last episode then cease therapy
Continue until age 18 then cease if no recurrence of ARF
Cease now as 2 years of prophylaxis is adequate for mild RHD
Switch to oral penicillin V daily until age 21 for convenience
Continue until at least age 35 or for a minimum of 10 years

subtopic_detail: Nephrotic syndrome: steroid-sparing agent in frequent relapse
stem: A 6-year-old boy with steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome diagnosed at age 4 presents with his fifth relapse in 12 months. Each relapse responds to prednisolone but he relapses within 2 weeks of dose reduction. He has developed cushingoid facies, striae, and his growth velocity has fallen to 3 cm/year. He has no haematuria or hypertension.

data_table.Investigations: Urine protein:creatinine ratio 850 mg/mmol (nephrotic range), albumin 18 g/L, eGFR normal, C3 and C4 normal
data_table.Examination: Cushingoid facies, abdominal striae, periorbital oedema, weight 28 kg (90th centile), height 108 cm (10th centile)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his management?

options.text: Add mycophenolate mofetil as a steroid-sparing maintenance agent
Increase prednisolone dose and extend taper over 6 months
Commence an ACE inhibitor as the sole antiproteinuric strategy
Refer for renal biopsy to reclassify the histological subtype
Give IV cyclophosphamide pulse therapy for definitive remission

stem: A 10-year-old girl presents with recurrent severe headaches occurring 3-4 times per month for 6 months. Each headache is unilateral, throbbing, associated with nausea and photophobia, lasts 4-8 hours, and prevents school attendance. She has trialled regular paracetamol and ibuprofen at onset with partial relief. She has a family history of migraine in her mother. She has no aura symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination including fundoscopy, visual acuity, and visual fields, BMI 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated given typical presentation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence topiramate 1 mg/kg/day as migraine prophylaxis
Commence propranolol 0.5 mg/kg/day with slow dose titration
MRI brain to exclude secondary cause before starting therapy
Commence amitriptyline 10 mg nightly as preventive treatment
Prescribe sumatriptan nasal spray for acute migraine attacks

subtopic_detail: Guillain-Barre syndrome: IVIG timing and monitoring
stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with progressive lower limb weakness over 4 days following a gastroenteritis illness 2 weeks ago. He initially complained of leg pain, then difficulty walking, and today cannot stand independently. He has no bowel or bladder symptoms. His upper limbs have mild weakness proximally.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral lower limb weakness MRC grade 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally, upper limbs 4/5 proximally, absent knee and ankle reflexes, flexor plantar responses, no sensory level, normal cranial nerves
data_table.Investigations: CSF: protein 1.2 g/L (ref <0.4), WCC <5 cells, glucose 3.8 mmol/L, nerve conduction studies pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Commence IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/day for 5 days
Begin plasma exchange with 5 sessions over 7 to 10 days
Commence IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days with FVC monitoring
Observe in hospital with physiotherapy and reassess in 48 hours
Commence IVIG 1 g/kg as a single dose with repeat if needed

subtopic_detail: Infantile spasms: vigabatrin versus ACTH selection
stem: A 5-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department after his mother noticed clusters of brief jerking movements where he flexes his trunk and extends his arms, occurring in clusters of 10-15 on waking. The episodes started 5 days ago and are increasing in frequency. He was born at term with no perinatal complications. His development had been normal until 2 weeks ago when his mother noticed he stopped reaching for objects.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, RR 32, T 36.8 C, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Decreased visual tracking, intermittent flexor spasms observed in clusters, no skin stigmata of tuberous sclerosis
data_table.Investigations: EEG: hypsarrhythmia (high-amplitude chaotic slow waves with multifocal spikes), MRI brain: normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Commence sodium valproate at 20 mg/kg/day in divided doses
Commence vigabatrin 50 mg/kg/day with ophthalmology review
Commence levetiracetam 20 mg/kg/day as broad-spectrum agent
Commence high-dose prednisolone 15 mg/kg/day for 14 days
Arrange urgent epilepsy surgery consultation for resection

subtopic_detail: Sickle cell disease: acute chest syndrome management
stem: A 10-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) presents with fever, pleuritic chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea over 24 hours. He was admitted 2 days ago with a vaso-occlusive crisis affecting his long bones. His baseline haemoglobin is 80 g/L. He is receiving IV morphine and maintenance fluids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 125, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min nasal prongs, T 39.1 C, BP 95/55
data_table.Investigations: Hb 62 g/L (dropped from 80), WCC 18.2 x10^9/L, reticulocytes 2%, CXR: new bilateral lower lobe infiltrates, ABG: pH 7.38, pO2 58, pCO2 34
data_table.Examination: Bilateral basal crackles, reduced air entry at both bases, tender chest wall, tachypnoeic and using accessory muscles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate antibiotics to IV piperacillin-tazobactam and review
Commence high-flow nasal cannula and monitor oxygen saturations
Administer IV dexamethasone to reduce pulmonary inflammation
Perform an urgent whole blood exchange via femoral line access
Urgent simple red cell transfusion to raise Hb and reduce HbS

subtopic_detail: Thalassaemia trait versus iron deficiency discrimination
stem: A 3-year-old boy of Mediterranean heritage is found to have a microcytic anaemia on routine blood tests. His parents are concerned as he has been a fussy eater with low meat intake. He has no history of blood loss, pica, or chronic illness. His growth and development are normal.

data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L, MCV 62 fL (ref 70-86), MCH 22 pg (ref 24-30), RCC 5.8 x10^12/L (ref 4.0-5.5), RDW 13.5% (ref 11.5-14.5), ferritin 45 mcg/L (ref 15-200), iron 12 micromol/L (ref 9-21), transferrin saturation 22%

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Beta-thalassaemia trait with normal iron stores confirmed
Iron deficiency anaemia requiring oral iron supplementation
Combined iron deficiency and thalassaemia trait together
Alpha-thalassaemia trait based on the Mediterranean heritage
Anaemia of chronic disease with adequate iron stores present

subtopic_detail: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: investigation and management
stem: A term male neonate born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery develops widespread petechiae and purpura within 6 hours of birth. The mother is healthy with no history of thrombocytopenia, autoimmune disease, or medication use during pregnancy. The pregnancy was uncomplicated and the mother's platelet count at booking was 245 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 40, T 36.9 C, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Investigations: Neonatal platelet count 12 x10^9/L, Hb 165 g/L, WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, blood film: reduced platelets, no fragmentation, no blasts
data_table.Examination: Widespread petechiae and ecchymoses, no hepatosplenomegaly, fontanelle soft and flat, active and feeding well

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Maternal platelet-compatible random donor platelet transfusion
IVIG 1 g/kg and urgent cranial ultrasound for ICH screening
Commence oral prednisolone to the mother via breast milk
Observe and recheck platelet count in 24 hours with precautions
Exchange transfusion to remove circulating maternal antibodies

stem: A 2-year-old boy has had 8 courses of antibiotics in the past 12 months for recurrent acute otitis media, 2 episodes of bacterial pneumonia requiring hospitalisation, and one episode of bacterial meningitis at 18 months. His growth has been poor. His immunisation history is complete for age. There is no family history of immunodeficiency but his maternal uncle died in infancy from an undiagnosed infection.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, T 37.0 C, weight 10.2 kg (3rd centile)
data_table.Investigations: FBC: Hb 110 g/L, WCC 8.2 (neutrophils 4.5, lymphocytes 2.8), platelets 280
data_table.Examination: Small tonsils, no palpable lymph nodes, no hepatosplenomegaly, healed bilateral tympanostomy tube sites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening investigation?

options.text: HIV antibody and viral load testing with parental consent
Complement pathway screen with CH50 and AP50 functional assays
Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with IgG subclasses panel
Lymphocyte subsets with T-cell and B-cell enumeration panel
Neutrophil oxidative burst test to exclude chronic granulomatous

stem: A 9-year-old girl underwent emergency splenectomy 4 weeks ago following blunt abdominal trauma in a motor vehicle accident. She has recovered well from surgery. Her parents attend to discuss her long-term infection prevention plan. She had received all routine childhood vaccinations on schedule prior to the splenectomy, including 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine.

data_table.Medications: Currently taking amoxicillin 250 mg daily since discharge
data_table.Investigations: FBC post-splenectomy: Hb 125 g/L, platelets 650 x10^9/L (reactive), WCC 12.5 with Howell-Jolly bodies on film

lead_in: What is the most appropriate vaccination schedule from this point?

options.text: No additional vaccines needed as routine schedule was complete
Single dose of 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide now only
Annual influenza vaccine only as pneumococcal series is done
23vPPV plus meningococcal ACWY and B boosters and Hib booster
Defer all vaccination for 6 months post-splenectomy to allow

stem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after her mother witnessed her swallow a button battery from a remote control. She is drooling, refusing to swallow, and intermittently crying. She has not vomited. There is no stridor or respiratory distress.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 135, RR 28, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.9 C
data_table.Investigations: AP chest and lateral neck X-ray: 20 mm diameter coin-shaped radiopaque object at the level of the thoracic inlet with a visible double-ring (halo) sign on AP view and step-off on lateral view
data_table.Examination: Drooling, distressed but no stridor, soft abdomen, no subcutaneous emphysema

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer honey 10 mL every 10 minutes until endoscopy is ready
Observe for 24 hours as most batteries pass spontaneously
Attempt to dislodge the battery with a nasogastric tube push
Arrange outpatient gastroenterology review within the next week
Emergency rigid oesophagoscopy for removal within 2 hours

subtopic_detail: Paediatric burns: fluid resuscitation and referral criteria
stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after pulling a pot of boiling water from the stove 30 minutes ago. He has scald burns to his anterior chest, abdomen, and both upper arms. The burns are erythematous with blistering and are painful to touch. He weighs 15 kg.

data_table.Examination: Superficial partial-thickness burns: anterior chest and abdomen (18% using Lund and Browder chart for age 3), both upper arms circumferential (8%), total burn surface area estimated 26%, no airway burns, no soot in oropharynx

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid resuscitation strategy?

options.text: Modified Parkland: 3 mL/kg/% BSA over 24 hours plus maintenance
Standard Parkland: 4 mL/kg/% BSA over 24 hours without extras
Normal saline bolus 20 mL/kg then reassess for further boluses
Oral rehydration only as burns are superficial partial thickness
Albumin 5% infusion to maintain oncotic pressure and perfusion

subtopic_detail: Adolescent deliberate self-harm: risk assessment and disposition
stem: A 14-year-old girl presents to the emergency department at 10 pm after her parents found her with superficial lacerations to her left forearm. She tells you she cut herself with a razor blade after an argument with her boyfriend. She denies suicidal intent and says she wanted to feel something other than emotional pain. She has had 3 previous presentations for self-harm over the past 6 months. She has a diagnosis of anxiety but is not currently receiving treatment.

data_table.Examination: Multiple superficial lacerations to left volar forearm (none requiring sutures), older healed scars visible on both forearms, alert and cooperative
data_table.Mental state: Euthymic, denies current suicidal ideation, no psychotic symptoms, good rapport established

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home tonight with GP follow-up within 48 hours
Admit overnight for comprehensive psychosocial assessment next day
Commence fluoxetine 10 mg tonight for underlying anxiety
Refer to headspace for outpatient assessment within 2 weeks
Arrange involuntary psychiatric admission under the Mental Health Act

subtopic_detail: Orbital cellulitis: preseptal versus postseptal discrimination
stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with a 2-day history of progressive left periorbital swelling, redness, and pain. He had a runny nose and cough for the preceding week. Today he developed painful eye movements and his mother noticed his left eye appears more prominent. He has not had any trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 115, T 38.8 C, SpO2 98% RA
data_table.Examination: Left eye: marked periorbital oedema and erythema, 3 mm proptosis compared to the right, painful and restricted eye movements in all directions, visual acuity grossly intact, consensual pupillary reflex normal, relative afferent pupillary defect absent
data_table.Investigations: WCC 17.5 x10^9/L, CRP 95 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and review in 24 hours
Commence IV flucloxacillin alone targeting staphylococcal cover
CT orbits with contrast and IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole
MRI orbits without contrast and IV vancomycin monotherapy
Immediate surgical drainage without prior imaging assessment

subtopic_detail: Peritonsillar abscess: drainage decision and antibiotic choice
stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with 4 days of worsening left-sided throat pain, difficulty swallowing, muffled voice, and trismus. He was started on oral phenoxymethylpenicillin by his GP 2 days ago without improvement. He has been unable to eat or drink today. He has no stridor or drooling.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 100, T 38.5 C, SpO2 99% RA
data_table.Examination: Trismus with mouth opening limited to 2 cm, left peritonsillar bulge with uvula deviation to the right, muffled hot-potato voice, tender left anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, no airway compromise
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.8 x10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Switch to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and reassess in 48 hours
IV benzylpenicillin alone and observe for spontaneous resolution
Urgent tonsillectomy as definitive surgical management now
Needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus IV antibiotics
CT neck with contrast before any intervention to confirm abscess

subtopic_detail: Down syndrome neonate: cardiac screening and early intervention
stem: A 2-day-old baby girl born at 38 weeks is confirmed to have trisomy 21 on rapid FISH testing. She is feeding well and there are no clinical signs of respiratory distress. On examination she has typical features of Down syndrome including epicanthic folds, single palmar crease, and hypotonia. Her precordium is quiet with no audible murmur.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, RR 42, SpO2 98% right hand, 97% right foot, T 36.8 C, BP 65/40
data_table.Examination: No murmur detected, no hepatomegaly, well-perfused peripherally, bilateral red reflex present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate cardiac investigation at this stage?

options.text: No cardiac investigation needed as no murmur is detected
ECG alone to screen for conduction abnormalities initially
Chest X-ray to assess cardiac silhouette and lung fields
Defer echocardiography to 6 weeks of age at routine review
Echocardiography before discharge regardless of clinical findings

stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed girl is referred for prolonged jaundice. She has been icteric since day 3 of life. Her stools have become progressively pale over the past 2 weeks and are now acholic (white-grey). Her urine stains the nappy dark yellow. She is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 135, T 36.9 C, weight 4.2 kg (50th centile)
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 185 micromol/L, conjugated bilirubin 142 micromol/L (ref <20), ALT 95 U/L, GGT 520 U/L (markedly elevated), albumin 34 g/L, INR 1.1, abdominal ultrasound: non-visualised gallbladder, triangular cord sign at porta hepatis
data_table.Examination: Jaundiced, firm hepatomegaly 3 cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent referral for Kasai portoenterostomy within 1 to 2 weeks
Trial of ursodeoxycholic acid for 4 weeks then reassess flow
HIDA scan to confirm biliary obstruction before any referral
Percutaneous liver biopsy to confirm biliary atresia histology
Switch to formula feeding as breast milk jaundice is the cause

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis nephritis: biopsy threshold and monitoring
stem: A 7-year-old boy diagnosed with IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura) 3 weeks ago with palpable purpura and arthralgia presents for follow-up. His rash has resolved. Urine dipstick today shows 2+ blood and 2+ protein. His blood pressure is 118/78 mmHg (above the 95th centile for age and height). His serum creatinine is 52 micromol/L (upper limit of normal for age).

data_table.Investigations: Urine protein:creatinine ratio 120 mg/mmol (ref <20), urine microscopy: dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, albumin 30 g/L, C3 and C4 normal, ANA negative
data_table.Examination: No oedema, no rash, mild abdominal tenderness, BP 118/78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and repeat urine dipstick in 4 weeks at GP review
Refer to paediatric nephrology for consideration of renal biopsy
Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day without biopsy first
Commence an ACE inhibitor for proteinuria and hypertension
Check ANCA and anti-GBM antibodies to exclude other vasculitis

stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought by her parents after her teacher reported that she has frequent brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness lasting 5-10 seconds, occurring up to 30 times per day. During these episodes she stops mid-sentence and blinks rapidly, then resumes her activity without awareness of the lapse. She has no tonic-clonic seizures. Her development and neurological examination are normal.

data_table.Investigations: EEG: generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges lasting 5-8 seconds, provoked by hyperventilation, normal background activity
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination, no focal deficits, MRI brain not indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Sodium valproate 20 mg/kg/day in two divided daily doses
Carbamazepine 10 mg/kg/day as broad-spectrum anticonvulsant
Ethosuximide starting at 10 mg/kg/day with dose titration
Lamotrigine with slow titration over 8 weeks to target dose
Levetiracetam 20 mg/kg/day as well-tolerated first-line agent

subtopic_detail: Cystic fibrosis: borderline sweat chloride interpretation
stem: A 4-month-old boy was referred for sweat chloride testing after elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening followed by detection of one CFTR mutation (F508del) on the initial gene panel. He has been feeding well, gaining weight, and has had no respiratory infections. His parents are anxious about the result.

data_table.Investigations: Sweat chloride: 42 mmol/L (borderline range 30-59), repeated: 45 mmol/L, initial CFTR genotyping: heterozygous F508del, second mutation not detected on standard 38-mutation panel
data_table.Examination: Well infant, no respiratory signs, no clubbing, weight and length on 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat sweat chloride test in 6 months and continue monitoring
Faecal elastase and chest X-ray to assess for CF end-organ damage
Reassure parents that one mutation is carrier status not disease
Extended CFTR gene sequencing to identify a second mutation
Nasal potential difference testing at a specialist CF centre

subtopic_detail: Marfan syndrome: aortic root surveillance and management
stem: A 14-year-old boy with confirmed Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation positive) attends for his annual cardiology review. He is tall (>97th centile) with arachnodactyly, pectus excavatum, and lens subluxation. He has been on atenolol 50 mg daily since age 10. He reports he is feeling well and playing basketball.

data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: aortic root diameter 42 mm (Z-score +3.5, increased from Z-score +2.8 one year ago), mild mitral valve prolapse with trivial regurgitation, normal LV function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management change?

options.text: Continue current atenolol and repeat echocardiogram in 1 year
Cease atenolol and commence valsartan as an alternative agent
Increase atenolol dose and repeat echocardiogram in 6 months
Urgent referral for prophylactic aortic root replacement surgery
Add losartan, restrict collision sports, repeat echo in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Type 1 diabetes: sick day management and ketone thresholds
stem: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes managed on a basal-bolus insulin regimen (glargine and aspart) calls your after-hours service. He has been vomiting for 6 hours with gastroenteritis. He last ate 8 hours ago. His mother has checked his blood glucose and blood ketones at home.

data_table.Home monitoring: Blood glucose 16.8 mmol/L, blood ketones 1.8 mmol/L (ref <0.6)
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine 18 units at bedtime, insulin aspart 1 unit per 10 g carbohydrate, correction factor 1 unit per 3 mmol/L above target of 6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Give extra rapid-acting insulin correction dose and present to ED
Withhold all insulin until vomiting stops and glucose falls
Give extra rapid-acting insulin and increase oral fluids at home
Halve the basal insulin dose and recheck glucose in 2 hours
Administer ondansetron orally and increase fluid intake at home

subtopic_detail: Haemophilia A: factor replacement and desmopressin trial
stem: A 3-year-old boy with mild haemophilia A (factor VIII level 12%, baseline) presents to the emergency department after a fall from playground equipment, striking his forehead on the ground. He has a large forehead haematoma and was briefly dazed but did not lose consciousness. He is now alert and interactive with no focal neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 105, BP 95/55, GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Examination: Large frontal haematoma, no palpable skull fracture, neurologically intact, no other bleeding, no haemarthroses
data_table.Investigations: Factor VIII level: 11% (baseline 12%), APTT 52 seconds (ref 25-38)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Observe for 6 hours with neurological observations and review
IV desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg and urgent CT brain without contrast
Recombinant factor VIII 50 IU/kg IV and CT brain with contrast
Tranexamic acid 25 mg/kg orally and CT brain in the morning
Cryoprecipitate infusion to rapidly replace factor VIII now

stem: A male infant is born at 39 weeks via emergency caesarean section for placental abruption. The Apgar scores were 2 at 1 minute and 5 at 5 minutes. He required positive pressure ventilation and was intubated at 3 minutes of life. At 30 minutes of age he is on mechanical ventilation. He was born 45 minutes ago.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130, SpO2 92% on FiO2 0.4, T 36.5 C (not actively cooled yet)
data_table.Investigations: Cord gas: pH 6.88, BE -18, lactate 14 mmol/L. Postnatal arterial blood gas at 30 minutes: pH 7.05, pCO2 38, BE -14
data_table.Examination: Hypotonic, absent suck and gag reflexes, intermittent clinical seizures (rhythmic limb jerking), sluggish pupillary responses, fontanelle soft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence active warming to maintain normothermia at 37 degrees
Administer IV phenobarbital 20 mg/kg for seizure control first
Initiate therapeutic hypothermia to 33.5 degrees within 6 hours
Arrange urgent MRI brain before deciding on cooling eligibility
Commence aEEG monitoring and cool only if seizures are confirmed

stem: A 6-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community presents with periorbital oedema, dark urine, and a severe headache for 2 days. His mother reports he had skin sores 3 weeks ago that were treated with topical mupirocin. He has no history of renal disease. In the emergency department he has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 95, BP 165/105 (well above 99th centile + 5 mmHg for age), RR 24, SpO2 97% RA
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick: 3+ blood, 2+ protein, urine microscopy: dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts, Na 138, K 5.1, creatinine 95 micromol/L (elevated for age), C3 0.25 g/L (low, ref 0.75-1.40), C4 normal, ASO titre 380 (elevated), anti-DNase B 450 (elevated)
data_table.Examination: Periorbital and peripheral oedema, seizure resolved, post-ictal drowsiness, no rash, skin sore scars on legs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment for the hypertension?

options.text: Oral amlodipine 0.1 mg/kg and recheck blood pressure in 1 hour
IV furosemide 1 mg/kg to reduce fluid overload and pressure
IV enalaprilat 5 mcg/kg as first-line rapid antihypertensive
IV hydralazine 0.2 mg/kg bolus with continuous BP monitoring
Sodium nitroprusside infusion at 0.5 mcg/kg/min titrated to BP

subtopic_detail: Gillick competence: contraception in an adolescent under 16
stem: A 15-year-old girl attends your GP clinic alone requesting contraception. She reports being in a consensual sexual relationship with her 16-year-old boyfriend. She does not want her parents to know about the consultation. She has no significant medical history, takes no medications, and has never been pregnant. She appears mature, articulates her reasons clearly, and understands the risks and benefits of contraception when you discuss them.

data_table.Examination: No clinical concerns, no signs of coercion or abuse on careful assessment

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to managing her request?

options.text: Decline to prescribe and insist on parental consent first
Report to child protection services as she is under 16 years
Prescribe emergency contraception only and defer regular options
Prescribe contraception but contact her parents to inform them
Assess Gillick competence, prescribe contraception, maintain privacy

stem: A 3-day-old term male neonate (birth weight 3.4 kg, gestational age 39 weeks) is referred from postnatal ward for worsening jaundice. He was born via uncomplicated vaginal delivery and has been breastfeeding well. The mother is blood group O positive and the infant is blood group A positive. Direct Coombs test is positive. He has been receiving intensive phototherapy for the past 12 hours.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 155 bpm, RR 42/min, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, weight 3.25 kg
data_table.Examination: Deeply jaundiced to soles of feet, mild hepatomegaly, no bruising, anterior fontanelle soft and flat, tone and reflexes normal
data_table.Investigations: Total serum bilirubin (TSB) 425 mcmol/L (up from 380 mcmol/L 6 hours ago despite phototherapy), direct bilirubin 18 mcmol/L, haemoglobin 132 g/L, reticulocytes 8.2%, blood group A positive (mother O positive), DAT positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Prepare for double-volume exchange transfusion
Increase phototherapy to triple-surface devices
Optimise oral breastfeeds and recheck in 4 hours
Recheck total serum bilirubin level in 6 hours
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg
